en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Praise of Homage:
To the Well-Gone One, the most excellent, who has abandoned both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
I bow to the Leader, the Leader of the world, who gives the Deathless, the Deathless, the Peaceful, the Peerless, the Peerless;
who is the Refuge, the Refuge for the world, who makes the Untroubled, the Untroubled;
the Fearless, the Fearless State.
Whose body-limbs are beautiful to behold,
who is endowed with a most sweet voice,
and who is the support for an immeasurable multitude of virtues.
I pay homage to the peerless One of Ten Powers,
the Buddha who, being steadfast and a bearer of wisdom,
experienced physical [suffering] within saṃsāra.
I pay homage to that auspiciousness for men and gods, who has transcended worldly mental suffering and whose body is variegated with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
I pay homage to the Sage who has reached his final birth,
from whose body radiates a blazing light, and who is a treasury of the flood of virtues consisting of wisdom, concentration, and moral discipline.
Like the rising sun in the midst of ascetics, graceful with splendors,
his face resembling the full moon, he was unshakable.
I pay homage to the Omniscient One, the Lord of Sages.
Having approached the foot of the sublime Bodhi tree,
the Sugata conquered Māra together with his army.
At the rising of the dawn, Abojjhi attained enlightenment;
I pay homage to you, the invincible Conqueror of Māra,
who wields the stainless sword of knowledge that cuts through passion and the rest.
I pay homage to him who holds the fruit known as "Satī," who is adorned with the ornament of the flood of virtue,
and who is endowed with the supreme supernormal power of direct knowledge.
To the abode of compassion, who performs what is difficult in every way,
who has reached the path that transcends the ocean of existence,
the Lord of the Three Worlds, well-composed and beneficial—
I bow to him who possesses the all-seeing eye.
Having accumulated the mass of perfections here and there,
he has reached that state which is the source of happiness for the virtuous.
I pay homage to the bull among Jinas, who is free from pride,
whose existence brings about the arising of happiness for humans and non-humans alike,
and who is the skilled navigator of the ship of the factors of the Path.
I pay homage to that Buddha, the destroyer of the great darkness, who, as a seeker using the instrument of knowledge,
embarked upon that [path] and crossed over many oceans of existence.
The accumulation of the thirty-two perfections,
the vision of the Four Noble Truths beneath the supreme Bodhi tree,
and the attainment of the sublime success for the benefit of humans and gods—
I pay homage to the Victor, who has brought the three worlds to peace;
who is stainless, marked by the signs of a hundred merits;
whose mind is like the sky, and whose fortitude is equal to Mount Meru.
I bow to the Victor, who possesses a virtue as cool as a lotus-pool and who endures like the earth—
the Buddha of noble mind, who shines day after day like the sun.
Shining upon his stone throne, generating delight,
he sat and taught the Dhamma that bestows the bliss of peace;
I bow forever to him, who is peerless among the gods.
The Protector attained that which is truly beyond comparison—
by means of the three worlds, which were free from agitation and possessed of beautiful,
high-rising lines upon his lotus feet.
I pay homage to that peerless one, honored by the entire world—
the Buddha, whose mind is steadfast, who has dispelled the darkness with the radiance of the lamp of wisdom, and who is the meeting place for both humans and non-humans.
I pay homage to that compassionate one, the path to liberation, whose infinite wisdom brings benefit to gods and men who desire their welfare.
To that Lord of Sages, the treasury of all virtues, who approached—

I pay homage to that which is called the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the abode of those who are self-restrained, where unwholesome states are cut off— that peerless, desirable, and worthy of veneration wheel.
Surrounded by a pure retinue, radiant with beautiful luster,
redolent with a multitude of glories, guarded and endowed with the sense faculties,
and adorned with the marks beginning from the orbs of the sun and moon.
I pay respectful homage to the Sugata, honored by gods and men.
By means of the raft of the Path, you have crossed the flood of saṃsāra—
its turbulent waves of momentary aversion and craving— and reached the fearless further shore for the sake of all beings.
I pay homage to the King of Dhamma, the refuge, the shelter, the peerless resort, the sole ford, the foundation, the field of merit, the bestower of supreme bliss.
He who sat at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree, the Lord of Sages, acting for the welfare of others.
He performed a miracle that was wondrous, swift, beautiful to behold, yet agitated by a mass of flames— a miracle difficult to achieve,
abandoned by other sages, supreme, bringing the highest delight, and endowed with the powers of psychic mastery. I pay homage to him, the Best One, who possesses such qualities.
The Sage alone, whose face is reddened by rising compassion and whose form is broad with wisdom,
has crossed the flood of living beings by means of the excellent rays of Dhamma described as lotuses;
he brings to perfect enlightenment those who are pure within the cave of the three realms of existence and whose fame has spread abroad.
I pay homage to that Great Sage, the eye of the three worlds, who cannot endure suffering.
That Victor, throughout many births, even gave away his children, wife, limbs, and life itself—
his mind unattached due to his love for Awakening— to whoever was in need.
I pay homage to that Sole Lamp, who thereafter fulfilled the perfection of generosity as well as the perfections of virtue and the rest; who has reached the path of their success;
the God of gods beyond gods, who bears a body subject to death, yet is the vanquisher of Māra and himself invincible.
I perpetually bow down to that Lord of Sages, the Lord of Sages— who is the lamp for those seeking a lamp, who attained the state of awakening upon the supreme victory-seat,
who is the preeminent speaker with the voice of Brahma among those who have reached the Brahma-world,
who is free from evil and has abandoned [all defilements], and who delights as the light of the world.
The Buddha has limbs like the banyan tree, with soft hands and feet;
his calves are like those of the enija antelope and his private parts are enclosed in a sheath. Furthermore, the Sugata has well-placed feet;
the hair on his body grows upward and is fine; moreover, the Sugata possesses the stature of a Brahma.
With blue eyes, long heels, delicate skin, and a voice like the call of the cuckoo;
with forty teeth, even and well-formed, broad between the shoulders,
feet marked with wheels, teeth without gaps, and hands and feet like those of an elephant.
Standing, he does not bend; both his knees touch the ground as he touches them with his soft hands.
The Victor has a rounded torso, eyelashes like those of a young bull, and the upper half of his body is like that of a lion.
He is full-bodied, has long fingers, and, O Sugata, each hair grows from a single pore.
With perfect, white teeth, a skin like refined gold, and hair on the upper body that is deep blue;
with a broad tongue, a lion-like jaw, webbed feet and hands,
and a cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) on his head— I bow to that Great Seer who is endowed with these qualities, the Fully Enlightened One, the Protector.
The mere sound of the word "Buddha" is exceedingly difficult to encounter; what need is there to speak of the state of Buddhahood itself?

Therefore, virtuous persons in this world who aspire to various benefits and happiness [should seek it] from one who brings about the desired goal, who is honored by gods and men, who is fearless, and who is worthy of offerings.
May they always pay homage to that peerless One of Ten Powers, who increases the joy of the worlds.
By this merit, may I be of subtle intellect and mindful, satisfied in future lives;
may I be skillful, possessing straight vision and wisdom, with unflagging energy, wealthy, and generous in sharing.
Sharp-witted, brave, firm-minded, acting for the welfare of both self and others, long-lived, free from disease, wealthy, handsome, famous,
possessing great strength, renowned, and endowed with patience; faithful,
possessed of the marks of a great man, bearing supreme glory, and detached from the things of this world.
May I be modest, possessed of virtuous friends, delighting in what is wholesome, and guarding the five precepts and so forth;
may I have few desires, little anger, and an exceedingly upright heart;
may I possess supernormal powers, be immeasurable, praiseworthy, affectionate in speech, a knower of the qualities of noble beings, and one who holds me dear.
Thus, O Protector, regarding these inexhaustible qualities illuminated by their characteristics,
the wise person remembers even a single verse among those indicative verses.
Such a one is liberated from the four states of misery and possesses the two kinds of accomplishment.
One who has destroyed the web of calamities and is a recipient of benefit and happiness,
may become a lord of men and gods,
or even a sovereign of the four continents in his final body— such another as this [is the result of] the white parasol.
Having mounted the vehicle of meditation, the one of virtuous conduct will attain equanimity;
even in this very life, he shall be healthy and long-lived.
Honored by all the worlds, his mind will delight in meditation.
Beloved by the people and pleasing to the mind—what need is there to speak of his unyielding retention?
The *Namakkārapāḷi* is finished.
The *Namakkāraṭīkā*.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having paid homage to the Victor who is praised by such epithets as "Sugata" and the like, who bestows happiness,
and having saluted the pure Dhamma and the supreme Assembly, [I shall speak].
Having written down and established this merit— the *Namakkāra*— composed by those seeking welfare and by the ancient teachers,
may it increase the wisdom of those who pay homage. I shall now provide a commentary on its meaning,
which brings about the easy understanding of its profound significance.
Requested by the venerable Movipuna, who is endowed with virtue,
I shall explain the meaning of this according to the method set forth in the various commentaries and other sources.
O virtuous ones, listen with faith!
It is called *namakkāra* because it is a bowing (*namana*), or because one bows (*namati*) by means of it, or because one performs that [bowing] toward him; thus it is termed *namakkāra*.
And that was composed by the teacher Buddhaghosa, having been previously heard [by him].
Furthermore, in the *Buddhaghosuppatti* and in various other discourses,
no specific reason for its composition has been seen; therefore,
it was stated by me that it was established by those seeking welfare and by the ancient teachers.
That cause should be investigated and understood by the wise:
"The Well-Gone One is the most excellent Well-Gone One; he has abandoned both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
he is the Deathless, the peaceful Deathless; he is the Unequaled, the giver of the Unequaled."
I bow to the Refuge, the refuge of the world; to the One who has made the passionless, the passionless;
to the Fearless One, the state of fearlessness; to the Leader, the leader.
1. [Ka] Now, first of all, having praised the Buddha with the eighteen qualities beginning with "the Well-Gone One" (sugata), [the author proceeds].
The two verses beginning with "By one desiring to pay homage to the Sugata... have been commenced.

This, however, should be understood as a verse composed of *vatta* (repeated) *yamaka* (rhyme) at the beginning of every line. Furthermore, that *yamaka* is stated in the *Subodhālaṅkāra* to be the fault known as *kiliṭṭha-dosa* (the defiled fault).
For it is said there:
“Whatever defiled expression the dull-witted might employ, such as *yamaka* (chiming) and the like,
that too is included within the faults of defiled expression. Furthermore,

this [verse] here is endowed with the poetic ornament of sound (*saddālaṅkāra*), which is designated as the quality of clarity (*pasāda-guṇa*), precisely because it is composed of words that are easily understood.
Therefore, that *yamaka* should be regarded as well-spoken. This applies likewise to the other *yamaka* verses. Thus it was said again by Laṅkā:
“That *yamaka* which is composed of past sounds, possesses smooth word-connections, and is endowed with the quality of clarity—such is considered the [proper] *yamaka*.”
In this context, "Sugata" means one who has gone to a beautiful place because his going is beautiful, and because he has gone rightly;
for he is called "Sugata" because he goes beautifully by means of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). The root *gam* preceded by the prefix *su-* [forms this word]. The word *su-* has the sense of beauty.
He has gone without attachment to the direction that is completely pure, blameless, and secure through the going by way of the Noble Path.

This is the meaning. Furthermore, that "going" is twofold: physical going (*kāyagamana*) and cognitive going (*ñāṇagamana*). In this context, the Blessed One’s approaching of those who are to be trained is called "physical going" because it is a beautiful going by body, resulting in the absolute production of their welfare and happiness.
However, the Self-Existent One (*sayambhū*), by means of his knowledge, [traverses] the entire world through the realization of full comprehension (*pariññābhisamaya*).

"Going by means of knowledge through thorough comprehension is called *ñāṇagamana* (going by knowledge). However, it is *ñāṇagamana* that is intended here. In the *Aṅguttara-ṭīkā*, however, it is stated:
"He whose going (*gamana*)—that is, his movement—is beautiful (*sobhana*) is a *sugata*. It is also said that he is a *sugata* because he goes to a beautiful state;
the meaning is that he has gone to the deathless Nibbāna by way of making it his object (*ārammaṇakaraṇa*). [He is so called] correctly and without error.
"He goes well," thus he is called "Sugata. The prefix *su-* has the sense of "perfectly" (*sammā*).

The meaning is that he does not bring back, does not return to, and does not go back to those defilements which have been abandoned by each respective path. Alternatively, he is called "Sugata" because he has come perfectly (*sammā āgacchati*);
from the time of the feet of Dīpaṅkara until the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), [he has proceeded] by fulfilling the thirty perfections (*pāramī*).

The meaning is: he has come, performing only the welfare and happiness of the entire world through right practice, without falling into these extremes—namely, eternalism (*sassata*), annihilationism (*uccheda*), sensual pleasure (*kāmasukha*), and self-mortification (*attakilamatha*). "I bow to that Sugata, the Buddha"—this is the connection [of the words].
Again, he is called "Sugata" because he has gone rightly (*sammā gadattā sugato*). For he is called "Sugata" because he goes and speaks rightly (*sammā gadati bhāsatīti sugato*).
In this language, *supubbagadadhātu* means "in distinct speech" or "in articulate speech"; [the rule] is that *ta* becomes *to*.

The meaning is that in the six modes of speech, one speaks with double articulation (*dvivāca*) precisely where it is appropriate. For it is said in the *Abhayarājakumārasutta* of the *Majjhima Nikāya*:
"Prince, whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial..."
And even that speech which is unpleasant and disagreeable to others, the Tathāgata does not speak. 2.

Furthermore, whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true and factual, yet unbeneficial and unpleasant and disagreeable to others—that speech too the Tathāgata does not speak. 3. But whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true and factual, and beneficial—
And that speech is unpleasant and disagreeable to others; yet the Tathāgata knows the proper time for explaining it.

4. Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, even if it is pleasant and agreeable to others, the Tathāgata does not utter such speech. 5. And whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true and correct...
Even if it were connected with what is beneficial, yet disagreeable and unpleasant to others, the Tathāgata does not speak such speech.
But as for that speech which the Tathāgata knows to be true, real, and connected with what is beneficial,
and which is agreeable and pleasant to others— in that case, the Tathāgata is one who knows the proper time for the explanation of such speech.”
Herein, this [classification] should be understood in brief for the sake of easy comprehension from the text.
For how is it that there is speech which is untrue, unbeneficial, and unpleasant; speech which is true, unbeneficial, and unpleasant; speech which is true, beneficial, and unpleasant;
speech which is untrue, unbeneficial, and pleasant; and speech which is true, unbeneficial, and pleasant? True... [and so on].

"Speech that is beneficial and pleasant" is of six kinds. In this context, speech that should be spoken in such a way as "He is not a thief, yet he goes about as a thief," and so forth, is called the first kind of speech.
Speech that should be spoken in such a way as "He is indeed a thief, and he goes about as a thief," and so forth, is called the second kind of speech.
[One who is] poor, ugly, and of little influence due to having failed to perform merit—yet, even while remaining here, [one performs] merit again...
He does not do so. In the second mental cycle, one asks: "How will he be liberated from the four states of misery?

Thus, the speech to be uttered with the welfare of the great masses as the primary concern, with the Dhamma as the primary concern, and with instruction as the primary concern, is called the third speech. A certain rogue said:
"Sirs, when I was in my mother’s womb, she had a craving for *kapiṭṭha* fruit. She [sought] another who brought *kapiṭṭha*..."
Finding no one else, she sent for me. Having gone there, being unable to climb the tree myself, I took hold of my own feet and flung them over the tree like a club.
Then, moving from branch to branch and gathering fruits, I was unable to descend; so I went home, brought a ladder, climbed down, and stood before my mother.
Having gone, I gave the fruits to my mother. They were indeed large, the size of bowls.
Then, while my mother was seated on a single seat, she ate sixty fruits from me. Speech such as this, which is to be spoken in this manner, is called the fourth type of speech.
Furthermore, speech that praises others in various ways for the sake of material gain, through flattery and the like, as well as talk concerning kings—this is [the fifth].
Idle chatter (*tiracchānakathā*) proceeding in the manner of talk about thieves and so forth is called the fifth kind of speech.
Discourse on the Dhamma based upon the Noble Truths is called the sixth kind of speech. Even if they hear it for a hundred years, the wise never reach satiety with it.
Of these, the Blessed One speaks only two kinds of speech—the third and the sixth. Therefore, by those who are true men...
"She herself should be expressed by two words. This is the summary method as it appears in the *Aṭṭhakathā* on that [text].

However, in the *Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā* and the *Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā*, it is explained in a different manner. One should consult those works and take [the explanation] from them. Here, moreover, is the summary verse:
“He who speaks two kinds of speech at the proper time— speech that is true and beneficial but unpleasant to others, and speech that is true,
beneficial, and pleasant to others— he is called ‘Well-Gone’ (Sugata).”
And it is said: "By making the letter *da* understood as *ta*.
"Excellent" (*seṭṭha*) means more praiseworthy due to the greatness of its qualities. For he is called "excellent" because he is especially praiseworthy among those who are praiseworthy.

In the word *pasattha*, the suffix *iṭṭha* is applied to the word *pasattha* in the sense of a superlative derivative (*visesa-taddhita*). Of the word *pasattha*... [among] those who are praiseworthy.
The meaning is that he is especially praised for his qualities, such as virtue, concentration, and wisdom, compared to those such as the Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*).

Alternatively, he is the "Best" (*seṭṭha*) because he seeks (*esi*) or searches for (*gavesi*) the beautiful (*sundara*) phenomena distinguished by the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth;

or he is the one who has sought them. The prefix *su-* is used here in the sense of seeking. His realm is [the Buddha-realm]. The word *su-* has the sense of "beautiful. By the virtuous and true persons...

It is "seṭṭho" because it is to be sought (*esitabbo*) or pursued (*gavesitabboti*). Here, the suffix *ta* follows the word *santa*, with the change of the vowel *o* to *e*, and the substitution of *ṭṭha* for *ta*.

Alternatively, it is "seṭṭho" because it is desired (*icchiyati*) or longed for (*kantiya*) by the good people (*santehi sappurisehi*). Here, the suffix *ta* follows the word *santa* in the sense of seeking (*isa*) or desiring and longing (*icchākantīsu*).
Or else, he is "seṭṭho"—the Buddha—because he desires the welfare and happiness of the good people (*santānaṃ sappurisānaṃ*).

This is an agentive derivation (*kattusādhana*). Alternatively, he is "best" (*seṭṭha*) because he seeks (*esati*) or awakens (*buddheti*) to the various sublime states such as the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
This is a causal derivation (*hetusādhana*). The root *esa*, preceded by the prefix *su*, signifies awakening (*buddhi*). That which is best (*taṃ seṭṭhaṃ*).

Regarding the analysis of the words in the phrase "they abandon what is wholesome and unwholesome" (*kusalaṃ-akusalaṃ jahanti*), one should divide it as follows: they abandon the wholesome and the unwholesome. [The word] *kucchitaṃ*...

It is called *kusala* because it makes the unwholesome (*pāpa-dhamma*) fade away (*salayati*), wavers (*calayati*), trembles (*kampeti*), and destroys (*viddhaṃseti*); thus, wholesome states belonging to the four planes are obtained.

The root *sa-* preceded by *ku-* is the element *a*. Therein, sense-sphere wholesome states make the unwholesome fade away, waver, and tremble through abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-ppahāna*);

sublime wholesome states make them fade away and tremble through suppression (*vikkhambhana-ppahāna*); and supramundane wholesome states [make them fade away] through eradication (*samuccheda-ppahāna*).
The meaning is that it "shakes off" or "destroys" by means of abandonment through complete eradication (*samucchedappahāna*).

Alternatively, it is *kusala* because by means of this, the virtuous (*sādhava*) "shake off," restrain, or close the wretched door to the states of misery (*apāya*). This is an instrumental derivation (*karaṇasādhana*).
However, since the word "they abandon" (*jahanti*) is used here, only the wholesome states belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmaka-kusala*) are intended. That, moreover—

It has the characteristic of having blameless and pleasant fruition; its function is the destruction of the unwholesome; its manifestation is purification, or alternatively, the manifestation of desirable fruition;
its proximate cause is wise attention. "Not wholesome" means unwholesome;

the meaning is that it is the opposite of the wholesome by way of being something to be abandoned, just as an enemy is the opposite of a friend. Furthermore, it has the characteristic of having blameworthy and painful fruition.
It has the characteristic of being blameworthy with an undesirable ripening; its function is the production of harm; it is manifested as an undesirable ripening;

and its proximate cause is improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*). Wholesome and unwholesome [volitional formations] comprise the wholesome volitional formation known as the meritorious (*puñña*), the immovable (*āneñja*), and the unwholesome volitional formation known as the demeritorious (*apuñña*).
Furthermore, that term refers to the state of action (*kamma*) in the context of the "states to be abandoned."

"Abandoning" means destroying by means of abandonment through eradication (*samuccheda-pahāna*) at the moment of the path, and by means of abandonment through subsidence (*paṭippassaddhi-pahāna*) at the moment of the fruit;

that is to say, he is "shattering" [the defilements]. For he abandons and relinquishes them by means of the knowledge of the path of Arahatship, and he has abandoned, relinquished, or caused them to subside by means of the knowledge of the fruit;
thus he is "Buddha. The verbal root *hā* signifies giving up (*cāga*). Furthermore, although here it is wholesome...

It is not said that [the wholesome formation] is abandoned by the path; however, when the defilements such as ignorance and craving—which constitute the root of the round of existence—are abandoned by the knowledge of the path of Arahantship, the wholesome formation is unable to produce rebirth-linking again in saṃsāra because of the absence of ignorance and craving, which are the roots for the arising of mundane wholesomeness.
Therefore, when the defilements that constitute the root of the round are abandoned...
By way of metaphorical designation, even the wholesome is said to be "abandoned," as in such passages as: "Bhikkhus, form is not yours; abandon it.

For it should be understood that although the Arahat performs the duties of proper conduct (*abhisamācārika-vatta*), these are not called "wholesome" (*kusala*); rather, they are called "functional" (*kiriya*).

For it is said in the *Nidānavagga-saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*: “Action performed by one whose taints are exhausted is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; having no result, it remains as mere functional activity. And in the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā* it is stated:
“The path of arahantship leads to the destruction of wholesome and unwholesome karma; thus it is by that [path] that karma is broken. Therefore, it is said in the *Cūḷaniddesa-pāḷi*:
“By means of the knowledge of the path of arahantship, through the cessation of volitional consciousness...”
“Whatever name-and-form might arise, herein they cease, are stilled, come to an end, and subside.
“The Deathless” means being devoid of death.
For that Victor has not died; he is the Deathless, [the opposite] of those things subject to death which produce [rebirth].
It is called "deathless" (*amata*) because, due to the complete eradication of the defilements (*kilesa*) by means of the path of Arahantship, it is free from death once again.
Alternatively, it is called "deathless" because for that Victor (*jina*), having attained Nibbāna by way of making it his object, there is no death—that is, no passing away.

For although the Victor has conquered the Māra of the aggregates (*khandha-māra*), he has also conquered the Māra of the defilements (*kilesa-māra*), since those [other two] are inevitably subject to being defeated.
It should be understood that it is called "the deathless" (amata) by way of a metaphorical designation for its fruit.
Furthermore, "the deathless" means being endowed with the deathless Nibbāna. It is called "the deathless" because there is no death or dying therein; that is, Nibbāna.
Moreover, it has the characteristic of peace, the flavor of non-decay, and it is manifested as signlessness and as escape.
However, no proximate cause (*padatthāna*) for Nibbāna is found.
For it was said by the Elder Nāgasena in the *Milindapañha*: "Nibbāna does not arise by any cause whatsoever.

That which has this [immortality] is "deathless" (*amata*); [it refers to] the Conqueror (*jina*). According to the rule *saddhādi-to-ṇo*, the suffix *-ṇa* is applied in the sense of possession (*assatthya*). One who possesses faith is a "faithful one" (*saddho*).

As in the case of [the word] *paññā* and so forth. The meaning is that for this Victor (*jina*), there exists the deathless (*amata*) Nibbāna realized through the knowledge of the four paths; that is the "deathless.
It is "peaceful" (*santa*) because it is perfectly stilled from all the fevers of the defilements (*kilesa*) and from the sufferings of saṃsāra (*vaṭṭadukkha*).

For that Buddha is called "peaceful" because he has calmed and stilled all the fevers of the defilements and the sufferings of saṃsāra. [The suffix] *-ta* is used in the sense of calming from the root *sam*. There is the elision of the final part of the root.
The formation of the word should be understood by applying the substitution of *santa* for the suffix *-tappa*.

Because the defilements that cause distress within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāravaṭṭa*) have been utterly eradicated at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) through the knowledge of the path to Arhatship, he is said to be "one whose body and mind have become cool" (*santakāyacitta*); thus, it is called *santa*.
It is *asama* because he is peerless among any person in qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and the rest; for there is no Buddha equal to him in such qualities as virtue.

"One who has no equal" (*asama*) is so called because there is no one equal to him. The meaning is that in this world of beings, there is no human, deva, or Brahmā who is the Buddha’s equal in qualities such as virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
For the Blessed One’s physical body is adorned with the eighty minor marks and is variegated in form by the thirty-two marks of a Great Man in every respect.
The Dhammakāya is enriched by the jewels of qualities such as the aggregate of pure virtue (sīlakkhandha),
and it has reached the highest excellence through qualities such as greatness of merit, greatness of power, greatness of psychic potency, greatness of tranquility, and greatness of wisdom; therefore,
it is said that the Blessed One is peerless and incomparable in his qualities of virtue and the rest.

They give what is incomparable (*asama*): by means of the knowledge of teaching, they bestow upon beings who are ready to be trained the Dhamma of the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna, which is peerless in terms of worldly phenomena.
Herein, "incomparable" (*asama*) means that there is no worldly phenomenon equal or similar to these;
thus it is "incomparable," and the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna are obtained therein. Alternatively, "incomparable" (*asama*) refers to its state of being the foremost among all other phenomena.
Nirvana is said to be that which is to be realized by means of the fourfold Noble Path. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (*virāga*) is declared to be the foremost among them.
Furthermore, the word *tassa* (of it) is connected with the word *dadanti* (they give) as its object. *Dado* means "the giver"; [it refers to] the Buddha. [The root is] *dā*, the element of giving.

The meaning is: he gives to those beings who are to be trained, through his knowledge of teaching—which consists in demonstrating the practice for attaining the Deathless and is dominated by great compassion—the supramundane state known as the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna, which is peerless and incomparable with any mundane state.
Thus, "giving that which is peerless."
(Kha) In the second verse, however, *saraṇaṃ* means one who has become the refuge, the ultimate resort, the shelter, and the protection for the entire world of beings;
this is what is meant. For that Buddha is called *saraṇa* because the world of beings (*sattaloka*) remembers (*saranti*) and turns back to him (*paṭisaranti*).

[The suffix] *-yu* is added to the verbal root *sar*. Alternatively, it is called *saraṇa* because the world of beings remembers (*saranti*), approaches (*osaranti*), and gathers together (*samosaranti*) there.
*Saraṇa* means "that which is remembered" or "thought of" by gods and humans who possess faith and confidence; thus it is called *saraṇa*.

Furthermore, it is called *saraṇa* because gods and humans who have approached it remember and penetrate the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*). In the sense of "remembering," the suffix *-yu* is applied to the root *sara*.
However, in the sense of going for refuge, *saraṇa* means that [the Buddha, etc. "removes" (*sarati*), that is, destroys, fear, anguish, suffering, and defilement.
"Ratanatta" (the three jewels) is what is stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). That is the refuge.
Furthermore, "saraṇaṃ lokaṃ" means one who remembers—that is, knows—the world, which is comprised of the world of sentient beings and the world of space.

For here, it is called "loka" because merit and demerit, as well as their maturation, "locate" (*lokayati*) themselves and find their footing (*patiṭṭhayati*) therein; thus, the world of sentient beings is obtained.
“Lokadhātu” means “the world-system. It is called “loka” because it breaks up and disintegrates; thus, it is the world of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*).
It is called “loka” because it is seen in various modes through the root *luj* (to break); or, it is called “loka” because mobile and stationary beings dwell and find their support therein;
thus, the world-space consisting of the world-sphere (*cakkavāḷa*) is obtained. This is “lokadhātu. And herein, [the view] that “the world is eternal” is...

In passages such as "Is the world eternal? or "Is the world non-eternal?", the term *sattaloka* (the world of beings) should be understood as the collection and continuum of the aggregates—form and so forth—that are bound up with the faculties, according to the etymological sense of "world" (*loka*) being "being" (*satta*). In the passage, "The world is one:
all beings subsist by nutriment," it refers to those [aggregates] that are either bound up with the faculties or not bound up with the faculties.
The aggregates (khandhas) are called *saṅkhārā* because they are conditioned by conditions (*paccayehi saṅkhariyanti*), both as a collection and as a continuum.
Since the world is these very formations, it is called the "world of formations" (*saṅkhāraloka*) according to the meaning of the term.
"As far as the moon and sun revolve..."
The directions shine forth, resplendent;
even throughout this world-system of a thousand worlds,
your sovereignty prevails here.

The "world as space" (*okāsaloka*) should be understood as follows: in the sense that it is a place where the collection and the continuum of form and so forth—which are not bound to the faculties—descend and establish themselves, it is called "space.
That very thing is the world; thus, by the meaning of the word, it is "the world as space.

"Lokaṃ" refers to that world. "Saraṇo" means one who remembers, knows, or understands; it is the Buddha. [The suffix] *-yu* is added to the root *sṛ*, meaning "to remember. The connection is: "the world which is remembered (or known)."

It is said that the Buddha penetrates with unobstructed knowledge the manifold worlds, beginning with the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*), the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*), the world of space (*okāsaloka*), the world of defilements (*kilesaloka*), the world of existence (*bhavaloka*), the world of faculties (*indriyaloka*), the world of aggregates (*khandhaloka*), the world of bases (*āyatanaloka*), and the world of elements (*dhātuloka*).
"Without conflict" (*araṇa*) means free from defilement, or devoid of the "conflict" (*raṇa*) known as the defilements. Furthermore, the word *raṇa* refers both to defilements and to battle.

And it is seen in the sense of grinding into powder. For instance, in such passages as "states with conflict" (*saraṇā dhammā*) and "states without conflict" (*araṇā dhammā*), it is seen in reference to the defilements (*kilesa*).
For those are called "conflicts" (*raṇa*) because beings quarrel and wail by means of them.
"The archer is peerless, the prince of great strength..."
“Having made war against all his friends, he entered upon self-restraint.
This is seen in the *Asadisa-jātaka* regarding battle. For “having made war” means having fought;
“he entered upon self-restraint” means he entered upon the self-controlled life of a seer’s renunciation (*isipabbajjā*). While making war on grass and wood, they fled in the eight directions.
"Samantato" (on all sides) is seen in the *Chaddanta-jātaka* in the sense of being "crushed to powder.

For "making *raṇa*" means making [them] crushed (*cuṇṇa*) and pulverized (*vicuṇṇa*). "Them" refers to all eight thousand nāgas; however, here it should be understood as referring to the defilements (*kilesa*).

This, moreover, is the etymological explanation (*vacanattha*) here: they are called *raṇā* because they crush (*cuṇṇenti*) and afflict (*pīḷenti*) sentient beings with passion and so forth; thus they are *raṇā*. They "raṇanti" (they clash/struggle).
The defilements (*kilesā*) are called *raṇā* because beings cry out and lament because of them. The verbal root *raṇ* belongs to the class of sounds.

One who has no *raṇā*, that is, no defilements, is called *araṇa*. Since the Victor was defeated by the Māra of the defilements at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the meaning is that he possesses no *raṇā*, that is, no defilements; thus it is *araṇa*. That is *araṇa*.
They create *araṇa* (freedom from conflict), which means the absence of the defilements known as "conflict" (*raṇa*) within the mental continuum of those to be trained.
In this context, "conflict" (*raṇa*) is a designation for passion and the other defilements by which beings are overcome and thus wail and lament;

the meaning is that he brings about their absence in the mental continuum of those to be trained through his knowledge of teaching. Alternatively, "he makes" (*karoti*) is *kara*, referring to the Buddha; [the term] is *taṃ karaṃ*.
It is "fearless" (*nibbhaya*) because it is devoid of the fears of birth and so forth.

For here, fear is fourfold: the fear of mental trepidation, the fear of knowledge, the fear of objects, and the fear of moral dread (*ottappa*). Among these, that which one fears with the mind is the fear of mental trepidation;
that which one fears after investigating with knowledge is the fear of knowledge; and that from which one fears is [the fear of] objects.
The fear of the object (*ārammaṇabhaya*). It is called "fear" (*bhaya*) because one is afraid of it; thus, it is the fear of moral dread (*ottappabhaya*).
The verbal root *bhī* is used in the sense of fearing, with the suffix *ṇa*. Furthermore, those mentioned in the *Mahāniddesa* commentary are:

the fear of birth, the fear of aging, the fear of illness, the fear of death, the fear of kings, the fear of thieves, the fear of fire, the fear of water, the fear of self-reproach, and the fear of reproach by others.

The fear of punishment, the fear of an unhappy rebirth, the fear of waves, the fear of crocodiles, the fear of whirlpools, the fear of sea-monsters, the fear for one’s livelihood, the fear of ill-repute, the fear of timidity in assemblies, the fear of intoxication, and the fear of an unhappy rebirth—these and others are included.
One who has no such fears is "Abhaya," the Buddha. Of him, [the following concerns] the causes of those fears...
Because all defilements have been utterly eradicated by the path of Arhatship, the meaning is that "there is no fear whatsoever.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the fearless place, the Leader," here the word *abhayaṃ* (fearless) is an adjective qualifying the word *ṭhānaṃ* (place).
The word *ṭhānaṃ* is the object (*kamma*) of the word *nāyakaṃ* (Leader). The meaning of the word *bhaya* (fear) has already been explained above. There is no fear whatsoever here.
*Nibbāna* means that which is fearless; it is *nibbāna*. It is called a *ṭhāna* (abode) because Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants abide and arise therein;
it is *nibbāna*. He leads (*neti*) those beings who are ready to be trained, thus he is the *Nāyaka* (Leader), the Buddha.

The verbal root *nī* signifies leading, and the suffix *ṇvu* is added. That Buddha, by means of his teaching of the Dhamma, causes capable sons of noble family to attain the knowledge of the paths and fruits through their progress along the path.
The meaning is "he leads to the state of Nibbāna"; thus, he is the Leader (*nāyaka*).
Furthermore, "I bow to that Leader, I bow to the Buddha, the Leader"—this is the grammatical connection.
In this context, "Leader" refers to the Buddha, for he leads those beings who are to be trained from the ocean of *saṃsāra* to the further shore of Nibbāna; he is indeed like a boatman.

Just as a boatman leads people from this shore to the further shore by means of a boat, so too does he lead beings across the ocean of saṃsāra to the further shore of Nibbāna by means of the boat of the factors of the Path;

this is the meaning. Alternatively, "Leader" (nāyaka): because he has attained the state of being the eldest among the three worlds, he is the Leader—the eldest, the most excellent, the most senior. For he leads to, goes to, and attains the state of being the eldest; thus he is called the Leader.

It is said: the root *nī* with the suffix *ṇvu* signifies "going. Here, however, the meaning is that he has attained the state of being the most excellent, the eldest, and the most senior among all beings, because he was born into the noble birth after having first of all split open the shell of the egg of ignorance for all progeny in this world by means of the path of Arahantship.
"To him, the Leader"—the meaning is: "I bow down to him with reverence through the three doors. In this context:

Indeed, in some instances, the substitution of *e* occurs for the present tense suffix by the rule beginning with *dhātutyādi*. However, the method for determining the meaning of the word here is as follows:
since the word *nameti* is a verb (*ākhyāta*), its lexical meaning (*vacanattha*) need not be explicitly stated. For it has been said by those learned in grammar:
“Conventional usage (*ruḷhī*), the verb (*ākhyāta*), the particle (*nipāta*), likewise the prefix (*upasagga*), the vocative (*ālapana*),” [and so forth].
"In all these [instances] ending in *nāma*, no dispute has been made regarding the six [cases].
Furthermore, that word (*pada*) is a verbal form (*ākhyāta-pada*) consisting of the root *nam*, the present tense marker, the suffix *-a*, and a case-ending.
Alternatively, the meaning expressed by the root *nam*—the act of bowing—is understood as a wholesome state of consciousness (*kusala-cittuppāda*) through its predominance.
In the case of the *mīva*-case ending (*mivibhatti*), the meaning expressed by it is a person who possesses arising and is characterized by that particular state of consciousness;

this is obtained in a secondary sense. However, the meaning expressed by the entire word-group is obtained as the agent among the categories of agent, object, and action, and as the present time among past times and so forth;
it is specifically the activity denoted by the verbal root. This is the summary here.

The detailed explanation should be understood as follows: In the case of the mind-element (*manodhātu*), it is a wholesome arising of consciousness dominated by faith, volition, and wisdom, which—having made the Buddha’s qualities such as those of a "Well-Gone One" its object—proceeds in the mode of homage and originates bodily and vocal intimation;
and there is also the wholesome arising of consciousness proceeding in the mode of homage at the mind-door, without originating the two intimations.

And it is obtained primarily through the recollection of the Buddha’s qualities. The arising of wholesome states of consciousness—preceded and followed by wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) and so forth—which proceeds by way of recollecting the Buddha’s qualities, is [the homage] in a figurative sense as the fruit.

Furthermore, the successive fruits known as pertaining to this life and the future life, the absence of obstacles such as disease and the like, and the bliss of attaining heaven and liberation, are [the homage] in a figurative sense as the cause. And "reverence at every step" is [the homage] in a figurative sense as the similar [action].
The designation "veneration" (*vandana*) is by way of proximity of location; the object, door, and focal point are by way of proximity of location;

the person-substance (*puggala-dabba*) characterized by the quality of veneration is by way of proximity of quality (*guṇūpacāra*); the state of being superior, middling, or inferior is by way of proximity of the possessor of qualities (*guṇyūpacāra*);

veneration as a constituent part is by way of partial metaphor (*ekadesūpacāra*); veneration as a whole collection is by way of metaphor of the part-possessor (*ekadesyūpacāra*); and the prior arising of wholesome states of consciousness is [by way of sequence].

By way of proximity (*samīpūpacārena*), the subsequent arising of wholesome consciousness is [designated] by way of proximity; the state of non-activity of the ultimate phenomena (*paramatthadhamma*) that constitute the arising of wholesome consciousness for the purpose of prostration is [designated] by way of metaphorical designation of those phenomena (*taddhammūpacārena*).

Their state as suchness (*dhammatā*) is [designated] by way of metaphorical designation of what is not those phenomena (*ataddhammūpacārena*); the act of salutation is [designated] by way of metaphorical designation of identity-in-difference (*abhedabhedūpacārena*).
The capacity for salutation is obtained by way of metaphorical designation of difference-in-identity (*bhedābhedūpacārena*). [This is expressed] in the locative case (*mivibhattiyā*).
That [action] is to be expressed by means of the primary [verbal roots] and so forth, as characterized by a specific agent,
by a specific verbal suffix termed the present tense, by a specific word termed the third person, by a specific first-person form,
by a specific personal ending, by a specific verbal root, by a specific singular number, and by a specific present time.
The continuum known as "I" (ahaṃ), which is designated as the aggregates (khandha), is obtained as secondary (appadhāna) when characterized by the specific meaning of the verbal root (dhātu),
the specific action (kriyā), the specific gender (liṅga), the specific class (gaṇa) such as *bhū-vādi*, the specific suffix (vikaraṇa), and the specific distinctions of state,
object, agent, or causal agent. Because the verb expresses the action as primary, the meaning of the verbal root alone is primary.

It is obtainable. Or rather, for that which is to be expressed (*vācya*), there is obtained a smoothness of expression consisting merely in the formation of words that indicate the *bhū-vādi* class [of roots].

Alternatively, "he who says 'I bow'—he bows. This is an analysis according to common usage (*sāmañña*). However, the meaning of what is to be expressed (*vācyattha*) should be understood by the method already stated.
And here, "bowing" (*namana*) refers to the performance of an act of prostration by way of being inclined and leaning toward the Buddha’s infinite qualities, such as virtue (*sīla*) and the rest.
Wholesome volition. And that [volition], for those who pay homage to those worthy of homage, becomes visible-in-this-life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya) due to the excellence of the field and the intention;

by way of providing support for the prior karma that is the cause of the prosperity thus obtained, it wards off obstructing (*upapīḷaka*) and interrupting (*upacchedaka*) karmas, and ensures the non-occurrence of obstacles such as disease during the course of existence for the stream of result (*vipākasantati*) produced thereby.
It accomplishes [this]. And in the future life, having become something to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), it produces the happiness of attaining heaven and liberation (*mokkha*).

This, however, is the method for the purpose of exposition here. By the word *namo*, the threefold wholesome volition (*kusala-cetanā*) consisting of prostration, which proceeds with reference to the Buddha’s qualities such as being a Sugata, is primarily shown. By that [prostration], its causes—such as wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*)—are indicated.

And by way of metaphorical designation (*phalūpacāra*), he illustrates the perfection of the four wheels, the supreme field of the Buddha’s appearance, and the arising of wholesome states of consciousness characterized by faith, wisdom, and exertion occurring in the prior stage.

By illustrating these, he reveals—by way of metaphorical designation for the primary cause—the destruction of obstacles such as diseases in this very life and the bliss of heaven and liberation, which are the fruits thereof.
By revealing these, [he demonstrates] the Blessed One’s state of being worthy of homage.

He clarifies this by means of the second figurative application (*kāraṇūpacāra*). By that clarification, he further emphasizes—by means of the third figurative application—the fact that for me, the worshiper, [the Buddha] has become a field (*khetta*) and the object to whom homage (*paṇāma*) should be rendered.

This, however, is the method of ornamentation (*alaṅkāranaya*) here. The threefold wholesome volition (*kusala-cetanā*) directed toward the Buddha constitutes the expressed meaning of the word "namo" (homage).

It is called the state of evenness (*samaṭṭhāyī-bhāva*). Why? Because it is the body [of the Buddha]. Alternatively, the great wholesome consciousness-arising, which is associated with the threefold wholesome volition that is the homage to the Buddha and is dominated by concentration, is called the state of evenness. Why?

Because of the one-pointedness of mind regarding the qualities of the Buddha such as being the Well-Gone One (*sugata*), or because of the state of having a concentrated mind. That very same [state] is also called the flavor of peace (*santarasa*). Why?
The volition of bowing to the Buddha is an unwholesome factor because it has abandoned the wholesome factor.

Or rather, the Buddha—who is the expressed meaning of the remaining words of the "Buddha-ant" recitation—is called the objective manifestation (*ārammaṇavibhāva*). Why? Because he assists that arising of a wholesome mind of bowing by way of being its object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*). The qualities of the Buddha, such as being a Sugata and so forth, are called the stimulating manifestation (*uddīpanavibhāva*). Why? [Because they incite the mind toward him.]
Because it is the cause of homage. Its "majesty" (ānubhāva) is to be understood by way of its state as a cause, namely:
the absence of diseases in this very life and the absence of obstacles in future lives, as well as the attainment of the bliss of heaven and liberation in the world beyond. Why?
Because it has the quality of being a fruit of benefit (ānisaṃsa). For although there is no word therein that explicitly indicates majesty, a cause cannot exist apart from its fruit.
"The fruit of the cause is to be understood. Alternatively, it should be seen that the power (*ānubhāva*) is indeed shown through the force (*sāmatthiya*) of the word "nameti" (bends/bows).

Manifestation, eagerness, the understanding of the benefits of bowing to the Buddha, intelligence, the absence of sloth, clarity of mind, concentration, and so forth, are what is called the state of non-deviation (*abyabhicārībhāva*).
The state of horripilation and so on is the state of being possessed of courage (*satvaṅkābhāva*).
The method of ornamentation (*alaṅkāra-naya*) should be understood through the names. Thus it is in each subsequent verse.
Here, however, is the concise interpretation (*saṅkhepa-yojanā*): *Sugata* means one who has gone to what is beautiful, or gone to the excellent state of Nibbāna, or one who has gone rightly;
*sugada* means right speech, utterance, or discourse—excellent and more praiseworthy—regarding the various divisions such as the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
Whether it be the Dhamma being sought, or that which is to be sought by the peaceful ones, or the welfare and happiness desired for beings;
whether it be the wholesome or the unwholesome, the abandoned or what has been abandoned; the Deathless, which is devoid of death and endowed with the Deathless Nibbāna;
the Peaceful, which is the subsiding of the distress of the defilements; and the Unequaled, which is incomparable to worldly phenomena—the Dhamma of the Path, the Fruit, and Nibbāna.

Giving—that which is given or the giver—He is the refuge, having become the resort for the entire world of beings. He knows the world—the world designated as "beings" and the world designated as "space"—that is, the triple world, as His refuge;
He is *araṇa*, free from defilements, or devoid of the crossing (*raṇa*) that is synonymous with the defilements.
He creates (*karaṇaṃ*) among beings the absence of the dust of defilements through the knowledge of His teaching; He is fearless (*abhayaṃ*), utterly without fear.

"I respectfully bow with my three doors to the Buddha—the fearless one, the state of fearlessness, the direction of Nibbāna; the Leader who leads beings to the further shore of Nibbāna; the Leader of the three worlds, the eldest, the foremost.
The commentary on the first two verses of homage is complete.
Whose bodily limbs are beautiful to behold,
who possesses a most sweet and excellent voice,
and who is the support for a multitude of immeasurable virtues.
I pay homage to the Incomparable One Possessing the Ten Powers. 2.

Having thus paid homage to the Buddha with the first two verses, he now speaks the verse beginning with "nayanasubhagakāyaṅga" in order to worship the Buddha after praising him with five qualities, such as his body-limbs being beautiful to behold. This...

However, it should be understood that these "good verses" (sugāthā) among the *bhujagasusuma* meters are characterized by nine syllables because they are not joined with a *nagaṇa*. For it is said in the *Vuttodaya*:
"That which has the name *bhujagasusuma* [is so called].
Here, however, the application is as follows: in whichever verse each quarter-foot (*pāda*) should consist of a *nagaṇa*, two *nagaṇas*, and a *magaṇa*.

"She is considered to be known by these verses, which are beautiful as a serpent. In that context, however, "one whose body-limbs are beautiful to behold" means one endowed with body-limbs that are pleasing to the eyes of all beings.
For here, "eye" (*nayana*) is so called because it leads (*neti*) the personal existence (*attabhāva*) toward what is even or uneven;
thus, "eye" (*cakkhu*) is obtained [as its synonym]. It is derived from the root *nī* with the suffix *yu*. It is "beautiful" (*subha*) because it goes (*gacchati*) toward what is lovely (*sobhana*).

A beautiful limb of the body (*kāyaṅga*) is obtained. [The compound] *kāyaṅga* is formed from the root *gam* preceded by the word *subha*, with the suffix *kvi*. A limb or part of the body is "a limb of the body.
A beautiful limb of the Blessed One’s body is obtained. This is a genitive *tappurisa* compound.
A beautiful eye is "a beautiful eye" (*nayanasubhaga*); that which has such a beautiful-limbed body is "one whose body-limb is a beautiful eye" (*nayanasubhagakāyaṅgo*), namely, the Buddha. He...
The meaning is that he is endowed with a physical body that is beautiful to the eye of faith of all beings because it possesses unsurpassed qualities,
and because that bodily form is marked by the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics.

“Endowed with a sweet and excellent voice” means possessed of a sound that is dear, beloved, and most charming. For the Blessed One is called *madhura* because he is *madhiyati*—that is, he is dear, beloved, cherished, or flows [with sweetness].
The root *madha* means “excellent” (*uro*). Indeed, it is stated in the *Majjhima-paññāsa-ṭīkā*:
“*Madhura* means dear, beloved, and unobstructed. Alternatively, *madhura* is so called because he is *madhiyati*, meaning he is tasted or relished; he gladdens (*madhati*) all sentient beings.

It is "sweet" (*madhura*) because it moistens and increases rapture (*pīti*); the root *madh* means to moisten, with the suffix *-ura*. Thus it is stated in the *Saddanīti*: "The root *madh* [means] to moisten.
It is "sound" (*sara*) because it is sought after, desired, or longed for; the root *var* means to desire, with the suffix *-a*.
It is "sound" (*sara*) because it moves or goes toward the state of being an object for auditory consciousness; the root *sar* means to go, with the suffix *-a*. It moves...

It is called *sara* because it goes (*gacchati*) while being heard (*suyyamāna*), or it is called *sara* because it is remembered (*sariyati*) or heard (*suṇiyati*). Thus, the Blessed One’s voice is obtained as possessing eight factors.

"Possessed" (*upeto*) means one who has approached (*upeta*); the root *i* is preceded by the prefix *upa*. That voice is both sweet (*madhura*) and excellent (*vara*), thus it is a "sweet and excellent voice" (*madhuravarasara*).
One who is possessed of, endowed with, or equipped with that is called "possessed of a sweet and excellent voice" (*madhuravarasaropeta*).
But because the Blessed One’s heart-organ is utterly purified and unobstructed by bile, phlegm, and so forth,

he is said to be "endowed, possessed, and furnished" with a voice and sound that is sweet, dear, and pleasing to gods and humans— a voice characterized by the desired and wished-for eightfold qualities.

And here, although it is stated in general terms as "possessing the voice" (*saropeta*), the meaning should be understood as referring specifically to the Blessed One’s voice being endowed with eight qualities:
it is expanded, intelligible, sweet, pleasant to hear, distinct, non-diffuse, deep, and resonant.
For it is said in the *Brahmāyu Sutta* of the *Majjhima Nikāya*: "Endowed indeed with eight qualities... [and so forth].
From the mouth of Master Gotama issues a sound that is distinct and intelligible, sweet and pleasant to hear,
clear and not diffuse, deep and resonant. Furthermore,
Master Gotama makes himself understood by his voice according to the assembly present, yet his voice does not issue beyond the assembly."
In the commentary on this [verse], however: "Visaṭṭha" means smooth, unobstructed. "Viññeyya" means intelligible or clear;
it is intelligible precisely because it is smooth. "Mañju" means sweet. "Savanīya" means pleasant to the ear; it is pleasant to hear precisely because it is sweet.
"Bindu" means condensed. "Avisārī" means not spreading out; it does not spread out precisely because it is condensed.
It exists. "Deep" means it originates from the deep. "Resounding" means it flows forth; it resounds precisely because of its depth.
It makes itself understood as a single, unified assembly, extending from the gathering of listeners out to the limits of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
"Not outside" means it does not go even a finger's breadth beyond the assembly. Why? Because such a sweet voice does not [arise] without cause.
“May it not perish! Thus, the Blessed One’s voice was described as moving with just enough strength for the assembly to hear.
And in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*, the summary verse states:
“Expansive, charming, and intelligible, pleasant to hear and far-reaching;”
“With a deep, resonant, and far-reaching sound— such is the eightfold voice.
For just as the voice of a Brahmā is pure and sweet because it is unobstructed by bile or phlegm,
and just as small animals fleeing from predators such as lions and tigers [seek refuge] in the warbling of the karavīka bird...
Having heard the sound, because of its sweetness, they abandon the fear of death and listen while standing with their feet lifted and not set down;
thus the sound of the *karavīka* bird is sweet, dear, and pleasing by virtue of its natural quality (*dhammatā*).
In this way, the deed performed by the Blessed One purifies the basis (*vatthu*); and because of the purity of that basis, [the voice is free] from bile and phlegm.

Because the Blessed One’s voice arises from his navel without obstruction, it is endowed with the eight factors, perfectly pure, exceedingly sweet, very dear, and most pleasing. However, this is a lowly comparison;
for the Blessed One’s voice is far sweeter, more dear, and more pleasing than those sounds by a hundredfold or a thousandfold part—just like the sound of the Dhamma.
Queen Asandhimittā, having heard the sweet sound of the karavīka bird, thought:
"The sound of this animal is sweet; what indeed must the exceedingly sweet sound of the Blessed One—who has attained the glory of omniscience—be like?
Having given rise to rapture and not relinquishing that rapture, she [attained] the fruit of stream-entry together with seven hundred attendants.
It is established; therefore, one praises the Blessed One as being "endowed with the most excellent sweet nectar.
"The support for the multitude of immeasurable qualities" means that which has become the foundation for the collection of immeasurable qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.
In this context, *mita* means "measured," derived from the root *mā* in the sense of measurement; *amita* means "not measured. "Qualities" (*guṇa*) refers to virtue and the rest.
*Dhammas*. For they "string together" (guṇenti) the person possessing them, making that person manifest; thus they are called *guṇas*. In the *Guṇadhātu-pakāsana*, [the root] *a* is used.
However, in the commentary on the *Maṇisāramañjūsā*, it is stated: "*Guṇā* means they make their own support manifest, thus they are *guṇas*.
And in the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā*: "*Guṇa* in the sense of addressing; *guṇas* are qualities such as virtue (*sīla*). In what sense are they *guṇas*?"

"Guṇo" means that which is called upon (āmantāpiyati) and invited (āmantāpiyati). It is "guṇo" because it is a person established in themselves who is desired by people wishing to see, hear, and honor them.

Although there is no actual calling upon or inviting of the phenomena such as virtue (sīla) and so forth, nevertheless, it is said thus because it is those very phenomena that, through that cause, perform the calling upon and the invitation. Others, however, [say] they are "guñjante" and "abyayante."
Thus they speak of the meaning as "guṇa. However, we do not see the word *dhātu* used in that sense; we see it only in the sense of "addressing" (*āmantane*).

It has been said: "It should be understood after careful investigation. *Amato guṇo* is "immeasurable quality" (*amitaguṇo*); the collection or multitude of those is the "multitude of immeasurable qualities" (*amitaguṇagaṇo*), [belonging] to them.
That which supports—that is, that wherein it stands—is the "support for the multitude of immeasurable qualities" (*amitaguṇagaṇādhāro*); thus the Victor (*jino*) is obtained.

The meaning is that, like the water of the ocean which cannot be measured by means of a hollowed leaf, it is the receptacle and foundation for an immeasurable multitude of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*).
"Endowed with the ten powers" (*dasabala*) means possessed of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, which are not shared by others. For here, "power" (*bala*) refers to... [by some].
Because they prevail against opposing causes, do not waver, and remain steadfast, they are called *bala* (powers).
One who possesses ten such powers is a *dasabala*, namely, the Buddha. That power is twofold: the bodily power of the Tathāgata and the power of his knowledge.
Among these, the bodily power is to be understood according to the lineage of elephants. For this has been stated by the ancients:
“Kālāvaka, Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tambapiṅgala, Gandhamaṅgala, Hema, Uposatha, and Chaddanta—these are the ten breeds of elephants.
These indeed are the ten elephant breeds. Therein, “Kālāvaka” should be understood as the ordinary elephant breed. As for that which...
The bodily strength of ten ordinary men is equal to that of one Kālāvaka elephant.
The strength of ten Kālāvakas is equal to that of one Gaṅgeyya. The strength of ten Gaṅgeyyas is equal to that of one Paṇḍara.
The strength of ten Paṇḍaras is equal to that of one Tamba. The strength of ten Tambas is equal to that of one Piṅgala.
The strength of ten *piṅgala* elephants is equal to that of one scent-elephant (*gandhahastin*).
The strength of ten scent-elephants is equal to that of one *maṅgala*. The strength of ten *maṅgala* elephants is equal to that of one *hemavata*.
The strength of ten *hemavata* elephants is equal to that of an *uposatha* elephant. The strength of ten *uposatha* elephants is equal to that of one *chaddanta* elephant.
That which is the strength of ten Chaddanta elephants is said to be the Nārāyaṇa-saṅghāta strength of a single Tathāgata.
In terms of ordinary elephants, this is the strength of a thousand million elephants; in terms of men, it is the strength of ten thousand million men.
This is the bodily strength of the Tathāgata. Now, among those...
This is not found in those canonical texts (pāḷi); it is found only in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā). Therefore, it is said in the *Aṅguttara-ṭīkā* on the *Dasaka-nipāta*:
"The knowledge of the ten powers (dasa-bala-ñāṇa), however, is indeed included in the canon.

The intention is that it is not merely a matter of traditional commentary (aṭṭhakathārūḷha), as is the case with physical strength (kāyabala). And here, regarding the phrase "the Nārāyaṇa-composed strength," "nārā" refers to reins (rasmiyo). These...

Because many things of various kinds arise from this, it is called *nārāyaṇa*, which means "diamond" (*vajira*). Therefore, the meaning is "the power of the Nārāyaṇa-composition" or "the power of the diamond-composition.
Furthermore, the ten powers of knowledge (*ñāṇadasabala*) are found in the Vibhaṅga-pāḷi, in the Mahāsīhanāda-sutta of the Mūlapaññāsa, and in the Dasaka-nipāta of the Aṅguttara-pāḷi.
This has already been explained in detail. However, for the sake of easy comprehension, I shall present it here in brief.
Namely: the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible; the knowledge of the ripening of karmic actions undertaken; the knowledge of the path leading everywhere;
the knowledge of the world with its many and diverse elements; the knowledge of the various inclinations of beings; and the knowledge of other beings and other persons...
The knowledge of the higher and lower degrees of the faculties; the knowledge of the defilement, purification, and emergence regarding the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments;
the knowledge of recollecting past lives; the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings; and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
This, moreover, is the sequence as it appears in the Abhidhamma Vibhaṅga-pāḷi.

Regarding the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (*cutūpapātañāṇa*), however, the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*) is mentioned in the *Mūlapaṇṇāsa* of the Pāḷi Canon, in the *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta*, and in the *Dasaka Nipāta* of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*.
In terms of meaning, it is indeed identical [to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth], because the passing away and rebirth of beings is seen by means of the knowledge of the divine eye.
In that context, "knowledge of what is possible and impossible" (*ṭhānāṭhānañāṇa*) is the knowledge that knows, as they truly are, causes and non-causes.
For it is called a "ground" (*ṭhāna*) because the fruit abides therein; since it arises and proceeds in dependence upon that ground, it is so designated.

"Knowledge of the ripening of the undertaking of kamma" refers to the knowledge of the ripening—consisting of rebirth-linking in happy or miserable destinies—and the fruit of Nibbāna, of wholesome and unwholesome kamma performed after having been undertaken in the past, future, and present.

Knowledge that understands things as they truly are (*yathābhūtaṃ pajānanañāṇaṃ*). Knowledge of the practice leading everywhere (*sabbatthagāminipaṭipadaṃ ñāṇaṃ*) is knowledge that understands, as they truly are, both the practice and the path leading to all destinations.
In this context, "practice" (*paṭipadaṃ*) means the path (*maggaṃ*), because by means of it one practices and reaches [the goal].
"Leading to destinations" (*gatigāminī*) means leading to the five destinations, such as hell and so forth. "Leading to no destination" (*agatigāminī*) means leading to Nibbāna.
For it is said: "Sāriputta, I understand Nibbāna and the practice leading to Nibbāna.

Regarding the phrase "knowledge of the world with its many elements and its various elements": here, "many elements" refers to the manifold elements, such as the eye-element and so forth, or the elements of the sense-desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Various elements" refers to those same elements as being of diverse kinds due to their distinct characteristics and dissimilar natures.
"World" refers to the world of aggregates, bases, and elements. "Knowledge" is the knowledge that understands things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-pajānana-ñāṇa*).
"Knowledge of the inclinations of beings" is the knowledge that understands, as they truly are, the state of having diverse inclinations in beings through their low and other types of inclinations.
Regarding "knowledge of the high and low faculties of other beings and other persons," here the term "other beings" refers to principal beings.
"Of other persons" means of those inferior beings who are beyond them; or else these two phrases have the same meaning, though stated in two ways for the sake of those to be trained (*veneyya*).

"Knowledge of the higher and lower faculties" is the knowledge that understands, as they truly are, the superior state—namely increase—and the inferior state—namely decrease—of the faculties such as faith and the rest.
"Knowledge of the defilement, cleansing, and emergence of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments":
here, "of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments" refers to the four jhānas beginning with the first; the eight liberations beginning with "one possessing form sees forms";
the three concentrations beginning with "accompanied by applied and sustained thought" (savitakka-savicāra); and the nine attainments beginning with the attainment of the first jhāna.
Of the successive attainments (*anupubbasamāpatti*). "Defilement" (*saṃkilesa*) refers to states conducive to decline. "Purification" (*vodāna*) refers to states conducive to distinction.

"Emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*) refers to the cause by which one emerges from the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so forth. "Knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) is the knowledge that understands things as they truly are.
"Knowledge of recollection of past lives" (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*) is defined as the recollection of the aggregates (*khandha*) in which one previously dwelt.
The knowledge of discerning. "Knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings" means the divine eye-knowledge that discerns both the death and the rebirth of beings.

"Knowledge of the destruction of the taints" means the knowledge that discerns, as it truly is, Nibbāna—the cessation of the taints—consisting in the destruction of the taints of sensual desire and so forth.
These knowledges, moreover, are not shared by others with the Tathāgata.
These should be understood as the ten powers of knowledge (*dasabalañāṇāni*).
And herein there are these verses:
"Knowledge of what is possible and impossible, and of the ripening [of kamma]; knowledge of the path [to liberation];"
The world of manifold elements and the inclinations of beings;
the degrees of the faculties, the defilement of the jhānas and so forth, their purification, emergence, and knowledge; and the recollection of past lives.
“Knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings, and knowledge of the destruction of the taints—these ten are the Buddha’s unique knowledges.
[This should be understood as a verse on commonality.
Is it not the case that there is no such thing as a “knowledge of the ten powers” distinct from omniscience (*sabbaññutā-ñāṇa*)? If so, why is it [listed separately]?

"It is said that knowledge is described as being of ten kinds. This is explained as follows: The knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabala-ñāṇa*) is indeed one thing, and the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) is another.
For the knowledge of the ten powers knows only its own respective functions; however, the knowledge of omniscience understands both that [which the ten powers know] and what remains beyond it.
Among the knowledges of the ten powers, the first knows only what is a cause and what is not a cause. The second [knows] the interval between karmic actions...
The third [section] concerns the differentiation of kamma itself. The fourth concerns the cause for the diversity of elements.
The fifth concerns the inclinations and resolutions of beings themselves. The sixth concerns the sharpness or dullness of the faculties themselves.
The seventh concerns their defilement and so forth together with the jhānas and other states. The eighth concerns the continuity of the aggregates in which one previously dwelt.
The ninth [knowledge] is simply the passing away and rebirth-linking of beings. The tenth is simply the analysis of the truths.
However, the knowledge of omniscience knows both what is to be known by these [other knowledges] and what lies beyond them;

yet it does not perform all their functions. For that [omniscient knowledge], being jhāna, cannot enter into absorption; being psychic power (*iddhi*), it cannot perform transformations; and being the path (*magga*), [it cannot produce the fruits].
It is not able to exhaust the defilements (*kilesa*). Such is the distinction between those two types of knowledge. However, it is these two types of knowledge that are intended here.
"Incomparable" (*atulam*) means peerless among persons in qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth. This, moreover, is the etymological derivation (*vacanattha*) here:
*tulā* is a weighing or measuring; [the root] *tula* means to resemble. For in the *Saddanīti*, it is stated: "*tula* in the sense of measuring. Alternatively, it is weighed (*tuliyati*).

That by which one weighs is a *tulā* (scale), namely, a standard scale (*pakatitulā*). It is called *tulā* because it is like a scale; thus, it is knowledge (*ñāṇa*). One who is measured by that is a *tula*.

In the formation of the derivative suffix, the elision of the suffix (*apaccaya*) occurs after the word *sammita*. A person measured by knowledge similar to a scale is a *tula*. One who is not a *tula* is an *atula*. This is a compound (*samāsa*) consisting of a *kammadhāraya* mixed with a *tappurisa*.
The Blessed One is found to be incomparable with any person whatsoever in qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth. Alternatively, there is none—
One who has no equal (*atula*) person is called *Atula*, the Blessed One. This is a *bahubbīhi* compound meaning "one whose qualities are recognized as incomparable.

The meaning is that he is the supreme person, being unlike anyone else in his qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth, because he is the foremost person in the world including the devas. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are beings—whether footless, two-footed, or four-footed—the Tathāgata is declared to be their chief."
"Dispassion is the best of all things, and the Visionary is the best of bipeds. This is to be connected with "the incomparable Buddha.
"I pay homage" means that, having recollected the qualities of the Buddha’s body—such as the beauty of his eyes and other limbs—I respectfully pay homage through the three doors.
And here, it should be understood that the *ekāra* (e) is the case-ending (*desa*) for the first person singular (*mivibhatti*) according to the *Mahāvisaya-sutta*.
Furthermore, homage is threefold, by way of bodily, verbal, and mental homage. As it is said: "Monks, there are these three kinds of homage.
Which three? One pays homage with the body, one pays homage with speech, and one pays homage with the mind.
In that context, having established a state of mind characterized by wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), [one touches] what are known as the two knees, the two elbows, and the forehead.
One is said to "pay homage with the body" when, having placed five limbs upon the ground, one prostrates oneself facing those worthy of veneration.
It is with reference to this that it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* and other texts: "having paid homage by means of the fivefold prostration.
One is said to "pay homage with speech" when one utters the words describing the qualities of the Buddha. For example: "Homage be to Vipassī; homage also be to Sikhī."
In such expressions as "Homage to Vessabhū, homage to Kakusandha, homage to Koṇāgamana, homage to Kassapa,
homage to Aṅgīrasa," it is indeed verbal veneration; for one venerates with the mind while recollecting the qualities of the Buddhas and others.
This, however, is the summary of the construction here: [He] whose bodily limbs are beautiful to behold, endowed with a body that brings splendor to the eyes of all beings;
who is possessed of a sweet and excellent voice, endowed with the highest sound which is delightful and pleasing to the taste;
and who is the receptacle for a multitude of immeasurable virtues, being the foundation for the infinite collection of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and the rest.
"I reverently worship, I worship the One Possessed of the Ten Powers— the Buddha who is endowed with the Tathāgata’s unique power of knowledge regarding the body, and who is incomparable,
being peerless in qualities such as virtue through any [other being]— through the three doors.
The commentary on the second verse of worship is complete.
The Buddha, who possesses fortitude and upholds the supreme knowledge,
has experienced within saṃsāra both physical and mental suffering from the world.
I pay homage to that auspicious one, O King of Men. 3.

Having thus paid homage to the Buddha with the third verse, he now speaks the verse beginning with "The Buddha who is steadfast and a bearer of wisdom," desiring to pay homage after praising him with the four qualities beginning with concentration (*samādhi*).
This [verse], moreover, because it is joined with the *masajaga* meter and the *ga* heavy syllable...
It should be understood that the *suddhavirājita* [meter] is characterized by eight syllables.
For it is stated in the *Vuttodaya*: "msā, jgā—this is considered *suddhavirājita*. Its meaning is as follows:

in each quarter-verse (*pāda*), if there should be *masagaṇas* (m, s, s) and *jagas* (j, g, g), that which is thus described is to be known as the one considered *suddhavirājita*. [The example is: *Dhitimā aññadhārako*.

The connection is as follows: "I pay homage to that Buddha," who, while in the world of *saṃsāra*, experienced both bodily suffering and mental suffering, he who is the auspicious one for men and gods.
In this context, the word "yo" (*yo*) is an indefinite designation;
its meaning is "whoever" or "of such a kind. And because it is a pronoun expressing indefiniteness, [it functions as such].
