The meaning of the word (*vacanattha*) need not be explained. However, its analysis of constituent parts (*padavibhāga*) must be performed.

Among those [words], while the denotation of the pronoun *ya* is indefinite and obtained as a subordinate factor, it is precisely the quality of being an indefinite universal form—consisting of such things as birth, name, clan, virtue, abiding, and resort—as joined with whatever [attributes] it may have, that is obtained as the primary factor. [This applies to] the nominative case ending (*paṭhamāvibhatti*).

The meaning expressed by the vowel *o* when it functions as a grammatical object receives the number of the first-person singular agentive case, which is designated as the natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*).
Alternatively, "yo" means that which goes to or attains the state of a pronoun; or, that which goes to or attains the state of expressing an indefinite [referent];
or, that which goes to or proceeds by way of the state of a pronoun; or, that which is to be gone to or known by way of the state of a pronoun.
Or *yo*: that by which one must go or know; or *yo* has the sense of indefiniteness.
Thus the Ancients said:
“Depending on various causes, there is the formation of verbal roots, suffixes, and compounds.”
"For those who reflect, reflection itself becomes the primary exertion.
"Buddha" refers to one who has penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. Herein, this is the etymological derivation (*vacanattha*):

he awakens to the four truths, thus he is the Blessed One, the Buddha. This is a formation where the agent alone is expressed. The verbal root is *budh*. Alternatively, he is the Buddha because he awakens the world.
This is a *hetu-kattusādhana* (an instrumental derivation based on the causal agent). The meaning is that he awakens others to the four truths.

Alternatively, he is called *Buddha* because, having become one whose awakening is unsurpassed (*anaññabodhi*), he awakens—that is, he wakes up—from the sleep of delusion together with its latent tendencies (*savāsanā-sammoha-niddā*).

Like a lotus that has blossomed upon encountering the rays of the sun, attaining the highest excellence of beauty and splendor, he is adorned with an immeasurable multitude of qualities through his encounter with the knowledge of the supreme path.
Alternatively, he is called *Buddha* because he awakens to or blossoms into the attainment of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*).
Or, he is called *Buddha* because he awakens to or goes along the "one-way path" known as Nibbāna. Indeed, the word *buddha* applies to four meanings, beginning with knowledge.
Therefore it has been said:
“The word *buddha* occurs with respect to these four meanings: knowledge, blossoming, going, and wakefulness.
Alternatively, he is called *Buddha* because he awakens to—that is, knows—all knowable phenomena (*sabbañeyyadhamma*), by means of wisdom (*paññā*) developed through the perfections (*pāramī*).
He is called *Buddha* because he awakens, has awakened, or will awaken to conditioned and unconditioned phenomena;

or he is called *Buddha* because he is to be understood through the specific qualities of knowledge he has attained, such that "the Blessed One is indeed a Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*);"; or he is called *Buddha* because that which is to be understood and known by the Blessed One is "the Awakened" (*Buddha*).
What is that? It is the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*); he possesses this, thus he is the Blessed One, the *Buddha*. In terms of its meaning:

However, when the perfections have been cultivated, the continuum of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*)—in which the defilements (*kilesa*) have been destroyed and shattered along with their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) by means of self-born knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*), and which is the locus of an immeasurable multitude of qualities such as great compassion and omniscience—is the Buddha. As it is said:
"A Buddha is that Blessed One who is self-born, without a teacher, regarding dharmas unheard of before, having [realized] the truths for himself..."
He fully awakened, attained omniscience therein, and achieved mastery over the powers.

In this context, one called a “Buddha” is fourfold: by way of the Omniscient Buddha (*sabbaññubuddha*), the Private Buddha (*paccekabuddha*), the Buddha of the Four Truths (*catusaccabuddha*), and the Buddha by way of learning (*sutabuddha*).
Among these, for four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus a hundred thousand aeons, he fulfilled the thirty perfections (*pāramī*).

Having fulfilled [the perfections], one who has attained full enlightenment is called a *sabbaññubuddha* (an omniscient Buddha). Having fulfilled the perfections for two incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus one hundred thousand aeons, one who has attained self-enlightenment is called a *paccekabuddha* (a solitary Buddha). The rest, those whose taints are exhausted, are called *catusaccabuddha* (those enlightened in the Four Truths).
One who is learned is called *sutabuddha* (one enlightened by what is heard). However, in this context, the *sabbaññubuddha* is intended.
Regarding the phrase *dhitimāññadhārako*: here the word-division should be made as *dhitimā* and *aññadhārako*. *Dhitimā* means "possessing concentration" (*samādhivanto*).

It is called *dhiti* because it holds (*dhāreti*) the associated mental states upon a single object; thus, *dhiti* is concentration (*samādhi*). This is derived from the verbal root *dhā*. The vowel *ā* is replaced by the vowel *i*.
It is called *dhiti* because it holds—that is, it establishes—the associated states upon a single object. This [stability] occurs through the mind's application (*yoga*) to a single object.
The meaning is that he establishes the mind upon its object by means of making it steadfast.
One who possesses fortitude (*dhiti*) is "possessed of fortitude" (*dhitimā*); this refers to the Buddha.

For just as Mount Meru does not waver when violent winds blow from the four directions, so too he does not waver before opposing wrong views, nor before desirable and undesirable objects, nor before gain and loss.

He does not waver because of worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) consisting of gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, or pleasure and pain; what is meant is that he remains possessed of concentration (*samādhivanta*).
"Bearing another burden" means bearing the fruit of arahantship. Or, it means bearing the white parasol of the fruit of arahantship, which is designated as liberation (*vimutti*).
He knows the "other" (*añña*), which is the fruit of arahantship, by not overstepping the boundary of the truths already seen through the first path.
The suffix *kvi* follows the verbal root *dhṛ* preceded by *ā*. The word *ā* has the sense of a limit (*maryādā*). Because it is followed by a conjunct consonant, the vowel *ā* is shortened;

thus, "that which holds this" is *aññadhāraka*. The suffix *ṇvu* follows the root *dhṛ* with the word *añña* as its prefix. [It functions] within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) that proceeds without interruption, consisting of the aggregates (*khandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).
For it is said in the Commentary:
“The uninterrupted succession of the aggregates, elements,
and bases as they proceed is called ‘saṃsāra’.”

*Samsāra* is so called because, through the mutual connection of the aggregates (*khandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), one repeatedly remembers, goes toward, and proceeds [through them].
It is derived from the verbal root *sar*, preceded by the prefix *sam*, in the sense of "going," with the suffix *ṇa*. Alternatively, the etymological meaning should be understood as follows:

it is *saṃsāra* because the aggregates, bases, and elements remember, go toward, and proceed there continuously (*saṃ abbocchinnaṃ*) without interruption. In that [state], you experience (*anubhosīti*).
"Again and again he ate"; the meaning is "he experienced. "Bodily" (*kāyika*) means occurring in the body, in the physical frame.

"Mental" (*cetasika*) means occurring in the mind. These two terms are qualifiers for the word "suffering" (*dukkha*). "Suffering" (*dukkha*) refers to the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
It is called "suffering" because it is the act of suffering, or alternatively, it is called "suffering" because it causes one to suffer; the suffix *-a* is applied to the root *dukkh*. This...
However, the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) is stated by way of its function (*kāritavasena*). What is meant is that it causes that in which it arises to suffer.

"From the world" (*lokatoti*) means for the sake of the world of beings (*sattaloka*). It is called "the world" (*loka*) because merit and demerit, as well as their respective results, arise and proceed therein;
thus, *loka* + *dhātu* + *ṇa*. Alternatively, it is called "the world" because it takes (*lāti*) or grasps (*gaṇhāti*) wholesome states and so forth; the root *lā* with the suffix *oka*. Beings...

The world indeed attains [this]. The steadfast one, the upholder of other [teachings], who— desiring to liberate from the suffering of the cycle of existence those beings submerged in the whirlpool of *saṃsāra* for the sake of their welfare—

performed the thirty perfections (*pāramitā*) along with the five great renunciations, which were exceedingly difficult to accomplish, throughout four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeya-kappa*) plus a hundred thousand eons, for the sake of the world of beings, [enduring] both bodily and mental...
It means that you experience the suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). "Him" (*taṃ*) refers to such a Buddha. "I revere" (*vandemi*) means I pay homage.

"An auspicious sign for men and gods" (*naradevamaṅgalaṃ*) means one who has become an auspicious sign for both humans and deities. Here, however, is the etymological explanation: a human (*naro*) is so called because he goes to or reaches hell (*nirayaṃ*);
the suffix *-aro* is used in the sense of reaching. Furthermore, a noble person (*ariyamanusso*) is so called because he has previously gone to the state of the Noble Ones (*ariya*).

"By way (*naya*) of a person (*nara*)," so it is said. Alternatively, he is called a *nara* because he leads (*neti*) toward excellence; the meaning is that he leads toward the supreme state of renunciation (*pabbajjā*).
In the *Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: "He is a *nara* because he leads toward the state of being the eldest (*jeṭṭha*).

For even a person who has become a son or a brother stands in the place of a father to his mother’s elder sister or elder brother, let alone one who has become a husband to other women. Thus it is said in the *Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā*.

But "narati" means "he leads," thus he is a *nara*, a man. For just as a being who has become the first in nature is called a *purisa* (man) because he lies (*seti*) or exists in a high (*puri*) or superior state by virtue of his excellence, so too he is called a *nara* in the sense of leading (*nayana*).
For even a person who is the son or brother of a woman stands in the place of a father to her mother, elder sister, or younger sister; how much more so, then, for others?

This has been stated regarding others. Therefore, although the word *nara* is used here in a general sense, it is understood specifically as "man" (*purisa-nara*), because it is appropriate to grasp it according to the principle of the primary subject.

They are called *devas* because they sport (*dibbanti*) with the strands of sensual pleasure, the meditative absorptions, supernormal powers, mental sovereignty, and so forth. [The root] *div* with the suffix *ṇa*.
Alternatively, they are called *devas* because they shine (*dibbanti*) with the splendor of their bodies and ornaments. And the *devas*...
There are three kinds of "deities": deities by convention (*sammutideva*), deities by birth (*upapattideva*), and deities by purification (*visuddhideva*).
Among these, kings, queens, and princes are called deities by convention because from the time of the Mahāsammata election onwards they have been designated as "deities" by the world.
Those born in the celestial realms are called deities by birth. Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) are called deities by purification. Here...
However, the gods of rebirth (*upapattideva*) are intended here.

"Auspicious" (*maṅgala*) means that which has become auspicious; it is an adjective for the word *tanti*. It is called "auspicious" (*maṅgala*) because by means of it, beings increase (*vaḍḍhenti*) in all attainments;
thus, the Buddha is the auspicious one. The verbal root *maṅg* is used in the sense of increasing (*vaḍḍhane*), with the suffix *-ala*. Alternatively, "fortune" (*maṅga*) is so called...

He is *Maṅgala* (the Auspicious One), the Buddha, because he reaps—that is, cuts away—evil through his teaching for those who are to be trained (*veneyya*). [Etymologically: from the root *lū*, with the prefix *maṅga-* and the suffix *kvi*.

Humans and gods are *naradeva*; he is their *Maṅgala*, thus *Naradevamaṅgala*, the Buddha. Furthermore, because he is worthy of worship by humans, gods, and Brahmas, he is represented by these symbols:
the conch, the wheel, the full vase, the lotus, the glory (*sirī*), the white parasol, the hook, and the banner.
Regarding the phrase *sovattikañca*: because it is the most excellent and supreme among the eight mundane blessings (*maṅgala*), it is called "the blessing";
therefore, the intended meaning is that he praises the Buddha as "the blessing of men and gods.
This, then, is the concise explanation here: one who is steadfast, possessed of concentration, a bearer of other [qualities], and a bearer of the fruit of Arhatship.

Or bearing the axe of the fruit of arahantship; whatever kind of Buddha he was, in the wandering through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), he experienced again and again—both the bodily suffering occurring in the body and the suffering of the cycle occurring in the mind—and from the world, the cause of the world;
he became, he felt, that auspiciousness of men and gods for men and gods.
"I pay homage, I bow down to that Buddha who is such a source of auspiciousness.
The commentary on the third verse of homage is complete.
[He whose] body is variegated with the thirty-two marks...
I pay homage to the Sage who has reached his final birth,
from whose body radiates a blazing light, and who is a treasury of the flood of virtues consisting of wisdom, concentration, and moral discipline.

4. Thus, having paid homage to the Buddha with the third verse, he now speaks the verse beginning with “bāttiṃsati lakkhaṇa citra deha” out of a desire to worship the Sage after praising him with six qualities, such as his body being variegated with the thirty-two marks.
This, moreover, is characterized by eleven syllables and is established as a *gāthā* because it is composed of the *ta*, *ja*, *ja*, and *ga* ganas along with two heavy (*garu*) syllables.

[The following] should be observed. For it is said in the *Vuttodaya*: "That in which the *tjā* (ta-jagaṇa) and *jgā* (ja-ga-ja-gaṇa) groups, together with a heavy syllable (*garu*), are established by means of a heavy syllable at the end of the foot—that is called an 'established' (*upaṭṭhitā*) verse.

The meaning of this is: in whichever quarter-foot the *tjā* (ta-jagaṇa) and *jgā* (ja-ga-ja-gaṇa) groups, along with a heavy syllable, are joined by a heavy syllable at the end of the foot, that verse is named "established.
And here, even though there is one heavy syllable as well as two heavy syllables, because the characteristic is the same, [it is so designated].

It should be understood that "gāthā" here means "established. In this context, "possessing a body variegated with the thirty-two marks" means having a body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
Here, "thirty-two" is thirty plus two; it is a substitution for the word *dvi*.

It is called a "mark" (*lakkhaṇa*) because by means of it the Buddha’s body is marked (*lakkhiyati*) and characterized. It is called "deha" because it is sustained (*dihiyati*), accumulated (*upaciyati*), and increased (*vaḍḍhati*).
Or, here "body" (*deha*) means the physical frame (*sarīra*). From the root *dih*, meaning accumulation or growth, with the suffix *ṇa*.

He whose body—his physical frame—is variegated and diverse with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man is called "one whose body is variegated with the thirty-two marks," which refers to the Sage (*muni*).
This, however, is a brief description of the nature of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man: (1) well-placed feet;... [and so forth].
And he has long heels; long fingers; soft and tender hands and feet; webbed hands and feet; high-arched feet; legs like those of the eneya antelope;
while standing without bending, he can touch and rub his knees with both palms;
his male organ is enclosed in a sheath; he is golden-colored, with skin like refined gold; he has delicate skin; and he has a single hair growing from each pore.

His body hairs point upward; his body is straight like that of Brahmā; he has seven prominent features; his torso is like that of a lion; there is no gap between his shoulders; his body is well-proportioned like a banyan tree; his trunk is symmetrical and rounded; he possesses the supreme sense of taste; his jaw is like that of a lion;
he has forty teeth; his teeth are even; his teeth are without gaps; his teeth are very white; he has a large tongue;
he has the voice of Brahmā and speaks with the voice of the karavīka bird; his eyes are intensely blue; his eyelashes are like those of a cow; and he has a tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
The hair-tuft is born between the eyebrows, and the head is like a turban; thus there are thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
Therefore it is said in the *Lakkhaṇa-sutta* of the *Pātheyya-vagga*:
"Monks, what are those thirty-two marks of a Great Man possessed by which a Great Man has two destinations and no other?"
If he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch...
[as before] ...but if he goes forth from the home life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, who has lifted the veil from the world.
1. Here, monks, a Great Man has feet with level tread. That a Great Man has feet with level tread—this, monks, is another mark of a Great Man.
Monks, this is a mark of a Great Man belonging to a Great Man.
Furthermore, monks, on the soles of the feet of a Great Man there are wheels produced, with a thousand spokes, with rims, with hubs, and complete in every detail.
This too, monks, is a mark of a Great Man belonging to a Great Man. Furthermore, monks...
The Great Man has long heels; 4. he has long fingers; 5. his hands and feet are soft and tender; 6. his hands and feet have webbed fingers and toes; 7. he has high-arched feet; 8.
he has calves like those of the eneya antelope; 9. while standing without bending, he can touch and rub his knees with both palms;
10. his male organ is enclosed in a sheath; 11. he is golden-colored, with skin like refined gold.
12. He has delicate skin; because his skin is so delicate, dust and dirt do not adhere to his body.
13. He has a single hair to each pore; the hairs grow one by one from each pore. 14. His body hairs point upward;
the upward-pointing hairs are blue, the color of collyrium, curled, circular, and grow turning to the right. 15. He has a body straight like that of Brahmā.
16. He has a prominent uṣṇīṣa. 17. His torso is like that of a lion. 18. He has well-rounded shoulders. 19. He is symmetrical like a banyan tree;
as is his span from hand to hand, so is his height from head to heels. 20. His body is evenly rounded. 21. He has the supreme sense of taste.
22. He has a jaw like that of a lion. 23. He has forty teeth. 24. His teeth are even. 25. His teeth have no gaps between them.
26. He has very white teeth; 27. he has a large tongue; 28. he has a Brahma-like voice, like the song of the cuckoo;
29. his eyes are intensely blue; 30. he has eyelashes like those of a cow; 31. a tuft of hair grows between his eyebrows, which is white and resembles soft cotton.
Monks, that the Great Man has a tuft of hair growing between his eyebrows, which is white and resembles soft cotton—[this is one of his marks].
This too, monks, is a mark of a Great Man. Furthermore, monks, a Great Man has a turban-like head.
That a Great Man has a turban-like head, monks, this too is a mark of a Great Man.
These, monks, are the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
“...the marks of a Great Man. Now, the meaning of these thirty-two marks of a Great Man will be revealed later.
“Blazing with the radiance issuing from his body”: it means shining all around with the six-colored rays of light emerging from the Blessed One’s physical body.
*Juti* means it moves or shines; it is derived from the verbal root *jud*. It goes forth (*nigacchati*).

"Niccharati" means "gone forth" (niggatā), [referring to] a ray (rasmi). This is derived from the verbal root *gam* preceded by the prefix *ni*. "Pajjalantaṃ" means shining, gleaming, or blazing intensely.

And here, although one should have said "the radiance gone forth from the body" (*dehaniggatajutī*), for the sake of preserving the meter, it is stated as "the radiance gone forth from the body's radiance" (*dehajjutiniggata*) through a transposition of words.

Therefore, the compound should be understood as "the radiance gone forth from the body" (*dehato niggatā jutī*). [It is] from the body, that is, from the form-body (*rūpakāya*), that they have gone forth.
"Blazing with rays and beams of light that stream forth"—thus is the Sage (muni) found, whose bodily radiance issues forth in a blazing state.
For from the front part of the Sage’s body, six-colored rays arise and extend for a distance of eighty cubits.
From the back part of his body, and from his right and left hands, six-colored rays likewise arise.
It occupied a space of eighty cubits. From the top of his hair-line upwards, a ray the color of a peacock’s neck emerged from every pore of his hair and occupied a space of eighty cubits in the sky.
From his soles downwards, a coral-colored ray emerged and occupied a space of eighty cubits in the solid earth; thus, it extended for about eighty cubits all around.
It is said that the six-colored rays of the Buddha, shining and quivering,
issued forth like golden-staffed torches and spread abroad like nets leaping into the sky, or like flashes of lightning emerging from a great cloud covering the four continents.
Therefore, he praises [the Buddha] as "one whose blazing bodily radiance has issued forth."
"Paññādhiti sīla guṇoghavindanti": herein, "paññā" (wisdom) is omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*). "Dhitī" (fortitude) is concentration associated with the jhānas, the paths, and the fruits.
"Sīla" (virtue) is the perfectly purified fourfold purification-virtue not shared by paccekabuddhas or noble disciples.
"Ogha" means a multitude or collection. "Vindanti" means they have obtained. It is so called because one knows or penetrates all knowable phenomena according to their specific nature and mode.

Wisdom (*paññā*). It is the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*). The verbal root *ñā* preceded by *pa-* and followed by the suffix *-a*. Furthermore, this wisdom has the characteristic of understanding (*pajānana-lakkhaṇā*), the characteristic of penetration (*paṭivedha-lakkhaṇā*), and the characteristic of illumination (*obhāsana-lakkhaṇā*);
it has the function of illuminating the object (*visaya-obhāsa-rasā*); it is manifested as non-delusion (*asammoha-paccupaṭṭhānā*); and its proximate cause is concentration (*samādhi-padaṭṭhānā*).
The etymological meaning of the word "steadfastness" (*dhiti*) has already been explained above. It is called virtue (*sīla*) because it cools (*sīlati*). Right bodily and vocal actions...

It burns away [defilements] and establishes [the mind] correctly; this is the meaning. Alternatively, it is *sīla* because one becomes cool (*sīlati*) and concentrated (*samādhiyati*), and because through the state of excellent conduct in bodily action and so forth, one does not become distracted.
Or, it is *sīla* because by means of it they concentrate the mind (*sīlanti samādahanti cittam*). It is the fourfold purity of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*).
The verbal root is *sīladhātu*. This, moreover, has the characteristic of establishing [the mind], the function of destroying misconduct (*dussīlya*), and the function of blamelessness (*anavajja*).
Alternatively, it has purity as its manifestation and moral shame and dread as its proximate cause. The etymological meaning of the word *guṇa* has already been stated above. Regarding *ogha*:
it is a collection (*samūha*) because it carries away (*uhanati*) or brings together the parts (*avayava*) therein.

It is derived from the verbal root *upahana* with the suffix *ṇa*. The *u* becomes *o*; the *han* becomes *gho*. Furthermore, in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā-ṭīkā*, it is said: "It is called *ogha* because it flows away (*byapiyati*) or goes toward the parts."
It is said, “a flood (ogho). “Vinda” means finding or obtaining; or, it is “vinda” because one has found or obtained.
Wisdom, fortitude, and virtue—these qualities are called *paññā-dhiti-sīla-guṇā*. A flood (*ogha*) of these is their collection; thus [the term is formed].
He who possesses that finding or obtaining is the sage (*muni*) known as *Paññā-dhiti-sīla-oguha-vindo*. Alternatively, *vinda* means that which is to be obtained.
"By whom [there is] a flood of the qualities of wisdom, concentration, and virtue" means "one who possesses a flood of the qualities of wisdom, concentration, and virtue.

This is a third-order *bahubbīhi* compound. The meaning is: "He is one in whom there exists a collection (*samūha*) of qualities consisting of wisdom, concentration, and virtue, which are to be found or attained.
"I worship him" means "I pay homage. "The Sage" (*muni*) refers to the Buddha. He is called a sage because he knows, understands, or discerns what is beneficial and what is harmful.
*Muni*, *buddho*. The element of a sage (*munadhātu*) is found in knowledge (*ñāṇe*). Alternatively, he is a sage (*muni*) because he knows and understands both types of welfare;

that is to say, having weighed the aggregates and so forth in the world as if placing them on a scale, the Blessed One knows the welfare of this world and the welfare of the world beyond by way of such methods as "these are internal aggregates" and "these are external," and so forth. Furthermore, he is a householder-sage (*agāriyamuni*) and a homeless-sage (*anāgāriyamuni*).
The sage (muni) is of many kinds: the trainee sage (sekha-muni), the non-trainee sage (asekha-muni), the solitary sage (pacceka-muni), and the sage of sages (munimuni).

Among these, the householder sage is a layperson who has attained the fruit [of the path] and understood the teaching. The homeless sage is one who has gone forth in such a manner. The trainee sage refers to the seven types of trainees (sekkhā).
The non-trainee sage is one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). The solitary sage is a paccekabuddha. The sage of sages is a perfectly enlightened Buddha (sammāsambuddha).
Among those [types of sages], however, it is the "muni" (sage) who is intended here; that sage. "Endowed with his final birth" means endowed with the final or last existence.

It is called *anta* because one reaches (*amati*) the end (*avasāna*). The verbal root is *am*. By the rule *massa no*, the *m* becomes *n*. That which exists at the end is "final" (*antima*); it refers to the last existence.
Birth (*jāti*) is the act of being born or produced; it is the manifestation of the aggregates (*khandhā*). It is so called because one is brought forth (*janiyati*) or produced by karma.
Or "birth" (jāti). Rebirth-existence (upapattibhava) is obtained. [The word] *jāti* is a verbal root (*dhātu*). There is the elision of the final part of the root.

One who is joined with his final birth is "joined with his final birth" (*antimajātiyutta*), the Sage (*muni*). For, because all defilements that produce rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the three realms of existence in the future have been utterly eradicated by the Supreme Path right there on the seat of enlightenment (*bodhipallaṅka*), there is no further becoming for the Blessed One in the future.
Therefore, it is said that this noble birth is joined with the final existence.
Thus it is stated in the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta*:
"Knowledge and vision arose in me; unshakable liberation has been attained; this is the final birth; now there is no more renewed existence."
This, however, is the summary of the application here: "Possessing a body variegated with the thirty-two marks" means having a physical body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man;
"blazing forth with the radiance issuing from the body" means shining all around with the six-colored rays issuing from the physical body;
"the Lord of the virtues of wisdom, steadfastness, and morality" refers to those [virtues] consisting of wisdom, steadfastness, and morality.

I reverently salute with my three doors the Sage, the Buddha—who possesses a multitude of virtues, or who possesses a multitude of virtues consisting of wisdom, concentration, and morality that are to be attained;
who is joined to his final birth, or joined to his last existence and last personal state. I salute him.
The commentary on the fourth verse of homage is completed.
Like the newly risen morning sun,
he shines with grace amidst the ascetics, radiant with splendors.
I pay homage to the Lord of Sages, the Omniscient One, who is free from agitation and whose face resembles the full moon. 5.
Having thus paid homage to the Buddha with the fourth verse, [he now praises him] by means of the four qualities beginning with "sporting with glories" (*sirīhi lalantam*).
Having praised [the Buddha], desiring to pay homage, he spoke the verse beginning with *pātodayanti*.

This, moreover, should be understood as an *indavajirā* verse, characterized by eleven syllables because it is composed of two groups of three syllables (*ta-ta-ja*) followed by a heavy syllable (*ga*). For it is said in the *Vuttodaya*:

"The *indādikā* [verses] are *vajirā* when they have *jagaṇa*, *gaṇa*, and *gaṇa*. The meaning of this is: in each quarter (foot), there are those two *gaṇas* (*ta-ta*) and a *jagaṇa* (*ja*) followed by a heavy syllable (*ga*).
And when there are *go* and *garu*, that [verse] beginning with the word *inda*—that is, beginning with the sound *inda*—is called a *vajirā* or *vajirāgāthā*.
In this context, the word division should be made as *pāto udayanti*; the meaning is that it has risen (*uggata*) from the eastern world-system in the morning, at the time of forenoon.
Because it rises (*udeti*), i.e., ascends (*uggacchati*), from the eastern world-system in the morning, it is the "morning-rising one" (*pātodayo*), namely, the sun.
"Before dawn" (*pātopubba*) means at the time of sunrise; that is *pātodaya*. "Like the newly risen sun" (*bāladivākaraṃ va*):
the word division is *bāla-divākaraṃ iva*. "Like the newly risen sun" means like the sun that has just emerged.
And here, "newly born" (*bāla*) refers to a recently born infant or a young chick. For it is "weak" (*balati*)—it lives merely by means of inhaling and exhaling, not by its own excellence.

"By means of wisdom as his life" refers to a fool, a young boy. The verbal root *bal* (to live) is used in the sense of breathing or living. Regarding *divā*: it is called *divā* because it shines (*divati*) or illuminates (*dibbati*).
The verbal root *div* with the suffix *a*. Alternatively, it is *divā* because darkness is destroyed (*dīyati*) by it;

the verbal root *dī* (to destroy) with the suffix *a* and the augment *v*. That which makes this [light] is the "maker of day" (*divākara*). Or, one whose light (*karo ābhā*) exists during the day (*divā*) is the maker of day.

*Sūriyo* means the sun. A maker of day who is like a child is a "child-sun" (*bāladivākaro*). Alternatively, one who is like a child in relation to the maker of day is a "child-sun" (*bāladivākaro*), referring to the newly risen sun.
Furthermore, the meaning is that he sports and plays with a thousand rays in the midst of the constellations and stars in the sky.
*Yatīnam* refers to the monks, for they strive, exert themselves, endeavor, and apply effort toward wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*).

They are called *yatī* because they strive (*yati*). The root *yata* means either "to prepare" or "exertion. Alternatively, they are called *yatī* because they restrain (*yamanti*) themselves and cease from unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*);
the root *yama* means "to cease," and the final vowel is elided. Of those *yatīs*. "Lalita" means playful or graceful. He is called *lalita* because he plays or sports; thus, the Muni is *lalita*.
The root *lala* means "play," and the suffix *ta* is added. That [is *lalita*]. "By means of glories" refers to the glories of the Blessed One.

"Glory" (*sirī*) refers either to the splendors consisting of the excellence of the limbs of the body, or to the attained splendors comprised of the thirty-two major marks, the eighty minor characteristics, and the six-colored rays.
It is "glory" because it rests upon those who have performed merit; the root *si-* means "to serve," with the suffix *-ra* and the feminine gender-indicating suffix *-ī*.
Alternatively, it is "glory" because it is served by those who have performed merit; thus, it is "attainment. In the *Mūlaṭīkā*, however, it says: "Glory is wisdom and merit..."
"...this is its designation," it is said. The connection is: "gracefully sporting with splendors in the midst of striving monks.

And here this is what is meant: just as the sun, risen and ascended at dawn, sports and plays with its thousand rays in the sky amidst the constellations and stars, even so does the Sage in the world, amidst the striving monks, [shine] with the thirty-two marks.
He sports and displays grace with a bodily splendor adorned by the six-colored rays of the cool secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), possessing a beauty that has attained true glory.
"With a face resembling the full moon" means he is endowed with a countenance like the full moon.
For just as the moon becomes diminished day by day from the first day of the dark fortnight, so too the mouth and countenance of the Sage are never diminished.
The Blessed One’s face, however, shines constantly, being no less than the full orb of the moon;
therefore, he praises it by qualifying it with the word "full" as "the face resembling the full moon. It is called *puṇṇa* because it is filled (*pūreti*) by the sixteen digits.

The verbal root *pūr* takes the suffix *ta*, and for that, there is the substitution *ṇṇa*. It is called *indu* because it exercises sovereignty (*issariya*) over the lunar mansions and stars; the verbal root is *idi*.
Sovereignty (issariyaṃ). Full (puṇṇaṃ). The full moon is *puṇṇendu*; it is the moon (*cando*). "Resembling" (*saṅkāsanti*) means similar (*sadisaṃ*).
For the word *saṅkāsa* is a particle expressing a simile. Indeed, it is stated in the *Subodhālaṅkāra*: [text follows].
“*Iva*, *iva*, *vā* mean ‘like’ (*tulya*); *samāna*, *nibha*, *sannibha*;
*yathā*, *saṅkāsa*, *tulita*, *ppakāsa*, *patirūpaka*,” and so forth.
It is called the face (*mukha*) because it shines like the full moon; it is the countenance (*ānana*). The word-element *mukha* [ends in] *a*. It is similar (*saṅkāsa*) to the full moon.
He whose face and countenance are similar [to the full moon] is "one whose face resembles the full moon" (puṇṇindusaṅkāsamukho), the Lord of Sages (munindo). Now, that Lord of Sages—
possessing a splendor like the thousand rays of the full moon, adorned in the midst of the monks with the glories of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics,
and surrounded by a fathom-wide halo of light— [shines] from one garland to another.
It is said that his face is radiant and adorned with what are called dense Buddha-rays, which issue forth in clusters, forming pairs upon pairs.
Therefore, he praises him as "one whose face resembles the full moon.
*Anejam* means free from craving (*nittaṇham*). *Ejā* is so called because it moves or trembles in dependence on gain, loss, and so forth; *ejā* is craving. The verbal root *ej-* signifies trembling.
"One who has no wavering (ejā) is called 'the unwavering' (anejo), the Lord of Sages (munindo). For it is said in the *Mahāniddesa* commentary:
'The Blessed One is found to be "unwavering" because he does not waver amidst gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain.

"Omniscient" (*sabbaññu*) refers to one who has penetrated all things that can be known. This is by way of the designation of Nibbāna, which is characterized by the absence of conditioned change (*saṅkhāra-vikāra*).
He is called the All-Knowing (sabbaññū), the Lord of Sages (munindo), because he knows and penetrates all fivefold knowable phenomena (ñeyyadhamma) through his virtue (*sīla*).

The word *sabbaññū* is derived from the verbal root *ñā* preceded by the prefix *sabba*. Here, "all" refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhatadhamma*), which are called "formations" (*saṅkhārā*) because they are formed by their respective conditions.
The two types of intimation (*viññatti*) and the triad beginning with lightness (*lahutā*) are called "mutations" (*vikāra*), because they cause the four great elements to become deformed.

Having done so: because the two types of intimation (*viññatti*) are respectively the specific qualities of the mind-born air element (*cittaja-vāyo-dhātu*) and the mind-born earth element (*cittaja-pathavī-dhātu*);
and because the triad of lightness and so forth (*lahutādi-ttaya*) is the specific quality of material phenomena produced by mind, nutriment, and birth;

and because the characteristic of touching and so forth belongs to phenomena such as contact (*phassa*), while the characteristics of hardness and so forth belong to the earth element and the rest, and the characteristic of cognizing the object belongs to the mind.

The characteristic of peace of Nibbāna, the characteristic of being afflicted (ruppana) of material form (rūpa), the characteristic of bending (namana) of name (nāma), the three characteristics of impermanence and so forth, and the four characteristics of matter such as accumulation—these are called "characteristics" (lakkhaṇa), because they characterize;
that is, the phenomena to be characterized are characterized by them. Furthermore, "craving" (vāna) is said to be the unconditioned element of Nibbāna.

It is called "derived" because it has emerged from that [primary matter]. It is called "conceptualization" (*paññatti*) because it is made known—that is, it is made known in a specific manner—as a delimiting form, as well as all conventional objects such as "woman," "man," "pot," and "cloth.

In this context, the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) and Nibbāna are ultimate realities (*paramattha-dhamma*). However, among the [types of] conceptualization, those characterized by transformation and so forth are treated separately because they are specific types of conceptualization.

These have been explained. However, it should be understood that those material phenomena (*rūpa*) excluded from these two categories, which serve as the basis for all conventional designations, are called "conceptual constructs" (*paññatti*).

In the *Apadāna-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: “One who knows everything—divided into the past and so forth—as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand is ‘omniscient’ (*sabbaññū*).

And regarding the term “omniscient,” there are five kinds: omniscience by succession (*kama-sabbaññū*), omniscience all at once (*sakiṃ-sabbaññū*), constant omniscience (*satata-sabbaññū*), omniscience by power (*satti-sabbaññū*), and omniscience by knowledge (*ñāta-sabbaññū*).
Thus, the Omniscient One (sabbaññū) is fivefold. Therein, one who possesses the quality of knowing everything in successive order is called a *kamasabbaññū*.
One who possesses the quality of knowing the Dhamma of the Four Truths—which is to be known by a single adverting consciousness followed by a series of impulsion moments—is called a *sakiṃsabbaññū*.
One who possesses the quality of knowing the fixed objects of the eye-consciousness and so forth is called a *satatasabbaññū*. [One who knows] all at once...
The quality capable of knowing all phenomena is called "all-knowing by power" (*sattisabbaññū*).
The quality of knowing all phenomena that are to be known through the differentiation of advertence is called "all-knowing by knowledge" (*ñātasabbaññū*).
Among these, two qualities—the once-all-knowing and the all-knowing by power—are exclusively path-knowledges; the remainder are all-knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*). That is "all-knowing" (*sabbaññu*).

Regarding the term *muninda*, the meaning of the word *muni* has already been explained above. *Munīnaṃ indo* means the lord (*issara*) of the sages; thus, the grammatical connection is: "I pay homage to that Lord of Sages.
This, however, is the concise construction here: "Risen before dawn," that is, risen early; like the young sun, like a newly risen solar youth;
in the midst of the *yatīs*, the monks, [he shone] with splendors consisting of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics.

I worship with reverence through the three doors the Lord of Sages, the Buddha, who is graced by splendors and playful charm, whose face resembles the full moon and possesses a countenance like the full moon,
who is unshakable and free from craving— or rather, unmoved by the worldly conditions— and who is omniscient, knowing all phenomena.
The commentary on the fifth verse of homage is completed.
Having approached the foot of the sublime Bodhi tree,
the Sugata, having conquered Māra together with his army;
At the rising of the dawn, Abojjhi attained enlightenment;
I bow to you, the invincible Conqueror of Māra. 6.
Having thus paid homage to the Lord of Sages with the fifth verse, he now wishes to pay homage again after praising him for his quality as the Conqueror of Māra.

He recited the verse beginning with "upetapuñño. This, however, should be understood as an *upendravajrā* verse, characterized by eleven syllables due to its being joined with two heavy (*ga*) syllables following the *ja*, *ta*, and *ja* groups.
For it is stated in the *Vuttodaya*: "That same [verse] beginning with *upa* is [an *upendravajrā*] when there are *ja*, *ta*, *ja*, *ga*, *go*. Its meaning is:
in each quarter-verse there are the *jata* (jagaṇa), *jagaṇa*, and *tagaṇa* groups, followed by *jagaṇa*, *jagaṇa*, and *ga* (a heavy syllable). *Go* refers to a heavy syllable.
And if it should be so, that very verse beginning with *sāva* and *upasaddādikā*, being in the *indavajira* meter, is called a *sāgāthā*. The connection [of the verse] is as follows:

"I bow to that Sugata who, having possessed merit (*upetapuñño*) at the foot of the supreme Bodhi tree, conquered Māra together with his army, and at the breaking of dawn attained enlightenment—the unconquerable Victor over Māra.
In this context, "possessed of merit" means one who has perfected the merit of the perfections (*pāramīs*), such as generosity and virtue.

Or, one who is endowed with the merit of the perfections (pāramī) such as generosity and virtue. "Endowed" (*upeta*), "fully endowed" (*samupeta*), "approached" (*upagata*), "fully approached" (*samupagata*), "accomplished" (*sampanna*), and "endowed" (*samannāgata*)—this is the meaning. Furthermore, the etymological analysis here is as follows:

that which has arisen and, having become accomplished, goes, moves, or proceeds, is "endowed" (*upeta*); it is merit (*puñña*). The root *i* preceded by the prefix *upa* signifies going; it purifies (*punāti*).
"Merit that makes for one's own welfare": this refers to the merit of the perfections (*pāramīpuñña*). [The suffix] *ṇya* is applied to the root *pu*, which means "to nourish" or "to purify.

Its [form] is *puñña*. In this context, "making for one's own welfare" means that through repeated occurrence, it "purifies," "nourishes," and "cleanses" both the continuity of one's own mind and the continuity of material form together with its basis, by means of the diffusion of sublime forms that have been generated. This is from the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-gaṇṭhipada*.

It is called *puñña*. Alternatively, it fulfills one’s aspiration (*ajjhāsayam*), thus it is *puñña*. The root *pūr* with the suffix *ṇya*. The meaning is that it fulfills the aspiration of the person who performs merit.
Or else, it produces a state worthy of honor (*pujja*), thus it is *puñña*; this is a derivative formed from the act of producing. From the base *pūja*, the suffix *ṇya* is applied.
The meaning is that for one who performs merit (*puñña*), it brings about a state of existence worthy of honor. Therefore, it is stated in the *Sammohavinodanī* commentary:
“It purifies (*punāti*), it fulfills its performer, and it produces a desirable state of existence in accordance with his intention;
thus it is ‘merit’ (*puñño*). And in the *Mūlaṭīkā*: “‘It purifies’ means it cleanses [the mind] from the results of demerit and from suffering and defilement through an intention for welfare.”
“It is called *puñña* because it fulfills the intention of the agent by bringing that [result] to completion;
and by way of its etymological characteristic, it should be understood as *puñña* because it fills and produces what is worthy (*pujja*). Thus it is said. And in the *Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā*:

“It is *puñña* because it purifies (*punāti*) one’s own continuum, cleansing it from the fruit of demerit and from suffering and defilement; it is so called through the aspiration for welfare and happiness.”
"It is called *puñña* because it fulfills the intention of the agent by bringing that [intention] to completion; or, it is *puñña* because it generates a state worthy of honor (*pujja*).
Thus, according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*), it should be understood as *puñña* because it fills and because it generates what is worthy of honor. So it is said.
One who possesses such endowed and perfected *puñña*, which is the *puñña* of the perfections (*pāramī*), is "one possessed of endowed *puñña*" (*upetapuñña*); thus the term *sugata* is obtained.
"At the foot of the excellent Bodhi tree" means in the vicinity of the supreme Bodhi tree. In this context, "excellent" (*vara*) means that which is to be chosen, sought after, or desired.
Regarding the term "foot of the Bodhi" (*bodhimūla*): here, "Bodhi" refers to the tree, the path, omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*), and Nibbāna. For it is said:
"He attained full enlightenment for the first time at the foot of the Bodhi tree," and "between [the sitting] at the Bodhi..."
Between Gayā and Gayāsīsa, there is a tree at the place where [the Buddha] arrived; this is called "Bodhi" in the context where it refers to the knowledge of the four paths.
In the passage "He attains the Bodhi of excellent and vast wisdom," it refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*).
In the passage "Having reached the deathless, unconditioned Bodhi," Nibbāna is called "Bodhi. However, here it is the "Bodhi-tree."

This is intended. Now, this is the etymological analysis (*vacanattha*) of those terms: It is "Bodhi" (Awakening) because one awakens (*bujjhati*), has awakened (*abujjhi*), or will awaken (*bujjhissati*) to the Four Noble Truths and all knowable phenomena (*ñeyyadhamma*) therein;
thus it is the Bodhi-tree. [The suffix] *ṇi* is added to the verbal root *budh*.

It is "Bodhi" because one awakens to the Four Truths; thus it is the Path (*magga*). It is "Bodhi" because one awakens to all knowable phenomena; thus it is omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*). By the Noble One...
That which is to be awakened to is *bodhi*; Nibbāna is what is attained there. The "excellent tree of awakening" (*varabodhirukkha*) is the supreme tree;
its root and vicinity is the "root of the excellent awakening" (*varabodhimūla*), and [the phrase refers to] being in that place.

"Māra with his army" (*sasena-māra*) refers to King Māra together with his host (*senā*). In this context, *senā* is so called because it "sits" (*siyati*) or is "bound" (*bandhiyati*); the verbal root is *sidh*.

*Bandhaneyu*. Because he proceeds together with that [army], he is *sasena* (with an army); [this refers to] King Māra. Since he leads beings toward misfortune and kills them by destroying their virtues, he is *māra*.
[The suffix] *ṇa* is added to the root *mar*. Alternatively, he is *māra* because he kills (*māreti*) and destroys the wholesome qualities of beings.

He is both *sasena* (with an army) and *māra*, thus *sasenamāra*; [this refers to] King Māra. *Taṃ* (him). *Jinitvā* (having conquered) is the object (*kamma*) in this word. *Upetapuñño yo sugato* (the Sugata who is endowed with merit).
The connection [is as follows]. The meaning of the word *Sugata* has already been stated above.

"Having conquered" (*jinittvā*) means having triumphed through the power of the merit of the perfections (*pāramī-puñña*) on the full moon day of Visākha, the day of the Buddha, even before the sun had set.
"He awakened" (*abujjhī*) means he penetrated or attained. "Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) refers to supreme, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-sammā-sambodhi*).

The meaning is "the omniscient knowledge of the path to Arahatship. For the knowledge of the path has omniscient knowledge as its proximate cause (*padatthāna*), and omniscient knowledge has the knowledge of the path as its proximate cause;
this is what is called "Awakening" (*bodhi*). "That Awakening":
the word division is *aruṇodayamhi* (not *aruṇodayam hi*). The meaning is "at the time of the rising of the dawn. In that context, *ā* [is used] in the sense of "all around."
It is called *aruṇo* because it rises while making light (*ālokaṃ karonto uggacchati*). [The derivation is: from the prefix *ā-* and the root *un-*, meaning "to go," with the suffix *ṇa*.
There is a shortening of the vowel *ā*, an insertion of the letter *r*, and the change of *n* to *ṇ*. The meaning is that before the rising of the sun, that which has risen higher is named *aruṇo*.
For it is said in the *Dasaka-nipāta* of the *Aṅguttara-pāḷi*: "Monks, this is the precursor of the rising of the sun; this is..."
“Just as the dawn is the precursor and the omen of the rising sun, even so, monks, right view is the forerunner and the omen of wholesome states.
It is with reference to this that it is said in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*:

“Before the rising of the sun, there may be the dawn, which is the light still standing [in the sky]. Furthermore, in the commentary to the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*, it is stated: “Because of its reddish-brown color...”
It is said that "aruṇa" means that which goes toward the dawn. "Udeti" means it rises; thus, "udaya" refers to the sun (*sūriya*). From the verbal root *ud* comes [the suffix] *a*.
The "aruṇa" of the rising sun—that is, its upward-shooting rays—is "aruṇodaya. At that time of the rising of the dawn, there is the connection: "he awakened to enlightenment" (*bodhiṃ abojjhi*).
For the Blessed One, on the full moon day of Visākha, even before the sun had set, having shattered the host of Māra, [stood] upon his robe...
As if worshipping with the falling shoots of the Bodhi tree that resembled red coral sprouts, he recollected his past lives during the first watch of the night;

purified his divine eye during the middle watch; and during the last watch, having reflected upon dependent origination in forward and reverse order, he produced the fourth jhāna based on mindfulness of breathing, making that very state the foundation.

Having performed insight meditation known as the Great Vajira-knowledge and having increased it, when the dawn breaks, he will— by means of the knowledge of the fourth path attained through the sequence of the paths—
exhaust all defilements and penetrate, that is, realize, all the Buddha-qualities such as omniscience; this is what is meant.

"Mārajina" means one who has conquered the five Māras. He is the Sugata, the Conqueror of Māra (Mārajina), because he conquers, has conquered, and will conquer the five Māras—consisting of the son of a deva, the defilements, the aggregates of conditioned formations, and death.

The meaning is that he conquers, has conquered, and will inevitably conquer the three Māras consisting of the son of a deva, the defilements, and conditioned formations, as well as the two Māras consisting of the aggregates and death.
If this is so, why is it called "the Victorious One" (*vijitāvin*)? Because he has never failed, being victorious in every respect.
"Unbreakable" (*abhaṅga*) means incapable of being broken or destroyed by Māra together with his army, or incapable of being broken or destroyed by anyone at all.
Herein, this is the etymological meaning: because it cannot be broken by Māra or by anyone else, it is "unbreakable."
It is "unbreakable" (*abhaṅgo*) because it is not broken or destroyed by that [Māra]. The verbal root *bhanj* is preceded by the negative particle *na*.
At the end of that root, there is a substitution of the letter *g*. Alternatively, "breakable" (*bhaṅgo*) refers to that which breaks or destroys—namely, Māra or anyone else.
One for whom there is no breakable Māra or anyone else is "unbreakable" (*abhaṅgo*), the Sugata. That is the unbreakable one. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to the Sugata.
The connection [of the verse] is: "I pay homage to that Sugata, the conqueror of Māra, who is indestructible.

Furthermore, regarding this verse, the Buddha’s victory over Māra and so forth should be understood in brief according to the method found in the *Ekanipāta Jātakaṭṭhakathā* and the *Apadānaṭṭhakathā*, for the sake of the great learning of those who hear it. [Thus ends the section on] Bodhisatta.
Having experienced great prosperity and having cast aside the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch that had come into his hands as if it were a globule of spittle without regard for it,
at twenty-nine years of age, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha when the moon was conjoined with the Uttarāsāḷha constellation,
he made the Great Renunciation; then, on the bank of the Anoma River, he received from the brahmin Ghaṭīkāra the eight requisites which serve as the banner of Arahantship.
Having accepted it, put it on, and gone forth into the ascetic life, he practiced austerities for six years; then, at the foot of the Nigrodha tree in the village of Senāni,
after consuming the entire offering of milk-rice mixed with honey— worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold, served in a golden bowl,
and consisting of forty-nine mouthfuls each about the size of a single palm fruit— he ate his meal together with Sujātā, the daughter of the householder Sena.
At the time of evening, while proceeding toward the Bodhi tree along a path adorned by deities,

he accepted eight handfuls of grass given by a grass-cutter named Sotthiya; having ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and knowing that this place is the site never abandoned by all Buddhas,
the immovable site, and the site for the shattering of the defilements (kilesa), he sat down.
Taking those grasses by the tips, he shook them. At that very moment, they became a couch fourteen cubits long.
Those grasses were spread out and settled in such a form that even a most skilled painter or weaver would not be capable of painting or weaving it.
Then the Bodhisatta [placed] the Bodhi trunk behind him.
Having made this resolve, he stood facing the east with a firm mind, thinking:
"Let my skin, sinews, and bones wither away;
let every bit of flesh and blood in my body dry up."

But thinking, "I shall not break this cross-legged posture until I have attained supreme perfect enlightenment," he sat down, and that cross-legged posture—which was truly indestructible even by a hundred thunderbolts—could not be broken.
At that moment, Māra the son of a deva thought, "Siddhattha Kumāra desires to transcend my domain;
I will no longer allow him to transcend it," and [went] to the presence of the Māra-force.
Having gone there and reported this matter, he caused the proclamation known as the "Proclamation of Māra" to be made and set forth, taking the Māra-force with him.
That army of Māra extended twelve yojanas in front of him; twelve yojanas to his right and left;
it stood reaching as far behind as the edge of the world-system (cakravāḷa), and its height was nine yojanas. Of which—
From Māradēvatā’s loud shouting, the sound was heard for a thousand *yojanas*, like the sound of an earthquake.
Then Māra the son of a deity, having mounted his elephant named Girimekhala, which was one hundred and fifty *yojanas* in height, manifested a thousand arms and seized various weapons.
Among the rest of Māra’s retinue as well, two persons held the same weapon.
They did not seize him. Taking on various forms and various faces, they came swarming over the Great Being.
However, the devas of the ten thousand world-systems stood praising the Great Being. Sakka, the king of the gods, stood blowing his victory-conch, Vijayuttara;
it is said that this conch was one hundred and twenty cubits long. Once—
Having plunged into the wind and trumpeted for four months, it became silent after making its sound.
King Mahākāḷanāga stood praising him with more than a hundred verses. Great Brahmā stood holding a white parasol.
But when Māra’s forces approached the seat of enlightenment, not even one of them was able to remain standing.

They fled right there, from face to face. A nāga king named Kāḷa, having submerged into the earth, went to his own nāga abode at Mantira, five hundred yojanas away, and lay down covering his face with both hands.
Sakka, placing the Vijayuttara conch upon his back, stood at the rim of the world-system (cakravāḷa). Mahābrahmā held a white parasol at the tip [of the staff].
Having taken it, he went straight to the Brahma-world. Not even a single deity was able to remain there.
The Great Man sat all alone. Māra also said to his own retinue: "Sons, there is no other man equal to Siddhattha, the son of Suddhodana.
We will not be able to give him battle face-to-face; we must do so from behind."
“Let us give [them]. The Great Being also looked toward the three sides and saw that they were empty because all the deities had fled.
Then, seeing Māra’s army overwhelming him from the northern side, he thought:
“This great multitude exerts such immense effort directed against me, all alone; in this place, neither my mother, nor my father, nor my brother...”
"Furthermore, there is no other relative or kinsman; rather, these ten perfections alone have been like children and attendants to me for a long time.
Therefore, it is right that I take these very perfections as my shield, strike with the essence of the perfections, and destroy this army.
Thus he sat, reflecting upon the ten perfections.
Then Māra the son of a deva, thinking, "I shall drive Siddhattha away by this very means," raised up a whirlwind.
At that very moment, winds of various kinds from the east and other directions arose, shattering mountain peaks measuring half a yojana, one yojana, two yojanas, and three yojanas in size;
they uprooted forests, thickets, and trees, and [devastated] the surrounding villages and market towns.

Although they were capable of pulverizing him into dust, by the power of the Great Being’s merit and his great majesty, they were unable to move even the hem of the Bodhisatta’s robe upon reaching him.
Then, thinking, "We shall kill him by drowning him in water," she unleashed a great rain.
By its power, there arose layers upon layers of rain, consisting of hundreds and thousands of distinct strata.
Clouds arose and rained down. By the force of the torrents of rain, the earth was split asunder.
Although the great cloud approached from above the forest trees and such, it was unable to moisten even so much as a drop of dew upon the Great Being’s robe.
Thereafter, he caused a rain of stones to arise; great mountain peaks appeared, smoking and blazing.
Having come through the air, they turned into divine garlands at the feet of the Bodhisatta.
Then he raised a rain of weapons. Single-edged swords, double-edged swords, spears, javelins, and so forth, smoking and blazing, came through the air;
having reached the Bodhisatta, they became divine flowers. Then he raised a rain of embers, the color of *kiṃsuka* flowers.
Embers came through the air and, having become divine flowers, scattered at the feet of the Bodhisatta.

Then he raised up a rain of glowing embers (*kukkuḷa*). The intensely hot, fire-colored embers came through the air and fell at the feet of the Bodhisatta, having become divine sandalwood powder. Then he raised up a rain of sand. It was exceedingly fine sand.
Smoking and blazing, they came through the air and fell at the feet of the Bodhisatta, becoming divine flowers.

Then he raised up a mass of mud-like water. That mud-like water, smoking and blazing, came through the air and fell at the feet of the Bodhisatta, becoming divine unguent. Then, having terrified Siddhattha with this—
Thinking, "I shall drive him away," he raised up darkness. That great gloom, possessing the four factors, reached the Bodhisatta and vanished like the light of the sun when it is struck down.
Thus did Māra [attempt to overcome him] with these nine showers of wind, rain, stones, blows, glowing embers, hot ashes, sand, mud, and darkness.
Failing to frighten the Bodhisatta away, he commanded his retinue, saying, "Hey! What are you waiting for? Seize this Prince Siddhattha!

Kill him! Drive him away! Then, sitting upon the back of the elephant Girimekhala and taking up his discus-weapon, he himself approached the Bodhisatta and said, "Siddhattha, rise from this cross-legged seat!"
"This does not belong to you; it belongs to me alone," he said. Having heard his words, the Great Being replied:
"Māra, neither have the ten perfections been fulfilled by you, nor the secondary perfections, nor the ultimate perfections;
neither have the five great renunciations been relinquished, nor the conduct for the benefit of relatives, nor the conduct for the benefit of the world, nor the conduct for the sake of Buddhahood."
“All these have been fulfilled; they were all fulfilled by me alone. Therefore, this couch does not belong to you; it belongs to me alone.
Enraged and unable to withstand the force of his anger, Māra discharged his discus-weapon (*cakrāyudha*) at the Great Being.
As the Great Being was reflecting upon his ten perfections (*pāramitā*), it stood above him, becoming a canopy of garlands. Indeed, it is said that...
Previously, when he was angry, he had released his weapon, the Khuracakka, which went along cutting through solid stone pillars as if they were bamboo canes.
But now, while that [wheel] stood there as a floral canopy, the rest of Māra’s retinue, thinking,
"Now he will rise from his cross-legged seat and flee," hurled down massive mountain peaks.
As the Great Being was reflecting upon those perfections (*pāramitā*), they turned into flower garlands and fell to the ground.

Deities standing at the rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-mukhavaṭṭi*) craned their necks and lifted their heads, watching and thinking, "Alas, the Prince Siddhattha’s body, which has reached the pinnacle of beauty, is lost! What indeed will he do?"

Then the Great Being said to Māra, who stood there having remarked, "The throne-seat reached on the day of the full awakening of Bodhisattvas who have fulfilled the perfections shall come to me alone," "Māra, who is your witness that you have ever given a gift?
Māra replied, "So many people are my witnesses," and extended his hand toward the Māra-host. At that moment, from the assembly of Māra—
The sound that arose, “I am the witness! I am the witness! was like the roar of an earthquake.
Then Māra said to the Great Being, “Siddhattha, who is the witness to the fact that you have given this gift?
The Great Being replied, “As for your gift, sentient beings are indeed witnesses; but as for my gift here, there is no sentient being—”
“There is no witness whatsoever. Let alone the gifts I gave in my remaining existences;
as for the fact that I gave the great seven-times-sevenfold alms-offering while dwelling in the Vessantara existence—even the great earth, though insentient, is my witness.
Having said this, he drew his right hand out from within his robe and [said], “In the Vessantara existence, my...”

When he extended his hand toward the great earth, saying, "Are you a witness, or are you not a witness, to the giving of the seven-times-seven great gifts? the great earth roared with a thousand cries,
a hundred thousand cries, as if trampling the host of Māra, declaring, "I am a witness to your gift!"

Then, as he contemplated the Great Gift given by the Great Being, Siddhattha—the supreme gift known as the Vessantara-gift—the elephant Girimekhala, who was one hundred and fifty yojanas in height, knelt upon his knees. The host of Māra fled in all directions;
there were none who went along the same path. Their head-ornaments and their clothing-ornaments...
Abandoning their positions face-to-face, they fled in every direction and intermediate quarter.
Then, seeing the host of Māra fleeing, the assembly of gods realized that Māra had been defeated and that Prince Siddhattha had won.

Thinking, "We shall perform a victory offering," the nāgas sent word to the nāgas, the supaṇṇas to the supaṇṇas, the deities to the deities, and the Brahmās to the Brahmās, [sending] perfumes, garlands, and so forth.
The hands came into the presence of the Great Being at the seat of enlightenment. And when they had thus arrived—
“This is indeed victory for the Glorious Buddha,
and defeat for Māra the Evil One;”
Then, on the seat of enlightenment, the hosts of nāgas, filled with joy,
proclaimed victory to the Great Sage:
"This is indeed the victory of the glorious Buddha!"
And there was the defeat of Māra the Evil One.
Delighted, the hosts of Supaṇṇas then proclaimed victory for the Great Seer at the seat of enlightenment.
"Victory indeed belongs to the Blessed Buddha,
and defeat to Māra the Evil One!
Thus did they cry out in jubilation upon the seat of enlightenment.
Then the hosts of gods rejoiced in the Great Sage.
For this is indeed the victory of the glorious Buddha and the defeat of Māra, the Evil One.
“Then, on the seat of awakening, the hosts of Brahmas, filled with joy,
also proclaimed victory for the Tathāgata.
In the remaining ten thousand world-systems, the deities, honoring him with garlands, perfumes, and ointments, [uttered] various kinds of...

And they stood praising him. Thus, even before the sun had set, the Great Being, having shattered the army of Māra, was honored by the sprouts of the Bodhi tree—which fell upon his robes—as if with shoots of red coral.
Having recollected his previous births during the first watch of the night, and having purified his divine eye during the middle watch, he [attained] dependent origination during the last watch.
He applied his knowledge to the simultaneous arising [of phenomena].

Then, as he contemplated the twelvefold formula of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, according to its progression and regression, the ten-thousandfold world system, bounded by the waters, shook twelve times.
Having caused the ten-thousandfold world system to resound, the Great Being, at the time of sunrise—
It is said that he penetrated the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*). Here, however, one should understand what remains unsaid by looking back at those [other passages].

This, then, is the summary of the construction here: He who is "endowed with merit" (*upetapuñño*), meaning possessed of the merit of the perfections such as giving (*dānādipāramīpuñña*) or perfected through the merit of the perfections such as giving;
he who is the "Sugata," near the root of the supreme Bodhi tree—that is, in the vicinity of the most excellent tree of enlightenment—[conquered] Māra together with his army...
Having conquered the King of Māra who had advanced with his army, and having triumphed through the power of the merit of the perfections (pāramī),
at the time of sunrise on the full moon day of Visākha— during the rising of the dawn— he awakened to, penetrated,
and attained the Bodhi known as the knowledge of the path to Arahatship and the knowledge of omniscience; he was the conqueror of Māra, victorious over the five Māras, and unshakable.
"I bow to that Sugata whom no Māra, even with his army, is able to overcome.
The commentary on the sixth verse of homage is complete.
[He who wields] the stainless sword of knowledge that cuts away passion and the rest...
I pay homage to him who has grasped the fruit known as "Satī," who is adorned with the ornament of the flood of virtue,
and who is endowed with the supreme supernormal powers of direct knowledge.

7. Having thus paid homage to the Sugata with the sixth verse, and now desiring to pay homage after praising him by means of the four qualities beginning with the knowledge of the path to Arahatship, he spoke the verse beginning with "Rāgāditya.

This, however, should be understood as an *upajāti* verse characterized by eleven syllables, because it is a mixture of the characteristics of the two verses *indravajrā* and *upendravajrā*. For it has been said:
In the *Vuttodaya*, it is said: “If the feet possess the characteristics just mentioned and are mixed, they are *upajātis*.

The meaning of this is as follows: if, in a particular meter (*vutti*), the feet possess the characteristics just mentioned—that is, those stated in the immediately preceding [section] regarding the *indravajrā*, *upendravajrā*, and *vajrāgāthā*—and if these feet are mixed or combined, then those meters are called *upajātis*.
In that context, regarding the phrase "the stainless sword of knowledge that cuts off lust and the rest" (*rāgādicchedāmalañāṇakhagga*):

here, the word division is *rāgādiccheda-amala-ñāṇa-khagga*. The meaning is: the sword consisting of the knowledge of the path of Arahatship, which cuts off the defilements such as lust and is free from stain.

Herein, this is the etymological analysis: it is called *rāga* because one is colored by (*rañjati*) forms and so forth; from the verbal root *ranj*, meaning "to color," with the suffix *ṇa*. Those things of which lust is the first are [called] *rāgādi*.
Lust and so forth are the defilements (*kilesa*). That which cuts these is the "cutting of lust and so forth," namely, the knowledge of the path of arahantship.

It stains and maintains what is wretched; thus it is "stain" (*mala*), referring to lust and so forth. Alternatively, that by which one is stained and defiled is "stain. The verbal root *mal* means to defile.
That which is devoid of stain is "stainless" (*amala*), namely, knowledge. One who knows and penetrates the four truths is "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*), namely, the knowledge of the path of arahantship.
It is "the stainless knowledge that cuts off lust and the rest" (*rāgādichedāmalañāṇa*); it is called *khagga* because it "cuts" (*khagga-ti*) trees and such things, according to its primary meaning.
Or, it is *khagga* because it is "like a sword" (*khagga-viya*); thus, it is knowledge.

He who possesses this sword, which is designated as the stainless knowledge that cuts off lust and the rest, is "the Buddha who wields the sword of the stainless knowledge that cuts off lust and the rest. By cutting off the defilements of lust and so forth, he is free from stain...
The meaning is: "endowed with the sword" which is designated as the knowledge of the supreme path (*aggamaggañāṇa*).
Regarding the phrase *satisamaññā phalakābhigāhī*: here the word division is *satisamaññā-phalaka-abhigāhī*. The meaning is: "one who firmly grasps the shield named Right Mindfulness.
Herein, this is the etymological analysis (*vacanattha*): mindfulness (*sati*) is so called because it remembers (*sarati*) the associated mental states.
*Sati* means that which comes toward [an object] or that which remembers; it is derived from the root *sar*. Alternatively, *sati* is that which remembers or destroys negligence;

thus it is "right mindfulness" (*sammāsati*). The root *sar* indeed signifies destruction. It is called *samaññā* because one rightly understands by means of it. "Mindfulness" (*sati*) is the conventional designation (*samaññā*), hence "the designation 'mindfulness'" (*satisamaññā*).

A *phalaka* is a shield; it is so called because it strikes or wards off weapons such as swords. The root *phal* is used in the sense of warding off, with the suffix *ṇvu*. [This refers to] the designation "mindfulness."
"He grasps the shield firmly" means he grasps the fruit of mindfulness; thus, "the Buddha is attained.

For just as a shield protects the weapons of an army, such as swords and the like, so too does the restraint of mindfulness protect by not allowing objects such as forms to enter through the doors of the eye and so forth.
Therefore, the Blessed One is the possessor of the dharma of mindfulness, because he is the protector against all unwholesome states and [the source] of all wholesome states.
Because it is beneficial to all phenomena and because it accomplishes all goals, it is said that one grasps the shield of mindfulness firmly.
For it has been said: "Whatever wholesome states there may be, they all have heedfulness as their root, they converge upon heedfulness;
heedfulness is declared to be the foremost of those states. And: "Monks, I declare mindfulness to be beneficial in every respect."
*Sīloghalankāravibhūsitaṃ*: the word division is *sīla-ogha-alaṅkāra-vibhūsitaṃ*. The meaning is:
"adorned with the ornament consisting of the collection of those whose virtue is purified. In that context, *sīla* refers to supramundane virtue (*lokuttara-sīla*).

Its meaning has already been explained above. Furthermore, that [virtue] consists of: volitional virtue (*cetanā-sīla*), mental-factor virtue (*cetasika-sīla*), restraint virtue (*saṃvara-sīla*), and non-transgression (*avītikkama*).

And "virtue" (sīla) is fourfold. Therein, virtue as volition (cetanā-sīla) is the volition of one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth, or of one who fulfills the performance of duties.
Virtue as mental concomitant (cetasika-sīla) is the abstinence (virati) of one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth.
Regarding "virtue as restraint" (saṃvara-sīla), here "restraint" refers to the restraint of the Pātimokkha, the restraint of mindfulness, and the restraint of knowledge.
It is fivefold: restraint through patience and restraint through energy; all of this is called virtue as restraint (*saṃvara-sīla*).
Virtue as non-transgression (*avītikkama-sīla*) is the non-transgression of body and speech by one who has undertaken the precepts. For this is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "What is virtue?
Volition is virtue, mental concomitants are virtue, restraint is virtue, and non-transgression is virtue. Here...
However, non-transgression is not what is intended here by "virtue" (sīla). Why? Because there is no undertaking of training precepts (sikkhāpada) for the Blessed One.
For indeed, there are no so-called training precepts for the Buddhas. "Flood" (ogha) means a collection; the word *ogha* denotes a multitude.
Thus it is said in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*:
“*Samūha*, *gaṇa*, *saṅghāta*, *samudāya*, and *sañcaya*;
*sandoha*, *nivaha*, *ogha*, *visara*, *nikara*, and *caya*,” and so forth.

It is called *ogha* (flood/mass) because it carries (*avahana*)—that is, goes (*gacchati*) or proceeds (*pavattati*)—and because its constituent parts (*avayava*) enter (*eti*) therein. The verbal root *hana* preceded by the prefix *ava* signifies motion (*gatimhi*).

No. By rule, *hanassa gho*: [the *h* of *ogha* becomes *gh*]. However, in the *Abhidhānappadīpikāṭīkā*, it is stated: "It is called *ogha* because, having become a constituent part (*avayava*), it flows through (*byāpiyati*) and pervades.
An *ogha* of virtues—that is, a collection—is a "flood of virtue" (*sīlogha*). "Adornment" (*alaṅkāra*) means that which is worn as an ornament.

It is called *alaṅkāra* because by means of it, one makes a person possessed of it beautiful (*alaṃ vibhusaṃ... karoti*). This refers to virtue (*sīla*). It is a verbal root (*karadhātu*) with the prefix *alam*.
No. "The flood of virtue itself is the ornament; thus, it is the 'ornament of the flood of virtue.

One who is adorned by that is 'adorned with the ornament of the flood of virtue,' namely, the Buddha. He is adorned by that extraordinary, supramundane ornament of virtue, which is not shared by others.

The meaning is that he is not adorned by ornaments such as robes and the like. For there is indeed no ornament equal to the ornament of virtue. That is what is meant by 'adorned with the ornament of the flood of virtue.'"
Regarding the phrase *namāmibhiññāvaramiddhupetaṃ*: here the word-division is *namāmi abhiññāvaraṃ iddhi upetaṃ*.
In that context, *namāmi* means "I pay homage. *Abhiññāvaramiddhupetaṃ* means "endowed with the supreme psychic power (*iddhi*) known as the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).

That which knows in a pre-eminent way (*abhivisesena*) is called *abhiññā*; it is sixfold knowledge. For that [knowledge] consists of the various kinds of psychic power (*iddhividha*), the divine ear (*dibbasota*), and so forth.

It is sixfold by way of the knowledge of the minds of others, the recollection of past lives, the knowledge of passing away and rebirth, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*).

Among these, "knowledge of the various kinds of supernormal power" (*iddhividhañāṇa*) is the knowledge that knows the exercise of supernormal powers occurring in such a manner as, "being one, he becomes many," and so forth.
"Knowledge of the divine ear" (*dibbasotañāṇa*) is [the knowledge] of the divine ear-element which has as its object sounds distinguished by being distant, near, and so on.
Knowledge of knowing. Knowledge of discerning the minds of others is the knowledge that discerns the mental boundaries of other beings.

Knowledge of recollecting past lives is the knowledge associated with mindfulness that recollects the aggregates and so forth in previous past existences, both by way of their occurrence within one's own continuum and by way of the dwelling place [of those lives]. Knowledge of passing away and rebirth...

It is the knowledge that knows the passing away and rebirth of beings. And here, because it establishes the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth (*cutūpapāta-ñāṇa*) in the commentaries, it is called the "divine eye knowledge" (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*).
"Knowledge of the destruction of the taints" (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*) is the knowledge that discerns the Truths;
it is the knowledge of the path of Arahantship. "Excellent" (*vara*) means supreme. "Success" (*iddhi*) means succeeding, achieving. It succeeds...

Or, *iddhi* means "it succeeds. The root is *idh*.
