One who is endowed with, fully endowed with, and possessed of the excellent *iddhi* known as the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) is "endowed with the excellent *iddhi* of the higher knowledges" (*abhiññāvaramiddhupeto*), namely, the Buddha. "I bow to that Buddha who is endowed with the excellent *iddhi* of the higher knowledges"—this is the grammatical connection.

This, however, is the concise interpretation here: he who wields the sword of stainless knowledge that cuts through lust and the other defilements—that is, the knowledge of the path to Arahatship characterized by being free from stain—and who firmly grasps the shield known as right mindfulness, which is designated by the name "mindfulness" and is equipped with the blade of mindfulness;
and who is adorned with the ornament of the flood of virtue, meaning the collection of moral precepts.

"I bow down to that Buddha who is adorned with ornaments, and who is endowed with supreme and excellent psychic powers— that is, possessed of, fully equipped with, and endowed with the highest, most excellent power known as the higher knowledges (abhiññā).
The commentary on the seventh verse of homage is complete.
To the abode of compassion, who performs what is difficult in every way,
who has reached the path for crossing the ocean of existence,
the Lord of the Three Worlds, well-composed and beneficial—
I bow to him who possesses the all-seeing eye. 8.

Having thus paid homage to the Buddha with the seventh verse, he now speaks the verse beginning with "Dayālayanti" (The abode of compassion), desiring to pay homage after praising him with nine qualities, foremost among which is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
This [verse], moreover, consists of twelve syllables because it is composed of *ja*, *ta*, and *ja* gaṇas.
It should be understood that the *vaṃsaṭṭha* verses consist of four-footed yamakas. For it is said in the *Vuttodaya*:
"The sages say this is *vaṃsaṭṭha* when there is *jatā*, *jatagaṇas*, and *jarā*, *jaragaṇas*. The meaning of this is:

in whichever verse each quarter contains *jatā* (the *jatabandha* meter), *jatagaṇas*, and *jarā* (the *jarabandha* meter), *jaragaṇas*, the wise ones—the seers—call this the stated *vaṃsaṭṭha*, namely, a *vaṃsaṭṭha* verse.

In this context, "abode of compassion" (*dayālaya*) refers to the basis for both great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and loving-kindness (*mettā*). For the word "compassion" (*dayā*) applies to both compassion and loving-kindness.

In the phrase "one who has become devoid of compassion" (*adayāpanna*), it applies to compassion; the meaning is "one who has fallen into a state of pitilessness. In the phrase "one who has become compassionate" (*dayāpanna*), it applies to loving-kindness;
the meaning is "one who has attained a mind of loving-kindness. However, here [in the present case], it refers to both of these.

It is appropriate. Therefore, the grammatical reduction (*ekasesa*) should be made as *dayā ca dayā ca dayā*, based on the similarity of the sounds. Furthermore, the meaning of the word here should be understood as follows:

it is called *dayā* (compassion) because it "protects" (*dayati*)—that is, it does not harm—the compassionate one; thus, it is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). For the verbal root *day* signifies "to harm," with the suffix *a*.
That which is compassion, as long as it has not reached the accomplishment of another's welfare as intended, [remains] the compassionate one.
The meaning is "it harms. Alternatively, *dayā* is so called because it protects (*dayati*), harms, or removes the suffering of others.

Or else, *dayā* is that by which the virtuous person protects (*dayati*)—that is, undergoes hardship even while abandoning their own happiness. Or again, *dayā* is that by which one protects (*dayati*), that is, shows favor, even toward wicked people.
Or, *dayā* is that by which Bodhisattvas protect (*dayanti*), that is, grasp after, perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). Thus, [it is] the Bodhisattvas...
The meaning is that, at the time of making the resolution for the state of Buddhahood, even though the supreme fruit was already in their hands, they cast it aside; out of great compassion,
desiring to rescue sentient beings from the ocean of *saṃsāra*, they accepted the immense suffering of *saṃsāra*— which brings no relief— and, in their final existence,
simultaneously attained the deathless element (*amata-dhātu*) and the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) adorned with manifold virtues.
*Dayā* (compassion) is so called because it gives (*dayati*) or bestows (*dadāti*) fearlessness upon beings; thus it is *mettā*. The verbal root *day* signifies giving.
It is *dayā* because it proceeds equally toward all beings without making distinctions, moving through them.

Just as water pervades all beings with its coolness and washes away dust and impurities, even so does *mettā* proceed without making distinctions between those who are evil and those who are virtuous.
The meaning is that it proceeds evenly.
Another method: they protect and guard beings by means of this, or it itself is compassionate, or its very nature is compassion;

thus it is *dayā*. Here, *karuṇā* (compassion) and *mettā* (loving-kindness) are obtained. It is called *dayālayo* because one rests (*ālayati*) or is established (*patiṭṭhati*) therein by means of that.

"Buddha. For the Blessed One remains constant and equal toward hostile beings such as Devadatta, as well as toward non-hostile beings and his own son Rāhula, by virtue of his benevolent intention, great compassion, and loving-kindness;
therefore, it is said that he is praised as "the abode of mercy. Indeed, this is stated in the Apadāna Pāḷi:
“Toward Vadhaka, Devadatta, the thief Aṅgulimāla, Dhanapāla, and Rāhula, the Great Sage was even-minded. Regarding the phrase “everywhere”:
it means in every single personal existence (*attabhāva*). That is, from the time he first made the aspiration for Buddhahood, throughout all his existences.
The meaning is as follows: "Difficult to perform" (*dukkara*) means that which must be done with hardship;
the task consisting of the five great renunciations (*pañcamahāpariccāga*) and so forth is what is meant by "difficult to perform.

In this context, the "five great renunciations" are fivefold: the renunciation of wealth, the renunciation of limbs, the renunciation of children, the renunciation of a wife, and the renunciation of life.

Therein, the relinquishing of animate wealth such as elephants, horses, female and male slaves, and so forth, or of inanimate wealth such as pearls, gems, silver, and so forth, is called the relinquishing of wealth (*dhanapariccāga*).
The relinquishing of one’s own limbs, such as hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose, and so forth, is called the relinquishing of limbs (*aṅgapariccāga*).
And the relinquishing of one’s son and daughter is called the relinquishing of children (*puttapariccāga*).
The relinquishing of a wife is called the "relinquishing of a wife. The relinquishing of the body, which is bound up with the life-faculty, is called the "relinquishing of life.

Although the relinquishing of wealth and so forth are already included within the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), they are nevertheless described here by way of "great relinquishings" in order to demonstrate their specific nature as acts of relinquishment and to show that they are extremely difficult to perform.
The intended meaning is that they are performed separately. However, in the *Mahāpadānasutta-ṭīkā*, it says:
“The five great renunciations are: the renunciation of limbs, the renunciation of eyes, the renunciation of self, the renunciation of kingdom, and the renunciation of wife and children.

Although, among these, the renunciation of limbs and so forth are indeed themselves the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*), nevertheless, [they are listed separately] for the purpose of showing the specific distinctions among types of renunciation.”
"The separate mention of the great renunciations (*mahāpariccāga*) is for the purpose of showing their extreme difficulty.

For that very reason, the renunciation of the eyes is mentioned separately even from the renunciation of the limbs. Furthermore, although there is a commonality in the nature of renunciation, the renunciation of kingdom and the renunciation of wife and children are mentioned separately," so it has been said.
That [renunciation] is difficult to perform. But this [act] they "do"—this is the verb (*kammapada*). They "do" means "performing."
He acts, thus he is a *kara*; [this refers to] the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "the path for crossing the ocean of existence" (*bhavaṇṇavātikkamamagga*): here, the word division is *bhava-aṇṇava-atikkamaṃ agga-taṃ*.

"Crossing the ocean of existence" means having crossed over the ocean—the sea—consisting of the realms of sense-desire, form, and formlessness. It is called "existence" (*bhava*) because beings (*sattā*) exist therein.
"Water" (aṇṇa) is what is called water. That which has this [water] is "watery" (aṇṇavā), namely, the ocean.
Since the ocean is a "watery expanse" (aṇṇavā) defined as existence (bhava), it is the "great ocean of existence" (bhavaṇṇavā).

Just as [the ocean] is beset by many dangers such as the force of waves, so too the threefold existence is beset by many fears of suffering such as birth, aging, and death; therefore, it is called the "ocean of existence. One has transcended that.
"Crossed over" means having transcended the ocean of existence; thus he is the Buddha.

For just as water flows and streams without interruption in the great mass of water that is the deep ocean, so too, within this saṃsāra comprised of the three realms of existence, the rebirth-linkings and deaths continue without interruption.
By means of the knowledge of the path to Arahantship at the seat of enlightenment, [the Buddha] [overcame] the one thousand five hundred defilements that produce these [rebirths].
Because he has utterly destroyed [rebirth], there is no further becoming in the three realms of existence.
Therefore, it is said that he is worthy of praise as one who transcends the ocean of existence (*bhavaṇṇava*). "That transcendence of the ocean of existence" refers to this.

"The state of being supreme" (*agga*) means the quality of being the most excellent among all sentient beings. Furthermore, in this context, the word *agga* [is used] in the senses of beginning, peak, portion, and excellence.
It is seen [in various senses]. For instance, it is seen at the beginning in such passages as, “Thus, from this day forward, I have gone for refuge for as long as life lasts.

It is seen at the tip in such passages as, “One might touch that very tip with that same finger-tip. It is seen in the sense of a portion in such passages as, “I allow you, monks, to divide [the property] by the dwelling or by the courtyard.
It is seen in the sense of the best in such passages as, “I am the foremost in the world.”
Even here, he should be understood as that very same person. He is called *agga* (the foremost) because he goes to (*ajati*) the state of being the best among gods and humans;
the meaning is that he is named the "foremost" and "best" in the sense of being peerless, in the sense of having distinguished qualities, and in the sense of being equal to the unequaled.

Alternatively, it is because his appearance is difficult to encounter, because he possesses a marvelous human nature, because he brings welfare and happiness to many people, and because he is without second or without equal.
And the meaning is that the Blessed One is the foremost and most excellent in the world. For it is said in the Aṅguttara Nikāya:
“Bhikkhus, as far as there are beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed—the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them.
The state of being foremost is *aggatā*. That, moreover, is the object of the verb *gata* (gone). *Gata* means attained; the sense is “having reached.”
*Tilokanātha* means the refuge for the three worlds, which are comprised of the realms of sense-desire (*kāma*), form (*rūpa*), and formlessness (*arūpa*).
Furthermore, the meaning of the word *loka* has already been explained above. The three worlds are *tiloka*. As for the word *nātha*, it is twofold:
derivative (*nipphanna*) and non-derivative (*anipphanna*). Among these, the non-derivative word *nātha* signifies "refuge" by way of conventional designation (*saṅketa*). Likewise...
For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "The conventional expression is true; it is the cause of worldly designation.

The Lord of the Three Worlds (*tilokanātha*) is the Buddha. He is the one who, through his consummate mastery of application—characterized by the prevention of all that is harmful, preceded by which he is intent upon the provision of welfare and happiness in its entirety—and through his unsurpassed service to the generation consisting of gods and humans, as well as his possession of immeasurable, incomparable, and distinguished qualities of power, is the refuge of the three worlds.
And the Blessed One, the supreme among all beings, is the name for the sole refuge of immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems;

such is the meaning. Furthermore, the word *nātha* (protector) is used in four senses: in the sense of requesting, in the sense of afflicting, in the sense of sovereignty, and in the sense of aspiration.

Among these, in the sense of requesting: he requests (*nāthati*) or asks (*yācati*), thus he is the *nātha*, the Buddha. The verbal root *nāth* [takes] the suffix *a*. He [the Buddha], moreover, [protects] the beings who are to be disciplined...

The meaning is that he enjoins others even after requesting them to act for their own benefit. Alternatively, by saying, "It is good, monks, that a bhikkhu should from time to time reflect upon his own excellence," and so forth, the Blessed One—being impelled by compassion—enjoins beings to practice various beneficial courses of action even after requesting them to do so.
Therefore, the meaning is that he is called the "Protector" (Nātha). Regarding *upatāpe*:
He is called *nātha* because he rules over (*nāthati*) the defilements residing in those who are to be disciplined (*veneyya*) and consumes them; thus, he is the Buddha.

The meaning is that through his teaching of the Dhamma, he causes the destruction of the defilements within the mental continuums of those to be disciplined. Furthermore, he is called *nātha* because he rules (*nāthati*) or exercises sovereignty (*issariyati*) over beings in terms of lordship.
The meaning is that the Blessed One, endowed with supreme mastery of mind, rules over all beings and overcomes them by means of the Dhamma.
One who desires blessings (*āsīsā*) is called a *nātha*; the meaning is that he seeks the welfare and happiness of those to be trained (*veneyya*) through the newness of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
A *tilokanātha* is a lord of the three worlds; [this refers to] the Buddha.
"Well-composed" (*susamāhita*) means possessing beautiful concentration because of being unshakable by the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) such as gain and loss. *Saṃsamaṃ*.

It is *samādhi* because by means of it one places (*ādhiyati*) the associated mental states upon a single object. The root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *saṃ* becomes *i*. A beautiful or praised concentration is *susamādhi*. One who possesses that is *susamāhito*, namely the Buddha. The suffix *-to* is used here in the sense of possession, as in words such as *pabbato* (mountain). [Just as] the great Mount Meru remains unshaken by winds coming from the four directions, so too is he. The root *dhā* with the prefix *saṃ* becomes *i*. A beautiful or praised concentration is *susamādhi*. One who possesses that is *susamāhito*, namely the Buddha. The suffix *-to* is used here in the sense of possession, as in words such as *pabbato* (mountain). [Just as] the great Mount Meru remains unshaken by winds coming from the four directions, so too is he. The root *dhā* with the prefix *saṃ* becomes *i*. A beautiful or praised concentration is *susamādhi*. One who possesses that is *susamāhito*, namely the Buddha. The suffix *-to* is used here in the sense of possession, as in words such as *pabbato* (mountain). [Just as] the great Mount Meru remains unshaken by winds coming from the four directions, so too is he. The root *dhā* with the prefix *saṃ* becomes *i*. A beautiful or praised concentration is *susamādhi*. One who possesses that is *susamāhito*, namely the Buddha. The suffix *-to* is used here in the sense of possession, as in words such as *pabbato* (mountain). The meaning is that the Blessed One is endowed with a concentration that remains unshaken by worldly conditions such as gain and loss, as well as by the winds of false views.
That is "well-concentrated" (*susamāhita*). "Beneficial" (*hita*) means bearing the welfare of all beings, including humans, devas, and brahmas; it is in accordance with the cause.
It is called *hita* because it leads (*hinoti*) or proceeds; it is the purpose (*payojana*). The root *hi* belongs to the sense of going. That which sustains (*dhāreti*) that [purpose] is *hito*;

this is a compound ending in a primary suffix (*kitanta*). While one might say "bearer of the beneficial" (*hitadharo*), the word *hito* is used by eliding the latter member for the sake of metrical prosody (*chandānurakkhaṇatthāya*), just as one says "lamp-stand" (*padīpo*) for "lamp-holder" (*samajjanī*).
Alternatively, it is *hita* because it destroys (*hiṃsati*) suffering; the root is *hiṃs*.

This is the etymological derivation (*tapaccaya*) for *hita*. Just as a medicine that counteracts a disease is called "beneficial" (*hita*) for those who are ill, so too it is called "beneficial" because it destroys suffering.
Alternatively, it is "beneficial" because it bestows happiness (*sukhaṃ vidadhāti*). The verbal root *dhā* signifies "to hold" (*dhāraṇe*).
Just as a nutrient that increases the elements such as blood and flesh is called "beneficial" for those seeking health, so too it is "beneficial" because it conveys happiness.
It is so called. He bears that purpose, thus he is "beneficent" (*hita*), the Buddha.

Furthermore, by means of his teaching of the Dhamma, he removes suffering from those susceptible to training and brings their wisdom to maturity; thus it is said that he "bears" worldly and supramundane welfare and happiness.
That is "benefit" (*hita*). Regarding the term "all-seeing eye" (*samantacakkhu*): here, "eye" refers to the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the knowledge-eye, and the all-seeing eye.
The divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) is fivefold. Among these, "Bhikkhus, with the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakkhu*) I surveyed the world" refers to what is called the Buddha-eye.
"The dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye (*dhammacakkhu*)" refers to the Dhamma-eye consisting of the lower paths.
"The eye arose" refers to the knowledge-eye (*ñāṇacakkhu*).
"Samantacakkhu" is said to mean "omniscient knowledge"—this is what is meant by "Samantacakkhu.
"I saw, monks, with the purified divine eye"—this is what is meant by "dibbacakkhu" (the divine eye). However, in this context, it is "Samantacakkhu" that is intended.
The meaning is: one who sees all knowable phenomena all around, being possessed of omniscient knowledge.
Now, this is the etymological explanation here: it is called *samantacakkhu* because it sees (*cakkhati*) all knowable phenomena (*sabbañeyyadhamma*) on every side (*samantato*).

It is the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutañāṇa*). [The root] *cakṣ* is the element of seeing. Thus it is said in the *Mahāniddesa* commentary: "The 'all-seeing eye' (*samantacakkhu*) is called the knowledge of omniscience.
One who possesses the all-seeing eye is "possessed of the all-seeing eye" (*samantacakkhu*), namely, the Buddha. For this has been stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*:
“There is nothing here that he has not seen,
nor anything unknown or yet to be known;
he has directly realized all that is to be understood.”
"The Tathāgata is therefore all-seeing.
This is its meaning: for that Tathāgata, there is no kind of phenomenon (*dhammajāta*) in this world that is unseen or unperceived;
nor is there any kind of phenomenon that is unknown, unrecognized, obscure, or not to be known. It is to be understood.
Whatever category of phenomena exists that is to be known, all those categories of phenomena the Tathāgata has directly known and penetrated.
Therefore, for that reason, the Tathāgata is named "the All-Seeing One" (*samantacakkhu*). That is the All-Seeing One.
Regarding the phrase "I bow to that Immeasurable One" (*paṇamāmi taṃmitaṃ*), the word division here is *paṇamāmi taṃ amitaṃ*. To that immeasurable Buddha, I—

The connection is with the word "I bow" (*paṇamāmi*). In that context, "immeasurable" (*amita*) means either immeasurable by knowledge—that is, not delimited by knowledge—or possessing qualities such as virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
Alternatively, it is "immeasurable" (*amita*) because it is that which should be measured, yet cannot be delimited by knowledge;

that is, the quality of virtue and so forth. The verbal root *mā* preceded by the prefix *na-* signifies measure. That which possesses this [quality] is "immeasurable" (*amita*), namely, the Buddha. For example, as in the great ocean...

It is not easy to calculate the measure of that water, saying, "there are this many *āḷhaka*s of water," or "there are this many hundreds of *āḷhaka*s of water," or "there are this many thousands of *āḷhaka*s of water," or "there are this many hundreds of thousands of *āḷhaka*s of water.
Rather, it is reckoned simply as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of water; even so, for a Buddha...

It is not easy to calculate the measure of one’s qualities such as virtue, thinking, "The quality of virtue is this much, the quality of concentration is that much, the quality of wisdom is so much," and so forth.
Rather, it is reckoned simply as a great mass of qualities that is incalculable and immeasurable.
Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna Pāḷi:
“Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of another Buddha for an entire eon,
without speaking of anything else,
that eon would be exhausted within its long duration.”
"And the praise of the Tathāgatas would not be exhausted. And:
"The names of the Great Seer are incalculable according to his qualities;
even from a thousand names, his name could not be fully enumerated by its qualities."
"By this he praises the Buddha as 'Immeasurable' (amita).
This, moreover, is the concise explanation here: [He praises him] as the abode of compassion, the foundation of great mercy and loving-kindness;
performing—while in every way, throughout every existence—the difficult deeds that must be accomplished with hardship, such as the five great renunciations and so forth.
One who has transcended the ocean of existence—that which is known as the three realms of being; one who has attained the pinnacle, the state of supremacy among all beings;
the Lord of the Three Worlds, the refuge for the triple world consisting of the realms of desire, form, and formlessness; one who is perfectly composed, possessing sublime concentration;
and one who is beneficial, maintaining the welfare of all beings through both mundane and supramundane means.
"I bow down to— that is, I pay homage to— that Buddha who possesses the all-seeing eye that perceives all knowable phenomena on every side,
who possesses the knowledge of omniscience, and who possesses immeasurable and boundless qualities such as virtue (sīla) and the rest.
The commentary on the eighth verse of praise is complete.
In each and every place, he accumulated a mass of perfections;
wherever he went, he followed the path trodden by the virtuous that leads to the state of happiness—
the existence that is the source of bliss for both gods and men.

Having thus paid homage to the Buddha with the eighth verse, now, desiring to pay homage after praising him with the five qualities beginning with "the one who accumulates the collection of perfections" (*pāramisañcaya*),
he spoke here and there the verses beginning with *pāramisañcaya-cayantī*. This, however—

Because it is composed of groups of *jata* and *jarā*, and is characterized by twelve syllables with *yamaka* (rhyme) at both the beginning and end of every foot, it should be understood as a *vaṃsaṭṭha-gāthā*.
For it is said in the *Vuttodaya*: “They call this *vaṃsaṭṭha* when there are *jata* and *jarā*. Its meaning has already been explained above.
In that context, the phrase “here and there” (*tahiṃ tahiṃ*) refers to in each respective birth or personal existence (*attabhāva*), starting from the time of the vow for the Supreme Buddha.

The meaning is that he blows through various existences and individual bodies (*attabhāva*). "The accumulation of perfections" (*pāramisañcaya*) refers to the collection of the perfections such as giving and the rest.

And here, the perfections (*pāramī*) are tenfold, by way of giving, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truth, resolve, loving-kindness, and equanimity. And it is said in the *Buddhavamsa*:
“Generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, and energy as the fifth;
patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity—these are the ten.

This, moreover, is the etymological definition of the word *pāramī*. By virtue of possessing the specific qualities of generosity, virtue, and so forth, the Great Bodhisatta attains supremacy among beings.

*Paramo*. Its meaning is as follows: it is called *pāramī* because it is an action (*kamma*) or a perfection; it is obtained in the sense of the activity of giving and so forth. The suffix *-ṇa* is applied here according to the rule for *taddhita* derivatives expressing the state of being one's own (*santaka-bhāva-kamma*).
Furthermore, the suffix *-ī* is added to indicate the feminine gender. Alternatively, *paramo* means "one who fulfills" (*pūreti*) giving and the other perfections;

thus, the Bodhisatta is the fulfiller and protector of the qualities such as generosity. The root *pūra-* takes the suffix *-ama*. He is so called because he causes other beings (*pare satte*) to exist within himself (*mavati attani*) and binds them to himself.

Or, he is "supreme" (*paramo*) because of his association with distinguished qualities; thus, he is the Bodhisatta. [Etymologically: the root *mudh* with the prefix *para-* in the sense of "binding" (from *para-saddūpapada-mudhātu-bandhane-kvi*).

Alternatively, he is "supreme" because he immerses (*majjati*) the stains of the defilements excessively (*atirekaṃ*); thus, he is *paramo*. [Etymologically: the root *majj* with the prefix *para-* in the sense of "purification" (from *para-saddūpapada-majjadhātu-saṃsuddhiyaṃ-kvi*). The word *para* has the sense of "excessive.

Or, he is so called because he especially (*visesena*) goes (*mayati*) to the supreme (*paraṃ*), excellent (*seṭṭhaṃ*) Nibbāna. [Etymologically: the prefix *para* has the sense of "excellence. (From *paraṃ-seṭṭhaṃ-nibbānaṃ-visesena-mayati-gacchati*).

*Paramo*. [This is derived from] the root *maya*, preceded by the word *para*, in the sense of "going," with the suffix *kvi*. There is elision of the final part of the root. The word *para* has the meaning of "excellent.
Alternatively, he who "measures" (*munāti*) or "delimits" (*paricchindati*) the other world (*param lokaṃ*) by means of a specific knowledge that serves as a standard, like this world, is *paramo*.

[This is derived from] the root *muna*, preceded by the word *para*, in the sense of "delimiting," with the suffix *kvi*. He whose own multitude of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth exceeds (*ati*) the other [world].

"Parama" means one who measures or casts away [defilements] within the continuum (saṃtāna); it is formed from the root *mid* with the suffix *kvi*, preceded by the prefix *para*. The word *para* expresses the sense of "excessive.

He is called "parama" because he measures—that is, destroys—the enemy, which is either something other than his own body of dhammas or the host of thieves that are the defilements (kilesa) which work against him;
thus, he is the Mahābodhisatta. It is formed from the root *mid* meaning "to harm," preceded by the prefix *para*, with the suffix *kvi*.
The word *para* signifies "other" or "opposite. It is called a *pāramī* according to the method explained in the passage beginning with "they go to the supreme (*parama*).

Furthermore, it is a *pāramī* because one immerses oneself (*majjati*) or purifies oneself (*sujjhati) in the further shore (*pāra*), which is Nibbāna; thus, the Greatly Awakened One (*mahābodhisatta*) is a *pāramī*. This is an analysis based on the pure active agent (*suddhakattu*).

With the word *pāra* as a prefix, the verbal root *maj* in the sense of purification takes the suffix *kvi*, and the vowel *i* is substituted. Thus, one who immerses oneself—that is, purifies oneself—in the further shore, which is Nibbāna, is a *pāramī*.
Alternatively, *pāramī* is a term formed by the agentive (*hetu*), active (*kattu*), or instrumental (*sādhana*) suffixes.

It is called *pāramī* because it causes beings to reach, binds them to, or joins them with the further shore, which is Nibbāna. Or, it is called *pāramī* because it itself goes to, reaches, or leads beings to the further shore, which is Nibbāna.
Or, it is called *pāramī* because it knows and discerns the further shore, which is Nibbāna, exactly as it is.

Or, it is a *pāramī* because it measures (*minoti*) or places beings in the further shore, which is Nibbāna. The verbal root *mid* has the sense of "placing" (*pakkhipana*), and the suffix *ī* is added.
Or, it is a *pāramī* because it measures—that is, harms—beings in the further shore, which is Nibbāna; [this refers to] the Mahābodhisatta.
Its state or activity is the deed, such as the acts of giving and so forth, which is the *pāramī*. In this manner, the etymological meaning of the word *pāramī* should be understood.

Although the etymological derivation of the word *pāramī* has been stated in brief, it should be understood that it is explained here in detail for the sake of the listeners’ proficiency in the method of grammatical analysis (*niruttinaya*).

Furthermore, that [perfection] is threefold: the ten perfections (*dasapāramī*), the ten secondary perfections (*dasaupapāramī*), and the ten ultimate perfections (*dasaparamatthapāramī*). Among these:
The requisites for enlightenment fulfilled by relinquishing wealth, both animate and inanimate, are called the ten *pāramīs*.
The requisites for enlightenment fulfilled by relinquishing hands, feet, ears, nose, and other major and minor limbs, are called the ten *upapāramīs*.
The requisites for enlightenment fulfilled by relinquishing the life-faculty are called the ten *paramatthapāramīs*.
The meaning of the perfections (pāramīs), such as giving and the rest, should be understood from the *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā* and other commentaries.

"Accumulation" (*sañcayo*) means that which "accumulates," "goes toward," or "proceeds" by way of gathering its constituent parts (*avayava*). [Etymologically,] the root *ci-* preceded by the prefix *sam-* denotes "going," with the suffix *-a*. Alternatively, it is an "accumulation" because it "accumulates" the constituent parts;

thus, it is a collection (*samūha*). The "accumulation of perfections" is the collection or mass of the perfections; that is, the "accumulation of perfections. That [is what is meant by] "that accumulation of perfections."
But "they accumulate" (cayanti) refers to his karma. "Accumulated" (caya) means that which has been built up, brought about, or produced; the meaning is "accumulated.

It is called "accumulation" (caya) because one accumulates (cayati) or builds up (upacināti), or because it was accumulated (ciyittha) or built up (upaciyittha); thus he is "the Buddha. [The root] *ci* means accumulation, with the suffix *ṇa*. "That accumulation" (taṃ cayaṃ) is connected with "gone together with" (sabbhigataṃ).

In this context, "together with" (*sabbhi*) means with the peaceful ones, the true persons (*sappurisa*). They are "peaceful" (*santa*) because they pacify or thoroughly calm the defilements such as lust; they are the true persons.

The prefix *sam-* becomes *sa-* when followed by a condition for elision (*paccaya*). Where one should say "by those who are peaceful" (*santehi*), according to the rule *smāhismiṃnaṃ mhā bhimhivā*, the letter *hi* of the case-ending is replaced by *bhi*.
Then, by the rule *santasaddassa so bhe bo cantē*, the letter *sa* of the word *santa* is changed to *sa* when the letter *bha* follows, and the letter *ba* is inserted at the end;
thus it is said "by those who are all" (*tehi sabbhi*).
Regarding the phrase "that which has been gone to" (*gata*): since the agent [of the action] has not been explicitly stated, it must be understood as something to be approached.

For it is called "gone to" (*gata*) because it is gone to, approached, and drawn near by gods and humans. It is said that this Buddha, who possesses infinite qualities such as virtue, should be honored with the conviction that he is a refuge by noble persons—both gods and humans—who desire their own welfare.

That has been traversed. The connection is: "He has gone to the state that brings happiness. In this context, "state that brings happiness" (*sukhappada*) means that which serves as the foundation for ultimate happiness.
"Happiness" (*sukha*) is the act of being happy; that wherein one goes to and abides is the "state that brings happiness," namely, Nibbāna.
"State" (*pada*) refers to Nibbāna. For it is called a "state" because it is traversed and reached by the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas and others.
"He has gone" (*gato*) means he has gone where it is called "gone" (*gatanti agaminti*).

It is said that the Buddha has reached Nibbāna—which is the state of absolute happiness unmixed with suffering and the like—by way of making it his object (*ārammaṇakaraṇavasena*). That [Nibbāna] is what he has gone to.

Regarding the phrase *narānarānaṃ*, the word division is *nara-anarānaṃ*. The meaning is "of humans and gods. [He has attained] the state of excellence, such as renunciation (*pabbajjā*), and so forth.
One who leads (*neti*) is a "man" (*naro*); or, one who is led (*narīyati*) by his own karma or destiny is a man, a human being, or a sentient being (*satto*).
The element *nara-* signifies leading (*nayane*), with the suffix *-a*. One who is not a man is a non-man (*anaro*), namely a god (*devo*). A man and a non-man are "men and non-men" (*narānaro*);
[the word] "of those men and non-men" (*tesaṃ narānarānaṃ*) is connected to the following phrase, "that source of happiness" (*taṃ pana sukhasambhavaṃ*).
*Sukhasambhava* means the cause of mundane and supramundane happiness. Alternatively, it refers to merit (*puñña*), which serves as the cause for obtaining the threefold happiness.
It is called *sukha* because it brings about happiness (*sukhayati*). This refers to the threefold happiness; the meaning is that it makes happy that person in whom it arises.

Alternatively, it is called *sukha* because it thoroughly digs up (*suṭṭhu khanati*) suffering. Here, the root *khan* preceded by *su-* is used in the sense of determination (*avadhāraṇe*). It arises (*sambhavati*).

"By means of this merit, [there is] the fruit known as happiness"—this is *sambhava*, meaning the production of merit. The root *bhū* preceded by the prefix *sam-* and followed by the suffix *-ana* signifies "existence.
*Sukhasambhava* is the production (*sambhava*) of happiness; that, moreover, is the object (*kamma*) in the verb *bhavanti*. *Bhavanti* means "they are arising" or "coming into being.

He who causes that production of happiness to come into being (*bhāveti*), i.e., brings it forth, is *bhava*, namely the Buddha. That is *taṃ bhavaṃ*. For he, preceded by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)—

It should be understood that by means of the teaching of the Dhamma, he causes gods and humans to perform merit—consisting of generosity, virtue, and meditation—which is the cause for obtaining both mundane and supramundane happiness; therefore, it should be seen that he praises the Blessed One as the source of happiness for both humans and non-humans.
Regarding the phrase *namānamānaṃ*, the word division is *name* and *anamānaṃ*. *Nama* has the meaning "I bow. Herein—
And it should be understood that there is a substitution of the vowel *e* for the case-ending *mi*. "Anaman" means those who do not bow, those who do not pay homage, or those who are disrespectful;
this is an adjective qualifying "gava. "Gava" refers to fools who are like oxen. For "gava" is a noun-word in the genitive plural.
Then, by the rule "after *nam*, when followed by *pati*, there is elision (*lutta*) and [the formation of] a compound," it is established through the application of that sutta.
By the inclusion of the word *ca* ("and"), one should understand the derivation of the form by applying the substitution of *aṃ* for the word *naṃ*, and the substitution of *o* for the word *go*.
Thus, "those that go" (*gacchanti*) are *gāvo*, meaning "oxen. "Like oxen" (*gāvo viya*) means "like oxen"; [the phrase] "of those oxen, of the fools" (*tesaṃ gavaṃ bālānaṃ*) follows.

Furthermore, in the phrase "to the Bull among Conquerors" (*jinapuṅgavaṃ*), this is the genitive case. "To the Bull among Conquerors" (*jinapuṅgavaṃ*) means: I pay homage to the Buddha, the supreme person who is victorious.

The connection is with the word "I bow" (*namāmi*). And here, the term *puṅgava* (bull) in a *kammadhāraya* compound expresses the sense of "best," as in examples such as *munipuṅgava* ("bull among sages").
And it is said in the *Amarakosa*:
"In the subsequent member [of a compound], the words *byaggha*, *puṅgava*, *usabha*, and *kuñjara* [denote excellence]."
“*Sīha*, *saddūla*, *nāga*, and so forth, when used as the final members in a *kammadhāraya* compound, denote the meaning of ‘best’ (*seṭṭha*) in the masculine. This is the meaning of that [rule].

In a *kammadhāraya* compound, when occurring as the final member, the words *byaggha*, *puṅgava*, *usabha*, *kuñjara*, as well as the words *sīha*, *saddūla*, *nāga*, and so forth—namely, the words *sīha*, *saddūla*, and *nāga*—denote the sense of ‘best’ in the masculine. Furthermore, in this context:

The meaning of the word: He is a *jina* because he conquers (*jināti*) or has conquered (*ajinī*) those who hold other views—fools who, like oxen, do not know and do not bow before the qualities of the Buddha.
He is a *puṅgava* because he goes upward (*uddhaṃ gacchati*) to a distinguished state or a preeminent state. The verbal root *gam*, preceded by *pa-u*, means "to go";

the suffix *ava* is added. There is the elision of the nasal (*niggahita*). By applying the rule beginning with "when *ya* etc. (*yadādi*), the final consonant of the class of gutturals (*ka-vagga*) is substituted for that [nasal], and there is the elision of the end of the verbal root.
The derivation of the word *rūpa* should be understood. He is both a Victor (*jina*) and a Bull (*puṅgava*), thus he is the "Victorious Bull" (*jinapuṅgava*), the Buddha.

Furthermore, it is said that he has "conquered" (*ajinī*) by means of the power of his perfections and merit—without weapons—those other holders of wrong views who are fools, ignorant of the immeasurable qualities such as virtue possessed by Buddhas like bulls, and who do not acknowledge, measure, respect, or worship them. That [Buddha] is the "Victorious Bull."

This, however, is the concise interpretation here: in various places, in those respective existences or personal identities, the accumulation (*sañcaya*)—the mass or collection—of the perfections such as giving;

that which has been gathered, built up, and fully produced; that which is to be gone to, approached, and attended upon by the good, the peaceful, and the virtuous; and the state of happiness, which is the foundation for absolute bliss.
I have gone to and attained the state of Nibbāna, which is the source of happiness for humans and non-humans— both gods and men—
and which brings about the arising of the threefold happiness, being the cause of both mundane and supramundane bliss, or merit that produces existence;
[I have attained this] by not bowing to those who do not bow, who are disrespectful, or who do not pay homage— the foolish who are like oxen— to the Bull among Conquerors.
"I bow, I bow to the Buddha, the Victor, the Supreme Person.
The commentary on the ninth verse of praise is complete.
The Sage is the skillful boatman; the factors of the Path are the boat.
I pay homage to that Buddha, the destroyer of great suffering, who, as a seeker using the instrument of knowledge,
embarked upon that [vehicle] and crossed over many oceans of existence.

10. Thus, having paid homage to the Buddha with the ninth verse, he now speaks the verse beginning with *maggaṅganāvantī* out of a desire to worship the Buddha after praising him for the quality of ferrying many beings across the ocean of saṃsāra—known as the three realms of existence—and for the quality of causing beings to abandon suffering.
Furthermore, because this [verse] is composed with groups of seven syllables, it consists of twelve syllables.
It should be understood that [the verse] "yuttā indavaṃsa gāthā" refers to this. For it is said in the *Vuttodaya*:

"Indeed, where there are two *tagaṇas* and *jarā*, that is *indavaṃsā*. The meaning of this is: in whatever verse (*gāthā*) those two *tagaṇas* and *jarā* (i.e., *jagaṇa* and *ragaṇa*) should occur, that verse is indeed exclusively called an *indavaṃsagāthā*.
Therein, the connection is "yo munidakkhanāviko," which means: he who is known as the Buddha, the skillful leader of the ship.
In this context, *muni* refers to the Blessed One (*bhagavā*), who is called a *muni* because he measures (*munāti*) and knows both worlds. The verbal root *muna* signifies knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
Alternatively, *mona* is said to be omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*); since he possesses that, he is a *muni*. The suffix *-i* is used here in the sense of possession (*assatthi-atthe*).
For it is stated in the commentary on the *Vaṇṇapatha Jātaka* in the *Ekanipāta*: "A *muni*—*mona* is said to be knowledge. [By means of his body...]"
Or, a person is called a "muni" because he is endowed with one or another of the qualities beginning with moneyya.

Furthermore, this [muni] is of many kinds: the householder-muni, the homeless-muni, the muni-in-training (sekha), the muni-beyond-training (asekha), the solitary-muni (pacceka-muni), and the muni-of-munis.
Among these, the "householder-muni" is a layperson who has realized the fruit and understood the teaching. The "homeless-muni" is one who has gone forth as a renunciant of such a nature.

"A learner sage (*sekkhamunī*) refers to the seven types of learners (*sattasekkhā*). An adept sage (*asekkhamunī*) refers to one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). A solitary sage (*paccekamunī*) refers to a paccekabuddha.
A sage among sages (*munimunī*) refers to a perfectly enlightened Buddha (*sammāsambuddho*).

However, in this context, "sage among sages" is what is intended. "Skilled" (*dakkho*) means clever. One who becomes skilled (*dakkhati*), that is, proficient, in crossing the ocean is "skilled," such as a navigator. This is the root *dakkha*.

In the sense of "going" (gati). Alternatively, he is called *dakkha* because he proceeds swiftly due to his lack of sluggishness regarding skillful karma (*kusalakamma*) and other duties and non-duties;
thus, any person who is skillful is *dakkha*. The root *dak-kha* has the sense of speed (*sīghattha*).
Like one who is skillful (*dakkha*), so too is the Buddha. However, in the direct sense (*nītattha*), the Buddha is the cause for the deliverance of beings from the ocean of saṃsāra.
One who sees and discerns by means of knowledge is called "Dakkha. A "nāvika" is one who crosses to the shore of the ocean by boat; thus he is a "nāvika," the master of a ship.
The suffix *-ika* is applied here according to the rule for derivatives meaning "one who crosses. Like a *nāvika*, the Buddha is a *nāvika*.
In its direct sense (*nītattha*), however, the Buddha is called a *nāvika* because he crosses to the further shore of Nibbāna by means of the boat of the eight factors of the Path. He is *dakkha*.
A *nāvika* (pilot) who is skilled (*dakka*) is a *dakkha-nāvika*; and since he is a *muni* (sage), he is a *munidakkhanāvika*. This is a *kammadhāraya* compound.
Alternatively, a *muni* who is as skillful as a skilled pilot is a *munidakkhanāvika*; [this refers to] the Buddha. This is a *upamā-kammadhāraya* compound.
For just as a pilot expert in crossing the ocean leads people to the far shore of the sea, even so does the Buddha [lead] those beings who are ready to be trained.
It is said that it leads to the further shore of Nibbāna.
The connection is: "having boarded the ship of the path-factors. "The ship of the path-factors" means the ship known as the eight path-factors.
"Having boarded" means having ascended; the sense is that, while destroying the defilements, one goes toward Nibbāna by way of making it the object of cognition.

*Magga*. It is derived from the verbal root *gam* with the prefix *māra-* and the suffix *kvi*. While it could be called *mārento* (one who kills), it is stated as *maggo* according to the rules of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*).

Alternatively, it is the *magga* because one seeks (*maggati*) or searches for (*gavesati*) Nibbāna; the root *magga* means "to seek," with the suffix *a*. Or else, it is the *magga* because it is sought or searched for by those desiring Nibbāna.
[It is the path] for those who are exclusively oppressed by the sufferings of birth, aging, sickness, death, and so forth.
It is called the *magga* (path) because it must be sought and pursued by sentient beings for the purpose of attaining Nibbāna, the destruction of suffering;
thus, there are four paths. For it is said: "In what sense is it the path? In the sense of seeking (*maggana*), and in the sense of being sought (*magganīya*) by those who desire Nibbāna.
It is called an *aṅga* (limb/factor) because one goes to the fruit and Nibbāna by means of it. The root *agi* signifies going; the suffix *a* is added. Thus, it is a limb of the path.

"Kāraṇa" means a factor of the path (*maggaṅga*). By way of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, the eight factors of the path are obtained.
It is called a "boat" (*nāvā*) because it is pushed (*nuyati*) or praised (*thavīyati*). The root *nud* is used in the sense of praising (*thaviya*).
Alternatively, it is a boat because it carries one from this shore to the further shore, or because they carry a burden by means of it.
Or "nāvā" means a boat. "Nayane avo" means that which carries across.
A boat consisting of the factors of the path is a "path-factor-boat. Alternatively, because the path-factors are like a boat, they are called a "path-factor-boat.

For just as a boat carries people who have boarded it to the further shore of the ocean or a river, so too do the eight dhammas that constitute the path-factors carry those practicing them to the further shore of Nibbāna; thus it is said.
That is the ship of the path-factors (*maggaṅga*).
"The oar of striving" (*īhāphiya*) refers to the rudder consisting of energy (*vīriya*). For it is said in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*: "By the oar means by the rudder.
It is called "striving" (*īhā*) because one strives (*īhati*) or exerts oneself; or else, it is called "striving" because one strives, exerts, and intends by means of it.
Vīriya. In the *Saddanīti*, however, it is stated: “*Īha* means striving (*cetāya*). Because one increases (*vaḍḍheti*) water by means of this, it is *phiyaṃ*.

The root *phā* is used in the sense of increasing; *iya* is the suffix. Or, because one strikes (*ghaṭṭeti*) against the water, it is *phiyaṃ*. Alternatively, because one goes (*gacchati*) by means of this boat, it is *phiyaṃ*.

It is made of reeds (*dabbisārakaṃ*). The root *phāyi* is used in the sense of going; *a* is the suffix, and the vowel *ā* becomes *i*. That which is reckoned as striving (*īhā*)—[this is the meaning].
*Īhāphiyaṃ*: "Like a boat, it strives" (*īhāti*)—thus it is *īhāphiyaṃ*.

Just as a boat goes to its desired destination by means of a sail (*phiya*), so too one accomplishes various tasks through energy (*vīriya*) designated as "striving" (*īhā*), and thus goes to the desired state of Nibbāna;

this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, in the phrase "the grasper of that," it is the object (*kamma*). By "the maker of knowledge" (*ñāṇakaraṇa*): by that which is designated as the knowledge of omniscience.

"With the hand": that which knows all knowable phenomena (*ñeyyadhamma*) is "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*); thus it is "omniscient knowledge" (*sabbaññutañāṇa*). That which performs various actions is a "doer" (*kara*), namely the hand.
Knowledge characterized as a doer is "knowledge-doer" (*ñāṇakara*); or, knowledge is like a doer, thus it is "knowledge-doer. By that knowledge-doer. "A grasper" means grasping firmly.
"By that" means by that ship, which consists of the eight factors of the path. "Many" [is the word].
"Many beings who were to be disciplined. "The ocean of existence" refers to the great ocean consisting of the three realms of existence (*tibhava*) or the cycle of saṃsāra;
its meaning has already been explained above.

"He ferried across" means he caused them to descend [into safety], that is, he made them transcend it. "Buddha" refers to one who has realized the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Destroyer of the abyss."

It means the one who abandons the suffering of beings; that is, the one who destroys suffering. Alternatively, it means the one who strikes down misfortune (*agha*), abandoning the defilements (*kilesa*) of beings; that is, the one who destroys the defilements.

For here, the word *agha* refers to both suffering and defilement. In this context, it is called *agha* because it "goes toward" (*aghati*) or "causes to go toward" (*dukkhayati*) suffering; and it goes toward [suffering] by way of the mode of suffering.

Alternatively, it is called *agha* because it occurs (*pavattati*). Furthermore, defilement (*kilesa*) is called *agha* because by means of it beings experience suffering (*aghayanti*) and commit evil (*pāpaṃ karonti*).

The verbal root *agha-dhātu* is used in the sense of performing evil. He abandons and destroys suffering, thus he is the "Destroyer of Suffering" (*agha-ppaha*), the Buddha. The verbal root *hā*, preceded by *pa* and having the word *agha* as its prefix, signifies relinquishing.
Through his teaching of the Dhamma, the Buddha [removes] both the suffering and the defilements of those beings who are ready to be trained.

The meaning is "he carries away. And here, in the first alternative, because suffering is a dhamma that cannot be abandoned [by itself], it is said that even though the Path does not abandon suffering, it "abandons suffering" by way of figurative designation (*phalūpacāra*).
The connection is: "I bow, I pay homage, to him"—namely, to the clever boatman who is the Sage.
This, then, is the concise interpretation (*saṅkhepayojanā*): He who is the clever boatman who is the Sage—that is, the skillful chief of the ship known as the Buddha.
Having boarded the ship of the path-factors— namely, the ship consisting of the eight factors of the path—
and having taken hold of the oar-handle of effort known as *īhā* with the hand of knowledge known as omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*),
grasping it firmly, he [the Teacher] ferries across many, numerous beings to be trained from the ocean of existence, the great sea known as the three realms of becoming.

"I cross over and cause others to cross over"—I bow, I pay homage to that Buddha who has penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, the dispeller of misfortune, the destroyer of the suffering of beings, or the destroyer of their defilements; to that Sage, the skillful ferryman.
The commentary on the tenth verse of homage is complete.
The accumulation of the thirty-two perfections,
the vision of the Four Noble Truths beneath the supreme Bodhi tree,
and the attainment of sublime success for the benefit of humans and gods—
I bow to the Victor who has attained the pacification of the three realms of existence.

11. Having thus paid homage to the Buddha with the tenth verse, he now speaks the verse beginning with “samatiṃsatipāramisambharaṇa” in order to praise and worship the Victor by means of five qualities, starting with the fulfillment of the thirty-two perfections of mindfulness. This is [the verse]:
However, because it is composed of four *sagaṇas*, it should be understood as a *toṭaka* verse consisting of twelve syllables.
For it is said in the *Vuttodaya*: "In this [work], *toṭaka* is measured by four *ambudhi-sagas*. Its meaning is as follows:
that which is measured, defined, composed, or characterized in each quarter-verse by four *ambudhi-sagas* (groups of four syllables) is called *toṭaka* here in the *jagatī* meter.

In that context, "the accumulation of the thirty perfections" means that which has been brought together and fulfilled by the thirty perfections—namely, the ten *pāramīs*, the ten *upapāramīs*, and the ten *paramatthapāramīs*.
The distinction between these and the etymological meaning of the word *pāramī* have already been explained above.

It is called *sambharaṇo* because he accumulated (*sambhari*) and fulfilled them; thus, the Victor is the one who performed the act of accumulation (*sambharaṇo*). This refers to the verbal root *bhar* preceded by the prefix *sam*.

The suffix *yu* is used in the sense of completion (*pūraṇe*). "One who has accumulated the thirty perfections" (*samatiṃsatipāramisambharaṇo*) means the Conqueror (*jino*) who fulfilled the thirty perfections.

The meaning is that, starting from the time he received the prophecy at the feet of Buddha Dīpaṅkara, he fulfilled the thirty perfections for four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus one hundred thousand aeons.
That is "the accumulation of the thirty perfections. [He did this] "at the noble Bodhi tree" (*varabodhidume*).
"At the foot of the tree of supreme enlightenment. Here, the meaning of the term *varabodhi* has already been explained above.
It is called a *dumo* (tree) because it moves (*davati*)—that is, it goes—toward growth, increase, and abundance by means of its roots, trunk, bark, branches, twigs, shoots, and fruits;
or alternatively, because it reaches an extreme state of beauty through the splendors of silver, gold, gems, and precious stones. On the very day the Bodhisatta was born...
Born together with the Bodhisatta, there was a king of trees called Asattha, sixty cubits in height.
Regarding the word *dudhātu*, it means "in the state of motion. However, in the *Apadāna-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "It is called a *duma* because it causes trembling (*dunāti kampati*);

or else, it is a *duma* because it fills (*dumati*) the expanse of the sky. *Varabodhi* means excellent awakening; since it is both that excellent awakening and a tree (*duma*), it is the *varabodhiduma*. [The phrase refers to] "in that [tree]."
The vision of the Four Truths means that the four noble truths have been penetrated by means of path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*).
Furthermore, the word *sacca* (truth) is seen in many different senses. For example: in such passages as "One should speak the truth and not be angry," it refers to verbal truth;

in such passages as "Samanas and brahmins established in truth," it refers to the truth of abstinence (*virati-sacca*). [As it is asked: "Why do they speak of various truths, those who propound diverse views?"...

In passages such as “skilful declarations,” it refers to the truth of view (*diṭṭhisacca*). In passages such as “for there is one truth, not a second,” it refers to ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*), namely Nibbāna and the Path.
In passages such as “of the four truths, how many are skilful?,” it refers to noble truth (*ariyasacca*).

Therefore, it should be understood that here too, it refers to noble truth. *Sacca* means being real, being non-false (*avitatha*). The root *sath* [is used] in the sense of non-falsity, with the suffix *-nya*.

Just as the intrinsic nature of fires is exclusively heat and never cold, so too the intrinsic nature of suffering and the rest—namely, oppression and so forth—is exclusively true, real, not unreal, and not otherwise. That, moreover, is fourfold:
the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path. Among these, the truth of suffering is:
“Dukkha” means that which is wretched (*kucchita*) and empty (*tuccha*). This is a *kammadhāraya* compound. For this has been stated in the *Saccavibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*:
“The word *du* is seen in the sense of ‘wretched. For they call a wretched son a ‘bad son’ (*duputta*).
The word *kha*, however, [denotes] the empty. For empty space is called ‘*kha*. And this first Truth is wretched, because it is the locus of manifold calamities.”
It is devoid of the state of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood as imagined by foolish, common people. Therefore, because it is contemptible and empty, it is called "suffering" (*dukkha*).

And because it is both suffering and a truth, it is the "truth of suffering" (*dukkhasacca*); the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) belonging to the three planes is what is meant. As for the "truth of origin" (*samudayasacca*):
it is called *ayo* because by means of it one goes (*ayati*) or proceeds toward the fruit of suffering; thus, *ayo* is greed (*lobha*). The root *aya* pertains to going.
a. *Samudaya* (the origin): When there is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of the remaining suffixes, *sam* signifies the arising of suffering, and *udaya* signifies the cause (*kāraṇa*).
This is a genitive *tappurisa* compound. For this has been stated in the *Saccavibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*: "The word *sam* indicates conjunction, as in *samāgama*, *sameti*, and so forth;
the word *u* indicates arising, as in *uppanna* and *udita*; and the word *aya* indicates a cause."
It illuminates. And this second truth is the cause for the arising of suffering when there is the conjunction of the remaining conditions.
Thus, because it is the cause for the arising [of suffering] through its conjunction with suffering, it is called "the origin of suffering" (*dukkhasamudaya*).

It is both an origin (*samudaya*) and a truth (*sacca*), hence "the truth of the origin" (*samudayasacca*); here, craving (*taṇhā*), which is characterized by greed (*lobha*), is obtained. As for "the truth of cessation" (*nirodhasacca*): it ceases...

It moves and proceeds, thus it is *rodha* (the moving); this refers to the phenomena of the cycle of existence belonging to the three planes. [The suffix] *ṇa* is added to the root *rudh* in the sense of "moving. There is no moving—that is, no proceeding—of the phenomena of the three-planed cycle of existence here;
thus it is *nirodha* (cessation), which is Nibbāna. Alternatively, it is *nirodha* because the suffering of saṃsāra ceases (*nirujjhati*) here;
thus it is Nibbāna. [The suffix] *ṇa* is added to the root *rudh* in the sense of "obstructing. For this has been stated in the commentary on the *Saccavibhaṅga*:

As for the third truth: since the prefix *ni-* signifies absence (*abhāva*), and the word *rodha* indicates confinement (*cāraka*), it is called "the cessation of suffering" because there is an absence here of the confinement of suffering known as saṃsāra, due to its being empty of all destinations;

or alternatively, when one has entered into concentration (*samādhi*), there is an absence of the confinement of suffering known as saṃsāra, because that [concentration] is its opposite. Thus it is "the cessation of suffering."
...is said. Or, because it is the condition for the non-arising and cessation of suffering, it is the "cessation of suffering" (*dukkhanirodha*).

And since it is both cessation and a truth, it is the "truth of cessation" (*nirodhasacca*); that is, *nibbāna*. The "truth of the path" (*maggasacca*): it is called the "path" (*magga*) because by means of it one seeks (*maggati*) or goes (*gacchati*) toward the cessation of suffering, which is *nibbāna*.
It is the eightfold path. The verbal root *maggh-* signifies going; the suffix *-a* is added. For this has been stated in the *Sacca-vibhaṅga*: [etc.]

In the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* it is said: “But as for the fourth truth, because it goes toward the cessation of suffering by way of being its object—since it is directed toward that—and because it is the practice for the attainment of the cessation of suffering, it is therefore called ‘the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
And since it is both the path and a truth, it is the ‘truth of the path. The eightfold path is found therein. Because...

These are penetrated by the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas; therefore, they are called "Noble Truths" (*ariyasaccāni*). Alternatively, they are penetrated by the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas; therefore, they are also called "Noble Truths.
Their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth should be understood as follows: herein, the truth of suffering has the characteristic of oppression (*bādhanalakkhaṇa*).
The truth of origination has the function of burning; its manifestation is occurrence, and its characteristic is being the source. The truth of cessation has the function of non-interruption;
its manifestation is an obstacle. The truth of cessation has the characteristic of peace; its function is deathlessness, and its manifestation is the signless.
The truth of the path has the characteristic of leading out; its function is the abandoning of defilements, and its manifestation is emergence.
Among these four truths, the first and third truths are the fruits; the second and fourth truths are the causes.
The first two truths are difficult to see because they are profound; the latter two truths are difficult to see because of their profundity.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the noble truth of the cessation of suffering is both profound and difficult to see.
Furthermore, by way of four meanings for each Truth, there are sixteen aspects of the Truths (*saccaṭṭhā*).

Therefore, it is said in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*: “The meaning of oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, and the meaning of changeability—these four are the meanings of suffering within suffering;
they are such, not otherwise, and not different. Thus is suffering.”

In that sense it is truth. For the origin, the meaning of accumulation, the meaning of source, the meaning of bondage, and the meaning of impediment—these four are the meanings of origin for the origin;
they are such, not otherwise, and not different. Thus, the origin is truth in the sense of being such.
For cessation, the meaning of escape, the meaning of seclusion, the meaning of the unconditioned, and the meaning of the deathless—these four...
The meaning of cessation as cessation is such, not otherwise, not different; thus, cessation is a truth in the sense of being such.

The meaning of the path as outlet, as cause, as seeing, and as predominance—these four meanings of the path as path are such, not otherwise, not different; thus, the path is a truth in the sense of being such.

*Dasanaṃ* means seeing; or, it is *dasanaṃ* because one sees (*passati*) with it; thus it refers to the knowledge of the four paths (*cattumaggañāṇa*). The root *dis-* has the sense of looking toward (*apekkhane*).

One who possesses the seeing of the four truths is a "seer of the four truths" (*catusaccadaso*), namely, the Victor (*jino*). Alternatively, he is a "seer of the four truths" because he saw (*adassi*) and perceived (*apassī*) the four truths;
the meaning is that he penetrated (*appaṭivijjhi*) the four truths by means of the knowledge of the four paths.
That [insight] has the vision of the four truths. Knowledge of the four truths, moreover, is twofold: knowledge of recollection (*anubodha-ñāṇa*) and knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*).
Therein, knowledge of recollection is mundane; it occurs with respect to cessation and the path by way of hearsay and so forth.
Knowledge of penetration is supramundane; taking cessation as its object, it penetrates all four truths by way of its function.
As it has been said: "Bhikkhus, he who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering; he sees the cessation of suffering;
he sees the path leading to the cessation of suffering"—all this should be stated.

Furthermore, the knowledge of penetration into the Four Noble Truths does not arise without the knowledge of awakening; therefore, for the sake of that knowledge of awakening, the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths was previously [taught].
"It should be undertaken by the wise. But surely noble disciples (ariyasāvaka) penetrate the Four Truths;

why then is it the Victor alone who is praised as "seeing the Four Truths"? It is because the Blessed One penetrates the Four Truths through the knowledge of the path to Arhatship—a unique instruction distinct from that of the noble disciples. Therefore, it is the Blessed One alone [who is so praised].
"He has praised the vision of the Four Truths. In this context, with the exception of craving and Nibbāna, all remaining phenomena are called the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
The eight hundred types of craving-investigations are called the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*). Nibbāna is called the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*).
The Eightfold Path is called the truth of the path (*maggasacca*). As it is stated in the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*:
“The round of existence in the three realms is suffering;
craving is its origin; cessation is called Nibbāna; and the supramundane path is considered the way.
“Supreme attainment of psychic power” means the best attainment of psychic power (*iddhigata*). The meaning is: having reached the supreme psychic power of the past Buddhas.
Alternatively, the meaning is that it is the foundation for the highest supernormal powers (*iddhi*).

*Iddhi* is so called because of succeeding (*ijjhana*), accomplishing (*samijjhana*), or because it succeeds, accomplishes, or is brought forth. Both the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power and the path of Arahantship are obtained therein.
For it is said in the *Visuddhimagga*: "Likewise, renunciation succeeds, thus it is 'success' (*iddhi*); and the path of Arahantship succeeds, thus it is 'success'."
And [the word] "iddhi. Alternatively, beings succeed (*ijjhanti*) by means of this; they become successful (*iddhā*), grown, and reached the pinnacle—thus it is *iddhi*.
The eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the four paths (*magga*) are obtained here. The verbal root *idh* signifies growth (*vuḍḍhi*).

Alternatively, the suffix *ta* indicates the feminine gender, and there is the suffix *ī*. One who has gone to success is "one who has attained success" (*iddhigata*), namely, the Victor (*jina*). Now...

That which one goes to or stands upon is called a "gata" (a resort). One who has gone to, that is, become the resort for excellent (*vara*) and supreme (*uttama*) psychic powers (*iddhi*), is thus "one who has attained excellent psychic power" (*varamiddhigata*);

this refers to the Conqueror (*jina*). Although noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*) have also attained psychic powers, Buddhas, however, are distinguished by this higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) as being preeminent, successful, grown, and having reached the highest excellence.
Therefore, it should be understood that only the Buddha is worthy of being praised as one who has attained the supreme success (*iddhi*).
"For the welfare of humans and gods" (*naradevahita*) means the welfare, purpose, and sustenance consisting of both mundane and supramundane benefits for humans and gods;

their meaning, however, has already been stated below. "The pacification of the three realms of existence" (*tibhavūpasama*) refers to the cessation of rebirth in the three realms of existence. Regarding the production of renewed existence...

The meaning is that he is "pacified," "extinguished," or "ceased" because of the non-existence of renewed existence (*punabbhava*) produced within the three realms of existence—namely, those designated as the realms of sense-desire, form, and formlessness. It is called *bhava* because beings (*satta*) come into being (*bhavanti*) therein; there are three such realms of existence, hence "the three existences" (*tibhava*).
He has attained peace through them, thus he is the "Pacifier of the Three Existences" (*tibhavūpasama*), the Victor. [This refers to] the Blessed One.

Because, at the very seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka), the formative forces (saṅkhāra) rooted in ignorance and craving—which produce rebirth-linking within the three realms of existence known as the sensual, fine-material, and immaterial—have been abandoned without remainder by means of the knowledge of the path to Arahantship, there is no further arising of renewed existence (punabbhava).
Therefore, it is said that he especially praises the Blessed One as the one who has brought the three realms of existence to rest. "The Victor" (Jina).
"I bow to the Buddha, the conqueror of the fifth Māra"—this is the construction, meaning "I, with a mind endowed with knowledge, pay homage with reverence. Here, however, is the concise construction:
*Samatiṃsa* means thirty; *sambharaṇaṃ* means accumulation; thus, it refers to the thirty perfections (*pāramiyo*) that have been accumulated and fulfilled.
At the excellent Bodhi tree, at the foot of the supreme tree of enlightenment, [he realized] the ten aspects of the Four Truths—the four noble truths.

To one who sees and penetrates with the knowledge of the path; to that which is the excellent attainment of supernormal power (*iddhi*), the supreme state of the past Buddhas, the foundation for the highest powers;
to that which maintains the welfare of humans and gods—the purpose consisting of both mundane and supramundane matters;
and to the pacification of the three existences, stilled from the three realms known as sense-desire, form, and formlessness.

I bow with a mind endowed with wisdom and with reverence to the Buddha— the Victor who has conquered the five Māras, whose rebirth has been stilled and extinguished within the three realms of existence known as Kāma, Rūpa,
and Arūpa. Thus ends the commentary on the eleventh verse of homage.
Possessing the marks born of a hundred merits, stainless,
with a mind like the sky and a steadfastness equal to Mount Meru,
endowed with a cool virtue like a lotus—
I bow to the Victor who endures the earth. 12.

Having thus paid homage to the Victor with the eleventh verse, he now speaks the verse beginning with “Satapuññajalakkhaṇikaṃ” (marked by a hundred merits and water-like signs), desiring to worship the Victor after praising him with these six qualities. This, moreover—
It should be understood that this is a *toṭaka* verse because it is composed of four groups [of syllables] and endowed with twelve syllables.
As for its proof, it has already been stated in the commentary on the immediately preceding verse.
In that context, "characterized by the water of a hundred merits" refers to the thirty-two marks of a Great Man produced by the power of the merit of numerous perfections (*pāramī*).
It is accomplished. And here, the word *sata* denotes a plural number, as in "hundredfold splendor" (*satatejo*), "thousand rays" (*sahassaraṃsī*), and so forth.

"Born of a hundred merits" (*satapuññajaṃ*) means that which is produced by a hundred—that is, many—meritorious powers of the perfections (*pāramī*). "Characteristics" (*lakkhaṇaṃ*) refers to the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and so on;

they are called characteristics because the state of Buddhahood (*buddhabhāva*) is characterized (*lakkhiyati*) or marked by them. The verbal root *lakkh-* signifies seeing or numbering. And [it is] born of a hundred merits...
"And that mark" refers to the mark born of a hundred merits (*satapuññaja-lakkhaṇa*).
He who possesses that is "one possessing the mark born of a hundred merits," namely, the Conqueror (*jina*). That [mark].

For if all beings in infinite world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) were each to perform a meritorious deed a hundred times, the Bodhisatta alone, having performed a hundredfold more merit than the total merit performed by all those people, [attained it].

The intention is that he praises [the Buddha] as "one whose marks are born from a hundred merits" because he is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor marks produced by the power of the merit of the perfections (*pāramī*).
For it is said in the *Buddhavamsa-aṭṭhakathā*:

“Regarding ‘the mark of a hundred merits’: if all beings in infinite world-systems were each to perform a meritorious deed a hundred times, the Bodhisatta was reborn having himself performed a hundredfold the merit performed by all those people.
Therefore, it is called ‘the mark of a hundred merits. However, some [explain] that it was produced by a hundredfold hundred merits.”
"Some say it is a single characteristic [for each mark]. If that were so, anyone could become a Buddha. This was rejected in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
However, in the *Pātheyya-aṭṭhakathā*, it says: "A hundredfold merit-characteristic means each individual characteristic is produced by a hundredfold meritorious deed.
If that were so, anyone could become a Buddha—this they did not approve of. But regarding the infinite..."

It is said: "If all beings in every world-system were each to perform a single deed a hundred times, the Bodhisatta alone was reborn having performed a hundredfold more merit than the deeds performed by all those people.
Therefore, they accepted this meaning as 'the mark of a hundred merits' (satapuññalakkhaṇa). As for the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, however, they will be revealed further on."
"Virajaṃ" means free from dust (*vigata-rajaṃ*) due to the absence of the dust of passion (*rāga*), etc. "Dust" (*rajo*) refers to that which stains and clings to objects such as forms;
thus, it is the dust of passion and so forth. The verbal root *ranj* signifies passion. That which is free from such dust is "dustless" (*viraja*), namely, the Conqueror (*jina*).

For the Conqueror is indeed "free from dust" because he has conquered all the dust of the defilements (*kilesa-māra*) right there on the seat of enlightenment (*bodhi-pallaṅka*). "Gaganūpamaṃ" means like the sky.
Here, "wisdom" (*dhī*) refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*). Therefore, the meaning is: "possessing omniscient knowledge that is comparable to space.
It is called *gagana* (the sky) because birds and other creatures move within it; it is the atmosphere (*ākāsa*). The verbal root *gam* is used in the sense of "going," with the suffix *yu*.

The letter *m* becomes *g*. It is called *upamā* (comparison) because it is compared to something else. This is a noun derived from the action itself (*bhāvasādhana*). The verbal root *mā*, preceded by the prefix *upa*, is used in the sense of "measuring. It sustains all knowable phenomena (*sabbañeyyadhamma*).

*Dhī* means that which knows; it is the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*). [The suffix] *ī* is added after the verbal root *dhar* in the sense of knowledge, and the feminine marker *īp* is also applied.

An analogy connected with the sky or space is a "sky-like analogy" (*gaganūpamā*). The Victor is one whose wisdom is like that—his omniscient knowledge is similar to it—and thus he is "one of sky-like wisdom" (*gaganūpamadhi*).
That is "the one of sky-like wisdom. This, however, is an analogy for the excellence of the Dhamma, because of his being devoid of qualities such as finitude.
Indeed, it is said in the *Subodhālaṅkāra*: "The lotus-face of the Sage is like the Dhamma.

For just as space is infinite because it is called "infinite space" and thus expands infinitely, so too, because the Blessed One’s Buddha-knowledge is called "infinite," and because the object of omniscient knowledge is infinite, that knowledge itself becomes infinite.
It expands. Therefore, he praises [the Buddha] as "one whose resolve is like space.
Here, "resolve" (*dhiti*) refers to concentration (*samādhi*). The meaning is: one who possesses unshakable concentration, similar to Mount Sineru.

It is called "resolve" (*dhiti*) because by means of it, the associated mental states are held (*dhiyati*) and established upon a single object; thus, it is the mundane and supramundane meditative absorption and concentration of the Blessed One.
*Dhī* is the root meaning "to hold. *Meru* means that which measures or destroys darkness by its radiance; it is the king of mountains.
The root *mī* signifies "to harm," and the suffix is *ru*.
Regarding this etymological explanation, it is said that the eastern face of Sineru is made of silver, the southern face of jewels, the western face of crystal, and the northern face of gold.
This was said with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). Alternatively, it is called *Meru* because it measures or overcomes all mountains by its own superior height;

one whose steadfastness (*dhiti*) and concentration (*samādhi*) are equal to Meru is "one whose steadfastness is like Meru," namely the Conqueror (*jina*). That [Conqueror] is equal to the Meru of steadfastness.
For just as King Meru does not shake or tremble when winds come from the eight directions, so too the Conqueror [is unshaken] by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).
Having abandoned [defilements], because he is endowed with supramundane jhāna-concentration, he is neither shaken nor moved by the eight worldly conditions or by the winds of wrong views;
thus he is praised as being like Mount Meru in steadfastness.
He is joined with a virtue as cool as a lotus born in water—that is, with a virtue that is exceedingly cool and incalculable.
It is connected. For it is said in the *Apadāna* text: "His virtue is incalculable. And in its commentary: "But the Blessed One’s virtue is indeed incalculable.
It shines and glows, thus it is *jala*, meaning water. The root *jal* [denotes] radiance; the suffix *a* is added.
That which is born in water (*jale*) is *jalaja*, namely the lotus. They compare it with, that is, liken it to, the lotus which is born in water.
Virtue (*sīla*) is like a lotus born in water. It is "cool" (*sītala*) because it is practiced by those seeking happiness; here, the root *sī-* means "to serve," with the suffix *-tala*.
Alternatively, it is "cool" because it takes up or grasps the quality of coolness (*sītaguṇa*); here, the root *lā-* preceded by the prefix *sī-* means "to grasp," with the suffix *-i*.
Just as a lotus born in water is as if cool because the heat has been neutralized by the water, so too is the virtue of the Buddha.
Furthermore, because it is composed of the absence of defilement, it is absolutely cool.
For well-guarded, purified virtue, by means of the abandoning of defilements, pacifies the fever of defilement in beings—not so green sandalwood, pearl necklaces, gems, water, wind, or moonbeams.
Therefore, virtue alone is "cool," and thus it is called "absolutely cool. This is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*:
