“Neither the winds laden with water, nor even yellow sandalwood;
neither pearl necklaces nor jewels, nor the rays of the moon’s beams—
none of these can soothe the fever of beings here, however well-guarded it may be.”
"That which allays this fever of the noble ones, this virtue that is supremely cool"—this is the meaning of those two verses.
This virtue, well-guarded, thoroughly protected, noble, pure, and supremely cool, allays whatever fever there is for beings in this world; just as a rain-cloud, a giver of water, [allays the heat].
The winds blowing together with the clouds do not harmonize; even the green sandalwood does not harmonize. Necklaces and pearl strings do not harmonize at all.
Jewels, such as beryl and other gems, do not harmonize. The sprouts of the moon’s rays—the rays of the moon—do not harmonize.
It is called *sīla* because it cools (*sīlati*) and composes (*samādhiyati*) bodily actions and so forth by means of excellent conduct.
It does not scatter; thus it is virtue (*sīla*). The root *sīl* is used in the sense of concentration (*samādhi*). Alternatively, it is virtue because by means of it they concentrate the mind;
or, it is virtue because by means of it they hold fast, that is, they firmly maintain wholesome states (*dhamma*) as excellent;
thus it is virtue. It is understood as the state of volition (*cetanā*) or an arising of wholesome consciousness. The root *sīl* is used in the sense of holding fast. For this has been said:
In the *Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā*: “In what sense is it ‘virtue’ (*sīla*)? It is virtue in the sense of ‘cooling’ (*sīlana*). What is this so-called virtue?
It means either composure, in the sense of the non-distraction of bodily action and so forth through the state of good conduct;
or it means upholding, in the sense of being a foundation through the establishment of wholesome states. By way of the simile of water, [it is] like a lotus.
He is endowed with cool, exceedingly cool, and incalculable virtue; thus he is "endowed with virtue as cool as a lotus," the Victor.

He is that one endowed with virtue as cool as a lotus. For just as a lotus born in water is cooled by the water, so too, because the Blessed One has abandoned the burning of the defilements through the virtue of the Path, that virtue of his is cool, exceedingly cool.
"Endowed with that" means he praises him as being "joined with a cool virtue (sīla) like a lotus pond.

"Earth-enduring" (pathavīsahana) means one who is endowed with patience (khanti), or one possessing patience, like the earth. It is called "earth" (pathavī) because trees, mountains, and so forth rest (patiṭṭhahanti) upon it;
it is the ground. The root *path* signifies "resting," and the suffix *-avī* is added. Alternatively, [it may be explained differently].
It is called *pathavī* because it has arisen (*jāta*) as something distinct (*puthu*). The suffix *-ī* is applied in the sense of a taddhita derivative from the root *jan*.

*Sahanaṃ* (patience) means that which is endured (*sahayate*) or forgiven (*khamiyate*); or, that which endures or forgives is *sahanaṃ*, meaning patient forbearance (*adhivāsanakhanti*). The verbal root *saha-* takes the suffix *-ana* in the sense of patience.
One who possesses such endurance or forgiveness like the earth is *pathavīsahano*, namely, the Conqueror (*jino*). That is *pathavīsahanaṃ*. For just as the earth—

Just as the earth endures everything placed upon it, whether pure or impure, and does not give rise to aversion or attachment, so too the Victor endures all objects—whether desirable or undesirable—and does not give rise to aversion or attachment therein;
this is the intended meaning when he is praised as "the Earth-Endurer. Thus it is said in the Apadāna-pāḷi:
“They do not cling to gain or loss, nor to honor or dishonor;
the Buddhas are like the earth, therefore they are not to be offended.
The connection is: “I bow down to the Conqueror, I pay homage to him.”

This, however, is the summary of the connection here: [He is] endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, born from the power of the merit of manifold perfections, characterized by the water of a hundred merits;
stainless, being free from dust due to the absence of the dust of passion and so forth;
possessing the likeness of the sky, meaning he possesses the omniscient knowledge comparable to space; and having fortitude equal to Meru, like Mount Sineru.

I reverently bow down and pay homage to the Victor, the Buddha, who has conquered the five Māras; who possesses immovable concentration (*acalasamādhi*); who is endowed with virtue as cool as a lotus in water;
who is associated with incalculable virtue that is exceedingly cool like a lotus born in water; who, like the earth, is patient and endowed with forbearance (*khanti*);
or rather, who is possessed of patience. Thus I worship him with due respect.
The commentary on the twelve verses of homage is completed.
He who is the Buddha, the wise one, shining day by day like the sun,
generating joy while seated upon his stone throne;
Seated, he taught the Dhamma that bestows the bliss of peace, incomparable even for the gods; I bow to him constantly. 13.
Having thus paid homage to the Jina with these twelve verses, [he now speaks] regarding those in the city of Tāvatiṃsa, headed by the mother, the gods, and the sons.

Having praised the Buddha—who, by virtue of being the teacher of the Abhidhamma to the devas born [in the Brahma-world]—and wishing to pay homage to him, he spoke the verse beginning with "yo buddho sumati...

This verse, moreover, should be understood as a *pahassiṇī* consisting of thirteen syllables, because it is composed of the *ma*, *na*, *ja*, and *ra* ganas, along with three heavy syllables (*ekagaru*) and ten light syllables (*yatī*). For this has been stated in the *Vuttodaya*: "mnā jarā..."
"Go tidasayatippahassiṇī sā":

this is its meaning. In whichever foot there are the *magaṇa* and *nagaṇa*, followed by *ja*, *ra*, and *ra*, and then a *go* (long syllable), and if it "tidesayati," "tiyati," and "dasayati," that verse is called a *pahassiṇī* verse. In that regard:
The connection is: "Sumati, the Buddha, who taught the Dhamma to the gods. *Yo* is an indefinite pronoun (*sabbanāmapada*).
Its specific denotation (*vacanattha*) need not be explained. For it has been said by those learned in grammar:
"Conventional terms, verbs, particles, prefixes, and vocatives;..."
"Regarding the term *sabbanāma*, no grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) has been made for these six.
Alternatively: that which goes to the state of being a pronoun (*sabbanāma*); or, that which goes to the state of expressing the indefinite;
or, that which goes—that is, proceeds—by way of being a pronoun; or, that which goes—that is, proceeds—by way of expressing the indefinite. By way of being a pronoun...
That which is to be gone to or known is "yo"; or that by means of which there is no fixed object [of going or knowing] is "yo.

The word "ya" is obtained as a designation for all nouns. "Yo," "yā," etc., have the meaning of "so" (that). A "Buddha" is one who has penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, or one who has penetrated all knowable phenomena.
Furthermore, the etymological explanation of that term has already been stated above. A "Sumati" is one who possesses the beautiful knowledge of omniscience, or the knowledge of teaching.
Or rather: because it is said that he "taught the Dhamma to the gods," here *sabbaññuta-ñāṇa* (omniscient knowledge) is called *sumati*.
It is *mati* because it "thinks" (*manati*) or knows all knowable phenomena (*sabbañeyya-dhamma*) or the phenomena to be taught. The root *man* means "knowledge.

*Sumati* is beautiful wisdom (*sundarā mati*), capable of knowing all knowable phenomena according to their true nature (*yathāsabhāva*), and capable of knowing those various kinds of phenomena that are to be taught.
And it is endowed with the threefold capacity, being capable of discerning the inclinations, dispositions, and so forth, of those persons who are to be awakened.

By the term "Sumati" (Possessor of Good Wisdom), he indicates that it is only the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*) that is capable of being the source for the Abhidhamma discourse, and nothing else; thus he demonstrates the unique, non-common nature of the Abhidhamma discourse.
[The text] shows this. One who has beautiful wisdom (*sumati*), or in whom it exists, is *sumati*; that is, the Buddha. This is a compound ending with a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).

According to the rule *tadassatthīti vā*, by the word *vā* (or) in the sutta, the suffix *ap* is applied. It is just like the term *pītisukha*. For it is said in the commentary on the *Pārājika-khaṇḍa*:
"This joy (*pīti*) and this happiness (*sukha*) belong to this jhāna, or exist in this jhāna; therefore, this jhāna is called 'joy-and-happiness' (*pītisukha*)."

*Diveti* means on the day. It is called *divo* because it shines (*dibbati*) there by means of the sun’s radiance. The verbal root *div-* signifies brilliance; with the suffix *-a*, it becomes *diva*.

On that day (*tasmiṃ dive*). *Sūriyo iva* means like the sun. He who makes the day is the maker of the day (*divākara*), namely the sun. [The compound] *divā-kara* consists of the word *divā* (day) and the verbal root *kar-* (to make), with the suffix *-a*.
Alternatively, he who has rays (*karo*) during the day (*divā*) is the maker of the day (*divākara*). For the word *kara* denotes a ray.
"Sobhanto" means being resplendent. He is "Sobhanto," the Buddha, because he shines and radiates with six-colored rays and so forth.

[The root] *subh* belongs to the *sobha* group, or it is used in the sense of splendor (*ditti*), with the suffix *-anta*. The meaning is that the Blessed One shines and radiates in the midst of the gods by means of his six-colored rays, his thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*), and his eighty minor characteristics (*anubyañjana-lakkhaṇa*). Regarding the phrase "in the generation of joy":
It is for the purpose of producing the joy and gladness that does not cause the gods to burn, or for the production of affection. *Ramaṇaṃ* means delight. The root *ram* signifies sporting.

That which generates or produces this is "delight-generating" (*ratijanana*). It is a stone throne (*silāsana*). The suffix *-yu* is added to the root *jan*, preceded by the word *rati*, in the sense of generating.

"In that delight-generating [throne]" refers to the stone throne located in the abode of the Thirty-three (*tidasālaya*), produced or placed at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, sixty *yojanas* in length.

On a stone seat (silāsana) fifty yojanas in length, fifteen yojanas in width, and the color of a red *kampa* flower—resembling the *jayasumana* blossom—smooth, delicate, and known as "Pale *Kampa*" (*paṇḍukambala*).
It is called a "stone" (*sila*) because it is frequented by Sakka; from the root *sidh* meaning "to serve," with the suffix *alap*.
It is called a "seat" (*āsana*) because one sits upon it; or alternatively, because one comes (*āgantvā*) [to sit].

It is called a seat (*āsana*) because one sits upon it (*seviyati ettha*). The root *sidh* preceded by the prefix *ā-* signifies sitting; with the suffix *yu*, it becomes *āsana*. A stone itself as a seat is a "stone-seat" (*silāsana*).

The "stone-seat of Paṇḍukambala" is what is meant here. Upon that stone-seat: "sitting" (*āsīno*) means sitting while surrounded by a host of devas who have come from ten thousand world-systems and sat down together. Sitting is the act of sitting; thus, he is "sitting. All around...

*Āsīno* means "he sits" or "he dwells. He sits—that is, he settles down—facing toward the discourse on the Abhidhamma; thus he is *āsīno*. The verbal root *sīd-* preceded by the prefix *ā-* denotes sitting.

Alternatively, it is derived from the roots *visar-* (to spread) or *gati-avasāna-* (the end of going), with the suffix *-tap*. For this, there is the substitution of *ī*, the replacement of *ṇ* by *n*, and the elision of the final portion of the root.
*Sivasukhadaṃ* means "bestowing the bliss of Nibbāna. It is called *sivaṃ* because it is cultivated (*seviyati*) by the Noble Ones; it is Nibbāna.
May this service be successful. Alternatively, *sivaṃ* (peace) is that wherein one is completely (*sam-*) calmed (*upa-samati*) from the fire of passion and so forth;
it is *nibbāna*. The root *sidh* [is used] in the sense of calming. However, in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā-ṭīkā*, it is stated: "It is *sivaṃ* because it makes for the state of security (*khemabhāva*);
or it is *sivaṃ* because it is to be cultivated by those who fear *saṃsāra*; the suffix *-vap-* is applied by means of the rule beginning with *yadādi*. It brings happiness (*sukhayati*).
*Sukhaṃ*. The meaning is that whatever arises [in one] makes that person happy. Alternatively, it is *sukhaṃ* because it thoroughly (*su*) digs away (*khanati*) suffering;

the root *khan* preceded by *su* is used in the sense of "tearing open" (*avadāraṇe*), with the suffix *kvi*. The bliss of *siva*, which is Nibbāna, is *sivasukha*; that which gives this is *sivasukhada*, namely the Abhidhamma Dhamma.
For he who [studies] the Abhidhamma Dhamma... [suffix *a*]. (The compound is formed from the words *sivasukha* and the root *dā* with the suffix *a*.)
"He hears" means that he bestows upon him the bliss of Nibbāna.
"He taught the Dhamma to the gods" is to be connected as "he taught the Dhamma to the gods.

And here, "Dhamma" refers to the Abhidhamma—the Dhamma that is diverse through various methods, profound, subtle and delicate, and difficult to see. It is called "Dhamma" because it maintains its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
The Abhidhamma Piṭaka is the Dhamma that is "retained by the wise, not by fools. The verbal root *dhr* (dhar) means "to retain," and the suffix *-ma* is a gerundive (*ramma-paccaya*).
That Dhamma [is for] "the gods" (*devānam*), meaning for the gods of rebirth, headed by those sons of the gods who were one's mother in the human world in the past.
For this is stated in the Aṭṭhasālinī commentary:
“Placing his mother at the forefront, by the power of her wisdom, he set forth the path of the Abhidhamma discourse for the devas.
And here, the meaning of the word *mātaraṃ* should be understood as “a son of the devas who had previously been a mother in the human world. For this has been stated in the *Jinālaṅkāra-pāḷi*:
“Then, taking her son, the mother went to her own home;
having passed away on the seventh day, she went and attained the state of a son of the gods.
And in the commentary (*Ṭīkā*) it says: “The Bodhisatta’s mother, having died seven days after the birth from the womb, [was reborn] in the Tusita city...”
It is said, "He was reborn as a son of the gods. And here, it is precisely by the term *devaputta* (son of a god) that this is expressed.
Furthermore, in the *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā* regarding the Elder Kāḷudāyī, it says:

"'Surrounded'—this feminine designation is made with reference to the female state established in his previous existence, or his status as a deity; however, his rebirth among the gods occurred in the form of a male."

It has been stated [thus]. And in the *Jātakaṭīkā*, it is expressed by the term "Mātudevaputta" as follows: "At the time of descending from the deva-world, having taught the Abhidhamma Piṭaka for three months to Mātudevaputta. Furthermore, in the *Abhidhammāvatāraṭīkā*, it says:
"'Of the devas'—that is, of those who at that time received the Dhamma, the inhabitants of ten thousand world-systems, headed by Mātudevaputta."
Regarding the phrase "upapatti-devānaṃ," it is expressed by the term *devaputta* (son of a god) in the case of Queen Mahāmāyā. In the *Sirīmahāmāyā-saṃyutta*, it is stated using the term *devaputta*:
"Queen Sirīmahāmāyā, having lived for only seven days, passed away and was reborn as a son of the gods (*devaputta*) in the Tusita heaven through the power of her own merit.
And in the *Maṇidīpa-ṭīkā*, regarding the word "mother" (*mātaraṃ*), it says: "In a previous existence in the human world..."
The meaning is "a son of the gods who has become one's mother. For it is said: "After giving birth to the Bodhisatta, Queen Mahāmāyā remained for only seven days;
having passed away from here, she was reborn in the Tusita heaven in male form, not in female form.
Therefore, the primary meaning of the term *mātaram* should be understood as "a son of the gods who has become one's mother."
In the *Madhusāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā*, however, it says:
“The father of the Great Sage was named Suddhodana,
and the mother of the Buddha was named Māyā.”
Having carried the Bodhisatta in her womb,
Gotamī rejoices in the Heaven of the Thirty-three after the breaking up of the body;
she, having passed away from here, has died.
“Endowed with divine sensual pleasures,
she rejoices in the five strands of sense-desire,
surrounded by those hosts of gods.”— The Elder’s Commentary.
In the commentary on that [passage], they say: "The feminine designation ‘surrounded’ (*parivāritā*) was made with reference to her established feminine nature or her status as a deity;
however, because it is stated that her rebirth as a deva occurred in a male form, the word ‘mother’ (*mātaraṃ*) is used here in the sense of her human existence.
But this is not included in the *Thera-aṭṭhakathā*. In the commentaries and sub-commentaries on other [texts]...

Furthermore, there is no such statement [to that effect]. Nor is there a resolution made at the time of the aspiration [to become a Buddha] such as, "Having been the mother of a Buddha, may I later become a man.
Moreover, according to the thirtyfold nature [of the Bodhisattva], there is no state of masculinity for the mother of a Buddha.
Therefore, it is said that the wise declare this should be investigated. However, that [objection] is not to be accepted. Why? Because of the statement involving doubt.
It must be investigated because it is stated that "the wise say so," and because it directly contradicts the explanations found in the aforementioned commentaries and sub-commentaries.
For the word *devatā* applies to a son of the gods (*devaputta*), to Brahmā, and to a daughter of the gods (*devadhītā*).
Thus, in such passages as "Then a certain deity, at the end of the night, of surpassing beauty... it refers to a son of the gods.
For it is said in the *Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā*: "‘A certain one’ (*aññataro*) is an indefinite designation. She was not well-known by name or clan;
therefore she is called ‘a certain one. ‘Deva’ is the same as ‘devatā. This term is common to both male and female, but here it refers specifically to a male.
He is a son of a god (*devaputta*), yet he is called ‘devatā’ by way of a gender-neutral name. — *Sunīta Thera Apadāna*
In the canonical texts, in passages such as “Then those seven hundred sublime deities and Brahmās, having emerged from their celestial mansions,” it refers to *brahmā*.
In the *Padīpavimānavatthu* of the Canon, it is said:
“O deity, you who stand there with such exquisite beauty;”
"Shining in all directions like a star among the herbs"—in such passages [the word *devadhītā*] refers to a celestial maiden (*devadhītā*).
Furthermore, the word *parivāritā* should also be understood in this way.
Therefore, the statement made in the *Theraṭṭhakathā* composed by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla, as well as the statement in the *Jātakaṭīkā* by the Elder Ācariya Sumaṅgala—
Having taken the words stated in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā* as authoritative, the meaning should be understood simply as "the son of Mātādevī.
However, some teachers nowadays, relying on the word *parivāritā* found in the *Therāpāḷi* and the statement in the *Madhusāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā*, say she was "the daughter of Mātādevī.
But that should be regarded as merely their own opinion. [The word] *adesi* means...
He spoke by means of omniscient knowledge preceded by great compassion. "The peerless discourse" is the connection [of the phrase].
Here, "discourse" (tanti) refers to the Buddha. "Peerless" (asadisa) means one who has no counterpart. He is "peerless" because there is no person who is his equal;
the meaning is that in the world with its devas, there is no person equal to the Buddha in qualities such as virtue. Therefore he said:
In the Vinaya Mahāvagga Pāḷi:
“I have no teacher; there is none equal to me.
In this world with its devas, there is no one who is my peer.”
"Constantly, perpetually, and continuously"—this is the meaning of "all the time, without interruption. "I bow always to that peerless Buddha"—this is the grammatical connection.
This, then, is the concise interpretation here: *Sumati* refers to one who possesses the wind (or flow) of beautiful omniscient knowledge, or the wind of the knowledge of teaching.
To such a Buddha as he is—shining and radiant like the sun (*divākara*) day after day—he [bows] while generating delight.
Seated upon the stone throne named Paṇḍukambala, which produces joy and gladness for the Atappaka deities—

or rather, which generates affection— he, while sitting, taught and spoke the Dhamma— the Abhidhamma— which bestows the bliss of Śiva, that is, the bliss of Nibbāna, to the deities who had been reborn there,
headed by the mother of the gods and the sons of the former deities; [a teaching] peerless and without equal.
"I always and constantly bow down to and worship that Buddha.
The commentary on the thirteenth verse of praise is completed.
He whose lotus-feet have beautiful, fine lines...
The Protector attained that which is truly beyond comparison— unperturbed by the three worlds and free from all agitation.
I pay homage to that peerless one, honored by the entire world.

14. Having thus paid homage to the Buddha with the thirteenth verse, he now speaks the verse beginning with "yo pādapaṅkaja" (he whose lotus-feet...), desiring to pay homage after praising the Buddha for the hundred-and-eight marks of wheels with variegated patterns appearing on the soles of his feet.
This, moreover, is a *vasantatilakā* verse, consisting of fourteen syllables and composed of the *ta*, *bha*, *ja*, *ja*, and *ga* ganas, along with two *garu* (heavy) syllables.
It should be recognized. For this has been stated in the *Vuttodaya*: "The *vasantatilakā* is said to have the gaṇas ta, bha, ja, ta, bha, ja, followed by a *jagaṇa*, a *guru*, and another *guru*.

This is its meaning: that verse in which each quarter-verse consists of the gaṇas *ta*, *bha*, *ja*, *ta*, *bha*, *ja*, a *jagaṇa*, a *guru*, and a *guru*, is called a *vasantatilakā* verse by the masters of prosody.

In this context, the connection is as follows: "I bow to that Protector (Nātha), who has attained incomparability in the world through his two lotus-feet—whose soles are flawless and undisturbed—and who is honored by the entire world, peerless.

Here, rather than following the sequence of the words, we shall provide the commentary according to the sequence of the meaning. "Yo nātho" means "he who," referring to one such as he for all sentient beings.
The Buddha is the refuge. Furthermore, that word [“attains”] should be connected as the agent to the phrase “he shall surely attain that state.

As for the meaning of the word *nātha*, it has already been explained above. Regarding the term *avikalehi*: the meaning is “complete with all the characteristics of the wheels on the soles of the feet, lacking nothing whatsoever.
That which moves or goes in an uneven manner is *vikala*. [This is derived from] the verbal root *kal* preceded by the prefix *vi* in the sense of “going,” with the suffix *a*.

"Avikalā" means there is nothing deficient in her lines; it refers to the lines on the feet. The meaning is that in both feet, there is no deficiency whatsoever in the clearly manifest form of their configuration.
"By those which are avikalā" means by those that are not deficient. "Nirākulehi" means by those devoid of confusion.
"Asaṃmissehi asaṃsaṭṭhehi" means by those that do not intermingle with or mix together one another among the marks of the wheel-signs on the feet.

Meaning: It binds thoroughly and firmly, thus it is *ākula*; the root *kul* preceded by the prefix *ā-* has the sense of binding. Alternatively, it thoroughly covers what is beautiful, thus it is *ākula*;
that foot-print (*pādarāji*) which has no such *ākula*—that is, no mutual intermingling—is *nirākulā*.
[This refers to] the foot-print. By those two [terms], *nirākulehi*. Furthermore, those two words [refer to] the phrase "by the soft ridges of the lotus-like feet."
This is the qualification. Regarding the phrase "with the lines on the soles of his lotus-feet":
it is called a *pāda* because one moves (*padati*) by means of it; the root *pada* signifies "going.
It is called a *paṅkaja* because it is born in mud (*paṅka*); thus, it is a lotus (*paduma*). A lotus that is reckoned as a foot is a "lotus-foot" (*pādapaṅkaja*). It is like a lotus.
A foot, or a lotus-foot; [this refers to] the foot. It is "mudu" because it is soft and functions through its quality of smoothness;

the root *muda* means "to go," with the suffix *u*. It is "talaṃ" because one stands or rests upon it; the root *tala* means "to stand," with the suffix *a*. That which is both soft (*mudu*) and a surface (*talaṃ*) is "muduttalaṃ.
The soft surface of the lotus-foot is "pādapaṅkajamuduttalaṃ. It is "rājikā" because it shines or is seen; the root *rāja* means "to shine," with the suffix *ika*.
*Rājikā* means that which shines or is beautiful (*rājati sobhati etena*). The suffix *ṇika* is used in the sense of "shining" (*sobhane*) after the root *rāj*.
The term *pādapaṅkajamuduttalarājika* refers to those [marks] on the soft soles of the lotus-feet known as the one hundred and eight marks of the wheel (*cakralakkhaṇa*).
Furthermore, those one hundred and eight marks of the wheels on the feet should be understood in this way: on the soft soles of the Blessed One’s lotus-feet...

The hub is visible in the middle. The circular lines concealed by the hub are visible. The rim encircling the face of the hub is visible. The opening of the axle-hole is visible. The spokes are visible.
The circular lines on the spokes are visible. The felly is visible. The jewel-like ornaments on the felly are visible.
This much, for now, is exactly as it appears in the text (*pāḷi*). However, the section on the "fully expanded" (*sampahula*) has not yet been included; it is as follows:
It should be depicted: a spear, a *śrīvatsa*, a *nandyāvarta*, a *sovattika* (lotus), an ear-ornament (*vaṭaṃsaka*),
a *vaḍḍhamānaka* (vase of fortune), a pair of fish, a *bhaddapīṭha* (auspicious throne), a hook, a lance, a palace, an archway, a white parasol, a sword,
a palm-leaf fan, a peacock-feather fan, a yak-tail whisk, a turban, an alms-bowl, a garland of jewels and flowers, and a blue lotus.
The red lotus, the white lotus, the *paduma*, the *puṇḍarīka*, the full water-pot, the full bowl, the ocean,
the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), the Himalayas, Sineru, the moon and sun, the constellations, the four great continents, and the two thousand minor islands—
even including the retinue of a wheel-turning monarch— all this is merely the entourage of the mark of the wheel. Thus it is only to that extent.
It should be understood that this was stated in the *Majjhima-ṭīkā*.
However, in the *Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā*, it says: "The mark of the wheels [on the soles] means that on the two soles of the feet, two wheels have arisen;
in each [sole], there are about a thousand spokes joined together. The rim is golden in color."
The hub is the color of a sapphire. In its center, around its circumference, and facing its hub, there are circular lines;
in the middle there is a hollow, and around the rim of the wheel, outside the felloe, there are [the following designs]:
a spear, a śrīvatsa, a nandyāvarta, a sovatthika, an ear-ornament, a vardhamānaka, a bhadrāsana, a hook, a palace, a gateway, and a white parasol.
A sword, a palm-leaf fan, a peacock-feather whisk, a yak-tail fan, a turban, an alms-bowl, a jewel, a garland of jasmine,
a blue lotus, a red lotus, a red water-lily, a white water-lily, a white lotus, a full vase, a full bowl, the ocean,
the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, the Himavat mountain, Mount Meru, the solar disc, and the lunar disc.
The lunar mansion with its retinue; the four great continents with their retinues; the wheel-turning monarch endowed with the seven treasures with his retinue;
the right-spiraling white conch shell; the pair of golden fish; the discus-weapon; the seven great Ganges rivers; the seven principal mountain ranges;
the seven seas of milk; the golden king of swans; the crocodile; the bannered flag; the golden palanquin; and the golden yak-tail fan.
Mount Kelāsa, the lion king, the tiger king, the horse king Valāhaka,
the elephant king Uposatha-Chaddanta, the nāga king Vāsuki, the swan king, the bull king, the elephant king Erāvaṇa, the golden makara,
the four-faced golden ship, the cow with her calf, the kiṃpuruṣa, the kinnarī, the karavīka bird, the peacock king, the crane king, and the cakravāka king.

It is said: "The king of the *jīvañjīvaka* birds, the six celestial worlds (*devaloka*), and the sixteen Brahma worlds—these many marks of supreme auspiciousness are discernible on the soles of his feet.
By this statement, it should be understood that the mark of the hundred-and-eight wheels on the feet is complete.

This is connected with the phrase "by the three worlds. The meaning is: "by the three worlds of sense-desire (*kāma*), form (*rūpa*), and formlessness (*arūpa*). Furthermore, the literal meaning of that [phrase] is as follows:
This has already been explained below. Furthermore, this [term] is used in the instrumental case to express the sense of the locative (*katvatthe karaṇavacana*).

The connection of that word with the word *nirupameyya* is by way of its being the agent (*kattubhāvena*). *Nirupameyyatan* means the state of being immeasurable (*appameyyabhāvaṃ*). That which is to be compared is *upameyya*. The suffix *ṇya* is applied to the root *mā* preceded by the prefix *upa* in the sense of measurement (*pamāne*).
The state of being that which is to be compared is *upameyyatā*. There is no state of being that which is to be compared for it (*natthi upameyyataṃ assa*).

*“Of the mustard seed” (*rājikassa*) means “the state of being beyond comparison” (*nirupameyyatam*). Alternatively, that which has no object of comparison (*upameyya*) is “beyond comparison” (*nirupameyyo*);

here, the mark of the wheel on the foot (*pādacakkalakkhaṇa-rājika*) is what is obtained. The abstract state of that is *nirupameyyatam*. Furthermore, that word [is the object] in the phrase “only when he attains that state” (*sampāpuṇeyeva*).
The connection is with the words “only when he attains” (*sampāpuṇeyeva*). The meaning is “he goes rightly. But why?
It attains incomparability through the three worlds by means of the soft soles of its lotus-like feet.
This is because no other being—whether god or human—possesses the mark of the wheel on the center of the sole of the foot except for the Buddha.

Indeed, it is only on the soft soles of the Blessed One’s lotus-like feet that the one hundred and eight marks of the wheel, produced by the power of his perfections and merit, are fully present, and not on those of others.
Therefore, he attains incomparability.
"Honored by the whole world" means worshipped by the entire world. He is one who should be honored and worshipped by the whole world of gods and humans;
thus he is "honored by the whole world," and a Protector (Nātha) is found. For when a Tathāgata has arisen, whatever gods and humans possess great influence—
They honor the Buddha, let alone others. For instance, Brahmā Sahampati honors the Tathāgata with a jeweled garland as large as Mount Sineru.

Likewise, other gods and humans—such as King Bimbisāra, the King of Kosala, and others—even though the Blessed One has attained *nibbāna*, have offered ninety-six crores of wealth in his name; and the Great King Aśoka [did so] throughout the entire Jambudīpa.
He established eighty-four thousand monasteries; what need is there to mention the honor paid to others?
It is said that he was "unequalled" (*asama*), meaning peerless among all humans, gods, and Brahmas; the sense is that there is no person equal to him.
He is "the Peerless Lord" (*asamo nātho*). Furthermore, he was adorned with the eighty minor marks and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
He possesses a body of diverse forms. He is the Dhamma-body, perfected with the jewels of qualities such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) which is pure in every aspect.
Furthermore, he has reached the supreme pinnacle of greatness in merit, greatness in strength, greatness in supernormal power (iddhi), greatness in fame, and greatness in wisdom;
therefore, the meaning is that there is no one equal or similar to the Tathāgata. That is the "Unequaled. "Him" refers to the Protector (Nātha).
"I bow" is the connection [of the words].

This, however, is the concise explanation here: To that Lord, who is such as he is, the refuge for all beings, the Buddha, whose lotus-feet possess complete and unimpaired, unconfused and free from disorder, soft and smooth rows of toes—[to him I bow].
With the hundred royal marks of wheels produced on the smooth soles of his feet— which are counted as lotuses— and which have become the makers of the three worlds,
he surely attains, reaches, or arrives at incomparability, immeasurability, or the state of being beyond measure;
he is honored by the entire world and worshipped by the whole world, peerless among all humans, gods, and brahmās.
"I bow to that peerless Lord.
The commentary on the fourteenth verse of homage is complete.
[I pay homage] to the Buddha, the assembly of men and non-men, whose mind is steadfast.
I pay homage to that compassionate one of infinite wisdom,
who has dispelled the darkness with the radiance of the lamp of insight, and who brings benefit and welfare to both gods and humans through his longing for their true well-being.

15. Thus, having paid homage to the Protector with the fourteenth verse, and now desiring to worship the Buddha by praising him with seven qualities beginning with "The gathering of men and non-men" (*narānarasamosaraṇa*), he spoke the verse beginning with "The gathering of men and non-men.
This verse, however, consists of fourteen syllables and is composed in the *Vasantatilakā* meter, being constructed from the *ta*, *bha*, *ja*, and *ga* gaṇas along with two heavy syllables (*garu*).
They are to be seen. As for the proof here, it is exactly as stated below.
Regarding the phrase *narānarasamosaraṇaṃ*, the analysis of the words is *naraanarasamaṃ osaraṇaṃ*.
The meaning is "the common gathering place, the place where humans and gods meet together. The etymological definition of the term *narānara* has already been explained above.
It is called a *samosaraṇa* because people come together and assemble there; thus, the Buddha is a *samosaraṇa*. The root *sar* preceded by the prefixes *sama* and *ava* means "going" (*gati*).
He is the *samosaraṇa* for humans and non-humans—that is, for gods and men—therefore he is the *narānarasamosaraṇa*, the Buddha.
For just as a great banyan tree is a gathering place for flocks of birds desiring fruit, so too is the Buddha for those in the world.
It is a gathering place, a meeting point, or a refuge for humans and devas who desire supramundane attainment;
therefore, he praises it as "the assembly of humans and non-humans" (*narānarasamosaraṇa*).

"Steadfast" (*dhīta*) means one whose mind is concentrated (*samāhitacitta*). Here, the word *atta* is the same term found in expressions such as "right aspiration toward oneself" (*attasammāpaṇidhi*).

It should be understood as denoting the mind (*citta*). That by which, or in which, associated states (*sampayutta-dhammā*) are supported (*dhiyati*) or established (*ṭhapiyati*) upon a single object is *dhiti*;
this is concentration (*samādhi*). The root *dhā* is used in the sense of supporting. That which eats (*adati*) or takes hold of (*ādadāti*) the object is *atta*;
this is the mind (*citta*). The root *ada* is used in the sense of taking. One whose mind is *dhita*—that is, concentrated (*samāhita*)—is *dhitatta*; such is the Buddha. That is *dhitatta*.
"By the radiance of the lamp of wisdom" means by means of the light of the lamp consisting of the knowledge of the path to arahantship, which acts as the instrument.

"Wisdom" (paññā) is that which understands; it is the knowledge of the path to arahantship. The meaning is that it penetrates the Dhamma of the Four Truths in all its aspects according to their true nature.
Wisdom itself is the "lamp of wisdom" because, through the abandoning of the obscurations of the knowable, it illuminates the true nature of phenomena in every way.

It illuminates, thus it is *juti* (radiance); it is the light of the lamp of wisdom. The root *judh* means "to shine. Wisdom itself as the lamp is the radiance; thus, it is the "radiance of the lamp of wisdom" (*paññāpadīpajuti*).
Alternatively, it is the radiance of the lamp of wisdom; this compound, however, should be understood according to the method of non-distinction and distinction (*abhedabhedūpacāra*).
By that radiance of the lamp of wisdom.

"Having destroyed the darkness" (*vihata-andhakāraṃ*): this refers to the gloom of delusion (*moha*), which is synonymous with ignorance (*avijjā*) and is to be destroyed. It is "destroyed" (*vihata*) because it is specifically eliminated through the abandonment of the defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā-kilesa*). The verbal root *han* (in *vipubbahanadhātu*) signifies injury or destruction.

It is called "darkness" (*andhakāra*) because it makes [reality] blind and dark; it is the delusion known as ignorance. Delusion is termed "darkness" because it resembles darkness in its quality of concealing the true nature of objects.
It is so called. Alternatively, it is "darkness" (*andhakāra*) because it makes the eye of wisdom blind; that is, delusion (*moha*).
It is formed from the root *kṛ* with the prefix *andha* and the suffix *ṇa*. One by whom darkness has been destroyed is "one who has destroyed darkness," namely, the Buddha.
To him, the one who has destroyed darkness. For just as in the world a lamp destroys darkness by its own radiance, so too does the wisdom of the Buddha’s path to Arhatship.
It is said that it destroys the darkness of ignorance. However, this [lamp] is called a "low comparison.
For one possessed of wisdom, even while sitting in a single cross-legged posture, the ten-thousandfold world system becomes a single illumination. Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, there are these four illuminations. Which four? The illumination of the moon, the illumination of the sun, the illumination of fire, and the illumination of wisdom."
“Lamp. Monks, these are the four lamps. Of these four lamps, monks, the foremost is this:
the lamp of wisdom. Regarding the phrase “the darkness dispelled by the radiance of the lamp of wisdom,” here, by the expression “the radiance of the lamp of wisdom,” [it refers to] the Buddha’s...

He shows the knowledge of the path to arahantship primarily. By that [knowledge], he illustrates the knowledge of the perfections (*pāramī-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), and the knowledge of the lower paths and fruits through figurative designation (*phalūpacāra*).
By illustrating those, he proclaims the abandoning of the darkness of ignorance through the figurative designation of the first cause.
By proclaiming that, he indicates the attainment of the knowledge of the fruit of arahantship through the figurative designation of the second cause.
He contemplates it. By means of that contemplation, he magnifies the attainment of all the Buddha-qualities, such as omniscience, by way of the third figurative cause.
Now, one might ask: "Is it not the case that for all those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), the destruction of darkness through the radiance of the lamp of wisdom is possible?

Then why is the praise of the Buddha made by means of a specific quality not shared with others? [The answer is: Because of the state of being unique and unsurpassed due to the abandonment of even the latent tendencies (savāsanappahāna).

In terms of possibility: for although all those whose taints are destroyed possess the radiance of the lamp of wisdom that dispels darkness, the noble disciples and paccekabuddhas do not possess the abandonment of defilements together with their underlying tendencies (*savāsanā*).
Only in the case of the perfectly enlightened Buddhas (*sammāsambuddhā*) does a distinction exist in the abandonment of defilements through the abandonment of even the underlying tendencies;
thus, it is by virtue of this excellence, namely the abandonment of the darkness of ignorance, [that they are distinguished].
He praises the Blessed One alone as one who has dispelled the darkness by the radiance of the lamp of wisdom.
"Desiring the welfare" (*atthābhikāma*) means desiring exceedingly the purpose (*payojana*) of the world of beings, known as both mundane and supramundane.
"Welfare" (*attha*) is that which exists when its cause is present; it is the fruit. The root *as-* [is used] with the suffix *-tha* in the sense of "being. That [welfare] is "exceedingly" (*abhi*).
*Kāmeti* means "he desires," thus *atthābhikāmo* (one who desires the goal). The root *mud*, preceded by *abhi* and accompanied by the prefix *attha*, is used in the sense of desiring;
with the suffix *ṇa*, it forms *atthābhikāma*. *Taṃ atthābhikāmaṃ* refers to that one who desires the goal. *Naradevahitāvahaṃ* means bringing welfare to humans and gods.
One who leads (*narati*) humans to their welfare is a *naro* (human); alternatively, one who is led (*nariyati*)—that is, carried away—by one's own karma is a *naro* (human). [The root is] *nara*.

For it is said: "The world is led by karma. They are called *devas* because they sport and play with the qualities of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), the superknowledges (*abhiññā*), mental sovereignty (*cittissariya*), and so forth;
or else, they are called *devas* because they dwell among them. The verbal root *div* is used in the sense of playing and so on, with the suffix *ṇa*.

Humans and gods are *naradevas*. It is called *hita* because it increases or grows. The verbal root *hidh* is used in the sense of increasing; thus, it refers to the fruit (*phala*). [This is] for the *naradevas*.
"Beneficial" (*hita*) means beneficial for humans and gods; that which brings about this is "the bringer of benefit for humans and gods" (*naradevahitāvaha*), namely, the Buddha.
The root *vah* preceded by the prefix *ā* and accompanied by the words *nara*, *deva*, and *hita* is used in the sense of "carrying.

For it is said that the Buddha sustains all gods and humans through his teaching of the Dhamma for the sake of their mundane and supramundane prosperity; thus, he is the "bringer of benefit for humans and gods. [He is] compassionate, the path, and infinite.

Regarding "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*): here, the word-division is *kāruṇikaṃ aggaṃ anantañāṇaṃ*. In that context, *kāruṇikaṃ* means one who is endowed with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all sentient beings, or one who possesses great compassion.

*Karuṇā* [is derived as follows]: from the root *kṛ*, meaning "to scatter," with the suffix *-uṇa*. The sense is that it scatters or removes the suffering of others. The verbal root *kir* signifies "removal. The suffix *-uṇa* is applied. Thus, the meaning is: it scatters and removes the suffering of others.
Alternatively, it is called *karuṇā* because it "hurts" (*kināti*). Here, the root *ki-* means "to harm," and the suffix *-ruṇa* is applied.

The meaning is that when there is suffering in another, it "hurts" or afflicts the compassionate one. Or else, it is *karuṇā* because, when there is suffering in another, it causes the heart of the virtuous to tremble;

here, the root *kara-* takes the suffix *-uṇa*. Alternatively, *kaṃ* is said to mean "happiness" (*sukha*); it is *karuṇā* because it "obstructs" (*rundhati*) that [happiness]. This is with the word *kaṃ* as a prefix (*upapada*).
The suffix *yup* is added to the verbal root *rudh*, meaning "to obstruct. For this [compassion] has the characteristic of the desire to remove the suffering of others.

The meaning is that, through its disregard for one's own happiness, it obstructs—that is, hinders—the happiness of the compassionate ones. One who is endowed with compassion (*karuṇā*) or great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is "compassionate" (*kāruṇika*).

Alternatively, one who possesses compassion is "compassionate"; this refers to the Buddha. That state of being compassionate is "compassionateness" (*kāruṇikatā*). It is called "supreme" (*agga*) by virtue of the greatness of his birth, merit, and qualities.

He is called *agga* (the foremost) because he goes to (*ajati*), that is, attains, the state of being the most excellent among all beings; thus he is the Buddha. The verbal root *aja* signifies "going.

He is *Buddha* because, by virtue of his birth in an unadulterated kshatriya lineage, he is preeminent in terms of *jāti* (birth); because, through the merit of fulfilling the perfections (*pāramīs*), he is preeminent in terms of *puñña* (merit);
and because he is endowed with immeasurable and incomparable specific qualities such as virtue (*sīla*), he is preeminent in terms of *guṇa* (qualities).
He is called *agga* because he attains the state of being supreme among all beings in infinite world-systems; or, he is called *agga* because he goes to (*ajati*) or reaches *nibbāna*.
Alternatively, he is called *agga* because he exhausts (*ajeti*) or consumes the defilements—the Buddha.

The verbal root *aja* has the sense of "exhausting. That is the *agga*. "Infinite knowledge" (*ananta-ñāṇa*) is knowledge that is devoid of limits in terms of number, intrinsic nature, and objective domain.
It is by some person’s knowledge that [the Buddha] is infinite and unlimited, or possesses omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*).
That which has no end is "infinite" (*ananta*); this refers to knowledge. It is called "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) because it knows all things to be known; such is "omniscient knowledge.
He who possesses infinite knowledge is "one of infinite knowledge" (*anantañāṇo*), namely, the Buddha. For the knowledge of the Buddha cannot be fathomed by any human, deity, or Brahmā.
It is impossible to delimit it as being "only this much"; therefore, it is said to be infinite and immeasurable.
For this was said in the *Apadāna* of the Elder Sāriputta:
"It might be possible to measure the water in the ocean by means of a *aḷhaka* measure;..."
"Indeed, it is not possible to measure your omniscient knowledge.
Regarding the phrase "the path of the compassionate one with infinite knowledge," here the mention of compassion shows the root of perfect enlightenment;
for the Blessed One, his mind impelled by great compassion, [set out] at the feet of Dīpaṅkara for the sake of lifting beings out of the mire of saṃsāra.
Having made his resolution, he gradually fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons, thereby attaining unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
thus, compassion is the root of perfect enlightenment.

By this term, "the highest," it is shown that because the Blessed One possesses immeasurable and incomparable qualities such as virtue (*sīla*), he is the supreme among immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems.
This shows the supreme state among beings. By the phrase "possessor of infinite knowledge," he shows Perfect Enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).

For the knowledge of the Supreme Path has omniscience (*sabbaññutañāṇa*) as its proximate cause, and omniscience has the knowledge of the Supreme Path as its proximate cause; this is what is called Perfect Enlightenment.

And by implication, it includes the knowledge of the four analytical insights (*catu-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence (*catur-vesārajja-ñāṇa*), and the six unique knowledges (*cha-asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa*).

"He shows the conduct of knowledge by way of many such classifications of wisdom as the six direct knowledges (*cha-abhiññā*), the unshakability amidst the eight assemblies, the ten powers of knowledge (*dasabala-ñāṇāni*), the sixteen modes of conduct of knowledge, the forty-four bases of knowledge, and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge.
'I pay homage with a serene mind to that Buddha'— this is the grammatical connection."
This, however, is the concise explanation here: "The assembly of men and non-men" is the gathering place where humans and devas meet together. "Steadfast" means one whose mind is concentrated.

"Dispelled darkness" refers to the darkness of delusion consisting of ignorance that is to be destroyed, by means of the light of the lamp of wisdom—the radiance of the knowledge of the path to Arahatship acting as the instrument. [He is] "desirous of the welfare" of the world of beings.
To him who intensely desires the goal known as the mundane and supramundane; who brings welfare to men and gods, being the sustainer of the benefit for humans and deities;
who is compassionate, endowed with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all beings or possessing such great compassion;
who is supreme, the highest of all beings by virtue of his preeminence in birth, merit, and qualities; and whose knowledge is infinite both in its extent and in its essential nature.
And with a mind full of serene confidence, I pay homage to that Buddha who possesses knowledge free from limits by way of both object and domain, or who possesses infinite omniscient knowledge.
Thus ends the commentary on the fifteenth verse of homage.
The Lord of Sages, the treasury of all virtues,
having approached the abode of the self-restrained known as Vanamisisapata,
set in motion there the Wheel of Dhamma which cuts away unwholesomeness.
I pay homage to him who is tranquil, lovely, and worthy of veneration. 16.

Having thus paid homage to the Buddha with the fifteenth verse, he now speaks the verse beginning with "The treasury of all virtues" (*akhilaguṇanidhāno*), desiring to pay homage to the Lord of Sages after praising him for his qualities such as setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma at Isipatana in the Deer Park. This [verse], moreover, consists of *na*, *na*, *ma*, and *ya* gaṇas.
It should be understood that a *mālinī* verse is composed of fifteen syllables. For it is said in the *Vuttodaya*:
"This *mālinī* is joined with *na*, *ma*, *ya*, and *ya*, by the serpents and lions. Its meaning is as follows:

if each quarter-verse (*pāda*) is joined by the "serpents and lions"—that is, by eight, seven, and six [syllables]—and is also joined by *na*, *ma*, *ya*, and *ya* (the *na*-group, *ma*-group, and two *ya*-groups), then this verse is a *mālinī* verse.

Regarding the name: here, the word division should be understood as *bhoga-isī* (the lion of enjoyments). It should be seen that the word *bhoga* denotes the number eight, and the word *isi* denotes the number seven.

In that context, "a treasury of all virtues" refers to the collection of virtues such as virtue (*sīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*), which comprise both the mundane and supramundane.
It is established. And here, the word *akhila* signifies "without remainder"; that is, the meaning is "all. For it is said in the Madhuṭīkā:
"In this context, the word *khila* signifies what remains. That which is not *khila* is *akhila*. Alternatively, it is *akhila* because it does not diminish (*na khīyati*); thus, it means "all.

The root *khid*, preceded by the negative particle *na*, occurs in the sense of diminishing; the suffix *lo* [is applied]. The etymological meaning of the word *guṇa* has already been stated above. [These are] the *akhilaguṇas*.
"All virtues" means all qualities without exception; "the treasury of those" means that which stands as the repository for them—thus the term "munindo" (Lord of Sages) is obtained.
"Yo" means "whoever" or "of such a kind. Regarding the phrase "munindopagantvā," the word division here is *munindo upagantvā*.

As for "munindo," it refers to the householder sage (*agāriya-muni*), the homeless sage (*anagāriya-muni*), the trainee sage (*sekkha-muni*), the one beyond training (*asekkha-muni*), and the solitary sage (*pacceka-muni*).
The meaning is: the lord and sovereign of the five sages. Its etymological derivation has already been stated above.

The connection is as follows: that Lord of Sages, a treasury of all virtues, having approached the forest called Isipatana—the abode of the self-restrained—set in motion there the Wheel of Dhamma which cuts off unwholesomeness.
The word division is: *vanam-isipatana-vhaṃ-ti* and *vanaṃ-isipatana-vhaṃ-ti*. Here, "forest" (*vana*) refers to the Deer Park (*migadāya-vana*).

For it is called a "forest" because it is to be sought after (*vanitabba*) and frequented (*sambhajitabba*) by those desiring seclusion; the verbal root *van* is used in the sense of "seeking," with the suffix *kvi*.
It is called "Isipatana" (Sages' Fall) because it is named Isipatana and is the place where sages (*isī*) fall [to earth]; thus it is designated as Isipatana.

Or, they are called *isi* because they seek (*esanti*) and search for the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth; thus, *isi* refers to the Paccekabuddhas and others. The verbal root *is-* means "to seek," and the suffix *-i* is applied.
That place where they fall together, gather, or assemble is *Isipatana*, the forest. [The compound is formed as follows:

with the word *isi* as a prefix, the root *pat-* meaning "motion" takes the suffix *-yu*. Alternatively, *Isipatana* is the falling (*patana*) of the *isis*; it is the forest. That which is to be addressed or spoken to is *avhaṃ*.
The root *vhe* preceded by *ā*, with the suffix *kvip*, [forms *āvha*]. Due to the following conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), there is a short substitution for the vowel *ā*.

"Isipatana" means that which is to be called (*āvhetabba*); thus it is the "Forest Named after the Sages" (*isipatanavha*). "Of the restrained ones" (*saññatānaṃ*) refers to the virtuous ones who possess restraint of body, speech, and mind.

They are "restrained" (*saññatā*) because they restrain themselves; these virtuous ones include the Paccekabuddhas and others. The root *yam* preceded by *sam*, with the suffix *ta*, [forms *saṃyata*] in the sense of cessation. "Of those restrained ones" (*tesaṃ saññatānaṃ*).
*Niketanti* means a dwelling place or a delightful place. *Niketaṃ* is that wherein one dwells (*nivasati*) or finds delight (*rammati*);

thus it is a grove (*vanaṃ*). It is derived from the root *kit* preceded by *ni-* with the suffix *ṇa* in the sense of dwelling. *Upagantvā* means having gone. *Tahin’ti* means in that grove of deer named Isipatana.
*Akusalacchedanti* means the cutting off of unwholesomeness; it cuts off the unwholesome.

It is called the *Akusala-ccheda-sutta* because it cuts off unwholesome states by means of this discourse; it is the Discourse on the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (*Dhammacakka-pavattana-sutta*). The verbal root *chid*, preceded by the prefix *akuśala*, signifies "cutting" in the sense of making twofold, with the suffix *ṇa*.

The term *dhammacakka* refers to the Discourse on the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma. For here, the word *cakra* (wheel) is seen to signify success, a characteristic mark, a part of a chariot, a mode of conduct, a gift, and the wheel-jewels of a Universal Monarch, as well as the wheels of the Dhamma and so forth. "Monks, there are these four... [and so forth].

In such passages as "of gods and humans who are endowed with wheels," it is seen in the sense of excellence (*sampatti*). In "wheels were born on the soles of the feet," it refers to a mark (*lakkhaṇa*).
In "like the wheel of one who draws [a cart]," it refers to a part of a chariot (*rathaṅga*). In "four-wheeled, nine-gated," it refers to the modes of deportment (*iriyāpatha*).
And in "Give, enjoy, and do not be negligent; set in motion the wheel for all living beings," it refers to the Wheel of Dhamma.
"In this case, 'giving' refers to the gift. 'The divine wheel-treasure appeared' refers to the jewel-wheel (*ratnacakra*).
'The wheel set in motion by me' refers to the Wheel of Dhamma (*dharmacakra*). 'The wheel revolves on the head of the man overcome by desire' refers to the razor-wheel.
'With a wheel whose edge is like a razor' refers to the weapon-wheel. 'The thunderbolt-wheel' refers to the circle of the thunderbolt (*aśanimaṇḍala*)."

Furthermore, this should be understood here as the Wheel of the Dhamma (*dhammacakka*). For it is called the Wheel of the Dhamma because it wheels—that is, it sets in motion—the Dhamma consisting of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth.
Alternatively, it is called a wheel because it wheels—that is, it sets in motion—the Dhamma consisting of the Noble Truths and so forth.

Or else, because it does not deviate from the Dhamma, it is both the Dhamma and a wheel of authority; thus, it is the Wheel of the Dhamma. By way of the Dhamma, that is, by way of the proper method...
“Wheel” (*cakkam*) refers to the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*). Thus it is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*: “In what sense is it the Wheel of Dhamma?
It is the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets the Dhamma in motion and is itself a wheel; it is the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets the wheel in motion and is itself the Dhamma;
it is the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets [things] in motion by means of the Dhamma; it is the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets [things] in motion through the practice of the Dhamma; in the Dhamma...”

"Standing, he sets it in motion; thus it is called the Wheel of Dhamma," and so forth. Furthermore, "Wheel of Dhamma" refers both to the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*).

Therein, "knowledge of penetration" is that knowledge by which, while seated at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhipallaṅka*), he penetrated the Four Truths in sixteen aspects and sixty thousand methods.
"Knowledge of teaching" is that knowledge by which [he turned] the three revolutions and twelve aspects.
He set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*). Both of these are indeed the knowledge born upon the chest of the One Possessing the Ten Powers (*dasabala*).
Among them, however, the knowledge of teaching the Dhamma is what is intended here. The discourse (*sutta*), by way of figurative designation (*ṭhānūpacāra*), is called the "Wheel of Dhamma.
It was "set in motion" when he taught the group of five monks, beginning with: "These two extremes, O monks, are not to be pursued by one who has gone forth... and so forth.
*Tamatulamabhikantanti*: the word division is *taṃ atulaṃ abhikantanti*. Here, *taṃ* refers to the Lord of Sages (*muninda*).

*Atulaṃ* means one who is peerless in qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth. He is "peerless" (*atula*) because there is no person (*puggala*) equal to him; thus he is the Peerless One (*atula*), the Lord of Sages.
For indeed, throughout the immeasurable world-systems (*lokadhātu*), there is no person equal to him in qualities such as virtue and the rest. Because he is without equal...

The meaning is "equal to the Buddhas. *Abhikantaṃ* means exceedingly lovely, desirable, and endowed with the beauty of a body by all gods and humans; or, it means possessing a bodily beauty that surpasses even that of the Tusita heaven.

For while one might have said *abhikkantavaṇṇaṃ*, the word is stated as *abhikantaṃ* according to the rules of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), by eliding the letter *k* and omitting the word *vaṇṇa* for the sake of preserving the meter. This is an instance of the elision of the latter member of a compound (*uttarapadalopa*).

Or [it is] by way of [the root *kam*]. Furthermore, the bodily color (*sarīravaṇṇa*) of the Lord of Sages is desired (*kamiyati*) or delighted in (*tosiya*) to an extent that far exceeds all gods and humans;
thus it is called "exquisite" (*abhikanta*). The verbal root *kam*, preceded by the prefix *abhi*, occurs in the senses of wishing and desiring.
He whose bodily color is exquisite—that is, whose bodily color is exquisite—is the "Exquisite One" (*abhikanta*), the Lord of Sages. For he, by means of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man...
Because he is endowed with the eighty minor marks, the six-colored rays, and a golden complexion, his bodily splendor has reached its peak;
thus, being exceedingly desirable to all gods and humans, he praises it, saying, "The color of my body is delightful (abhikanta), it exists.
That which is "delightful" (abhikanta) is worthy of homage by gods and humans—thus, "worthy of veneration" (vandaneyya).
*Vandanaṃ* is that which is to be saluted by them, or that which is saluted and praised; it is a noun derived from the action (*bhāvasādhana*).

It is formed from the verbal roots *vand-* or *vad-*, with the suffix *yu* added in the senses of salutation and praise. One who is worthy of that is *vandaneyyo*, namely the Lord of Sages (*munindo*). The word *vandana* takes the suffix *ṇeyya* in the sense of being worthy of that.
Alternatively, he is "to be saluted" (*vandaneyyo*), meaning he is to be saluted and praised by gods and humans; thus he is the Lord of Sages (*munindo*).
For, because he is endowed with qualities from beginning to middle to end, he is worthy of homage from all gods and humans, or indeed, he is to be saluted by them.
In this context, the "beginning quality" refers to virtue (*sīla*) rooted in compassion, which proceeds from the abstention from killing living beings and so forth. The "middle quality" refers to...

Because of his connection with the three jhānas of samādhi, he praises the Blessed One as one worthy of veneration through his excellence; for the quality of ultimate perfection is wisdom, since there is nothing further to be done beyond it.
"I bow and pay homage" is the connection [of the words] through the three doors.
This, however, is the concise interpretation here: the treasury of all virtues—namely, the mundane and supramundane qualities of virtue, concentration, wisdom, and so forth.

Having approached—that is, having gone to—the forest called Migadāya, which is the abode, the dwelling place, or the delightful resort of the Lord of the Multitudes, the Lord of the five Sages, the Sovereign, the Blessed One;
[and] which is the home, the residence, or the delightful place of the virtuous ones who have restrained their bodies, speech, and minds;
[and] which is named Isipatana, so-called because it is called Isipatana or should be designated as Isipatana.

There, in that forest grove named Isipatana, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma—the Discourse on the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma—which effects the total eradication of unwholesomeness. He taught it to the group of five monks;
it was incomparable, peerless in qualities such as virtue, and most excellent, exceedingly lovely and desirable to all gods and humans, bringing them satisfaction.

"I bow down and pay homage with my three doors to that Lord of Sages (Muninda), who possesses the beauty of the body, who is worthy of being saluted by gods and humans, and who is deserving of their veneration.
The commentary on the sixteenth verse of praise is complete.
Surrounded by a pure retinue, radiant with exquisite splendor,
a dwelling place for an abundance of glory, guarded and endowed with the sense faculties,
adorned with the marks beginning from the orbs of the sun and moon.
I pay respectful homage to the Sugata, who is honored by gods and men.

(17) Having thus praised the Lord of Sages with the sixteenth verse, he now speaks the verse beginning with “suciparivāritan” out of a desire to honor him by extolling him through seven qualities, starting with his being surrounded by a pure retinue.
This verse, moreover, is composed not in *ja-bha-ja-ra* meters, but in *gaṇa* meters.
Furthermore, because it is composed with a single heavy syllable (*guru*) at the end, it should be understood as a *vāṇinī* verse endowed with sixteen syllables. For it is said in the *Vuttodaya*:
"When *na*, *ja*, *bha*, *ja*, and *ra* occur, and there is a *ga* [at the end], it is *vāṇinī*. The meaning of this is:

when in each quarter-verse (*pāda*) there are *na*, *ja*, *bha*, *ja*, and *ra*—that is, a *nagaṇa*, *jagaṇa*, *bhagaṇa*, *jagaṇa*, and *ragaṇa*—and they are joined with a *ga* (a heavy syllable) at the end of the foot, provided there are conjunct consonants (*saṃyoga*).
Then that woman, being so addressed, becomes what is called a "woman’s verse" (*vāṇinīgāthā*).
In this context, *suciparivārita* means surrounded by a retinue of noble disciples and others who are purified of the stains of passion and so forth;

or it means possessing requisites that are purified of the stains of the defilements. A *parisā* (retinue) is called *suci* because it cleanses and purifies itself from the stains of passion and so forth.

In purity, he belongs to the element of the pure (sucadhātu). That which is surrounded (*parivāryate*) on all sides (*parisamantato*) by noble monks and others, or by gods and humans, is a retinue (*parivāra*);

thus, he is the Sugata. The prefix *pari-* combined with the root *vṛ*, meaning "to cover" or "to surround," takes the suffix *ṇa*. He who is surrounded by pure assemblies is "one with a pure retinue" (*suciparivārita*);
this is the Sugata. This third [epithet] is a *tappurisa* compound. For the Blessed One is always [surrounded] by those purified of the stains of passion and the like.
The intended meaning is that he is surrounded by the four assemblies, beginning with the noble bhikkhus, or by the eight assemblies.
Alternatively, "one who has a pure retinue" (*suciparivārita*) means one whose retinue is completely purified; such is the Sugata.

By means of the instrumental phrase "by the rays of beautiful, radiant light" (*surucirappabhāhi*), it is meant that he is well-pleased (*suṭṭhu ruciyati*) or desired (*kamiyati*) by those rays—one fathom in length—issuing from his well-groomed body.

It shines beautifully, thus it is *suruci*; it is a ray (*raṃsi*). The root *ruc* preceded by *su-* means "to shine. It shines forth and is divine in its manifestation, thus it is *pabhā*; it is a ray.
The root *bhā* preceded by *pa-* means "to shine" with the suffix *kvi*. It is both beautiful to behold and radiance, thus it is *surucirappabhā*;
[the phrase] "by those beautiful radiances" (*tāhi surucirappabhāhi*). "Red" (*ratta*) refers to the body that is constantly to be colored. It is colored, thus it is "red" (*ratto*); it is the body.
*Rañjadhātu* means "in passion. One who is colored (*rakta*) by that is "colored" (*rakta*), namely the Sugata.

This is a compound formed by the elision of the latter member (*uttarapadalopa*). Just as the state of form is called "form" (*rūpa*), so too is that which is colored [called] "colored. What is meant is that the Blessed One possesses a material body (*rūpakāya*) that is to be colored by the fathom-wide rays constantly streaming forth from his body.
"Sirīvisarālaya" means the abode of the multitude of fortunes (lakṣī) consisting of wisdom and merit.
In this context, "sirī" is a designation for wisdom and merit. Alternatively, it refers to the excellence of physical beauty and so forth produced by merit.
For that [excellence] exists in or depends upon one who has performed meritorious deeds, or it exists in or is depended upon by those who have performed meritorious deeds; thus it is called "sirī."
It is wisdom and merit, or sovereignty. Or else, excellence such as the beauty of the physical body is obtained. For it is said in the *Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā* and other texts:
"‘Sirī’ is a designation for intelligence and merit; ‘sirī’ is sovereignty; and ‘sirī’ is the excellence of the form-body.
Here, the root is *si*, with the suffix *ra*, and the feminine-indicating suffix *ī*. Thus, by way of the long vowel, it is *sirī*.
It should be stated that it is expressed in the short form for the sake of preserving the meter (*chanda*) due to its composition as a verse (*gāthā*).

The word division is *visarālayanti* / *visara-ālayanti*. *Visara* means a collection (*samūha*). It is called *visara* because the parts (*avayava*) enter (*visanti*) into it—that is, they enter into the collection.
The root *vis-* [meaning] "entering" takes the suffix *-ara*. Alternatively, it is *visara* because the parts converge (*visaranti*) into it.
In the *Samosaraṇa* [chapter], the verbal root *vipubb-saradhatu* is used. However, in some manuscripts, the reading *visayāla* is seen with the letter *y*;
that is not correct. Why? Because only the word *visara* denotes a collection (*samūha*). For it is said in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*: "A collection (*samūha*) is called a *gaṇa* or a *saṅghāta*."
“Collection (samudāya) and accumulation (sañcaya);
mass (sandoha), multitude (nivaha), flood (ogha),
dispersion (visara), heap (nikara), and pile (caya),” and so forth.
*Ālaya* means a foundation. It is called *ālaya* because they rest (*ālayanti*) or settle (*patiṭṭhanti*) upon it; thus, the Sugata is the *ālaya*.
The root *li*, preceded by the prefix *ā*, with the suffix *ṇa*, signifies "adhering. A multitude (*visara*) or collection of glories (*sirī*), that is, of the marks numbering fifty, is *sirīvisara*;
the *ālaya* of those is the *sirīvisarālaya*, the Sugata. That [is] the *sirīvisarālaya*. He is "endowed with guarded faculties" (*gopitindriya*), meaning [endowed] with those things to be guarded.
It is endowed, fully endowed, and possessed of the six faculties, beginning with the eye, which are to be restrained.

They are called *gupitāni* because they guard (*gupiyanti*) and protect; the verbal root *gup* signifies protection. They are called *indriyāni* because they exercise sovereignty over their co-nascent states;

the verbal root *id* signifies supreme sovereignty, and the suffix *-iya* is added. Thus, the guarded faculties are the "guarded faculties" (*gupitamindriyāni*), namely the faculties of the eye and so forth.
They are obtained. One who approaches and accomplishes [them] is "approached" (*upeta*); thus he is the Well-Gone One (*sugata*). The root *idh* preceded by *upa* signifies going;

that which is approached is "approached. Although the sense-faculties such as the eye are guarded by other noble disciples and individuals besides the Buddha, it is the Buddha alone who, at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhipallaṅka*), has destroyed all defilements along with their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) by means of the path of Arhatship.
"He is one whose sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth, are guarded by the sublime"—thus he praises him as "one endowed with guarded faculties" (*gupitindriya*).
"Adorned with the characteristics of the solar and lunar discs, etc. means his feet are exquisitely variegated with the wheel-marks on the soles, such as the solar disc, the lunar disc, and so forth.
Here, the prefix *upa-* denotes intensity (*bhusa*). [His feet are] exquisitely variegated with the solar disc, the lunar disc, and so forth.

That by which something is characterized is a "mark" (*lakkhaṇa*). The mark of the wheel with its thousand spokes on the soles of the feet, as well as the orbs of the sun and moon and so forth—these being marks, they are called "the marks beginning with the orbs of the sun and moon.

One whose foot is adorned (*upacitta*) and exceedingly variegated by those [marks] is "one whose foot is adorned with the marks beginning with the orbs of the sun and moon," namely, the Sugata. Alternatively, *upacitta*...
He is "Thus-Gone" (*tathā*) because he possesses the wheel-mark on his feet and other characteristics such as the radiance of the sun and moon mandalas, which are exceedingly wonderful.
He is "Worshipped by Gods and Men" (*suranarapūjita*), meaning he is worthy of being honored by gods and humans. "Gods" (*surā*) are so called because they sport with sovereignty and the like;
they are divine beings (*devā*). The verbal root *sur* means to sport. Alternatively, they are called "gods" (*surā*) because they rejoice, attain divine sovereignty, and shine.
*Surā* means gods (*devā*). They are called *surā* because they possess the element of splendor (*suradhātu*) in their sovereignty and radiance;

or alternatively, they are *surā* because they have beautiful sounds (*sundarā rāvā*). *Narā* means humans (*manussā*); they are called *narā* because they lead (*niyantīti*) the continuum of the aggregates (*khandhasantāna*) or their own karma (*sakakamma*) by means of the element *nara*, which signifies leading (*nayane*).
Gods and humans are *suranarā*; he who is worthy of being honored by them is *suranarapūjita*. [This refers to] the Sugata. Thus, "the Sugata."

"Buddha. For he is called "Sugata" because his going (*gata*)—his movement—is beautiful (*sobhana*). Indeed, the Blessed One’s approaching of those who are to be trained is beautiful, because it invariably brings about their welfare and happiness.

Likewise, his physical body is adorned with the primary marks (*lakkhaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*), and is free from faults such as being too fast or too slow, stumbling, dragging, being stiff, frowning, or crookedness. Thus he is "Gone Well."
The movement of his body was like that of a royal swan, a bull, an elephant, or the king of beasts;

[And] by means of the convergence of its cultivation, the path leading to the cessation of the world...

He is called the "Sugata" because he has gone rightly and practiced rightly; that is to say, he does not go back to, does not return to, and does not re-approach those defilements which have been abandoned by the path of stream-entry—this meaning should be clarified in such a manner.
Alternatively, he is the Sugata because he has gone to or attained a beautiful state, namely, perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) or Nibbāna itself. Or else, because he has [spoken] what is real...
He speaks the Dhamma that is auspicious, beneficial, and appropriate for those to be trained according to their needs;
therefore, he is "Sugata," meaning "one who has spoken rightly" (the *da* being changed to *ta*). Thus, he is Sugata because of his beautiful gait and other such qualities;

[I bow] to that Sugata. "Ādaraṃ" means with respect (*sakkaccaṃ*); "ādaranaṃ" is "ādara. The verbal root *dar* preceded by *ā-* signifies respect, with the suffix *-ṇa*. [I bow] to that respect. "Namāmi" means...
The meaning is: "I pay homage.
Herein, this is the concise construction: [He who is] surrounded by a pure retinue—surrounded by a circle of noble disciples and others purified of the stains of passion and so forth;
or who possesses the requisites purified of the stains of defilement; or who is well-polished with beautiful radiance.
With rays the measure of a byāma extending from his body acting as the instrument, he constantly colors his body red;

he is an abode of manifold glory, a foundation for the multitude of marks consisting of wisdom and merit; he is guarded by the six faculties—the eye and so forth—which are to be guarded and restrained;
he is endowed, fully endowed, and possessed [of these]; and he is adorned with the characteristics beginning with the orbs of the sun and moon.
I respectfully and reverently bow down and pay homage to the Sugata, the Buddha, whose feet are exquisitely adorned with the marks of the wheels—

such as the solar disc, the lunar disc, and so forth— or who possesses the marks of the wheels on his feet that are as exquisite as the solar disc, the lunar disc, and so forth; he who is honored by gods and men, and is worthy of being worshipped by deities and humans.
The commentary on the Seventeen Verses of Homage is completed.
By means of the raft of the Path, cross the flood of saṃsāra—
whose turbulent waves are the immediate resistance of the mouth and other such [defilements]— and reach the fearless further shore for the sake of all beings.
I pay homage to the King of Dharma, the refuge, the shelter, the peerless resort, the sole ford, the foundation, the field of merit, the bestower of supreme bliss.
