In whichever quarter, if there are four, six, seven, and eight syllables respectively, and if the *magaṇa*, *bhagaṇa*, *nagaṇa*, *tagaṇa*, *tagaṇa*, and two long syllables (*go*)— that is, a long syllable followed by another long syllable—
are joined together, it is called the *mandakkantā* metre. Regarding the phrase "by the numbers of the pairs" (*yugutvassakehi*), here the word *yuga* (pair) refers to the number four,
because the term *yuga* denotes the fourfold pair of persons consisting of those on the path and those who have attained the fruit.
Since the seasons—namely, winter, cold, the rainy season, summer, the rains, and autumn—are sixfold according to their seasonal nature, the word *utu* (season) denotes the number six.
It should be understood that the word *assa* denotes the number seven; for in the *Chappaccaya-ṭīkā* and other works, it is stated:
"The word *assa* has the status of denoting the number seven."

In this context, the connection is as follows: "I pay homage to that Dhamma King, who has crossed the ocean of saṃsāra—whose waves are the turbulence of delusion, aversion, and so forth—by means of the raft of the Path;
who has reached the shore of fearlessness; who is the refuge, the shelter, the peerless resort, the sole ford, the foundation, the field of merit, and the giver of supreme bliss.
Now, according to the sequence of the meaning of this [verse]:

I shall explain it. "The tossing waves" refers to the great surges known as delusion (*moha*), defilement (*dosa*), craving (*taṇhā*), and so forth, along with the minor ripples such as the desire for mouthfuls of food.
It is called *muha* because associated states are deluded by it, or it itself is deluded, or it is merely the state of being deluded;
thus it is *moha*. The root *muh* takes the suffix *ṇa* when there is a change in meaning. Associated states are struck by it, or it itself is struck.
*Paṭigha* (aversion) is so called because it is merely striking back (*paṭihaññanamattam eva*). For the root *han*, preceded by *pati*, occurs in the senses of harming and going;
*han* becomes *gha*. *Āsā* (craving) is the act of desiring (*āsana*) or wishing (*icchana*); or, it is that which desires (*isati*) or wishes (*icchatī*), thus *āsā*;

it is craving (*taṇhā*). The root *is* occurs in the sense of wishing; *ā* is the suffix. *Moha*, *paṭigha*, and *āsā* constitute *mohapaṭighāsā*; those which have these as their beginning are *mohapaṭighāsādi*, namely the defilements beginning with greed (*lobha*).

[They] are obtained. And here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), pride (*māna*), views (*diṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), sloth (*thina*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), shamelessness (*ahirika*), and fearlessness of wrongdoing (*anottappa*)—these defilements (*kilesa*) as well as unwholesome states of consciousness (*akusalacittuppāda*)—are included.
It is called *ullola* because it causes the water above to surge and become agitated; it refers to a great wave.

[The root] *upubbala-lola* belongs to the class of roots meaning "madness" (*ummādane*), with the suffix *ṇa*. Alternatively, it is *ullola* because it moves toward or reaches the shore (*tīra*). The root *ula* means "going" (*gatiyaṃ*).

The *olapaccaya* suffix. That which gathers (*cinoti*) diverse (*vicitta*) wonder is *vīci*, meaning a small wave. This is derived from the root *cid* preceded by *vi*, with the suffix *kvi* in the sense of accumulation (*caya*).
"Ullola" and "vīci" together form *ullolavīci*. In some manuscripts, the reading *kullolavīci* is seen;
however, that is not appropriate. Why? Because the word *kulla* denotes a raft (*uḷumpa*). Indeed, it is the word *ullola* alone that signifies a great wave.
It is called *vācaka* (expressive). For it is said in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*: "The terms *ullola* and *kallola* are used for the great waves (*mahāvīci*).
And in the commentary on the *Mūlapaṇṇāsa*: "'A raft' (*kulla*) is that which is bound together by being constructed for the purpose of crossing;
whereas a basket made of reeds and the like, bound by spreading [materials], is a 'float' (*uḷumpa*). A wave that strikes the mouth and so forth is an *ullola*. This [is what is meant] here.

"In the flood of saṃsāra" (*saṃsāroghe*) means "possessing the waves and billows of momentary aversion, craving, and so forth. This is a compound ending in a *taddhita* suffix, as in the cases of *pītisukha*, *mahāsanna*, *rattidivam*, and others.
Thus, the meaning of the word here should be constructed as follows: joy (*pīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*) are "joy-and-pleasure" (*pītisukha*).
That [joy-and-pleasure] exists in this jhāna, or it is found within it; therefore, it is "joy-and-pleasure jhāna. A great seat (*mahantaṃ āsanaṃ*).
*Mahāsanaṃ*: the state of that is *mahāsannaṃ*. *Ratti ca divā ca* means night and day; thus, "night-and-day" (*rattidivaṃ*) is formed as a compound meaning "night-and-day.
Alternatively, like waves that surge up, the craving for food and so forth is "surging waves" (*ullolavīci*); this is understood as the flood of *saṃsāra*.
This is a simile expressed as a *bahubbīhi* compound. Just as in the great ocean there are great waves, surges, and currents that must be feared...
And just as crocodiles, *timi*, *tipiṅgala* fish, and various kinds of fish such as the *makara* are strewn about,
so too it is said that the defilements such as delusion (*moha*), unwholesome states of consciousness, the many terrifying sufferings such as birth,
aging, sickness, and death produced by them, and the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, are all strewn about. "The flood of saṃsāra" refers to the flood known as *saṃsāra*.
The flow of the ocean’s waters. It is called *saṃsāra* because it flows (*sarati*), goes, and proceeds continuously and repeatedly without interruption.
The verbal root *sar-* preceded by the prefix *sam-* signifies "going. The meaning is that the aggregates, elements, and bases proceed without interruption.
Thus it is said in the commentaries:
“The succession of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, occurring without interruption, is called ‘saṃsāra.
It is called an *ogha* (flood) because it overwhelms, completely submerges, and carries beings away from below; it is a flow of water. [The prefix] *ava-*...
The root *han* (to strike) takes the suffix *ṇa*. For *han*, there is the substitution *gho*. The word *ava* has the sense of "covering over" (*ottharaṇa*).

That which strikes (*haneti*) or causes to sink beings who have fallen upon it, placing them beneath, is called a *ogha*—a torrential flow of water. The root *han* preceded by *ava* takes the suffix *ṇa* in the sense of causing to sink.

The word *ava* has the sense of the lower part. It is called a *ogha* because it is like a flood; thus, it refers to *saṃsāra*. Alternatively, it is so called because it covers over and completely overwhelms the aggregates of sentient beings.
It is called a *ogha* (flood) because it overcomes, strikes down, and carries away within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*);

or, it is called a *ogha* because it causes one to sink or to be submerged within the cycle of existence—that is, the defilements such as lust and so forth are found there. *Saṃsārogho* means the flood that is itself the cycle of existence; [one crosses] that flood of the cycle of existence.
Regarding the phrase "by the raft of the Path" (*maggoḷumpena*), the word division here is *magga-olumpena*. It means by the boat consisting of the eight factors of the Path.
This is the meaning. Here, "path" (*magga*) refers to the Eightfold Path. It is called a "path" because Buddhas and noble disciples go by it toward the as-yet-untraversed direction, which is Nibbāna;
thus it is the Eightfold Path. The verbal root *maggh* (from which *magga* is derived) signifies going.
For it is said in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*: "By this path, Buddhas and disciples go to the as-yet-untraversed direction, which is Nibbāna."
“The Eightfold Path. Alternatively, it is called the path (*magga*) because one seeks (*magga-ti*) or searches for Nibbāna;

or it is called the path because it is sought or searched for by those who desire Nibbāna—thus, the Eightfold Path. The meaning is that it is to be seen by means of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). The verbal root *maggh* is used in the sense of seeking.
For this has been stated in the commentary on the Mahāvagga Saṃyutta: “In what sense is it a ‘path’? Nibbāna...”

"Because it is to be sought in the sense of a path, and because it is to be traversed by those seeking Nibbāna. Alternatively, it is called a *magga* (path) because it is to be sought (*maggīyati*) or practiced (*paṭipajjiyati*).
The meaning is that the Eightfold Path is to be practiced by those seeking Nibbāna. *Uḷu* means water; one who protects from that is an *uḷupa*.
That same word becomes *uḷumpo* through the addition of the nasal *niggahīta*, meaning a raft or boat. This is derived from the prefix *uḷu-* and the verbal root *pā-*.
Regarding the term *maggoḷumpo*: it is a raft that is itself the path; or a raft designated as the path;
or a raft similar to the path; or a raft like the path; or the path and the raft together constitute the "path-raft.
Alternatively, the raft itself is the path, thus it is a "raft-path"; or the path designated as a raft; or a path similar to a raft.

Likewise, the path is like a raft; thus, "the raft and the path" or "the path-raft"—in this way, the meaning of the words should be understood through a simile based on a physical object, and by way of the purpose of equanimity toward both the opposing side and one's own side.
By means of that "path-raft," he "crossed over" (tarī). For the King of Dharma, having crossed the flood of saṃsāra by means of the ship of the eight factors of the Path, [reached the further shore].
One reaches the shore of Nibbāna. It is said that the Buddhas of the past reached it, and the Buddhas of the future will reach it.
For it is stated in the Mahāvagga Saṃyutta: "The path leading to the single goal is for one who sees the destruction of birth."
"He who is compassionate for their welfare understands the path;
by this path, those of old have crossed over, they will cross, and they are crossing the flood. And in the *Buddhavaṃsa*:
“Having cut off the stream of saṃsāra and having shattered the three realms of existence, having boarded the ship of the Dhamma, I shall ferry across the multitude of people.
It is called “fearless” because of the absence of fear such as that of birth, aging, sickness, death, and so forth. For that Blessed One is indeed fearless.

Because fear does not exist for him, he is called "fearless" (*abhaya*). Alternatively, "fearless" means security. For that *nibbāna* is called "fearless" because there is no fear of birth and so forth therein.
In this second interpretation, however, that word is an epithet for the word "the further shore" (*pāra*). Regarding the phrase "one who has reached the further shore" (*pārapatta*):
here, "the further shore" (*pāra*) refers to *nibbāna* by way of its being the opposite bank of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra-vaṭṭa*).

It is called *pāra* because it protects (*pāti*) and guards (*rakkhati*) that water; thus, it is the "far shore" (*samuddapāra*). The verbal root *pā* is used here in the sense of protecting (*rakkhane*), with the suffix *aro*.

Alternatively, it is called *pāra* because it enables one to cross (*pāreti*) and wards off waves and the like; the verbal root *pār* is used here in the sense of enabling (*samatthiyaṃ*), with the suffix *a*. It is called *pāra* because it is like the far shore (*pāraṃ viya*).
However, the derivation of the word should be understood according to its direct meaning (*nītatthena*) as follows: it is where birth, fear, and so forth, are protected and guarded against.
*Pāram*: that which wards off (*pāreti*), is capable of warding off, or wards off birth, fear, and so forth; thus it is *pāram*, namely Nibbāna.
One who has reached that—having gone to it, having attained it—is a *pārapatta*, a King of Dhamma. [This is derived from] the root *pad* in the sense of going, preceded by the word *pāra*.

Alternatively, it refers to the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*) proceeding according to the method beginning with "I am liberated" and "may I liberate," and to the entirety of the suffering of *saṃsāra*.

Or, one who has reached, attained, or gone to the further shore (*pāra*)—the limit—of qualities such as omniscience (*sabbaññutañāṇa*), is thus called "one who has reached the further shore" (*pārapatta*), the King of Dhamma.
For the word *pāra* denotes a limit. [The epithet] "having reached that further shore" (*taṃ pārapattaṃ*). They understand [the nature of] all beings.
They are called "beings" (*pajā*) because they are born (*jāyati*) or produced in various ways (*pakārena*) by those karmic defilements. [He understands] of those beings.
"Refuge" (*tāṇa*) means refuge in the sense of protecting (*tāyana*). He is a "refuge" (*tāṇo*) because he protects and guards beings from the fear of *saṃsāra*; thus he is the Dhamma King.

The verbal root *tā* signifies protection, with the suffix *-yu*. Alternatively, "refuge" (*tāṇa*) means refuge in the sense of fully preserving beings from the suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra-vaṭṭa*).
For that Dhamma King, through his teaching of the Dhamma, [bestows] upon beings the happiness of the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna from the suffering of the cycle of existence.
Because he gives and protects, he guards; thus he is called a "refuge" (*tāṇa*). That is the refuge. A "shelter" (*leṇa*) is so called in the sense of a place of concealment.

It is a shelter because beings who are oppressed by the fears of birth and so forth hide and take refuge therein; thus [the Dharma King] is a shelter. The verbal root *lī* is used in the sense of hiding.
Alternatively, a "shelter" is a place of concealment for those who perceive the fear of *saṃsāra*. For he—
Because those who seek escape from *saṃsāra* dwell and take refuge therein, it is called a "refuge" (*leṇa*).
That is the refuge. For it is said that the Dhamma King is the protection, the refuge, the shelter, the resort, and the standing place for all beings oppressed by the fears of *saṃsāra*.
*Asamasaraṇaṃ* means the incomparable refuge for all beings. He is "incomparable" (*asama*) because there is no one equal or like him in qualities such as virtue;
thus he is the Dhamma King. A *saraṇa* is that wherein one remembers, goes, or takes refuge; thus he is the Dhamma King. The root *sar-* signifies going.
Being incomparable and without equal, he is a refuge—thus he is the Incomparable Refuge, the Dhamma King. This is not a *kammadhāraya* compound.
The meaning is that the Dhamma King, because he is the giver of all success and happiness, is for all beings an incomparable refuge, an unequal shelter, and a final resort—none other than himself.
That is the "unequal refuge" (*asamasaraṇa*). It is the "single ford" (*ekatittha*), having become the one ford for those going to the further shore of Nibbāna.
A "ford" (*tittha*) is so called because they cross over, or ascend, by means of it or at it from the ocean of existence (*najja-samudda*). [Regarding] the ocean of existence...

A place for crossing is obtained for the purpose of going to the further shore (*pārimatīra*). The verbal root *tar* is used in the sense of "crossing"; [with the suffix] *tha*, the vowel is shortened, and the letter *i* is inserted.
A single ford for humans is "one-ford" (*ekatittha*); like that, he is "one-ford," namely the Dharma-King.

For just as people crossing a river or similar body of water by means of a proper ford reach the further shore easily, but not by an improper ford, so too by means of the one who has become supreme...
By means of the Buddha as the single ford, the beings to be trained (*veneyya-sattā*), crossing the flood of *saṃsāra*, reach the bliss of the further shore of *nibbāna*;
they do not do so by means of a non-ford or the ford of another sect. Therefore, he praises the Dhamma King as "the single ford" (*ekatittha*).

Furthermore, in the definitive sense (*nītattha*), it is called "the single ford" because, having become the one supreme one, the Dhamma King is that wherein they cross and traverse to the further shore of *nibbāna*. It is secure (*khema*).
Sentient beings who are to be trained, desiring to cross to the further shore of Nibbāna, hear the Dhamma taught at this Buddha-ford;
having practiced in accordance with the Dhamma taught, they cut through the flood of saṃsāra by means of the ship of the Eightfold Path and happily cross to the secure further shore of Nibbāna.
Therefore, by the word "here" (ettha), that Buddha is indicated as the one supreme ford for all sentient beings.
The meaning is: "They do not become followers of another sect (*ekatitthā*)"; thus it is called *ekatittha*.

It is a refuge (*patiṭṭha*), meaning it serves as a support and a foundation like a great island for all beings; the meaning is that it is a shelter (*paṭisaraṇa*), a cave, and a final resort (*parāyana*).
It is a "refuge" (*patiṭṭha*) because beings take their stand (*patiṭṭhanti*) therein—the Dhamma King. [This is derived from] the verbal root *ṭhā* preceded by the prefix *pati*.
Regarding "in the turning back from rebirth": the Dhamma-king is indeed like a great island, a foundation, a refuge, a shelter, and a final resort for all beings who desire happiness;
this is the meaning. "Field of merit" means it is the field for the seed of merit for those desiring the bliss of Nibbāna;
it is the field-like place for sowing the seed of merit for those desiring merit.
Alternatively, it is *puñña* (merit) because it purifies (*sodheti*) its own agent; thus it is wholesome (*kusala*). [The suffix] *-ṇya* is applied to the root *pudh* in the sense of purification.

Or else, it is *puñña* because it produces (*janeti*) the state of being venerable (*pujja*) for another; or it is *puñña* because it produces that which is always worthy of honor (*pūjita*); thus it is wholesome. [The suffix] *-ṇya* is applied to the root *jan* preceded by the word *pūja*.

The derivation of the word should be understood according to the method of etymological analysis (*nirukti*). The remainder is non-merit (*apuñña*), because it purifies—that is, cleanses—[the opposite].

Or it is merit (*puñña*), which is wholesome (*kusala*). [The term] *khetta* is derived from the root *sudh* (to cleanse) with the suffix *ṇya*. It is called a field (*khetta*) because it protects (*tāyati*) or guards (*rakkhati*) the sown (*khitta*) seed;

that is, a rice paddy and so forth. The root *tā* (to protect), preceded by the word *khipa* (sown), takes the suffix *kvip*. The meaning is that it protects the seed by causing it to yield great fruit for those people who sow the seeds.
Alternatively, it is a field (*khetta*) because seeds are sown (*khipanti*) or planted (*vapanti*) therein. The root is *khip*.
It is called a field (*khetta*) because it is sown (*khette*) or scattered (*khepe*). It is the King of Dhamma.

Furthermore, in its direct sense (*nītatthena*), it is a "field" because it protects (*tāyati*) and preserves (*rakkhati*) the seeds of merit sown by sentient beings, thereby making them bear great fruit.
Alternatively, it is a "field" because the seeds of merit are scattered and sown therein by those seeking *nibbāna*.
He should be called the "Dhamma-King" (*dhammarāja*). A field for merits is a "merit-field" (*puññakkhetta*);

thus, he is the Dhamma-King. For just as the place where a king or his ministers grow rice or barley is called the king’s or the ministers’ “rice-field” or “barley-field,” so too the Dhamma-King, by causing all the world to become possessed of great strength through merit, is [the field of merit].
In the place where [seeds] have perished, various kinds of merit conducive to welfare and happiness for the world of beings flourish by depending on the Dhamma-king;
therefore, it is said that the Dhamma-king is praised as a "field of merit. That is the field of merit.
It is "giving supreme happiness" because it bestows the highest happiness of Nibbāna. For it has been said: "Nibbāna is the supreme happiness."
And here, the word *parama* expresses the sense of "supreme" (*uttama*) as an unformed (*anipphanna*) and non-derivative (*pāṭipadika*) term.

Alternatively, it is *parama* because it is "excellent" (*paraṃ atirekaṃ*) and "to be honored by the Noble Ones" (*ariyehi mānitabba*); thus, it is Nibbāna. [The derivation is: from the root *mā* preceded by *para*, with the suffix *a*. Or alternatively, it is *parama* because "the Noble Ones delight in it in various ways" (*pakārena ariyehi ramiyati ettha*);
thus, it is Nibbāna. [The derivation is: from the root *ram* preceded by *pa*, with the suffix *ṇa*. [This is stated] in the *Abhidhānaṭīkā*.
However, it is said: “It is *parama* because it kills the adversary (*paccanīka*). It is *parama* because it delights in the state of excellence (*pakaṭṭhabhāva*).

[The suffix] *ṇo*. Its happiness is supreme happiness (*paramasukha*). Or, supreme (*parama*) and excellent (*uttama*) happiness is supreme happiness; he who gives that is the giver of supreme happiness (*paramasukhada*), namely, the Dhamma King (*dhammarājā*).

[The compound is formed as follows: the verbal root *dā* in the sense of giving, preceded by the word *paramasukha*, with the suffix *kvi*. Furthermore, the Dhamma King [bestows this upon] those beings who are to be disciplined (*veneyya-sattānaṃ*).
It is said that he gives the bliss of Nibbāna through his teaching of the Dhamma and through his acceptance of the four requisites.

That [teaching] bestows the supreme bliss. "Dhammarāja" refers to the Buddha; for he is called "Dhammarāja" because he delights and satisfies gods and humans with both mundane and supramundane Dhammas.
Alternatively, having attained Buddhahood by means of the Dhamma of the perfections (pāramīs) alone, he became a king.
"Dhammarāja" means: he is called "Dhammarāja" because he was born as a king by means of the Dhamma of the perfections (pāramī) alone.
The connection is: "I bow to that Dhammarāja.

This, however, is the concise interpretation here: the Dhammarāja who [overcomes] the surging waves of delusion, hatred, and so forth, known as the defilements of delusion, fault, craving, and the like...

The flood of saṃsāra—known as saṃsāra, a mass of great waves and small whirlpools, a torrential flow of ocean water—I crossed by means of the raft of the Path, which is reckoned as the eightfold path.
I reached the fearless and secure shore, which is called "fearless" because of the absence of birth and the like;
I attained the further shore of Nibbāna, having reached it for the sake of all beings.
It is a refuge (*tāṇa*) in the sense of providing protection; it is a shelter (*leṇa*) in the sense of being a place of concealment, a place of concealment.
It is the peerless resort for all beings, an incomparable asylum. It is the sole ford for those traveling to the further shore of Nibbāna, having become the one and only crossing.
It is the foundation for all beings, serving as a support like a great island. It is a field of merit for those who long for the bliss of Nibbāna.
I [bow to] the Buddha, who is like a field for the seed of merit; who is like a field for those seeking merit to sow the seed of merit;
who bestows the supreme bliss of the highest Nibbāna;
who is the Dhamma-king, having conquered or gladdened the world through mundane and supramundane qualities; or who has become a Buddha by means of the perfections (pāramīs) alone.
"I bow through the three doors.
The commentary on the eighteenth verse of homage is complete.
At the foot of the *kaṇḍamba* tree, the Lord of Sages, who works for the welfare of others, sat;
He performed a miracle that was wondrous, swift, beautiful to behold, yet agitated by a mass of flames—
a miracle difficult to master, abandoned by other sages,
and endowed with the supreme delight of psychic powers. I pay homage to that most excellent one, who possesses such qualities.

19. Having thus paid homage to the Dhamma King with the eighteenth verse, he now speaks the verse beginning with "At the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree" (Kaṇḍambamūle), desiring to pay homage after praising the Lord of Sages with his qualities such as the miracle of psychic power at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree in Sāvatthī.

This verse, however, being composed of the *mata*, *naya*, and *yaya* meters, with pauses at five, six, seven, and three syllables respectively, is endowed with eighteen syllables and is known as the *Kusumitalatā*.
It should be understood as *vellitāgāthā*. For it is said in the *Vuttodaya*: "The *kusumitalatā* [verse] consists of *ma*, *ta*, *na*, *ya*, *yā*, *ku*, *su*, *vi*, *si*, and *hi*.
Here is the application (*yojanā*) of this rule: That verse which, in each quarter, is composed of the syllable-groups *ma*, *ta*, *na*, and *ya*;
and *yā*, two instances of *ya*; and *ku*, *su*, *vi*, *si*, and *hi*—that verse is the *kusumitalatā*.
"Vellitā" means "curled," and "kusumitalatā" means "flowering creeper"; thus, "vellitā gāthā nāmā" [is the name].

Furthermore, since the word *akkha* denotes the five faculties (*pañcindriya*), the word *akkha* should be understood as denoting the number five. Since the seasons (*utu*) are sixfold—namely, winter, cool season, rainy season, summer, the period between rains, and autumn—the word *utu* denotes the number six.
Since the Buddhas beginning with Vipassī are seven, the word *isi* [denotes the number seven].
It should be understood that this refers to one who expresses the number seven.

In this context, however, the connection is as follows: "I pay homage—I do homage—to that Lord of Sages (muninda), the benefactor of others, who, while seated at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree, swiftly performed a miracle. I shall, however, explain this according to the sequence of the meaning.

"Benefiting others" (*parahitakara*) means one who effects the welfare and benefit of others—that is, of all sentient beings. "Benefit" (*hita*) is so called because by it one "prospers" (*hinoti*) or "increases" (*vaḍḍhati*) in happiness;
it refers to either welfare or a purpose. The verbal root *hidh* signifies "to increase. The meaning is that the mundane and supramundane happiness of one who possesses that [benefit] increases.

"The benefit of others" is *parahita*; one who performs that is a "benefactor of others," the Lord of Sages (*muninda*). He— (Note: The text provided appears to be a commentary on a verse, likely from the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*. The translation focuses on the grammatical and etymological analysis of the term *parahitakara*.)
Indeed, from the time he received his prophecy at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara,

renouncing his own happiness for the sake of the welfare and happiness of the world of beings, he practiced the thirty perfections and the five great sacrifices for four incalculable eons plus one hundred thousand aeons;
and when the time came for him to attain the state of an omniscient Buddha, [he spent] forty-five years.
He is praised as "one who brings about the welfare of others" because he creates mundane and supramundane benefit and happiness for the world of beings through his teaching of the Dhamma.
"Who" (yo) means whoever or of whatever kind. "Lord of Sages" (munindo) refers to the Buddha;

for he is called the Lord of Sages because he is the sovereign among the five types of sages—namely, the householder sage, the homeless sage, the training sage, the adept sage, and the solitary sage. "At the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree" (kaṇḍambamūle).
Here, the word division is *kaṇḍa-amba-mūle*. The addition of the vowel *i* (the *bindu*) is for the sake of euphonic protection (*chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ*).
The meaning is: "in the vicinity of a white mango tree planted by the park-keeper named Kaṇḍa, who served King Pasenadi of Kosala.
In this context, *Kaṇḍa* is his very name. Alternatively, *kaṃ* refers to happiness (*sukha*); it is so called because one goes to (*ḍeti*) or attains that [happiness] through it.
Kaṇḍo is a park-keeper (*uyyānapāla*). The verbal root *ḍi* preceded by the prefix *kaṃ-* means "to go.
Since water (*kaṃ*) is so called, and he sprinkles that [water] upon the trees—meaning he knows how to do so—he is called *kaṇḍo*, a park-keeper or a leader of the park.

It is called *ambo* because it is frequented (*amiyati*) or approached (*gamiyati*) by people who desire fruit; thus, it is a mango tree (*setambarukkha*). The verbal root *ama-* means "to go," with the suffix *-bo*. By one named Kaṇḍa...
"Kaṇḍambamūle" means at the root of a *kaṇḍamba* mango tree planted by a park-keeper; "at that root of the *kaṇḍamba* tree.

"Nisinno" means dwelling there. "Accharaṃ" (a marvel) is so called in the sense of causing amazement. For this word "acchara" is an un-derived (*anipphanna*) primary noun (*pāṭipadika*) expressing the meaning of wonder.
Alternatively, it is a "marvel" (*pāṭihāriya*) because an intense wonder (*vimhaya*) moves about or occurs therein.
The verbal root *car* (to move) with the prefix *ā-* takes the suffix *a* in the sense of motion. There is a substitution of *acchera* for *car*. The vowel *ā* becomes short (*rassa*).

It is called *acchera* (a marvel) because it does not move or proceed constantly, like a blind man’s climbing of a mountain; it is a miracle (*pāṭihāriya*). The verbal root *car* (to move) with the prefix *na-* takes the suffix *a* in the sense of motion.
Just as a blind man’s climbing of a mountain is not constant but occurs only occasionally, even so [is the case] with the Blessed One.
A marvel (*pāṭihāriya*) does not occur constantly; it occurs only at certain times. Therefore, it is called "wondrous" (*acchera*).

Thus it is said in the *Nettippakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*: "That which does not occur frequently is wondrous. Alternatively, it is "wondrous" because it is worthy of a snap of the fingers (*accharaṃ paharituṃ yoggam*);
the suffix *-iya* is applied here according to the rule for taddhita derivatives meaning "worthy of. For while one might say *acchara*, [the form becomes] *acchariya*.
The word *acchariya* is stated with the elision of the syllable *iya* for the purpose of preserving the meter (*chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ*). For this has been said in the *Sīlakkhandhavagga-ṭīkā*:
"It is called *acchariya* because it does not occur constantly, like a blind man’s climbing a mountain.

This, first of all, is the method of [interpreting] the word. But this is the method of the *Aṭṭhakathā*: that which is worthy of a *accharā* (a finger-snap) is *acchariya*; the meaning is 'fit to strike with a finger-snap'."
*Nayanasubhagaṃ* means that which has attained beauty for the eye of serene confidence (*pasādacakkhu*) of gods and humans.

It is called *nayana* because it leads one’s own form (*attabhāva*) to perceive what is even and uneven; thus, *nayana* refers to the eye of serene confidence. [The root] *nī* with the suffix *yu* is used in the sense of leading.

That which goes to what is beautiful (*subha*) or lovely (*sobhana*) is *nayanasubhaga*, namely, the miracle (*pāṭihāriya*). [The compound] *nayanasubha* is formed with the prefix *sadū* and the root *gam* (in the sense of going) with the suffix *kvi*. That is *nayanasubhaga*.
Regarding the phrase *ākulaṇṇaggijālaṃ*, the word-division here is *ākula-aṇṇa-aggi-jālaṃ*. It means "surrounded by streams of water possessing tongues of fire. Alternatively, the meaning is:
"on all sides (*parisamantato*), the family (*kula*) is scattered (*pakiṇṇa*); that which possesses twin (*yamaka*) nets of water and nets of fire mixed together with one another.
It is called *ākula* because it thoroughly (*ābhuso*) makes the nets of water and fire mixed with one another; thus, it is the net of water and fire.
*Āpubbakuladhātu* [is used] in the sense of "making. Or, it is *ākula* because they bind (*kulati*) one another together (*ābhusam*).
Alternatively, it is *ākula* because a pair upon pair of water and fire nets proceed all around (*āsamantato*); thus, it refers to the water and fire nets.
The meaning is that the water net is mixed with the fire net, and the fire net with the water net. *Ana* means "living."

By this [derivation], *aṇṇaṃ* means water (*udakaṃ*). From the root *ar*, with the suffix *-a*. For *na*, there is *ṇa*. For that, there is doubling (*dvittaṃ*), or the state of being double (*dvibhāvo*).

Alternatively, it goes to various places; thus, from the root *ar* meaning "to go," with the suffix *-aṇṇa*. There is the substitution of *a* for *ar*, elision of the end of the root, and the change of *n* to *ṇ*.
*Aṇṇaṃ* is the support (*dhāraṃ*) of *aṇṇaṃ*. By the elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopena*), [it refers to] by way of crookedness (*kuṭilabhāvena*).
It goes by not being born (*ajati gacchati*); thus it is *aggi*. The root *aja-* is used in the sense of going. Its suffix is *-go*. It burns and shines; thus it is *jālaṃ*, a flame.

The root *jala-* is used in the sense of shining, with the suffix *-ṇa*. The flame of the fire is *aggijālaṃ*. Both the embers (*aṇṇa*) and the flame of the fire (*aggijālaṃ*) constitute *aṇṇaggijālaṃ*.
That which has a confused (*ākula*) and scattered (*parikiṇṇa*) mass of embers and flames of fire is *ākulaṇṇaggijālaṃ*; thus, the twin miracle (*yamaka-pāṭihīra*) is obtained.
That [net] with its mass of tangled flames:
"dujjāladdhaṃsaṃ" means that the net known as the doctrine of false views has been utterly destroyed.

It is called "dujjāla" because it burns badly—that is, it binds one to the cycle of existence—and it is the net of the doctrine of false views. For the teaching of the non-Buddhist sects proceeds in such a manner as "there is no gift," and so forth.

The meaning is "difficult to unravel" (*dujjāla*) because it is like a net due to its inability to allow one to escape from *saṃsāra*. The prefix *du-* is used before the verbal root *jal* (in the sense of binding) with the suffix *-ṇo*.
That which destroys (*dhaṃsati*), i.e., utterly shatters (*viddhaṃsati*), is "the destroyer of the difficult-to-unravel" (*dujjāladdhaṃsa*), namely, the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*).

Regarding the phrase "not abandoned by the Sages" (*munibhirajahitaṃ*), the word division is "not abandoned by the Sages" (*munibhir ajahitam*). In that context, "by the Sages" (*munibhi*) means by all the Perfectly Enlightened Ones (*sammāsambuddha*). For they [possess] *mona*...

It is called "all-knowing knowledge" (*sabbaññutañāṇa*); because they possess this, they are called "sages" (*muni*). Alternatively, they are called *muni* because they possess bodily silence (*kāyamoneyya*), verbal silence (*vacīmoneyya*), and mental silence (*manomoneyya*); the suffix *-ṇī* is applied here to form the word *assattha*.

Or else, they are called *muni* because they "measure" (*munanti*)—that is, they know—the world of this life and the world beyond, their own welfare and the welfare of others, and what is beneficial and what is harmful; by those sages (*tehi munībhi*).
"Ajahitaṃ" means not abandoned (*avijahitaṃ*) or not relinquished (*apariccattaṃ*); "jahitaṃ" means that which is to be discarded or relinquished. The verbal root *hā* signifies giving up.
That which is not abandoned is "ajahitaṃ," namely, the miracle (*pāṭihāriyaṃ*). That is what is not abandoned.
For at the foot of the Kaṇḍama tree at the southern gate of the city of Sāvatthī, the Blessed One performed a miracle, and at the conclusion of that miracle, the Blessed One—
Having gone to the city of the Thirty-three, he sat down at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree upon the stone seat named Paṇḍukambala;
it is said that the teaching of the Abhidhamma to the devas is a natural law (dhammatā) never abandoned by any Perfectly Enlightened One.
For in the *Buddhavaṃsa-aṭṭhakathā*, among the thirty-two natural laws, it is stated regarding Sāvatthī:
The performance of the Twin Miracle at the city gate and the teaching of the Abhidhamma in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven are stated as being by way of natural law (dhammatā).
Therefore, he praises him, saying, "the Sage abandoned the miracle.
"Miracle" (pāṭihīra) means a marvel (pāṭihāriya) in the sense of warding off adversaries; having crushed the opposing heretics, he prevails (hinoti).
It is called *pāṭihāriya* (a miracle) because it proceeds (*pavattati*). The root *hi* preceded by *paṭi-* has the sense of "going" (*gati*), and the suffix *ṇo* is added; *hi* is replaced by *hera*.

Alternatively, it is called *pāṭihāriya* because it carries away (*harati*) or removes (*apaneti*) the heretics who stand in opposition to both the Blessed One and his Teaching; thus it refers to the knowledge of the various kinds of psychic power (*iddhividhañāṇa*).
The root *har* preceded by *paṭi-* has the sense of "removing" (*apanayana*); it is so called because it carries away or removes the minds of beings that have fallen into wrong views and conceit.

Or, it is called a *pāṭihīra* because it brings about confidence in those who lack it. Or, it is called a *pāṭihīra* because, when the mind is concentrated, free from defilements, and has accomplished its task, one must subsequently (*paṭi*) bring forth and exercise it.
For this word *paṭi* conveys the meaning of "subsequently" (*pacchā*), as seen in such passages as: "When he had entered therein, another brahmin arrived."
Alternatively, it is called a *pāṭihāriya* because it carries on or proceeds as a pair of water and fire, repeatedly and uninterruptedly;

thus it is the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*). Furthermore, that miracle is threefold by way of the miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*), the miracle of mind-reading (*ādesanāpāṭihāriya*), and the miracle of instruction (*anusāsanīpāṭihāriya*). Among these, it is the miracle of psychic power that is intended here.
*Sīghaṃ* means quickly, swiftly, or rapidly. That word, however, is an adverbial modifier for the phrase *akāsi*.
It is called *sīghaṃ* because it proceeds lightly or swiftly; the root *si-* is used in the sense of motion, with the suffix *-gha*, and the vowel is lengthened.
*Akāsi* means he performed. Furthermore, the miracle (*pāṭihāriya*) should be understood in this way: for in the seventh year after his full enlightenment, the Blessed One...

From the left shoulder a mass of fire, from the right shoulder a stream of water. From the right hand...
A mass of fire from the left hand, a stream of water from the right hand. A mass of fire from the left hand, a stream of water from the right hand.

from the spaces between the fingers a mass of fire, and from the fingers a stream of water. From each individual hair a mass of fire, and from each individual hair a stream of water;

A stream of water flows forth. Of six colors—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and crystal-clear—the waters surge together, and double by double streams of color flow out.

[It is] by means of the qualities comprised within the Buddha’s supernormal power (*iddhi*). For the word *dhamma* refers to a quality, as in expressions such as "Buddha-qualities" (*buddhadhammā*).
*Siddhi* (success) is the state of succeeding (*ijjhana*) or being accomplished (*samijjhana*). Or, it is called *iddhi* because one succeeds or is accomplished [thereby].

Or, it is called *iddhi* because by means of this, one’s desired purpose succeeds or is accomplished. The verbal root *idh* signifies growth (*vuddhi*); the suffix *i* is added, or alternatively, the suffix *tip*. By means of this *iddhi*, the Blessed One’s desired purpose is accomplished.
The meaning is that he is prosperous, grown, and has reached the highest excellence. It is called *dhamma* because it bears or manifests the substance of one who possesses it;

One approaches and accomplishes [it], thus one is "endowed" (*upeta*), O Lord of Sages (*muninda*). The root *upa-ai* is used in the sense of going. That which is so endowed is *tam upetam*.

In this context, one who is naturally single becomes many. Having adverted to a hundred or a thousand, he resolves with knowledge, "May I be many.

Here, when it is said, "From this body a monk emanates another body, a mind-made form," the power arrived at by this method is [the power of] a mind-made [body] within the interior of the physical body.
The supernormal power called "mind-made" (*manomaya-iddhi*) is so named because it proceeds by way of the production of a body.

The supernormal power called "expansion of knowledge" (*ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi*) refers to specific qualities produced through the power of knowledge, whether prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneous with the arising of that knowledge.
And in this regard, there was the expansion of knowledge of the Venerable Elder Bākula, the Venerable Elder Saṅkicca, and the Venerable Elder Bhūtapāla.

Success (iddhi) should be understood. The specific attainments produced through the power of serenity (samatha)—whether before, after, or at the very moment of concentration—are called success by the expansion of concentration (samādhivipphārā iddhi).

The miracle of the psychic power resulting from the expansion of concentration (*samādhivipphārā iddhi*) is to be understood as that of the female lay follower (*upāsikā*).
Furthermore, the noble miracle (*ariyā iddhi*), such as dwelling with the perception of the non-repulsive toward repulsive things and so forth, is called the noble miracle.

“For some gods, for some humans, and for certain beings in the states of deprivation, this is psychic power born of the ripening of kamma,” and so forth.

While performing his purpose, the Lord of Sages— who is such a Buddha— was seated near a white silk-cotton tree planted by the park-keeper named Kaṇḍa at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree in the garden of King Pasenadi of Kosala;
he was dwelling there, a marvel and a source of wonder, beautiful to behold for gods and men,
pleasing to the eye, possessing a radiant splendor, with a mass of disheveled hair like a cluster of flames and surrounded by water.
Possessing crests of flames like a torch, surrounding the family on all sides, intermingled with one another, paired and doubled,
possessing nets of water and nets of fire; the net known as the doctrine of evil views has been destroyed,
shattered by the Sage, never abandoned by any Perfectly Enlightened One— a miracle that is contrary [to such views].
Whether it be a miracle of manifestation (*pāṭihāriya*), a miracle of water and fire, or a miracle of pairs (*yamaka-pāṭihāriya*),
he quickly and swiftly performed it— most excellent, most praiseworthy, producing supreme delight for gods and humans,

generating the highest joy for the noble and the virtuous, or causing the minds of people to rejoice— by means of the inconceivable and immeasurable powers of a Buddha’s supernormal knowledge (*iddhi*).
I bow my head in homage to that Lord of Sages (Muninda), who is endowed and possessed of all virtues; I pay him homage.
Thus ends the commentary on the nineteenth verse of homage. 20.
The Lord of Sages alone is like the rising sun of compassion, with the vast orb of his wisdom; having crossed the flood of living beings, he is described as a lotus.
With the most excellent rays of Dhamma, you awakened those who were pure within the cavern of the three realms, you whose fame pervades the three worlds, the sole eye of the world;
I pay homage to that Great Sage who cannot endure suffering. 20.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Sages with this nineteenth verse, [I now praise him] who, through the teaching of Dhamma, leads the flood of living beings across.
Having praised the Dhamma of the Four Truths with nine qualities, such as being worthy of awakening, he spoke the verse beginning with "munindakko" out of a desire to pay homage to the Lord of Sages.

This verse, moreover, should be understood as a "Meghavipphujjitā-gāthā" consisting of nineteen syllables, because it is composed of the *ya*, *ma*, *na*, *sa*, and *ra* gaṇas, along with one heavy syllable (*garu*), seven light syllables (*laghu*), and seven heavy syllables (*garu*). For it is said in the *Vuttodaya*: "By *ra*, *su*, *tu*, and *assa*..."
“*Ymā na sa ra ra garū meghavipphujjitā sā*. This is the application (*yojanā*) here:

In whichever quarter, if there are six, six, and seven morae (*yati*) by means of the *rasu* and *tva* syllables, and if it is joined with the *ymā*—that is, a *yagaṇa* and a *magana*—and if *na sa rara garū*—that is, a *nagaṇa*, a *sagaṇa*, a *ragaṇa*, a *ragaṇa*, and a single heavy syllable (*garu*)—then that verse is called *meghavipphujjitā* (the Thundering Cloud).
Regarding the term *nāma*: here, since tastes (*rasa*) are sixfold—by way of astringent, bitter, sweet, salty, sour, and pungent—the word *rasa* should be understood as denoting the number six.
Since seasons (*utu*) are sixfold—by way of winter, cool season, spring, summer, rainy season, and autumn—the word *utu* denotes the number six.
It should be understood that the word *assa* denotes the number seven.
For the fact that the word *assa* denotes the number seven is stated in the *Chandaṭīkā*.

In that regard: "The rising sun of knowledge, whose orb is vast, the lone moon of the Sage—having dispelled the flood of living beings described as lotuses within the pure hollow of the three worlds—he awakened them with the excellent rays of Dhamma;
his fame is spread throughout the three worlds, and he is the eye for those in need."
The construction is: "I bow to that Great Sage, the sun among Munis, who is intolerant of suffering.
And for this verse, we shall explain it according to the sequence of meaning (*atthakkama*) for the sake of easy understanding, not according to the sequence of words (*saddakkama*).
Regarding the phrase *dayudayaruṇo*, the word division should be made as *dayā-udaya-aruṇo*. [He is] the dawn-sun risen upon the mountain of the arising of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Alternatively, the meaning is that great compassion shines forth like the dawn-sun risen from the mountain of sunrise.
And here, the word *dayā* (compassion) applies to both compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*mettā*). For in the phrase "one who is without compassion" (*adayā*), it refers to compassion;

in the phrase "one who has attained compassion" (*dayāpanno*), it applies to loving-kindness—the meaning being "one who has attained a state of mind characterized by loving-kindness. However, in this context, compassion is intended.

Now, this is the etymological explanation (*vacanattha*). It is called *dayā* (compassion) because it "protects" (*dayati*) or "sustains" (*hiṃsati*) the compassionate one until the accomplishment of the intended benefit for others is reached;

thus it is *mahākaruṇā* (great compassion). The verbal root *day* signifies "to harm" (*hiṃsā*). Alternatively, it is *dayā* because by means of it, even sinful people are "protected" (*anuggaṇhāti*) or sustained;
the root *day* here signifies "to sustain. It is *dayā* because it "protects" itself, meaning that having abandoned even its own happiness, it undergoes weariness [for the sake of others].
Or, it is *dayā*. The verbal root *day* means "to take. Alternatively, it is called *dayā* because by means of it Bodhisattvas take up both the suffering of *saṃsāra* and omniscient knowledge;

thus, *dayā* is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). For when Great Bodhisattvas make their formal aspiration (*abhinīhāra*) for Buddhahood, they set aside even the fruit of Arhatship already in their hands, desiring to rescue sentient beings from the ocean of *saṃsāra*, which provides no consolation.

The meaning is that they simultaneously grasp the most terrifying suffering of *saṃsāra* and, in their final existence, the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*) adorned with manifold qualities along with the attainment of the Deathless Element (*amatadhātu*).
For all the qualities of a Buddha have compassion as their root. Therefore, it is said in the *Aṅguttara-ṭīkā*:
"Compassion is the beginning of all the qualities of a Buddha, because they have that as their cause."

Furthermore, it is *dayā* because by means of it one feels compassion (*dayanti*) and protects (*anurakkhanti*) beings, or because one is oneself compassionate, or because it is merely the state of being compassionate.
The verbal root *day* is used in the sense of protecting, and the suffix *-ap* is added. It is called *udaya* because it rises (*udeti*) or increases; it refers to a mountain.

The verbal root *udi* is used in the sense of bringing forth, with the suffix *-a*. It is called *aruṇa* because, making light all around (*āsamantato*), it moves (*uṇati*) or goes; it is a specific ray of the sun.

The verbal root *ā-pubba* takes the suffix *ṇa* in the sense of "going. One whose dawn (*aruṇa*) has risen from the mountain of sunrise (*udaya-pabbata*), which is synonymous with compassion (*dayā*), is a "dawn-risen-compassionate one" (*dayudayaruṇa*).

Alternatively, one whose compassion—that is, great pity (*mahākaruṇā*)—is like the dawn of the sun risen from the mountain of sunrise is a "dawn-risen-compassionate one," namely the Moon of Sages (*munindakka*).
For just as the dawn of the risen sun is the beginning of light, so too...
At the feet of Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the Bodhisatta renounced the bliss of Nibbāna that was within his grasp;

out of great compassion (mahākaruṇā), desiring to rescue beings from the ocean of saṃsāra, he performed the ten perfections (pāramīs) beginning with giving—so very difficult to accomplish for the sake of Buddhahood—as well as the five great sacrifices, throughout four incalculable eons (asaṅkhyeyyas) plus one hundred thousand kappas. This is compassion.
"Beginning with 'for the state of Buddhahood' (*buddhabhāvāya*). Therefore, it is said that he alone is worthy of praise, as he causes the splendor of a Buddha to arise.

"The reflection expanded by knowledge" (*ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimbo*) means the circumference consisting of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*). Like the circle of the world-systems (*cakkavāḷamaṇḍala*) in its vast extent, he possesses the vast object of omniscient knowledge.
He knows all phenomena to be known, divided into the conditioned (*saṅkhata*) and the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).

Knowledge (*ñāṇa*), the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutañāṇa*). The verbal root *ñā* means "to understand. It is "extensive" (*vitthiṇṇa*) because it specifically stretches out or expands; thus, it is knowledge.

The prefix *vi-* precedes the root *tan*, which means "to expand," with the suffix *-ta*. There is the substitution of *i* for that [suffix], and the elision of the final syllable of the root, followed by the doubling of the dissimilar vowel (*asarūpa-dvitta*).
Alternatively, it is "extensive" because it spreads or extends; here, the specific difference lies only in the root *thar*. It "vomits" (or emits) in a circular form.

It is called *bimba* because it goes (*gacchati*) or proceeds (*pavattati*); [it refers to] the circle of knowledge (*ñāṇamaṇḍala*). Regarding the root *vam*: in the *Moggallāna* commentary on the *Ṇvādi* suffixes, it is stated:
"The root *vam* is used in the sense of vomiting (*uggiraṇa*). From *vam*, by the addition of the suffix *ṇvu*, we have *vitta*. That which vomits or emits is *bimba*, meaning the body (*sarīra*).
However, that definition is appropriate only when the word *bimba* denotes the body; it is not appropriate when it denotes something circular (*parimaṇḍala*).

However, here, because the word *bimba* denotes that which is circular (*parimaṇḍala*). The teachers, moreover, state that the meaning of the word *bimba* here is "the wheel-circle" (*cakkamaṇḍala*). But that should be examined. Why? Because in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*, it says:
"Bimba, however, [is used] for a reflection, for a circle, and for the fruit of the *bimbikā* tree"; and in its commentary, it says: "[It means] a circle, a secondary circle."

And because it is so stated: "He whose knowledge—consisting of omniscience—is wide, extensive, a full orb, and perfectly round, is one whose knowledge is wide and whose form is full (ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimbo).

Alternatively, he is one whose knowledge—omniscience—is wide, extensive, a full orb like the circumference of the world-system (cakkavāḷa), and possesses a vast object; thus he is Ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimbo, the Sage-Indra.

Just as the circle of the world-system (*cakkavāḷamaṇḍala*) is vast and great because the world-system itself is infinite, even so the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*) of the Buddha is vast and great because its objects are infinite. Therefore, he praises it as "the reflection of the expansion of that knowledge.
The word division is *yveko* = *yo eko*. Although the reading *yekoti* also occurs in some places, [it means] *yo eko* ("he who is one").
The word-division (*padaccheda*) should be made. Furthermore, both readings are indeed appropriate. For in the reading *yveko*, there is a sandhi of substitution (*ādesasandhi*);
whereas in the reading *yeko*, there is a sandhi of elision (*lopasandhi*). This is the distinction between them. The connection is: "He who is the Lord of Sages.

"One" (*eko*) means without companion, without a second; the meaning is that he has become the unique Buddha. And here, the word "one" (*eka*) [denotes] the best among others and the one without companion.
It is seen in the sense of number and so forth. Likewise, in such passages as "Thus some assert: 'The self and the world are eternal;
this alone is the truth, all else is vain,'" it is seen in the sense of "another. In such passages as "the state of one-pointedness of mind," it means "best.
In such passages as "one who is secluded," it means "without a companion. And in such passages as "There is, O monks, indeed only one moment and one occasion for the holy life," [it means "only"].
Regarding the term *saṅkhyāyaṃ*: here, however, it is intended in the sense of being without a companion (*asahāya*).

This is its etymological meaning: he goes, moves, or proceeds alone, thus he is *eko*; or, being without a second, he goes toward, knows, or penetrates unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, thus he is *eko*, the Sage-Indra (*munindakko*).
The suffix *-ṇvu* is applied to the roots *edh-* or *idh-* in the sense of "modes of knowledge. Alternatively, the Blessed One is *eko* by virtue of what is termed his renunciation (*pabbajjā*).

"Alone": he is alone in the sense of being without a second; he is alone in the sense of the abandonment of craving; he is alone as one who is entirely free from lust; he is alone as one who is entirely free from hatred;
he is alone as one who is entirely free from delusion; he is alone as one who is entirely free from defilements; he is alone as one who has gone by the single path;

he is alone as one who has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—and so forth. Herein, the meaning should be understood according to the method of the *Mahāniddesa* as it has been handed down.
Moreover, he is "one" because only one Buddha appears, arises, and flourishes even within infinite world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).

For it is said in the *Ekanipāta* of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*: "It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen that two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should appear simultaneously, neither before nor after, in a single world-system; such a thing is not possible. But it is possible..."
“Monks, it is possible that in a single world-system only one Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, might arise;
this is indeed possible. And in the commentary on that passage: “In a single world-system means in a ten-thousandfold world-system.
For there are three fields: the field of birth (*jātikkhetta*), the field of authority (*āṇakkhetta*), and the field of range (*visayakkhetta*). Among these, the ‘field of birth’ is as follows:”

The ten-thousandfold world system (*dasasahassī lokadhātu*). For this system trembles at the time of the Tathāgata’s descent into his mother’s womb, at the time of his birth, at the time of his awakening, at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, at the relinquishing of the life-force, and at his final Nibbāna.
However, a hundred thousand million world-spheres (*cakkavāḷa*) is called the "field of authority" (*āṇakkhetta*). [This includes] the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, the Mora Paritta, and the Dhajagga Paritta.
For here, the authority of the *Ratanaparitta* and other such protective discourses prevails. However, there is no limit to the extent of its objective field.
For the Buddhas, as far as their knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable; as far as the knowable extends, so far extends their knowledge.
Because of the statement, "The knowable is limited by knowledge, and knowledge is limited by the knowable," there is nothing that does not fall within their range.
Regarding these three fields, there is no sutta stating that Buddhas arise in another world-system (cakkavāḷa) apart from this one;
however, there is [a sutta] stating that they do not so arise. For there are three Piṭakas:
the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Suttanta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. There are three Councils (saṃgīti): the council of the Elder Mahākassapa, the council of the Elder Yasa, and...

Regarding the council of the Elder Moggaliputta, among these three councils recorded in the Buddha-word of the Tipiṭaka, there is no sutta stating that Buddhas arise elsewhere after leaving this Cakkavāḷa;
rather, there is one stating that they do not arise [elsewhere].
And here, by "one world-system," it is meant the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassi lokadhātu*), referring to the field of birth (*jātikkhetta*).
It has been stated. For this ten-thousandfold world system stands surrounding this [central] world system.
That these alone constitute the field of birth (*jātikkhetta*) is to be understood by way of the nature of things (*dhammatā*). By the phrase "in these three fields," it is meant:

in the field of birth consisting of the ten-thousandfold world system; in the field of authority (*āṇakkhetta*) consisting of one hundred thousand million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*); and in the field of infinite world-systems.

Regarding the phrase "and in the field of objects (*visayakkhetta*)," this shows that Buddhas do not arise in other infinite world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) beyond this [present] world-system among these three fields of a Buddha.

Having shown the threefold field of a Buddha, the expression "in these three fields" is stated in the sense of a locus (*ādhārabhāva*), not in the sense of a selection (*niddhāraṇabhāva*). Why? Because in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), the word to be selected...

Because of its non-existence. For if the commentator had intended the word *tassa* (of that) to have the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇattha*), then—having set aside the field of command among these three fields—it would have been said:
"this Cakkavāḷa," and so forth. But it is not so. Therefore, the word *tassa* must be understood as having the sense of a locus (*ādhārattha*) alone.
The construction of the meaning of that word is according to its state as a locus, based on the previous supports and the modes of conduct (*cariyā*).

Regarding the word "katā" (made): that reason has indeed already been presented in the Abhidhamma Vibhaṅga-pāḷi and its commentary, in the latter part of the Paññāsa (the *Bahu-dhātuka-sutta*) and its commentary, and in the Nettippakaraṇa-pāḷi and its commentary.
However, in the Aṅguttara-ṭīkā, it says: "But as for 'they do not arise,' there is no [evidence] for me..."
“There is a teacher; one equal to me does not exist,” and so forth.

When the Blessed One, speaking while standing in this world-system, was asked by [the Buddha], “But friend Sāriputta, is there now another ascetic or brahmin who is equal to the Blessed One in regard to perfect enlightenment?”—having replied, “No, venerable sir,” in order to show the reason for that, he said: “This is impossible, this has no occasion...”

"It was said: 'By one who cites this sutta—namely, "Could two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, arise simultaneously and not sequentially in a single world-system"—the intention is that, having set aside this world-system which constitutes a Buddha-field, non-arising elsewhere is stated. And likewise in the *Ñāṇavibhaṅgamūlaṭīkā*:

This is also stated in the commentary on the *Uparipaṇṇāsa-bahudhātu-sutta*. Furthermore, by the statement that there is no arising [of Buddhas] elsewhere "except for this world-system," it is shown that Buddhas do not arise in other infinite world-systems beyond this world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), which constitutes a Buddha-field.
For although the word "elsewhere" (*aññattha*) is used in a general sense, according to what is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*...
Regarding the phrase "in these three fields," by virtue of the proximity of other words, a specific meaning—namely, that which consists of infinite world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*)—should be understood.
For even a word of general application becomes restricted to a specific domain through the proximity of other words.
Furthermore, there is another way of explaining this: according to what is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, for Buddhas arise only in this very world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
They arise. However, when arising in this particular location is precluded, it follows that they do not arise in other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) than this;
thus, in this sentence, the word *eva* (only/just) attached to the term *imasmiṃ yeva* (in this very [place]) has the sense of exclusion and restriction.
By this, he excludes the arising of other Buddhas in other infinite world-systems. For even though in other...

Other Buddhas might arise in infinite world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). If that were so, our Blessed One—who knows and sees all phenomena, including the distinction between the conditioned and the unconditioned—would have to say, "Other Buddhas are arising in other world-systems. But he does not.
For the statement that the twenty-eight Perfectly Enlightened Ones, beginning with Taṇhaṅkara, arose in world-systems other than this one [is not what he said].
This is not found in the Buddha’s word contained within the Tipiṭaka, nor likewise in the commentaries or sub-commentaries.

Therefore, it should be understood that other Buddhas do not arise in other infinite world-systems beyond this world-system. For this has been stated in the commentary on the Mahāsamaya Sutta, in the commentary on the Mahāvagga of the Suttanta:
Then it occurred to him: "Only a Buddha such as myself would be able [to do this]. Is there perhaps another Buddha anywhere?
Spreading out his infinite knowledge across the infinite world-systems and looking about, he saw no other Buddha.
And this is not surprising, for even now he would see no one equal to himself; as was stated in the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta regarding the day of his birth.
"Seeing no one equal to himself, he uttered this irreversible lion's roar: 'I am the foremost in the world. Thus, seeing no other equal to himself, he thought.

It is exactly so. And in the *Purābheda-sutta-ṭīkā* and the *Mahāniddesa-aṭṭhakathā*, as well as in the commentary on the *Mahāsamaya-sutta*, according to the method found in the sutta regarding "one world-system," it is stated in all instances:
It is simply not the case that there are two Buddhas simultaneously, neither before nor after. For this very reason, he explains in the commentary: “In infinite world-systems...
[he] did not see [another].
And in the *Apaṇṇakajātakaṭṭhakathā*, it says: “The Teacher, O lay followers, [surveyed] from below the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence as his limit...”

It is said: "Having considered this, there is no one equal to the Buddha in qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) throughout immeasurable world-systems (*lokadhātu*). How much less could there be anyone superior?

In these two commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), the terms "in infinite world-systems" (*anantāsu lokadhātūsu*) and "in immeasurable world-systems" (*aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu*) are expressed by the words "infinite" (*ananta*) and "immeasurable" (*aparimāṇa*). By those two terms, according to the explanation in the *Ṭīkā*—
And it shows that there is no arising of other Buddhas in infinite world-systems.

However, in the *Sammohavinodanī-ṭīkā*, through the interpretation beginning with "But in these," it makes known that Buddhas do not arise in a world-system other than the hundred thousand million world-systems. We, however, reflect as follows: in another...

Regarding the term *cakkavāḷa*: if the meaning is taken as "in all other three Buddha-fields besides this *cakkavāḷa*," it is understood that Buddhas do not arise in any *cakkavāḷa* other than the hundred-thousand-million *cakkavāḷas*.

However, if the meaning is "in another *cakkavāḷa*"—that is, in a *cakkavāḷa* other than this one which serves as the field for the lineage of births (*jāti-āṇā-khetta*)—then [it refers to a single world-system].
It is understood from the text that when one hundred thousand million world-systems have been occupied, the arising of Buddhas in another world-system would be possible;

this is also known from such scriptural passages as: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should arise in a single world-system," and from such scriptural passages as:
"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that two Wheel-turning Monarchs should [arise] in a single world-system."

From the fact of their simultaneous discourse, it would follow that just as there is no arising of Buddhas within a hundred thousand million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), so too there would be no arising of a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*) in any other world-system. Furthermore, in the *Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa*, the arising of Buddhas in a world-system other than the hundred thousand million world-systems is not prohibited.
Therefore, [this restriction applies] only to the hundred thousand million world-systems that constitute the field of authority (*āṇakkhetta*).
"It might be that there is a Buddha in another world-system"—this is our position (*khanti*). It is said that this should be accepted after investigation.
Furthermore, regarding what was stated in the *Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa* and so forth, "it is not refuted," that [refutation] does not actually exist in the *Kathāvatthu* scripture itself.
However, in this discussion on all directions (*sabbadisākathā*), there is merely the hypothetical statement of the opponents.
Therefore, it is said in that scripture: “Buddhas stand in all directions. Yes. Does a Buddha stand in the eastern direction?
It should not be said so… [as before] …Does a Buddha stand in the eastern direction? Yes. What is the name of that Blessed One?
What is his caste? What is his clan? What are the names of that Blessed One’s mother and father? What is his name?”
“Who were the pair of disciples of that Blessed One? Who was the attendant of that Blessed One? What kind of robe did he wear?
What kind of bowl did he carry? In which village, town, city, kingdom, or province [did he dwell]?”—it should not be said thus, and so forth.
In the commentary on that [passage], however, it says: "Now there is what is called the discourse on all directions.

Therein, having generated their own imaginative construction—that the arrangement of world-systems exists all around in the four cardinal directions, below, and above, and that a Buddha exists in all world-systems—[they hold] that Buddhas abide in all directions, such as the Mahāsāṅghikas."...pe... they.
The question is posed with intentional ambiguity (*sandhāya*) by the proponent of the first position (*sakavādin*). The other [the opponent] grants the point (*paṭiññā*).
When asked "In the eastern direction?", he denies it, referring to Sakyamuni. Being asked again, he affirms it, referring to one residing in another world-system by way of his attainment (*laddhi*).
"What is the name of that Blessed One? and so forth is for the purpose of challenging him: "If you know him, tell me his name and so on."
It has been said: "By this method, the meaning is to be understood in all cases. It is further stated: "And here, in the four directions...
just as among the Mahāsāṅghikas," by which he shows the tenet of the opponents. Therein, however, the construction is as follows:
"In the four directions, below, and above—in this way, the arrangement of the world-system exists on all sides."
"Of those... [and so on] ...of the Mahāsāṅghikas" means: of those opponents who hold such a tenet. "Like the tenet of whom?

Like the tenet of the Mahāsāṅghikas"—this is the meaning. "With reference to them" means: with reference to those individuals who are opponents, having grasped it through knowledge and having observed it—this is the meaning.
"The question of the proponent" means: for the proponent, [the position is] that Buddhas stand in all directions.
There is a question. "The other's admission" means there is an acknowledgment by the opponent. "When asked 'from the east,'" etc., means when the proponent has asked "from the east" and so forth.
"The Sakyan Sage" refers to our Buddha Gotama, who was born into the Sakyan royal lineage. "He rejects" means the person who is the opponent sets it aside. "Again asked" means...
Furthermore, when the proponent asks, "Does a Buddha stand in the eastern [direction]?
the opponent—that person—admits, "Yes," based on a wrong view (*micchā-laddhi*), namely, the view that a Buddha exists and arises in another world-system.
If, however, a Buddha stands in another world-system, then [one must state] his name, clan, and so forth.
In order to show the challenging statement of the proponent, "Tell me," he said, "What was the name of that Blessed One?
and so forth. By this, he demonstrates that there are no other Buddhas in other infinite world-systems besides this one world-system.
Therefore, it is stated in the *Kathāvatthu* Pāḷi: "What was the name of that Blessed One? What was his clan?... [and so on] ...Was he from a certain province? It should not be said thus."
And here, when the proponent of the [opposing] side asks, "What is their name?

and so forth, the person representing the opponent—being ignorant of and not seeing the names and other attributes of the Buddhas arising in all world-systems according to his own tenets—rejects it, saying, "It should not be stated thus.
Therefore, in this context, regarding the tenets of the person [concerning] other infinite world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), the proponent of the [opposing] side...
It is understood that there is no arising of other Buddhas [simultaneously]. For even if other Buddhas were to arise in other infinite world-systems,

one who possesses great wisdom (*mahāpañña*), supernormal power (*iddhimā*), and the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) such as the divine eye, having realized and seen the Buddha’s intention as it truly is,
and having attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) according to the method of the matrices (*mātikā*) bestowed by the Teacher—
While teaching the *Kathāvatthu-pāḷi*, the Venerable Mahāmoggaliputta Thera might have spoken of the arising of other Buddhas in countless other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).

[This is not so. Therefore, both this *Kathāvatthu-pāḷi* and the words of its commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) serve to demonstrate the absence of other Buddhas in countless other world-systems, in accordance with the statements found in all the commentaries and sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*).
It should be understood that the statement regarding exertion is indeed more emphatic.
However, it is not the case that Buddhas alone do not arise in other infinite world-systems;

rather, there are also Mahābodhisattvas who have received their predictions, Paccekabodhisattvas, Bodhisattvas of the foremost disciples and great disciples, and Bodhisattvas of the disciple-vehicle whose faculties are fully ripened.
Furthermore, they arise only in this very world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), which has become a Buddha-field, and not elsewhere.

Why? Because Buddhas have not arisen in those other places; moreover, their resolution (*abhinīhāra*), the accumulation of the perfections (*pāramī-sambharaṇa*), and the ripening of their knowledge (*ñāṇa-paripācana*) are accomplished only here, and not elsewhere. Therefore, it is said in the *Mahāpadāna Sutta-ṭīkā*:

“The aspiration for the enlightenment of a disciple (*sāvakabodhi*), the accumulation of the perfections of a disciple (*sāvakapāramī*), and the maturation [of those perfections] for the arising of former Buddhas, Great Bodhisattvas, and Paccekabuddhas, succeed only here in this Cakkavāḷa,
specifically in Jambudīpa which serves as the Buddha-field, and not elsewhere. This is likewise stated in the *Ekanipāta-aṅguttara-ṭīkā*.

Now, however, other teachers say: "Buddhas arise in other world-systems (cakkavāḷa) than this one consisting of a hundred thousand million world-systems, which serves as the field of authority. But their statement is indeed improper. Why?

Because regarding the phrase "in another world-system" used in the Commentary, the word "another" (añña) refers to something other than this very world-system, and not to anything else [such as a different Buddha-field within the same system].
This is because it is impossible for there to be a source [of such a being], and because a Buddha is not a rarity even when many Buddhas have appeared throughout infinite world-systems.
For the Perfectly Enlightened One is indeed a marvelous person. Indeed, it is said in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the *Ekanipāta*:
"Monks, one person, appearing in the world, appears as a marvelous person. Who is that one person?"
“The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—this, monks, is the one person who arises in the world, a marvelous man.
Furthermore, other reasons for this should be understood by the wise through the method already stated by me above. Other teachers, however, [cite] in the *Buddhāpadāna-pāḷi*:
“The ten directions in the world have no end for one who travels through them;
and within that portion of space in the Buddha-field,
my radiance is proclaimed, borne by twin rays of light.”
"Within this interval, there would be a network of rays and vast illumination.

Having grasped the meaning of the first of these two verses according to their own interpretation rather than the Buddha’s intended meaning, they claim through false knowledge that the Buddhas arising in infinite world-systems are innumerable. However, this [claim] of theirs is indeed improper.
It is indeed not beautiful. Why? Because it contradicts the words of the Pāḷi, the Aṭṭhakathā, and the Ṭīkā, and because the interpretation of the meaning of that verse is incorrect.

For if, according to this verse in the Pāḷi, the meaning "other Buddhas arise in other world-systems" were accepted, [it would contradict] the statements in the Aṭṭhakathās: "But having set aside these three fields... and so forth.
There is no sutta stating that Buddhas arise in another world-system while [one] in this world-system [is already present], whereas there is a statement saying they do not arise.
For, in the Three Piṭakas...pe... in the word of the Buddha as established through these three councils...pe...
there is no such sutta. And by the statement "they do not arise," it is direct.

And it is contradictory. By claiming that the Aṭṭhakathā masters, such as the Venerable Buddhaghosa and others, did not see that Pāḷi, he incurs a false accusation against those Aṭṭhakathā masters based on his own misunderstanding.
How could these Aṭṭhakathā masters—who were bearers of the Tipiṭaka and possessed of sharp, keen, swift, and profound knowledge—not have seen it? They certainly would have seen it.
Therefore, that [previous interpretation] is indeed incorrect. It should be understood that the statement found in the commentaries—that "there is no such sutta"—is the more appropriate one.

Furthermore, in this context, the word *buddhakkhette* (in the Buddha-field) should be seen as a qualifier for the phrase *tasmiñca disābhāgamhi* (and in that direction), and the word *asaṅkhyā* (innumerable) should be seen as a qualifier for the word *pabhā* (radiance) in the second verse.
Here, however, is the construction: *loke* means in the world-system (*cakkavāḷaloke*).
The ten directions consist of ten sections. Regarding those sections, as I travel and continue traveling, there is no end or limit for me.
Within the Buddha-field—that field of birth consisting of ten thousand worlds—and in that region of space, my ray-vehicles appear in countless, inexhaustible pairs, arranged in pairs.

The rays (*raṃsi*)—whether carrying forth or emitting light—are described as the radiance of the Wheel-treasure (*cakkaratana*), the Jewel-treasure (*maṇiratana*), and so forth; they are manifested, made evident, or spread abroad.
Within this interval, throughout the ten thousand world-systems (*dasasahassacakkavāḷa*), there was a vast and abundant mass of light, a web of rays produced by a multitude of beams.
This is the meaning [established] by the one who received the title from the Great King of Dharma, the Supreme Sovereign whose banner is the True Dharma, the Lord of the Cakkindābhisiri dynasty.
It should be understood that this was written by Ācariya Budha.
For by these verses, the Blessed One demonstrates that during the time of his existence as a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*),

the immeasurable radiance of his wheel-treasure, jewel-treasure, and so forth, became manifest and spread throughout ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*)— which constitute the Buddha-field— and not throughout infinite world-systems.
"The state of being incalculable for Buddhas who are arising.
For this has been said in the *Buddhāpadāna-ṭīkā*: "The ten directions in the world means that in the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-loka*), the directions consist of ten kinds or ten sections.
Regarding those sections, there is no end for one who goes, who keeps going, who travels."

The meaning is as follows: During the time of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*), in whatever direction or region I went, within the Buddha-field—the domain of a Buddha—there were incalculable, unconditioned (*asaṅkhāra*) qualities.

"Radiance was manifested" means that at that time, during the reign of the wheel-turning monarch, my radiance—the light and splendors of the wheel-treasure, the jewel-treasure, and so forth—appeared clearly, manifesting in pairs, in couples, as vehicles of rays emitting beams of light.
"In this interval, within the ten thousand world-systems (cakkavāḷa), a network of rays, a mass of rays, a vast and abundant light came to be"—this is the meaning.

And here, because the first half-verse constitutes a single syntactical unit, it is said that "the ten directions in the world" refers to the world-system (cakkavāḷa-loka)... [and so on] ...that there is no end. As for the second half-verse...
Because it is included within the second verse, [it is said]: "At the time of a wheel-turning monarch... [etc]... immeasurable (asaṅkhayā) means light devoid of conditioned formations (saṅkhāra);

thus the meaning is that 'at that time, during the era of a wheel-turning monarch... [etc]... there was'. Therefore, the word *asaṅkhayā* should be understood as an adjective qualifying the word *pabhā* ("light") in the second verse.
In the *Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā*, however, after thus demonstrating his unimpeded range of knowledge regarding all phenomena, he now says— showing that there is no other such person in the world—
"Among infinite beings and world-systems,
