he alone is peerless; none at all are equal to him."
In that regard, among the infinite sentient beings in each of the infinite world-systems, there is not even a single one equal to that Tathāgata.
Even if it were granted that no single being is his equal, and that all sentient beings together as one might become his equal—even so, they do not exist;
for the intended meaning is that even if all were gathered together, they would not be equal to this one alone.
It has been stated. And here, by the phrase "in infinite world-systems" and so forth, he shows the absence of other Buddhas in other infinite world-systems besides this Cakkavāḷa.

However, by means of the most powerful supporting statements shown by me—like extracting the very essence of the earth—it is demonstrated that Buddhas arise in world-systems other than this Cakkavāḷa.

*Micchāvāda-sūriyo* means that just as the sun dispels darkness, so too is it to be understood as one who "dispels" (*paṭihaniyati*) and "removes" (*apaniyati*) [ignorance], and thus he is to be seen as a believer.

*Munindakko* is analyzed into the word-division *muninda-akko*; the meaning is "the sun among the lords of sages" (*buddhādicco*). One is a *muni* because they "think" (*manati*) and "know" (*jānāti*) all phenomena.

In the root *mani*, the vowel *i* signifies knowledge; the letter *m* is an augment. Alternatively, one is a *muni* because they "understand" (*munāti*) all phenomena by way of their specific and general characteristics and so forth.

He penetrates [reality], thus he is a *muni*. Or, he is a *muni* because he understands (*munati*) and discriminates between what is beneficial and what is harmful; this refers to the Blessed One. The verbal root *muna* signifies penetration.
Alternatively, *mona* is that by which one understands (*munāti*) or knows the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths; it is the knowledge of the four paths. For it is said in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*:
"‘Mona’ is the knowledge of the four paths. Indeed, it is called ‘mona’ because one understands (*munāti*) it; [it pertains] to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths."
The meaning is "he knows. He possesses silence (*mona*), thus he is a sage (*muni*), the Blessed One.

He is both a sage and a lord (*inda*)—one who rules over and surpasses those beings to be trained by means of the Dhamma—thus he is the Lord of Sages (*muninda*), the Blessed One. Alternatively, he is the Lord of Sages because he is the lord of the five sages;
thus he is the Lord of Sages, the Blessed One. He does not move or go with his feet, but goes by means of the celestial mansion born of his own merit.
*Akko*, *ādico*. [The suffix] *kvi* is added to the verbal root *kam* preceded by *na* in the sense of "going. There is elision of the final element of the root. *K* undergoes doubling (*dvitta*).
Alternatively, it is called *akko* because it moves (*arati*) through space at a height equal to the elevation of Mount Yugandhara.

The suffix *kap* is added to the root *ar* in the sense of "moving," and *k* undergoes doubling. Or else, it is called *akko* because it moves from one heap to another heap (*arati yāti*). Or again, because of its great speed...

He is called *Akka* because he is praised (*akkiyati*) and extolled (*abhitthaviyati*) by people who have faith in him; thus, *Akka* refers to the Sun (*Ādicca*). The verbal root *akk-* signifies praising (*thavana*).
He is both the Lord of Sages (*Muninda*) and the *Akka*, hence *Munindakka*; or, he is like the *Akka*, the Sun, and is therefore the Lord of Sages, *Munindakka*—that is, the Buddha.
For just as the Sun, with its thousand rays, dispels the darkness of gloom within a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) during the day...
Just as [the sun] moves shining, illuminating a region of nine hundred thousand yojanas,
or a region of a thousand kotis, or the ten directions day by day, even so the Blessed One, in his own field of the True Dhamma—
within the ten thousand world-systems that constitute the Buddha-field— dispels the darkness of ignorance among those to be trained, day by day, in each respective [place].

"He wanders as the Radiant One, illuminating the multitude of beings to be trained in every direction with the light of the Dhamma of the Four Truths"—thus he praises the Lord of Munis in a manner befitting his station.
This is a simile of abbreviation (*samāsopamā*), which should be understood as a "low" simile (*hīnūpamā*).

"Pure" (*suddhe*): purified of the stains of passion and so forth. It is "pure" (*suddho*) because it shines and is cleansed; [this refers to] the three realms of existence (*tibhava*). [The root is] *sudha*.
*Soceyya* means purity. *Tibhava-kuhare* means in the mire-pool known as the three realms of existence (*tibhava*). Just like a lotus-pool, beings exist within these three realms;
thus it is called *bhava*. The root *bhū* (to be) with the suffix *ṇa* denotes existence. The three realms of existence are the three worlds: the planes of sense-desire, form, and formlessness.
*Ku* refers to water; that which carries this is a *kuhara*. The root *hara* preceded by *ku* means "to carry," with the suffix *a*. These three...
"Bhava" (existence) and "kuhara" (cavity)—thus it is "tibhavakuhara"; or alternatively, because the three existences are like a cavity, it is so called.
In that "tibhavakuhara. Regarding "kamala": it should be explained as "uppala" (lotus). It is called "kamala" because it "alays" (adorns) "kaṃ" (water); thus it is "uppala.
The root *al* with the prefix *kaṃ-* has the sense of adorning (*vibhūsana*). Alternatively, it is "kamiyati," meaning it is desired.
*Kamalaṃ*. The root *kam* signifies desire; the suffix *alap* is added. That which is called "lotus" (*uppalā*) is "designated as a lotus" (*kamalakathitaṃ*).
Regarding the phrase *vineyyappāṇoghaṃ*, the word analysis is *vineyyapāṇoghaṃ*. The meaning is "the multitude of beings who are to be guided.

One who is to be guided, tamed, or trained by the Teacher is a "disciple" (*vineyyo*), that is, a being (*satto*). The prefix *vi-* combined with the root *paṇ* [in the sense of] taming takes the suffix *ṇya*. *Paṇanti*...

*Pāṇa* is that by which beings live; it is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). [The term is derived as follows: from the root *paṇ*, with the suffix *jīva* and the suffix *ṇa*. That which has this [life] or in which it exists is *pāṇa*; thus, a being (*satta*).

The suffix *ṇa* is applied here according to the rule for secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) beginning with *assa-atthi*. Furthermore, one who is to be disciplined (*vineyya*) and is a living being (*pāṇa*) is a "disciplinable being" (*vineyyappāṇa*).
An *ogha* (flood) is that which strikes, goes toward, or proceeds together with its parts; it is a collection. It is derived from the root *han* preceded by the prefix *ava*.
*Gatiyaṃ* [becomes] *ṇo*. *Avassa* [becomes] *o*. *Hana* becomes *gho*. "The flood (*ogha*) of those who have led away living beings" (*vineyyappāṇānaṃ ogho*) means a multitude; that [flood].
"By the excellent rays of the Dhamma" (*dhammaraṃsivarehi*) means by the rays designated as the supreme Dhamma.

And here, "Dhamma" is so called because it supports (*dhāreti*) sentient beings—who practice according to the instruction—by preventing them from falling into the four states of misery (*apāya*) and the sufferings of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
The earth element (*dhara-dhātu*) is the condition for support; the meaning is that it sustains and destroys the defilements that produce states of woe and so forth.
Both the Noble Eightfold Path and Nibbāna are obtained in the absolute sense (*nippariyāyato*). Why?

Because the Noble Path is the agent of eradication by way of the abandonment through cutting off (*samuccheda-pahāna*) of the defilements, and because Nibbāna is [the goal] by way of the abandonment as escape (*nissaraṇa-pahāna*).

Because, having become an object, it is the cause for the accomplishment of that purpose. Furthermore, the fruit of the four paths and the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti) are obtained in a figurative sense.
Why? Because the fruit conforms to the path by way of the subsiding and abandoning of those defilements which are to be destroyed by the path;
and because the Dhamma of the scriptures is the cause for the attainment of that [fruit] by way of abandoning through substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna).
Alternatively, it is called *dhamma* because it shakes, trembles, moves, and destroys the defilements (*kilesa*);
thus, it refers to the Fourfold Noble Path. The verbal root *dhun* signifies shaking. It is called *dhamma* because it is upheld, penetrated, realized, and taken as an object by the Noble Ones;

thus, it refers to Nibbāna. The verbal root *dhar* signifies knowledge. It is called *dhamma* because it destroys—that is, it pacifies—the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the defilements abandoned by the Path.
Dhamma is the noble fruit. The root *dhaṃsa* means destruction. It is called "dhamma" because it maintains its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and is maintained by the wise, not by fools;
thus, it refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*).

By the grammatical principle of "remainder of one" (*eka-śeṣa*), where "dhamma and dhamma and dhamma and dhamma" becomes simply "dhamma," ten kinds of dhamma are obtained. For this has been said in the *Chattavimāna*:
“The Dhamma free from passion, unshakable, sorrowless, unconditioned, and not repulsive—
sweet, well-mastered, and well-analyzed.”
"Come to this Dhamma for refuge.
Herein, the construction is as follows: "O young man, [come to] this Dhamma which is the fading away of lust and is free from lust;
and this Dhamma which is the Path-dhamma, unshakable and devoid of craving—termed 'shaking' (ejā); and this Dhamma which is the Fruit-dhamma, sorrowless and devoid of sorrow."
"Go to, approach, this Dhamma—the unconditioned, free from the conditioned, and the Dhamma of Nibbāna;

and this Dhamma—the scriptures—free from repulsiveness, non-opposing, sweet because it is endowed with both meaning and phrasing, proficient, possessing excellent qualities, well-analyzed, and thoroughly to be analyzed; go to, approach, its state of being a refuge."
For here, the path is described as "the fading away of lust" (*rāgavirāga*), because by means of it all lust—classified as sensual lust and so forth—is dispassionately detached from and abandoned.

The fruit is described as "the unshaken and sorrowless" (*anejam asokam*), because of the total exhaustion of craving—which is reckoned as "agitation"—and of sorrow, which is characterized by inward brooding, along with the conditions for their arising.
It is called "the unconditioned state" (*dhammam asaṅkhatam*) because it is not conditioned by any cause whatsoever.

Nirvana was spoken of. However, because it illustrates non-opposition, possesses excellence in both meaning and phrasing, reveals distinguished qualities, and is well-analyzed, the entire Dhamma of the scriptures was spoken of by way of the phrases "not repulsive" and so forth. For it is said in the commentary on that [text]:
"In this context, 'fading away of lust' refers to the Path; 'unshakable and sorrowless' refers to the Fruit; 'the unconditioned Dhamma'..."
"Nirvana. This [teaching] is non-repulsive, sweet, skillful, and well-expounded—meaning all the aggregates of Dhamma analyzed by means of the Three Piṭakas.
Here, however, "Dhamma" is tenfold in its general sense; but specifically, it is the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti) that is intended. Why?

Because it is being addressed as "that which makes [the meaning] easily understood" (*subodhesī*). As for "rays" (*raṃsī*): they are called rays because they are relished (*rasiyanti*) and enjoyed; they are called rays because they cause one to taste (*rasanti*) and experience enjoyment.

Alternatively, *raṃsī* is that by which beings delight; it consists of the *rasa*-element (*rasadhātu*) and the suffixes *assa* and *ī*. Or else, it is called *raṃsī* because it causes one to delight—that is, to feel affection—for those [beings];
the *rasa*-element means "affection. There is the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra). *Varo* means "supreme" (*uttamo*).
It is called *varo* because it is to be chosen (*varitabbo*) or longed for (*patthitabbo*), or because it wards off (*varati*) what is inferior; thus it is *varo*. The root is *vara*.
It is *dhamma* and it is a *raṃsi* (ray), thus *dhammaraṃsi*; or, the ray of the *dhamma*, thus *dhammaraṃsi*.
This compound, however, is expressed by means of figurative identification (*abhedūpacāra*). It is both excellent (*vara*) and a *dhammaraṃsi*, thus *dhammaraṃsivara*;

[the plural] *tehi dhammaraṃsivarehi* (by those excellent rays of the *dhamma*). "He awakened well" (*subodhesi*) means he caused [them] to thoroughly awaken by penetrating the *dhamma* of the Four Noble Truths.
The meaning is "he causes to blossom. For just as the sun, having touched it with its own rays,
causes the lotus born in a lake known as a hollow to blossom, even so the Blessed One, by means of the rays known as his own teaching of the Dhamma,

causes the flood of beings to be trained— who dwell within the three realms of existence known as a lotus-lake, who possess a basis of merit, and who are worthy of penetration— to blossom like a lotus.
"Penetrating the Dhamma of the Four Truths, he awakens and causes it to blossom by means of the Dhamma of the fruits"—this is what is meant.

"And whose fame is spread abroad" means whose renown is extended throughout the three worlds; the sense is that the sound of praise for his virtues, such as morality and so forth, has spread far and wide. Here, the word *ca* (and) serves merely to complete the meter.
Or else, [the name] is derived from the fact that he especially (*viśeṣena*) or variously (*vividhaṃ*) attains (*āpnoti*) increase (*vaḍḍhati*).

*Byāpito*. The root *āpa* preceded by the prefix *vi-* has the senses of pervading (*byāpana*) or increasing (*vaḍḍhana*). Alternatively, *byāpana* is the same as *byāpita*. *Kittiyate* means it is praised or extolled; thus, *kittinaṃ*.
This is a noun formed from the action itself (*bhāvasādhana*), and the act of praising is obtained [as its meaning].
That which is praised or extolled by gods and humans is *kittinaṃ*, the sound of praise. The root *kitta* has the sense of praising, with the suffix *yu*. *Byāpito* means spread out or extended.
"Byāpitakkittino" means one whose sound of praise is widespread; [thus he is called] Munindakka.

For the Blessed One’s fame—praised by gods and humans throughout the three worlds for his virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and for his qualities such as being an *Arahaṃ* and a *Sammāsambuddho*—rises up even to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*). Thus it is said that he is praised as "one whose fame is widespread."
*Tilokekaccakkhu*: the word division is *tiloke ekacakkhu*.

The meaning is that he is the one who has become the eye of wisdom for the three worlds, namely the worlds known as Kāma, Rūpa, and Arūpa. "Three worlds" is *tiloka*. He is *tilokekaccakkhu* because he possesses a single eye of wisdom that is like an eye for those three worlds;
[he is thus called] the Sage-Indra (*munindakka*). And here, there is an elision of the word *ekacakkhu*, as in the case of *brahmassara* and similar compounds.
Or alternatively, he has become the sole eye of wisdom for the three worlds; thus he is the "Sole Eye of the Three Worlds," the Sun among Sages (*munindāditya*).
Although one should have said *tilokekaccakkhubhūta*, the word *bhūta* is elided for the sake of metrical prosody (*chandānurakkhaṇattha*), and it is therefore stated as *tilokekaccakkhu*.
Or again, having become the sole being (*ekabhūta*) of the three worlds by means of the eye of wisdom, he sees all phenomena; thus [he is the Sole Eye of the Three Worlds].

The Sun among Sages, the Eye of the Three Worlds. For the Blessed One, because he possesses the eye of wisdom and because he produces it in sentient beings, has become the eye of the three worlds, the embodiment of knowledge, the embodiment of the Dhamma, and the embodiment of Brahma. Indeed, it is said in the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta:
"Friends, that Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen; he has become the eye, the embodiment of knowledge, the embodiment of the Dhamma."
“Having become Brahmā, he is the speaker, the one who sets the wheel of Dhamma in motion, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of Dhamma, the Tathāgata.
Therefore, he is praised as “the single eye of the three worlds.
“Enduring what is difficult to endure” means enduring that state which is exceedingly difficult for worldlings to endure; [a state] difficult for worldlings [to endure].

"Difficult to endure" (*kasirena khamitabba*) means painful; it refers to objects such as the desirable and the undesirable. Although it should have been called *dukkhama*, the letter *ka* has been elided for the sake of protecting the meter (*chandānurakkhaṇattha*) due to its being a "heavy syllable" (*gajja-bandha*), and thus it is stated as *dukhama*. One who "endures" (*sahati*) that is "difficult to endure" (*dukhama*) is a "sufferer of the difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*), namely the Sage (*munindako*). The verbal root *saha* is used in the sense of enduring. That is the state of being a sufferer of the difficult. For the Blessed One, compared to ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*)— [The text continues: ... [is superior]. The Blessed One, having attained the fruit of Arahantship through the power of his own exertion, is not dependent on others. Therefore, he is the one who is "difficult to endure. He is the one who endures even those things that are difficult for others to endure. Thus, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures all suffering, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Moreover, because he is the one who endures the various kinds of suffering arising from the five aggregates of clinging, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of cold and heat, hunger and thirst, wind and sun, and so forth, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being struck by clods of earth, sticks, swords, and weapons, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being bitten by gadflies, mosquitoes, snakes, and scorpions, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being reviled, abused, threatened, and beaten, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of disrespect and contempt, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being deprived of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of bodily pain, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of mental pain, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of both bodily and mental pain, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of worldly suffering, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of supramundane suffering, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are neither worldly nor supramundane, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are beyond conception, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are inconceivable, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are immeasurable, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are incomparable, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are unsurpassed, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are peerless, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are unique, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are extraordinary, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are unprecedented, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are unfathomable, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are unshakeable, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are unassailable, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are invincible, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are unvanquishable, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are unyielding, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are unbreakable, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are indestructible, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are imperishable, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are eternal, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are constant, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are uninterrupted, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are continuous, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are pervasive, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are all-encompassing, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is the one who endures the suffering of being subjected to various forms of suffering that are universal, he is the "Sufferer of the Difficult" (*dukkhamasahano*). Furthermore, because he is

He endures and patiently bears with extreme fortitude this very painful worldliness—consisting of desirable and undesirable objects, cold and heat, gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, and pleasure and pain;
therefore, he is praised as "one who cannot endure suffering.
He is called a "Great Sage" (Mahesi) because he seeks the great aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and so forth, or because he searches for the great Nibbāna.
One who seeks, searches for, and pursues the great aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth is a *mahesi*;

this refers to the Buddha. The word *mahesi* consists of the prefix *maha-* (great), the verbal root *es-* in the sense of seeking (*gavesana*), and the suffix *-i*. For it is said in the *Mahāniddesa*: "A *mahesi* is a *mahesi*.
The Blessed One sought, searched for, and pursued the great aggregate of virtue; therefore he is a *mahesi*. [He sought] the great aggregate of concentration and the great aggregate of wisdom."
"He is a great seer (mahesi) because he sought, searched for, and pursued the great aggregate of liberation and the great aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Alternatively, he is a great seer because he seeks and searches for the thirty-seven great factors conducive to enlightenment;
or he is a great seer because he seeks and searches for the great Nibbāna. For it is said in the *Mahāniddesa*: "The great foundations of mindfulness... [and so forth].
"He is a great seeker (mahesī) because he sought, searched for, and pursued the great right efforts, the great bases of psychic power, the great faculties, the great powers,
the great factors of enlightenment, the great noble eightfold path, and the great ultimate goal,
the deathless Nibbāna. Alternatively, he is a "great seeker" because he is sought, searched for, and pursued by beings of great influence.

"Where is our Buddha?"—thus [asked] the Great Queen (*mahesī*). For it is said in the *Mahāniddesa*: "By beings of great influence, he was sought and searched for: 'Where is the Buddha? and so forth. [The word] *taṃ* refers to that Great Queen.
[The word] *taṃ* refers to the speech of the Sage (*muninda*). The connection is: "I bow my head to him. Furthermore, this is the summary of the construction (*yojanā*) here:
*Dayudayaruṇo* means one for whom the dawn of the sun, which is the mountain of arising known as Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), has risen.

The section on arising (*udayapabba*): Then, like the risen sun and dawn, there is Great Compassion; the broad orb of knowledge, known as omniscience (*sabbaññutañāṇa*), is perfectly circular, possessing the omniscient knowledge of vast objects like the expansive circle of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
He is alone, without companion, the solitary Buddha, who, like the sage-sun, has purified himself of the stains of passion and the like.

In the pure hollow of the threefold existence, within the lotus-pond designated as the threefold existence, that which is called a lotus—the multitude of beings to be guided—must be described as blooming like a blue lotus.

Having crossed the flood of living beings, he caused them to awaken well and caused them to blossom by means of the cool rays known as the supreme Dhamma, making the Dhamma of the Four Truths understood through his realization; thus he whose fame is spread far and wide.

One whose renown is spread throughout the three worlds; or one whose voice of praise for virtues such as morality is widespread; the sole eye of the three worlds—that which has become the eye of wisdom for the three worlds known as the realms of desire, form, and formlessness;
one who endures suffering—that which endures a state of extreme hardship unendurable by ordinary people;
a great seer (mahesi)—one seeking the greatness of the aggregate of virtue and so forth.
"I bow my head and pay homage to that sage who, while seeking Nibbāna, [renounced] even his children, wife, limbs, and life.
The commentary on the twentieth verse of praise is complete.
The Victor, throughout many births—even at the cost of his children, wife, limbs, and life;
With a mind unattached even to love for enlightenment, he gave everything away to whomever it might belong;
thereafter, he fulfilled the perfection of giving as well as the perfections of virtue and the rest.
I pay homage to that sole island who has reached the path through the success of those very perfections.

21. Having thus praised the Sage with the twentieth verse, he now speaks the words beginning with "Yo jino" (He who is the Conqueror), desiring to worship the Jina after extolling him for his virtues—such as the sacrifice of life and so forth—while fulfilling the ten perfections of giving and the rest during his time as a Bodhisatta over many previous births.
This [verse], moreover, consists of twenty syllables, being composed with groups of three and four syllables that are heavy and light.

It should be understood that the verse has been explained. For it is said in the *Vuttodaya*: "The *vutta* [meter] consists of *ra*, *ja*, *na*, *ta*, *ga*, *la*, *ra*, *ja*, *ra*, *ja*, *ga*, *la*, *ra*, *ha*, and *u*.
Herein, however, the application is as follows: in each quarter-verse there are the groups *ra-ja-ra-ja* and *ra-ja-ra-ja-ra-ja*.
And if there were *garulha* and *ce* [particles], then such and such verses would be called by name; thus it is said, "verses by name" (*gāthā nāma*).

In that context, "he who is the Victor" (*yo jino*) refers to the Buddha. For he is called the "Victor" (*jina*) because he has conquered, is conquering, and will conquer the five Māras—namely, the Māra of the sons of gods (*devaputta-māra*), the Māra of defilements (*kilesa-māra*), the Māra of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra-māra*), the Māra of the aggregates (*khandha-māra*), and the Māra of death (*maccu-māra*). But are not the disciples of the Buddha also [victors over] the five Māras?

If it is argued that he is called a "Conqueror" (jina) because of his victory (*jinattā*), [the reply is: It is the Blessed One alone who is called a Conqueror because of his victory over the five Māras by way of the excellence consisting in the absence of dependence on another. For it is said in the *Dhātukathāmūlaṭīkā*:

"In that context, [victory] over the Māra of the Son of the Devas (*devaputtamāra*) is by way of the destruction of power and the transcending of its domain; [victory] over the Māra of Clinging to Existence (*bhavāsavamāra*) is by way of non-arising..."

Because the Māra of defilements, the Māra of volitional formations, and the Māra of aggregates were shattered at the very foot of the Bodhi tree through the full understanding that consists in the abandoning of their origin—
and because the Māra of death was likewise shattered— the Blessed One alone is praised as "the Shatterer of Māra," based on that unsurpassed shattering which is independent of any external support.
"Anekajātiyaṃ" means "in many births within saṃsāra. For here, this word *jāti* has multiple meanings.
Thus, in the expression "one birth, two births," it refers to a *bhava* (existence). In the expression "There is, Viśākhā, a class of ascetics called Nigaṇṭhas," it refers to a *nikāya* (class/type).
In the expression "The grass called *tiri*, having grown from the navel, stood touching the sky," it refers to a species of grass (*tiṇajāti*).
Regarding the term "conceptualization" (*paññatti*): 1. "Birth is comprised by two aggregates"—this refers to the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*).
2. "The first consciousness that arose in the mother’s womb, the first mind that became manifest; taking that as its basis, there is his birth"—this refers to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). 3.
"The Bodhisatta, Ānanda, has just been born"—this refers to actual physical birth (*pasūti*). 4. "Unreproached" (*anupakuṭṭho*)... [refers to the state of being free from blame].
"By way of birth" (*jātivādena*): here it refers to family. "Because I, sister, am born of noble birth" (*ariyāya jātiyā*): here it refers to noble virtue (*ariyasīla*).
But here [in this context], it occurs in the sense of existence (*bhava*). Therefore, the meaning should be understood as "through manifold existence in *saṃsāra*.

For that which is born, distinguished by its womb, destiny, and so forth, is called "birth" (*jāti*). Alternatively, it is called "birth" because the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth are born—that is, produced—within it.
Birth (*jāti*) and existence (*bhava*). The element of birth (*janidhātu*) means "to produce. It is not one, but many; that which is many and is birth is "multiple births" (*anekajāti*).
In those multiple births. Together with son and wife (*saputtadāra*): accompanied by both son and wife. He purifies, cleanses, and clears his own family (*kula*).
Or, he is a *putta* because he fills (*pūreti*) the heart of his mother and father; *pu* is the root meaning "to fill," with the suffix *ta*. Both son and daughter are called *putta*;
this is an example of the grammatical rule of "single remainder for dissimilar forms" (*virūpeka-sesa*). He is a *dāra* because he is supported (*dhariyati*) by the husband;

*dhar* is the root meaning "to support," with the suffix *ṇo*, and the change of *dh* to *d*. Alternatively, he is a *dāra* because wealth is given (*dīyati*) to him by the man; *dā* is the root meaning "to give," with the suffix *rapaccaya*.

Alternatively, *dāra* means "wife" because she is enjoyed (*ramiyati*) there by a man who is desirous (*dākucchita*). The suffix *kvi* is added to the verbal root *dā* (in the form *dāru*) preceded by *pu*, in the sense of enjoying.

The word *dā* has the meaning of "desirous. However, in the *Abhidhānaṭīkā*, it is stated: "It is *dāra* because they cause to tear apart (*dārayante*); [the root] *dara* is used in the sense of tearing apart (*vidāraṇe*).

The suffix *ṇo* is applied after a root that does not denote an agent, when forming a technical term (*saññāyaṃ*). A son (*putta*) and a wife (*dāra*) together are "son-and-wife" (*puttadāra*). This is also an example of a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandepi*).
For the teachers maintain that [the word] *putta* is masculine. That with which one dwells together is "together with son and wife" (*saputtadāra*), meaning the renunciation of son and wife.

That is "together with son and wife. "Even limbs and life" (*aṅgajīvitam-pi*): the parts of the body such as hands, feet, ears, nose, eyes, etc., and the entire body bound up with the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*)—it goes to the body (*kāya*), thus it is an "limb" (*aṅga*);
the limbs of the body such as the eyes, etc. [The root] *agi* is the verbal root *gi*.
*Gatiyaṃ a.* It is called *jīvitaṃ* (life) because beings live by means of it; it is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
The root *jīv-* is used in the sense of "sustaining breath" (*pāṇadhāraṇe*). *Aṅga* and *jīvita* together form *aṅgajīvitaṃ*. Here, the particle *pi* has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍanattho*).
By this, the renunciation of wealth and kingdom is included. For it is said in the *Sīlakkhandha-vaṇṇanā*:
“Having relinquished these five great relinquishments—the relinquishment of limbs, and the relinquishment of life, wealth, kingdom, children, and wife.
Alternatively, it has the sense of inspiring confidence (*sambhāvanattha*).

By this, the Blessed One inspires confidence by showing that even for the sake of omniscient knowledge, he relinquishes his children, wife, limbs, and life with an unattached mind, let alone external objects such as wealth.

"Bodhipema" means "dear to enlightenment," because it is dear to the enlightenment consisting of the path to arahantship and the knowledge of omniscience; for here the suffix *-to* is used in the sense of a cause (*hetvatthe*).
That which awakens to the four truths is "enlightenment" (*bodhi*); this refers to the knowledge of the path to arahantship. That which awakens to all knowable phenomena is "enlightenment";
this refers to the knowledge of omniscience. [The root] *budh* with the suffix *dhātu* [forms] *ñāṇe*; the suffix *ṇa* [is applied]. The suffix *ī* indicates the feminine gender.
For it is said in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*: "The word *bodhi* refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*) and to the noble path (*ariyamagga*), but not to a noble person (*ariya*).
Because both instances of *bodhi* are identical in form, they are combined into the singular as *bodhi*. *Pema* means affection; or, that which is to be loved is *pema*.
The verbal root *pī* [is used] in the senses of heating and desiring, with the suffix *man*. Affection for enlightenment is *bodhipema*; from that *bodhipema*. By the Blessed One...

Indeed, it is said that they hold the knowledge of enlightenment (bodhiñāṇa) dear a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even a hundred-thousandfold more than their own sons, wives, limbs, or life. For it is stated in the Vessantara Jātaka:
"Neither my two sons are to be given away, nor is Queen Maddī to be given away."
“Omniscience is dear to me; therefore, you have given what is dear. Regarding the phrase *alaggamānaso*:
having a mind that does not cling (*anallīyana-citto*) to children, wife, limbs, life, and so forth. *Lagga* means clinging, attachment, or being stuck.

It is called *lagga* because it clings (*lagati*), adheres (*saṅgati*), or sticks (*allayati*). The verbal root *lag* (in the sense of clinging or adhering) takes the suffix *gap*. That which is not *lagga* is *alagga*.
*Alagga*: "Unattached," meaning there is no attachment here to children, wife, limbs, life, and so forth; hence, *alagga*. *Mana*: that which knows or cognizes the object (*ārammaṇa*) is *mano*;
that very thing is *mānasa*. He whose mind (*mānasa*) is unattached (*alagga*) is *alaggamānaso*, the Conqueror (*jino*).
*Atthikassa*: one who desires children, wife, and so forth; the meaning is "one who asks" or "one who receives. One for whom there is desire (*attha*) is *atthika*.
...the one who possesses it. "He gave indeed" means that, out of a desire to honor and assist others, he did not fail to give through the volition of renunciation associated with wisdom;

for when the Bodhisatta was fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs), even while still possessing lust, hatred, and delusion, he would shave the heads of beggars who came and went—though they were fully adorned—and draw out blood from their necks, and [give] well-anointed...

Having gouged out his own eyes and having renounced, without regard, his son—who was the lamp of his family lineage—and his beloved wife as if they were a globule of spittle, it is possible to attain the knowledge of Perfect Self-Enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*) only while giving; it cannot be attained without renouncing even one's children, wife, limbs, and life.
Indeed, there has never been anyone who became a Buddha without having practiced the five great acts of renunciation (*mahāpariccāga*).

However, Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples (ariyasāvakas) are indeed capable of attaining the knowledge of the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha or a noble disciple even without renouncing their children, wives, limbs, or lives.

For this very reason, [the Blessed One] praises Kassapa, saying: "There is one who gave even his own children, wife, limbs, and life to the Blessed One alone, with a mind unattached due to love for enlightenment.
Indeed, this is stated in the commentary on the Vessantara Jātaka:
“There has never been anyone who became a Buddha without having relinquished these five great sacrifices:
the sacrifice of wealth, the sacrifice of children, the sacrifice of a wife, the sacrifice of limbs, and the sacrifice of life.
Having thus praised the Blessed One by means of the qualities of the five great sacrifices, [the author now praises him] by means of the quality of fulfilling the perfections such as giving.
Desiring to perform the praise, he spoke the words beginning with "the perfection of giving" (*dānapāramitā*). Therein, "giving" (*dāna*) is threefold:

the volition of relinquishment (*cāgacetanā*), abstention (*virati*), and the object to be given (*deyyadhamma*). For in passages where it is said, "faith, moral shame (*hiri*), and the wholesome are giving," the volition of relinquishment is what is called "giving.

In passages where it is said, "he gives fearlessness," abstention is what is called "giving. [And in the passage,] "he gives a gift of food... *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*

The gift to be given at the place where one has come to drink is called *dāna*. In this context, it is *dāna* because the volition of relinquishment (*cāgacetanā*) gives or causes the gift to be given;
by means of this, one gives the object to be given. Alternatively, it is *dāna* in the sense of cutting off (*avakhaṇḍana*) or lopping off (*lavana*).
For when it arises, it cuts away and lops off the unwholesome volition characterized by fear and dread; thus, it is *dāna*.
That which is given as a thing to be given is *dāna*. Here, however, three kinds of giving are intended.

The etymological meaning of the word *pāramī* has already been stated above. Alternatively, it is called *pāramī* because by means of it one goes (*eti*) or reaches (*gacchati*) the further shore (*pāra*), which is Nibbāna.
The suffix *kvi* is applied here to the root *i* with the prefix *pāra-*. The word division should be made as *pāram* + *iti*. Giving itself is *pāramī*.
The perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*); that is, the perfection of giving. "From that" means from the perfection of giving. "Another" means something else.
Regarding "the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramā*) and so forth": it is called *sīla* because it cools (*sīlati*). The root *sīl* [with the suffix] *a* pertains to concentration (*samādhi*).

The meaning is that it composes or causes to compose bodily and verbal actions. Alternatively, it is *sīla* because it cools, because it concentrates, or because it does not become distracted due to the excellent conduct of bodily actions and so forth.
*Śīla* means that by means of it, one composes (*samādahanti*) the mind; thus it is *śīla*. Alternatively, it is *śīla* because it steadies (*sīlayati*) or supports (*upadhāreti*).
The root *śīl* is used in the sense of supporting; the meaning is that it firmly holds (*ābhuso dhāreti*) wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) by way of being their foundation.
Or else, it is *śīla* because by means of it the virtuous ones steady or support wholesome states; it is steadied or supported.

Virtue (*sīla*) is so called because it brings one close to the very heart-flesh of the true persons (*sappurisa*), or because it supports (*sīleti*) and sustains the person endowed with it by way of preventing rebirth in the states of misery and leading to a happy destination and *nibbāna*. Virtue itself as a perfection is "virtue-perfection" (*sīlapāramī*).

That which has this as its beginning is "that which begins with the virtue-perfection. And here, by the word "beginning," the perfections of renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truth, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity are included.
He encompasses them. For this has been said in the Buddhavaṃsa-pāḷi:
“Generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, and energy as the fifth;
patience, truthfulness, resolve, loving-kindness, and equanimity—these are the ten.”
And here, the word *pi* has the sense of conjunction; by it, he conjoins [the deeds] with the five great renunciations.
"He fulfilled" means that he brought them to completion for the sake of perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).
For from the time the Blessed One made his aspiration for Buddhahood after combining the eight qualities at the feet of Dīpaṅkara, throughout many births, he [strived] for perfect enlightenment.
For one striving to penetrate [the truth], there is no such thing as a gift not given, nor any virtue not guarded.
There is no perfection (pāramī) that has not been fulfilled; indeed, he fulfilled them even to an extreme degree.
For when the Blessed One was a Bodhisatta, having surpassed the waters of the four great oceans, he gave a blood-donation that exceeded them. Having surpassed the dust of the entire earth...
He gave away flesh in abundance. Having surpassed even Sineru, the king of mountains, he gave away his head as a gift in abundance.
Having surpassed the multitude of stars in the sky, he gave away his eyes in abundance.
Therefore, it is said in the *Jinālaṅkāra*:
Thus he gave blood exceeding the waters of the ocean;
having conquered the earth, he gave it as a gift along with his own flesh;
and he offered his head together with its hair, equal in measure to Mount Meru.
“His eye became even more like a star in the sky.
This is a *vasantatilakā* verse.
In that context, “he” refers to the Bodhisatta of such a nature. “In the ocean” means among the four great oceans. “The sea” (*jaladhika*)—
"Having made it exceed water": she gave the gift of blood, that is, she gave a gift of red blood. "Having conquered the earth":
having conquered the dust of the dusty ground, she gave her own bodily flesh as something exceeding. "Exceeding the measure of Mount Meru":
having made it exceed even the measure of the king of mountains, which is six hundred and eighty thousand yojanas in height. "Together with the head and the hair."
He gave his head, together with the crown, after it had been consecrated. "Kheti" means in the sky, reaching as far as the edge of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) and the mountains.
"Tārakādhikataraṃ" means having made it even more excellent than the forms of stars and constellations. "Nayanaṃ adāsī" means he gave the gift of eyes; such is the meaning to be understood here.
Regarding "tāsamiddhiyopayātamaggataṃ," the word division is *tāsaṃ iddhiyā upayātaṃ aggaṃ*. "Tāsaṃ" refers to...

Of those perfections (*pāramī*). "By means of power" (*iddhiyā*) means by means of success (*samiddhi*); here the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause (*hetvattha*). "Attained" (*upayātaṃ*) means arrived at. "The state of supremacy" (*aggataṃ*) means the highest status among all beings; the meaning is the state of Buddhahood, which is the most excellent.
Furthermore, that word [supremacy] is the object (*kamma*) for the word "attained. And here, the word *agga* is a non-derived primary term (*anipphanna-pāṭipadika*) signifying "supreme."
Alternatively, he is called *Agga* because he reaches the highest state (*aggati*), the supreme condition, or the state of Buddhahood; thus he is the Conqueror (*jina*).

[The suffix] *-a* is used in the sense of going (*gati*) in the word *aggadhātu*. The state of being the highest is *aggataṃ*. For the Blessed One is the highest, most excellent, and most sublime among all beings in infinite world-systems—this is the meaning. Indeed, this has been stated in the *Dasanipāta* of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*:
“Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless;
whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost among them.
Regarding the phrase *tamekadīpakaṃ*: the word division is *taṃ ekadīpakaṃ*. *Taṃ* refers to the Conqueror (*jina*). *Ekadīpakaṃ* means [the sole lamp] for all beings.
It is that which has become the sole refuge or the foundation. For the word *dīpaka* is a derivative (*nipphanna-pāṭipadika*) denoting refuge and foundation.
Indeed, it is said in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*: "A lamp (*dīpa*) in the sense of providing a foundation.

Or else, he is the *Dīpaka*, the Conqueror (*Jina*), because beings take their stand (*dīpanti*) and find support (*patiṭṭhahanti*) in him by way of refuge. The verbal root *dīp* [in this context] means "to stand" (*patiṭṭhāyaṃ*), with the suffix *aka*. The word *eka*...
It expresses a number. "Ekadīpaka" means one who is a single lamp; [it refers to] the Jina.

Alternatively, "ekadīpaka" means that which has become the sole Buddha, serving as a refuge and a support for all beings—just like a lamp on an island in the ocean—serving as a refuge and a support for human beings.
Now, this is the etymological explanation here: it shines in the midst of the water, thus it is an island (*dīpa*).
Or, water flows on both sides of it, thus it is an island; that very thing is an "islet" (*dīpaka*). Having become a solitary Buddha, he comes, goes, and moves about alone;
thus he is a "solitary-island" (*ekadīpaka*), a Conqueror (*jina*). For just as in the great ocean, for people whose ships have been wrecked, the island in the sea is their refuge and their support.
In this way, the Jina becomes the sole Buddha, the refuge, and the support for all beings who are sinking in the ocean of *saṃsāra*, where no footing can be found;
thus he is praised as "the single lamp. The connection is: "I bow down to that Jina. This, then, is the concise explanation (*saṅkhepayojanā*) here:
the Jina, throughout many births and many *saṃsāra* existences, [protected] himself along with his children and wife...
Together with his son and wife, even his limbs and life— the life-faculty of the various parts of the body—
or alternatively, both the bodily members such as hands, feet, ears, nose, and eyes, and the entire body dependent upon the life-faculty;
"with a mind unattached" because of his love for enlightenment, meaning his affection for the path to Arahatship known as omniscient wisdom (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*).
Having become a mind that does not cling to children, wife, limbs, life, and so forth, he gave away his children, wife, and the rest to any seeker or petitioner who desired them;
indeed, he gave them through the volition of total relinquishment.

Furthermore, he fulfilled the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*), and beyond that, he also fulfilled the perfections beginning with morality (*sīlapāramī*) and the others, for the sake of attaining perfect enlightenment.

I bow with the three doors to that Conqueror who has attained—has reached—the state of preeminence, the supreme condition, or the status of the most excellent Buddha through the power and perfection of those perfections;
who is the sole island for all beings, having become their single refuge or single foundation;
who, like a lamp, has become their sole refuge and foundation.
The commentary on the twenty-first verse of homage is completed.
To the God beyond gods, the supreme god; the bearer of the body that is indestructible; the breaker of Māra, himself unbroken;
the island for the people, the lamp; who attained victory on the noble bed of the Bodhi tree, having reached his goal.

I perpetually bow down to that Lord of Sages, the Lord of Sages, who is praised by Brahmās and those who have reached the state of Brahmā, who speaks with excellent words, who is free from evil, who has abandoned [all defilements], and who delights the world and its inhabitants.
(22) Having thus worshipped the Victor with the twenty-first verse, he now [praises him] with the ten verses beginning with "Devādevātideva" (the God beyond the gods).
Having praised the Lord of Sages with his virtues, [the author], desiring to pay homage to him, spoke the verse beginning with "Devādevātideva.

This should be understood as a *saddharā* stanza, composed of twenty-one syllables through the *gaṇa*s *ma-ra-bha-na-ya-ya* and the *timuniyati* meters, and characterized by *yamaka* (rhyme) at both the beginning and the end.
For it is said in the *Vuttodaya*: "Where *ma*, *ra*, *bha*, *na*, *ya*, and *ya* occur, joined with *timuniyati*..."
"...is proclaimed as having six feet.
This, however, is the construction here: in which [verse] there is a *mr* (ma-ra) gaṇa, two *bhn* (bha-na) gaṇas, and a *yogaṇa*;
and together with that *yagaṇa*, there is a *yogaṇa*; and it is joined by pauses (*yatī*) consisting of three *muni* (ma-gaṇa), *yati* (ya-gaṇa), and *yuta* (ra-gaṇa), ending in seven syllables.
These may be so. Herein, in this natural meter (*pakaticchanda*), this verse is designated as a *saddharāgāthā*.

And here, the word *muni* should be understood as denoting the number seven. Because there are three repetitions of the pause (*yati*) at every seventh syllable within each quarter-verse (*pāda*), it is said to be "joined with the triple-muni-pause" (*timuniyatiyutā*). Thus, it is stated that it possesses twenty-one syllables.

And therein, "the god beyond gods" refers to one who is the most excellent and supreme among the gods of conventional designation—namely, those known as kings—and the gods by birth, such as the Four Great Kings, being a god of purified nature. For here, "gods" first refers to gods of conventional designation;
for they "shine" (devanti) by means of human sovereignty and prosperity, and thus human kings, queens, and princes are called "gods. Again, "gods" refers to gods by birth; for they...

They are called the *Cātumahārājika* devas because they shine with the attainment of divine sovereignty (*dibba-issariya-sampatti*). They shine, meaning they sport, dally, and play with the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) and so forth;
or else, they dwell among them. By virtue of their capacity for victory, they desire to conquer adversaries;

they conduct themselves by exercising authority, bestowing and receiving wealth and honors, and providing various instructions on matters of interest. This is due to the power attained through the influence of an abundance of merit (*puñña*).
They shine with splendor (*jutiyā jotanti*). They proceed toward their intended objects without resistance (*appaṭighātena*), and they are capable of accomplishing whatever they desire;
thus they are called *devas*. This should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā*.

"Surpassing the gods" (*atideva*) means that the Blessed One is superior to those gods—most excellent or most sublime—and has become a god through purification (*visuddhi-devabhūta*); such is the meaning. He...

Indeed, because he surpasses those gods of rebirth (*upapatti-deva*) by virtue of his superior qualities such as moral conduct (*sīla*), the Blessed One is called "the god beyond the gods" (*atideva*).
A god who is superior to gods, the most excellent, the best, the most distinguished—such a god is called "the god beyond the gods" (*devātideva*);
the Lord of Sages (*muninda*), having become a purified god, is thus attained. [I pay homage] to that God Beyond the Gods.
For it is said in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*: “‘Devas’ refers to three kinds of devas: conventional devas (*sammutideva*), devas by birth (*upapattideva*), and purified devas (*visuddhideva*).
Conventional devas are kings, queens, and princes. Devas by birth are those from the gods of the Four Great Kings upwards.
Purified devas are called the Arahants.”

The Blessed One, however, through his unsurpassed play of supernormal knowledge (*abhiññā*), by means of the supreme divine, brahma, and noble abidings (*vihāra*), through the manifestation of the power of mind that effects the conquest of the fivefold Māras within himself and others,

through the excellence of conventional expression— consisting of the seven treasures such as sovereignty of mind and right practice, and the acceptance and giving of honor based on verified confidence—
and through the radiance of the body of wisdom which conforms to the true nature of phenomena and the inclinations of individuals, [he taught].

Because he is endowed with splendor that is not shared by others, with the movement of the body of knowledge, and with unimpeded power in the accomplishment of the supreme benefit of the qualities of omniscience and victory over Māra, he is to be gone to for refuge by the world including the devas;
because he is to be praised and is desirable through devotion, he stands having surpassed all those devas by means of those very qualities; therefore, of those devas...
"He is the most excellent, the most supreme god" (*devātideva*) should also be understood according to the method found in the *Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā*.

"Bearer of the final body" (*nidhanavapudhara*): this refers to the maintenance of the very last physical body. Here, the word *nidhana* is an un-derived (*anipphanna*) primary noun (*pāṭipadika*) signifying "end.

Alternatively, it is *nidhana* because one brings [something] to an end (*nidheti pariyosānaṃ karoti*) by means of it; or else, it is so called because it brings [existence] to an end (*nidheti vināseti bhavaṃ*).
The final body is obtained. The root *dhā* preceded by *ni-* signifies destruction (*nāsa*). It is called *vapu* because one sows (*vapati*) the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma here;
thus, *vapu* means the body. The root *vap* signifies the continuity of seeds. That which is both an end (*nidhana*) and a body (*vapu*) is *nidhanavapu*;
he who bears (*dharo*) that is the Lord of Sages (*munindo*). [The compound refers to] him who bears that final body. For he, throughout the existences of the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra...

Because he has utterly severed all defilements that would otherwise lead to rebirth by means of the sword of the knowledge of the supreme path at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), there is no further production of renewed existence. Indeed, this birth as a Buddha is his final existence;
therefore, he specifically praises the Lord of Sages (Muninda) as one who bears the body of deathlessness. For it is said in the Aṅguttara Nikāya: "The Buddha is the bearer of the final [existence]."
*Mārabhaṅga* means the shattering of the five Māras, beginning with the Devaputta-māra. The meaning of the word *māra* has already been explained above.

[The term] *mārabhaṅga* refers to the Lord of Sages (*muninda*), who breaks, has broken, or will break the five Māras. The verbal root *bhanj*, preceded by the prefix *māra*, takes the suffix *-a* (tapaccaya) in the sense of crushing.
Following the root-final vowel, there is the substitution of *o* for the suffix-initial *a*. The nasal *n* is replaced by the *niggahita* (anusvāra). Of that...
The substitution of the *ka*-group [consonants] at the end [of the word]. That is "Mārabhaṅga. "Abhaṅga" means incapable of being broken or destroyed by the army of Māra;
that which is broken is a "bhaṅga. "Not a bhaṅga" is "abhaṅga. Alternatively, it is "abhaṅga" because it is not broken by the army of Māra.
The meaning is that it is not fit to be broken by the army of Māra. Or, it is "abhaṅga" because the army of Māra is not capable of breaking it.
"O Lord of Sages. That is the indeclinable [particle].
"They understand the island, the island of understanding"—here the connection is that they illuminate the island of understanding. In that context, "they understand" refers to sentient beings.
They are born and produced by those karmic defilements; or else, they are born and produced in a manifold way by way of rebirth-linking and death.

"Births" (pajāti) is what is said. "They illuminate" means they illuminate the lamp of wisdom. For it is called "illuminating" because, having analyzed wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, it illuminates, reveals, and makes them manifest;
thus it is said to "illuminate. Alternatively, it is a "lamp" (dīpa) because it shines and glows. The meaning is that it dispels darkness and reveals light.
The verbal root *dīp* is used in the sense of shining. "Like a lamp" (dīpamiva) refers to wisdom (*paññā*). For just as a physical lamp—
"Having dispelled darkness, it makes light manifest"—thus it is said that wisdom, having struck down the darkness of ignorance, makes the light of the Dhamma manifest.
That is the "island. Furthermore, "island" (*dīpa*) means "that which illuminates" (*dīpaka*), "that which makes manifest.

For it is called an "island" (*dīpa*) because it illuminates (*dīpeti*) and makes manifest. Indeed, by virtue of attending upon him, the Lord of Sages [illuminates] for those beings who are to be trained, whether they have come or gone.
It is said that through the teaching of the Dhamma, he illuminates the lamp of wisdom consisting of the knowledge of the four paths and so forth.
That lamp [is placed] upon the "Victorious Excellent Couch" (*jayavara-sayana*), which is the supreme Bodhi throne-seat that serves as the locus for conquering the five Māras.

It is called "Victory" (*jaya*) because one conquers the five Māras there; it is the Bodhi-tree throne. The root *ji* means "to conquer," with the suffix *ṇa*. It is called "excellent" (*vara*) because it is to be sought after and longed for.
*Vara*, *varadhātu*, *patthaṇe*: *a*. Or, it is called *vara* because it wards off (*varati*) or restrains (*nivāreti*) what is inferior; thus *varadhātu* is used in the sense of warding off: *a*.

A *sayana* is that which is resorted to (*seviyati*) or frequented (*bhajiyati*) by the Buddha; *sidhātu* is used in the sense of service or resorting to: *yu*. A *varasayana* is an excellent (*uttama*) bed (*sayana*).
A *jayavarasayana* is a victory-excellent-bed; [it refers to] the couch at the Bodhi tree. In that.
*Bodhipattaṃdhipattanti* is analyzed as *bodhipattaṃ adhipattanti*. "Bodhipatta" refers to that which has reached the path of Arahatship and the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutañāṇa*).
Furthermore, the word "bodhi" applies to the tree, the path, knowledge, omniscience, and Nibbāna.
For instance, in such passages as "He was first fully enlightened at the foot of the Bodhi tree," it applies to the tree. In the four [noble truths], "bodhi" is so called...

In such passages as "knowledge of the paths," it refers to the path. In such passages as "the one of excellent wisdom and vast intelligence attains enlightenment," it refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*).

In such passages as "having attained enlightenment, the deathless, the unconditioned," it refers to *nibbāna*. But here, what is intended is the Blessed One’s omniscient knowledge of the path to arahantship.
Enlightenment (*bodhi*) is so called because one awakens to the four truths; it is the knowledge of the path to arahantship. [It is that which] regarding all phenomena to be known...

It is called *bodhi* because one awakens (*bujjhati*); it is the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutañāṇa*). [The suffix] *ṇa* and the vowel *ī* are added to the verbal root *budh* in the sense of knowledge.

"Bodhi" and "bodhi" become "bodhi" by way of the grammatical rule of *sarūpa-ekasesa* (retaining only one of identical forms). He who has attained (*apajji*) that—meaning he has gone to it—is "one who has reached awakening" (*bodhipatto*), the Lord of Sages (*munindo*). That is "one who has reached awakening" (*bodhipatta*).
"One who has reached supremacy" (*adhipatta*) means one who has attained the state of being the eldest among all gods and humans in the world including the devas. Among all gods and humans...
"Adhippatto" means one who has attained, reached, or arrived at the state of being the eldest and the state of being the most senior; [this refers to] the Lord of Sages (Munindo).

Just as among chicks, that chick which breaks out of the eggshell first has attained the state of being the eldest and the state of being the most senior among them, even so the Blessed One [has attained this] among the world with its devas, amidst beings whose ignorance has departed.

Having burst open that eggshell of ignorance, he has reached—because he was the first to be born into the noble birth, because he excels all other qualities such as virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and because he is peerless—the state of being the eldest, the most senior, the best, and the incomparable among all gods and humans;
this is what is meant by "he has attained. Therefore, he praises him with the word *adhippatta*.
Regarding the phrase *brahmābrahmāgatānaṃ*: the word division is *brahma* and *abrahma-āgatānaṃ*. The meaning is:
"of those who have come"—that is, those who have come by way of attending upon—the assemblies of Brahmās, gods, and humans. In this context, "Brahmās" refers to the retinues of Brahmā and so forth;

for they are called "Brahmās" because they cause things to grow (*brūhanti*) or increase through qualities such as meditative absorption (*jhāna*). "Non-Brahmās" (*abrahmā*) refers to gods and humans.
For they are not called "non-Brahmas" (abrahma); they are "come" (āgatā) because they come for the purpose of paying homage;
thus Brahma and Brahmas are found. The root *gam* preceded by the prefix *ā-* signifies going (*gati*). "Come Brahma and non-Brahma" is *brahmābrahmāgatā*; [the word] belongs to them.
This is a qualifying term placed last (a *paranipāta*), as in such examples as *agyāhito*. Furthermore, that word [is used] in the phrase *varagirakathikanti*.
The recipient (*sampadāna*). "Of those who attend upon" means of the assemblies of Brahmas, devas, and humans.
"The speaker of excellent speech" (*varagirakathika*) refers to one teaching the supreme word of the Dhamma; or, teaching the Dhamma with the most excellent speech.
*Girā* means that which is sung or spoken; it is speech. The root *gā* signifies sound, and the suffix *-ira* is added. Excellent and most distinguished speech is *varagirā*.

"He speaks the Dhamma with that [voice]" means he is a speaker with a sublime voice, the Lord of Sages (*muninda*). The meaning is that he teaches the Dhamma with speech that is most excellent and pleasing.
"Devoid of evil" refers to base, unwholesome defilements (*kilesa*); for they are called "evil" (*pāpa*) because they cause one to reach suffering in the states of misery and so forth.
*Akusala-kilesa*: unwholesome defilement. *Pāpuṇane*: in the sense of reaching, the prefix *pā-* is used with the root *padhātu*.

That which is to be abandoned or cast off by a wholesome state (*kusala-dhamma*) is called "inferior" (*hīna*). It refers to a base state. The root *hā-* signifies abandoning; with the suffix *-ta*, it becomes *hīna*. Evil itself is inferior, thus *pāpa-hīna*.

"Abandoned" (*pahīna*) means completely eradicated by the knowledge of the path of Arahatship. "He abandons," thus he is "abandoned" (*pahīna*), O Lord of Sages (*muninda*). The root *hā-* is preceded by the prefix *pa-*.
"Relinquishing this": the meaning is that one completely eradicates all unwholesome states by means of the knowledge of the supreme path (*aggamagga-ñāṇa*).
"Delighting in the light of the world" (*lokālokābhirāma*): the word division is *loka-aloka-abhirāma*.

The meaning is that it is the place of delight for the human world, the world of devas, and the world of Brahmās. "The world" (*loka*) refers to the human world; for it is there that one surveys, establishes oneself, and proceeds.
Or, "world" (*loka*) here refers to merit and demerit, as well as their result; thus it is the human world. Having established the world-system (*lokadhātu*), [he says] "not a world" (*aloka*);

this is the world of devas and brahmās. Both world and non-world are "world-and-non-world" (*lokāloka*); because beings delight excessively in those worlds, it is called "delighting in the world-and-non-world" (*lokālokābhirāma*).
[This refers to] the Lord of Sages (*Muninda*). For he, by way of performing worship, assistance, and so forth for the three worlds...
"It is a delightful place" means he praises it as "delightful to the world-illuminator. "Constantly" means always; the meaning is "frequently day and night.
"Muninda" refers to the Lord of Sages (*munindra*); [the phrase] "that Muninda" is used. "I bow down" means "I bow with great reverence"—this is the connection.
This, then, is the concise construction here: [He praises him who is] the God beyond gods, the most supreme among conventional gods and gods by birth.
One who has become a pure deity, bearing the body of his final existence; the breaker of Māra, the destroyer of the five Māras beginning with Devaputta;
the unbreakable, whom the army of Māra is unable to defeat, or rather, one worthy of defeating the army of Māra;
the island for beings, the lamp of wisdom; illuminating the island that is action; on the supreme bed of victory.

On the supreme Bodhi-throne, which serves as the foundation for the state of victory over the five Māras, he attained the Bodhi-fruit— the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) consisting of the path of Arahatship—
and reached the preeminence among all gods and humans in the world with its devas;
he became the one who speaks with the most excellent voice to the assembly of Brahmā-gods and human beings who had come to attend upon him.
I constantly, perpetually, and repeatedly bow down with great reverence to that Lord of Sages— who teaches the Dhamma, who has abandoned evil, who has discarded base and unwholesome defilements,
who has utterly severed them by means of the knowledge of the path to Arahatship, who delights in the light of the world, who is the delight of the human world,
the world of devas, and the world of Brahmas, and who is the chief of the five sages.
The commentary on the twenty-second verse of homage is completed.
The Buddha has limbs like the banyan tree, soft hands and feet, shanks like those of an antelope with a divine voice,
private parts enclosed in a sheath, and, moreover, the Sugata has well-placed feet.
The Sugata has hair that curls to the right; his body is straight like a Brahma-column;
his eyes are blue-black; his heels are long; his skin is delicate; he possesses the most excellent of tastes;
he has forty teeth, even and closely set, with full cheeks.
With feet marked by wheels, with teeth without gaps, and with ankles like those of a Māra-elephant;
standing without bending, he touches his knees with both hands which are soft;
with a rounded torso, the Victor has eyelashes like a young bull’s and a body like the front half of a lion.
The Sugata has seven convexities, long fingers, and a single hair growing from each pore;
he has teeth that are perfectly white, skin the color of gold, and blue-black hairs on the upper part of his body;
the Fully Awakened One has a large tongue, a jaw like a lion’s, and webbed hands and feet.
I bow to that Great Seer, the Lord with the turbaned head, who is endowed with these aforementioned qualities.

(23) Having thus paid homage to the Lord of Sages with the twenty-third verse, [the author] now praises the Buddha for his qualities consisting of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man with three verses beginning with "The Buddha has a bimba-like complexion like a banyan tree," and so forth, [and then praises] the Great Seer.
Desiring to pay homage to the Buddha, he spoke these three verses beginning with "The Buddha, the image of the banyan tree. These three verses should be understood as being in the *saddharā* meter.
As for their accomplishment, it has already been explained below.
In that regard, in the first verse, the term "Buddha" refers to one who has penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, and who has penetrated all phenomena without exception.
Or rather, that term [Buddha] should be connected with terms such as *nigrodha* and *bimba* by virtue of having the same grammatical gender and number.
For he is called "Buddha" because he awakens, has awakened, and will awaken to the four truths;
and because he awakens, has awakened, and will awaken to all phenomena without exception. Regarding those two alternatives, in the first alternative:
The penetration of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths pertaining to the Buddha-element is primarily obtained through the knowledge of the path to Arahatship (*arahattamaggañāṇa*).

The knowledge of the lower paths and fruits, the knowledge of insight (*vipassanāñāṇa*), and the knowledge of the perfections (*pāramīñāṇa*) are so designated by way of figurative application to the fruit (*phalūpacārena*).

Furthermore, the knowledge of the fruit of Arahatship and the successive stages of knowledge culminating in omniscience (*sabbaññutañāṇa*) are so designated by way of figurative application to the cause (*kāraṇūpacārena*). This is what is expressed by the suffix *-ta*.

In the primary sense (*mukhyopacārena*), a specific being designated as "Buddha, Buddha" is obtained in dependence upon the five aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*), which are characterized by the ornament of an immeasurable multitude of qualities.
In the second alternative, the word-meaning of the root *budh* is obtained in its primary sense as the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*) capable of penetrating all knowable phenomena;
this includes the knowledge of the four paths and fruits, as well as insight (*vipassanā*) and the knowledge of the perfections (*pāramī*).

By way of metaphorical designation (*phalūpacāra*). The subsequent knowledges, beginning with the knowledge of latent dispositions (*āsaya*) and underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), are [designated as "Buddha"] by way of metaphorical designation of the cause (*kāraṇūpacāra*).

Or rather, that which is expressed by the suffix *-tappaccaya*—namely, a particular being designated as "Buddha, Buddha" in dependence upon the five aggregates adorned by an immeasurable flood of qualities—is characterized by that primary and metaphorical designation. What, then, is the referent (*vāccabhūta*) of the element "Buddha" (*budhadhātu*) in this context?
Is it knowledge itself that is called "Buddha"? Or rather, is the continuum of aggregates (khandhasantāna), which is the referent for that [term], what is called "Buddha"?

However, because the stains of the defilements (kilesas) together with their latent tendencies (savāsanā) have been abandoned without remainder by means of knowledge, the mental continuum becomes pure.
Because of its purity, the material body (rūpakāya), which serves as its support, also becomes pure. Therefore, regarding that referent...

The continuum of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*), which serves as the basis for the knowledge of the path to arahantship and so forth, and which constitutes the referent of the term "Buddha," is called "Buddha" by way of conventional designation (*nāmapaññatti-vohāra*). Thus it is said in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-ṭīkā*:
"The continuum of aggregates, which is cultivated by the attainment of the supreme liberation characterized by unimpeded knowledge regarding all phenomena..."
“The Buddha is a distinguished being designated in dependence upon either the state of omniscience or the perfect awakening to the Truths.

For it is upon the continuum of the aggregates—which constitutes ultimate reality—that the conventional designations “being,” “person,” and so forth, are superimposed for the sake of ease in communication.
Thus, as long as a being who has entered into such conventional usage does not strive for the sake of the knowledge of awakening nor make a formal aspiration, [so long...]

He is reckoned as a "being" (satta) indeed. However, from the moment he exerts himself for the sake of the knowledge of enlightenment (bodhiñāṇa) and makes his aspiration, the designation "Bodhisatta" comes into use.
But when he attains the knowledge of enlightenment, the designation "Buddha" comes into use.
Therefore, it should be understood that the continuum of aggregates (khandhasantāna), which is a conventional designation (paññatti), is what is called "Buddha."

For it is said in the *Mahāniddesa*: "‘Buddha’—this name was not made by his mother, nor made by his father, nor made by his brother, nor made by his sister, nor made by friends and colleagues, nor made by kinsmen and blood relations, nor made by recluses and brahmins, nor made by deities;
this is a term pertaining to liberation (*vimokkhantika*) for the Blessed Buddhas at the foot of the Bodhi tree."
"Simultaneously with the acquisition of omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutañāṇa), the realization-designation 'Buddha' occurs; therefore, he is called 'Buddha.
Alternatively, according to either the *paṭṭhāna* method or the *nānantara* method, the meaning is also consistent:
one whose mental continuum of the aggregates (khandhasantāna) is preeminent in knowledge and perfectly purified is called "Buddha."
*Nigrodhabimba* means one whose body is perfectly rounded like the circumference of a *nigrodha* tree.
It is called *nigrodha* because it obstructs the lower part; *nigrodha* refers to the *vaṭa* tree. The root *rudh* preceded by the prefix *ni-* has the sense of "obstructing" (*āvaraṇe*);

the suffix *ṇa* is added, and *ussa* is the augment. That which vomits or ejects is a *bimba*, meaning the body. The root *vam* has the sense of "ejecting" (*uggiraṇe*); the suffix *bo* is added. For the vowel *va* of *vami*, *bittaṃ* is substituted. [This is] of the *nigrodha*.
One whose body is like a *bimba* fruit that is perfectly circular is called "Nigrodhabimbo" (the Buddha with a body like a banyan tree).
Although one might expect the expression "nigrodhaparimaṇḍalabimbo," it is stated thus by eliding the word *parimaṇḍala*.
For just as a banyan tree—with its trunk and branches—whether fifty cubits or a hundred cubits tall, is of the same measurement in both length and breadth, so too is his body.
He is of one measure even as a fathom (*vyāma*). The meaning is that his body is not of uneven proportions, such as when the bodies of others are long but their fathoms are not, or vice versa.
For it is said in the *Brahmāyu Sutta*: "Master Gotama is well-proportioned like a banyan tree.
As is the extent of his body, so is the extent of his fathom; as is the extent of his fathom, so is the extent of his body."
*Mudukaracaraṇo* means having soft hands and feet. Here, the word *mudu* is an un-derived (*anipphanna*) primary noun (*pāṭipadika*) denoting smoothness and delicacy.

Alternatively, it is called *mudu* because it "pleases" (*modeti*) or "delights" (*modayati*) sentient beings; thus, *muda* [is derived from] the root *muda*, meaning "to delight" or "to laugh," with the suffix *u*.
*Karo*: that by which one performs various actions is the *kara*, namely the hand. *Caro*: that by which one moves or goes to various places is the *cara*, namely the foot.
*Carana* means foot. The verbal root *car* is used in the sense of "going. One whose feet are soft and beautiful is *mudukaracaraṇo*;

this refers to the Buddha. The meaning is that his hands and feet are always soft, like ghee poured into cream and set aside, or like a layer of cotton wool beaten a hundred times, or like the hands and feet of a newborn infant.
*Brahmaghoṣeṇijaṅgha*: the word division is *brahmaghoṣo* and *eṇijaṅgho*.
