Furthermore, in this context, "merit" refers specifically to the wholesome volition (*kusalacetanā*) that brings about the act of saluting the Buddha. And that [volition] belongs to both the one worthy of worship and the one who worships.
Through the perfection of field and intention, by way of providing reinforcement for the karma that has its sign as the prosperity obtained in the present life,
it wards off obstructive and interrupting karmas— which would otherwise create obstacles for the continuity of the resultant [vipāka] produced by that [root karma]—
and thereby accomplishes the non-occurrence of obstacles such as disease, which would otherwise hinder the attainment of the intended goal based on those [obstructive karmas].
And the meaning should be understood as follows. In the phrase "and in the future life" (*samparāye ca*), the word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of connecting a location (*aṭṭhānayoga*).
It is to be joined with such passages as "those of subtle intelligence" (*nipuṇamati*) and so forth. "In the future life" (*samparāye*) means in the other world (*paraloke*).

For it is called "the future life" because beings must go toward (*samparāyitabba*) or approach it; or else, it is called "the future life" because beings must go toward or reach it by way of karma and defilements (*kamma-kilesa*).
It is so called. For the root *ay* preceded by *sam-pari* takes the suffix *ṇa* in the sense of motion.

Alternatively, it is called *samparāya* because, by way of karma, one goes toward (*abhimukha*) and proceeds (*gacchati*) or continues to exist (*pavattati*). The root *par* preceded by *sam* takes the suffix *ṇya* in the sense of motion.
Thus, as in such passages as "Venerable Ānanda, wholesome virtues gradually lead to the highest," [the term is derived] according to the *cur-ādi* class of roots.
Those learned in grammar maintain that the word *para* signifies "going" (*gati*). In this context, it refers to the future life (*samparāya*).

The term *nipuṇamati* means one possessing subtle and refined wisdom (*saṇhasukhuma-paññā*), or one endowed with the wisdom capable of penetrating subtle and refined distinctions of meaning. Furthermore, in this instance, the word *nipuṇa* is an un-derived (*anipphanna*) primary noun (*pāṭipadika*) signifying subtlety and refinement.
*Mati* is that which thinks and knows what is beneficial and harmful; it is wisdom (*paññā*). As it is said: "The element of mind (*manadhātu*) is knowledge.
One who possesses such subtle and refined *mati*, or wisdom, is called *nipuṇamati*. *Sato* means being mindful (*satimā*). *Sati* is so called because one remembers;
as it is said: "The root *sar-* means to think. One who has this [mindfulness] is *sato*. *Titto* means satisfied; the meaning is that one is content with whatever object has been obtained.
*Tisanaṃ* means "satisfying. *Titta* is derived from the root *tappati* with the suffix *-ta*. The letter *sa* is replaced by *ta*.
What is meant is that he is "contented" through a threefold contentment: contentment with what is obtained, contentment with one's own strength, and contentment with what is appropriate.
*Dakkho* means clever and skillful in each respective task; for he is proficient in wholesome action as well as in other matters of what should and should not be done.
He is "dexterous" (*dakkha*) because he moves swiftly due to his lack of dullness. The verbal root *dak* signifies swiftness.
Regarding the phrase "one whose view and wisdom are straight" (*diṭṭhujjupaṇṇo*), the word division is *diṭṭhi-uju-pañño*. The meaning is: "one who is endowed with straight view and wisdom.
In some manuscripts, the reading is *diṭṭhijju pañño*. The word division is *diṭṭhi-uju-pañño*; this is the same matter. It is called "straight" (*uju*) because it exists by way of being non-crooked.

*Ajjava* (straightforwardness). From the root *uju*, with the suffix *kvi*, it becomes *ajjava*. Alternatively, that which proceeds by way of being straight (*akuṭila-bhāva*) and without crookedness is *uju*; it is without curvature.
From the root *ara* in the sense of "going," with the suffix *jupaccaya*, there is the substitution of *u* for *ari*. That which sees correctly is *diṭṭhi* (view) or *mati* (intellect).

From the root *dis* in the sense of "seeing," with the suffix *tapaccaya*, there is the substitution of *ra* for *ta*, the elision of the final part of the root, and the addition of *ī*. Straightness is *ajjava*; view and intellect are *diṭṭhi-mati*.

“Diṭṭhujju” is [an analysis] by way of a qualifying attribute followed by a particle. It is *paññā* (wisdom) because one knows clearly (*pakārena*) and understands by way of impermanence and so forth;

it is derived from the verbal root *ñā*, preceded by the prefix *pa*, in the sense of “understanding. One who possesses straight view (*ujudiṭṭhi*) and straight wisdom (*ujupaṇṇā*) is called “one of straight view and wisdom” (*diṭṭhujjupaṇṇo*), referring to a person.
“One of unimpaired energy” (*avikalavīriyo*) means one whose energy is neither deficient nor incomplete. “One who makes [it] perish” (*vihīnaṃ karoti*)... [meaning].
*Vikalo*: the *vipubbakara-dhātu* (the element that causes putrefaction) is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), hence it is short. *Vīriyaṃ* is the action of the heroic ones (*vīrānaṃ*).
One who possesses energy that is unimpaired and not deficient is "one of unimpaired energy" (*avikalavīriyo*).

It is not possible for one who is lazy to attain the nine supramundane states; it is only possible for one who has initiated energy. Therefore, it is said that he aspires to be "one of unimpaired energy."
"Bhogavā" means endowed with the happiness of success in what is to be enjoyed. "Bhoga" refers to that which is to be enjoyed; it is a success (*sampatti*).
From the verbal root *bhuj* in the senses of protecting and dealing with, the suffix *na* is added. One who thinks, "I have this enjoyment for myself," is "possessed of enjoyments" (*bhogavā*).

"Saṃvibhāgī" means one whose nature is to share, or one who is perfected in sharing; he is a "sharer" (*saṃvibhāgī*) because he shares by his very nature. "One whose nature is to share" (*saṃvibhajana-sīlo*)...
Or, one who shares is a "sharer" (*saṃvibhāgī*); that is, one whose nature is to share. Or, one whose nature is toward sharing is a "sharer. This is its meaning as a quality (*sīla*).

Alternatively, one who shares according to the Dhamma is "one whose nature is to share" (*saṃvibhajanadhamma*). Or, one whose nature is to share is a "sharer"; or, one whose nature is toward sharing is a "sharer. This is its meaning as a phenomenon (*dhamma*). Sharing...

"Good" (sādhukāra) exists for him. He is "one who shares" (saṃvibhāgī) either because he shares with one who has given a cry of "well done," or because he is one who gives a cry of "well done" in order to share, or because he is one who gives a cry of "well done" during the act of sharing. This is the meaning of the word "good.

The verbal root *bhaj*, preceded by the prefix *sam-*, signifies "dividing" (*vibhāge*); the suffix *ṇa* is added, and the *j* is replaced by *g*. Alternatively, the act of sharing is "sharing" (*saṃvibhāga*). He possesses that [quality], thus he is "one who shares" (*saṃvibhāgī*).
*Assathyatthe ī*: This means one who constantly practices the relinquishing of things such as food to other supplicants.

*Tikkho*: One who possesses sharp wisdom (*tikkhappaññavā*) or penetrative wisdom (*nisānapaññavā*). *Tijanaṃ nisanaṃ tikkhā, paññā*: "Tikkhā" is the wisdom that pierces through the three [realms]. The root *tij* is used in the sense of piercing (*nisāne*), with the suffix *kha*.
By the rule *jassa ko*, the *j* becomes *k*. Thus, "one who has this sharp wisdom" is *tikkho*. The suffix *ṇo* is applied in the sense of possession (*assathyatthe*). *Tikkha*.

The meaning is: "and endowed with wisdom. And because wisdom is the best of all wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) and the primary cause, he makes an aspiration for it to be sharp. For it is said in the *Milindapañha*:
"Wisdom is praised in the world, established for the sake of the persistence of the True Dhamma."
“Having destroyed doubt with wisdom, the wise man attains peace.
*Śūra* means a hero among the four assemblies and the eight assemblies; the meaning is one who possesses power and is fearless.

He is called *śūra* because he acts as a hero (*sūrayate*) and acts with valor (*virayate*). This is a noun derived from the action itself (*bhāvasādhana*). The verbal root *śūr* signifies prowess or heroism (*vikkanti*), or it is [formed] with the suffix *a*. Alternatively—
One who goes forth, proceeds, or acts with a state of being fearless, unshaken, and undaunted is a *sūra*. The verbal root *sūr* (from which *sūra* is derived) means "to go.
Thus, the meaning is: one who is endowed with heroic courage in the midst of an assembly, like a lion.

However, no etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) for the word *sūra* has been provided by those learned in the true Dhamma within the Teaching; rather, it is merely an explanation of the meaning as "a hero" or "an eminent hero."
It has been shown. Regarding the term *dhītatto*: here, the word-division is *dhīto* and *atto*. *Dhī* means concentration (*samādhi*). *Atta* means mind (*citta*).

Thus, the meaning is "one endowed with one-pointedness of mind. *Dhī* is so called because it stands firm through its objects (*ekārammaṇehi*), or because it sustains the mental factors associated with those single objects;
thus, it is concentration. The root *dhā* signifies "sustaining" (*dhāraṇe*). *Atta* is that which knows (*arati*) the object (*ārammaṇa*); thus, it is the mind.

*Cittaṃ*. [In the rule] *aradhātu gatiyaṃ ta*: [the suffix] *ta* is substituted for [the suffix] *ra* after a root ending in a short vowel (*rassa*). One whose mind is firm through concentration is *dhitatto*.
One who practices for the welfare of self and others is *attahitaparahitacaro*; the meaning is "one who has set out upon the path for the benefit of both oneself and others.
Because he practices—that is, proceeds—toward the welfare, benefit, and purpose of both himself and others, he is called *saparahitacaro*.

The term *saparahitasaddūpapadacaradhātu* [is used] in the sense of "conduct" (*caraṇe*). *Dīghajīvī* means one who has a long life (*dīghāyuko*), or one endowed with a long life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
Alternatively, he is called *dīghajīvi* because his life—his living—is long. The meaning is that he is endowed with a long life even for the duration of a lifespan (*āyukappa*).

*Arogo* means both freedom from disease (*rogaviraho*) and health (*ārogya*). Disease (*rogo*) is so called because the limbs and members of the body are afflicted (*rujjati*) and broken (*bhañjati*).

*Byādhi*. [It is derived from] the verbal root *ruj*, with the suffix *ṇa* in the sense of breaking. Alternatively, it is called *roga* because it breaks (*rujjati*) or harms (*hiṃsati*). [It is derived from] the verbal root *ruj* in the sense of harming, with the suffix *ṇa*.
"One who has no disease (*aroga*)" means one for whom there is no disease; the meaning is that there would be an absence of the ninety-eight diseases.

"Fortunate (*dhañña*)" means endowed with glory (*sirī*), merit (*puñña*), wisdom (*paññā*), and the auspicious marks (*lakkhaṇa*). For the word *dhañña* is a designation for glory, merit, wisdom, and the auspicious marks.
It should be understood thus. For it is said in the Vessantara Jātaka: "Grain is considered auspicious," and in the Temiya Jātaka:
"She gave birth to a son endowed with the marks of grain, merit, and fortune. This, however, is the etymological derivation: *dhañña* is the accomplishment (*sampajjana*) of wealth (*dhana*);
the meaning is that it is endowed with beauty, wisdom, merit, and the [auspicious] marks. The verbal root *dhan* means "to accomplish."
Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the suffix *ṇya* is applied. When the indicatory letter *ṇ* has been elided, the letter *n* is changed to *ñ* together with the suffix *ya*;

thus, the formation of the word *dhañña* (wealthy) should be understood. Alternatively, one who possesses (*atthi*) wealth (*dhana*), which consists of glory, wisdom, and the excellence of meritorious characteristics, is "wealthy" (*dhañño*).
Here, the suffix *ṇya* is used in the sense of possession (*assatthi*).
"Beauty" (*vaṇṇa*) means one who is endowed with beauty. And here, beauty is twofold: by way of physical beauty and by way of the beauty of qualities.

Therein, "physical beauty" refers to the possession of a pleasing form of the material body. "Beauty of qualities" refers to being endowed with qualities such as virtue, concentration, and wisdom, as well as the qualities of the practice of the ascetic virtues (*dhutaṅga*) and so forth.
This, however, is the etymological derivation: it is that which causes those things that have undergone transformation to... [be beautified].
*Vaṇṇa* means that which manifests the state residing in the heart; it is bodily form (*rūpa*).
*Vaṇṇa* means that which manifests one's own substance; it is a quality (*guṇa*). The verbal root *vaṇṇ* is used in the sense of manifesting. However, in this context, both meanings are applicable.
*Vaṇṇa* [is derived] from the thought "I possess beauty (*vaṇṇa*)"; the suffix *a* is used here in the sense of possession. *Yasassī* means endowed with a retinue or possessed of fame. And herein:

Fame is twofold, by way of retinue and by way of praise. In this context, "fame" (*yasas*) refers to the retinue; it is called "fame" because one is sacrificed to (*yajiyati*) and honored (*pūjiyati*) by means of that retinue.

The verbal root *yaj* is used in the sense of honoring. That which belongs to him is [the fame]. Alternatively, it is called "fame" because it goes (*yāti*), moves, and reaches the retinue of the master.
The root *yā* is used in the sense of motion with the suffix *-as*. It is also that by which one is sacrificed to and honored.
*Yaso* means fame; *kittisaddo* (the sound of renown). The verbal root *yaj* occurs in the senses of divine worship, gathering, performing, giving, and dharma.

*Jassa so*: "of whom that [fame] exists. Alternatively, it is *yaso* because it goes (*yāti*), moves, or pervades everywhere; it is the sound of renown or the sound of praise. The root *yā* is used in the sense of motion with the suffix *-as*.
By the rule of single-remainder (*ekasesanaya*), both instances of *yaso* are reduced to *yaso*. One who has this—meaning "I have this"—is called *yasassī* (renowned).
The suffix *sī* occurs in the sense of capability (*assathatthe*).
"One who possesses extreme strength" (*atibalavadharo*) means both one who maintains extreme power and one who maintains an exceedingly great physical strength and power of knowledge;
thus, he is "one who possesses extreme strength. Like King Ajātasattu and others, he is capable of sustaining the strength of ten elephants for every five elephants.
"And," the meaning is: "and may he be capable of maintaining the power of knowledge, like the Elder Sāriputta and others.

"Possessing fame" (*kittimā*) means possessing a reputation or renown. Fame (*kitti*) is that which is praised or spoken of as virtue; it is a sound of praise. The verbal root *kitta* is used in the sense of sound. "Fame-possessor" (*kittimā*) means "one who has this sound of fame for himself.
The suffix *-mantu* is applied in the sense of possession. "One who has patience" (*khantupeto*) [means one who is endowed with patience].
"Endowed" means possessed, fully possessed, and equipped with. "Patience" (*khanti*) is the bearing and enduring; it is derived from the root *kham* (to endure) with the suffix *ti*.

One who is "endowed with patience" (*khantūpeta*) is one who is possessed, fully possessed, and equipped with that [patience]. The meaning is that one should be endowed with patience like the ascetic Khantivāda.
For patience is difficult to practice, it is the foremost among all wholesome qualities, and it is the supreme austerity.
And he makes this aspiration: "May I be one who has attained patience. For this was said by the Blessed One:

"Patience is the supreme austerity, forbearance," and, "Nothing is found superior to patience," and, "The power of patience is the foremost of powers," and, "Of virtue, concentration, and wisdom, patience is the primary cause."
"And all wholesome states indeed increase by depending upon patience. This, moreover, is the concise explanation here:

"I, being such as I am, through this merit—this meritorious act of worshipping the Buddha—in the future world, may I possess refined intellect and subtle, delicate wisdom; may I be mindful and possessed of sati; and may I be contented and satisfied."
One who is content with whatever material things he has obtained; who is skillful and clever in his respective duties;

whose vision is upright and who possesses wisdom through straight view; who is not deficient in energy but possesses full and unimpaired vigor; who is wealthy and endowed with the happiness of enjoying attainments;
who is generous and disposed to sharing; who is sharp and possesses keen wisdom; and who is brave—such a person is one possessed of capability.

Fearless, steadfast in mind, and concentrated in thought—or rather, one-pointed in mind; practicing for the welfare of both self and others, one who has set out upon the path for his own benefit and the benefit of others;
long-lived and long-enduring; free from disease and devoid of illness; wealthy, endowed with beauty, merit, wisdom, and auspicious marks;
possessed of physical luster, perfected in complexion, renowned, and endowed with a retinue; and possessing great strength, a bearer of exceeding power.
"And may I be possessed of fame, possessing a reputation for renown; and may I be endowed with patience, fully endowed with patience, and possessed of it.
The commentary on the twenty-seventh verse is complete. 28.
Having thus made an aspiration for the future life with the verse beginning "By this merit," he now makes a wish for the present life (*diṭṭhadhamme*).

Desiring to act, he spoke the verse beginning with “the faithful one, endowed with the marks of a giver,” and so forth. Therein, “the faithful” (*saddho*) means one who is possessed of faith characterized by conviction in karma and other such matters.
Faith is that which believes; or, it is called faith because it believes. It is called faith because associated mental states believe by means of it.
The verbal root *dhā*, preceded by the prefix *sam*, has the sense of holding. That [faith], moreover, is characterized by conviction in karma and other such matters.
Or it has the characteristic of conviction (*okappana*). Its function is clarification, like a water-clearing gem; or its function is leaping forward, like one crossing a flood.
It is manifested as freedom from turbidity, or as resolution; its proximate cause is a thing worthy of faith, or the factors of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-aṅga*).
It should be regarded as being like hands, wealth, or seeds. For by the Blessed One, that [faith]...
Faith is described as: “The great elephant has faith as his hand”; “In this world, faith is the best wealth for a person”;
“Faith is the seed, austerity is the rain”; “By means of faith one crosses the flood”;
“Faith binds the provisions for the journey; faith is a person’s companion”; “Monks, the noble disciple has faith as his guide”; and “the treasure of faith.”
“Those who possess faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha, outshine me in longevity, fame, and glory. And:
“Relying upon faith, one gives gifts, undertakes moral discipline, performs the Uposatha rites, and attains meditative absorption (jhāna).”
“He arouses [insight], he arouses insight (vipassanā), he arouses the path (magga), he arouses direct knowledge (abhiññā), he arouses meditative attainment (samāpatti).
And it is said: “The perfection of faith is difficult to obtain. Therefore, one makes the aspiration: “May I be endowed with faith.

Furthermore, that faith is fourfold: faith based on scripture (āgama-saddhā), faith based on realization (adhigama-saddhā), faith based on conviction (okappana-saddhā), and faith based on serene confidence (pasāda-saddhā).
...and so forth. Therein, the faith of the omniscient Bodhisattvas is called "faith through scripture" (āgama-saddhā) because it has come down from their initial resolve (abhinīhāra).

The faith of the noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka) is called "faith through realization" (adhigama-saddhā) because it is attained through the penetration of the Truths (sacca-paṭivedha). The firm conviction (okappanā) characterized by immovability when the words "Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha" are uttered is called "faith through conviction" (okappana-saddhā).
The mere arising of clarity (pasāda) toward the Buddha and the others is called "faith through clarity" (pasāda-saddhā). Here—
However, because it is the locus of aspiration, all forms of faith are intended here. One who possesses faith (*saddhā*) is called "faithful" (*saddho*);

the suffix *-ṇa* is used in the sense of "possessing. "Endowed with the factors of giving" (*dātaṅgupeto*) means endowed, fully endowed, and possessed of the wealth that serves as the cause for the factor of giving.
One is fully endowed with three factors: the object to be given, the person who receives it, and faith.
And he is endowed with it. *Diyate* means "to be given. This is a word derived from the abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*). The verbal root *dā* signifies giving, and *a* is the suffix.

That by which one is marked (*aṅkīyati*) or known is a "mark" (*aṅga*), namely, the excellence of wealth. The mark of the giver is the "giver's mark" (*dātaṅga*); one who is possessed of that, fully possessed of that, or endowed with that is "endowed with the giver's mark" (*dātaṅgupeta*).
Alternatively, that which is given is the "gift" (*dāta*), meaning the object of giving. The mark of the gift is the "gift-mark" (*dātaṅga*); one who is possessed of that [is so called].
"Endowed and possessed" means that one makes an aspiration, thinking:
"I shall succeed by means of these three factors—the donor's qualities, the object to be given, the person who receives it, and faith. For it is said in the *Itivuttaka-aṭṭhakathā*:
"Indeed, a gift comes into being only when these three—faith, the thing to be given, and the recipient—are present together."
"Paramasiridharo" means one who possesses supreme glory (*siri*), or alternatively, one capable of maintaining supreme glory.

Here, "glory" (*siri*) is a designation for wisdom (*paññā*), merit (*puñña*), physical beauty (*sarīrasobhagga*), and excellence (*sampatti*). It is called "glory" because it is cultivated by those who have performed meritorious deeds;
or, it is called "glory" because it attends upon and relies upon individuals who have performed meritorious deeds—namely, wisdom, merit, physical beauty, and excellence.
It is obtained. [The root] *sidh* means "to serve"; with the suffixes *ira* and *ī*, it becomes *siri*. *Paramasiri* means supreme glory (*paramā uttamā sirī*).
One who bears that is a bearer of supreme glory (*paramasirīdhara*); the meaning is one capable of maintaining supreme glory.
*Diṭṭhadhamme* refers to the manifest personal existence (*attabhāva*). And here, "the seen dhamma" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) is said to be that which has become manifest.

The personal existence (*attabhāva*). For that which is to be seen is "seen," namely the personal existence. That which has the nature of a phenomenon (*dhamma*)—a phenomenon that is seen—is called "the seen phenomenon" (*diṭṭhadhamma*).
In that seen phenomenon. "Dispassionate" (*viratta*) means one whose passion for the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) has departed;

"passion" (*rajja*) refers to being colored by passion. The verbal root *rañj* signifies passion. One who has such passion departed is "dispassionate. "Conscientious" (*lajjī*) means one who shuns evil.

Or, he is endowed with a sense of shame (*lajjā*) characterized by revulsion toward evil. Alternatively, "one who has shame" (*lajjī*) means one endowed with both moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*).
For by the word *lajjī*, through the method of including the characteristic, *ottappa* must also be understood. Why? Because they are identical in their nature as wholesome characteristics.
Indeed, this is stated in the *Nettipāḷi*:
“When one single thing has been stated, whatever other things have the same characteristic are thereby stated as well;
this is the method of exposition known as ‘the characteristic. It is called *lajjā* (shame) because one feels shame (*lajjati*).
It is *hiri*. The element of shame is *hiriyaṃ*. It is called *lajjā* because one possesses it, thinking, “May I have this [shame]”; [it functions] toward bodily misconduct and so forth.

The meaning is: "endowed with moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*). "Possessing good friends" (*kalyāṇamitta*) means being endowed with excellent friends. For the word *kalyāṇa* is a primary (*anipphanna*) term used to denote "excellent.
Alternatively, it is called *kalyāṇa* because it brings (*aṇayati*) or causes one to attain (*pāpayati*) what is wholesome (*kalya*, i.e., beneficial);

thus, he is a "good friend" (*sumitta*). [Etymologically: the root *aṇ* preceded by the prefix *kalya* is used in the sense of motion, with the suffix *-na*. One is called a "friend" (*mitta*) because one is moistened (*mijjati*) or feels affection; it is derived from the root *mijj* (in the sense of being moistened).
Or, he is a "friend" (*mitto*) because he is affectionate; the verbal root *mid* signifies affection. One who has a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇa-mitta*) is thus a "virtuous friend.

The meaning is: "May one be endowed with a friend who possesses beneficial qualities. Here, however, a "virtuous friend" is intended as one endowed with the qualities of faith, virtue, learning, generosity, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. With reference to such a person, the Blessed One said in the *Siṅgāla-sutta*:
“The friend who provides assistance, the companion in both happiness and suffering,
the friend who points out what is beneficial, and the friend who is compassionate toward one’s friends—
these are the four kinds of friends. Having understood this, the wise person should treat them with due respect.”
"One should attend upon him as a mother attends to her own biological son"—thus it is said.
And in the *Visuddhimagga*:
"He is dear, venerable, and worthy of esteem; he speaks and is patient with what is spoken; he delivers profound discourse, yet not out of place..."
"May you employ me," he was told. Thus, because such a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta) is rare, it is said that one makes the aspiration: "May I be endowed with a spiritual friend.
"Delighting in the wholesome" means one who takes delight in the wholesome qualities of merit, such as giving and so forth. They "flow" (salanti) toward the base door of the states of woe (apāya).
It is "wholesome" (*kusala*) because by means of it, the virtuous restrain or close off [unwholesome states].
The root *sal* preceded by the prefix *ku-* has the sense of "restraining. One who delights excessively in these is "delighting in the wholesome" (*abhirata-kusala*); this is a *kitanta* compound.

Although one could have said "delighting in the wholesome" (*kusalābhirato*), it is stated thus by reversing the word order for the sake of protecting the meter. Alternatively, *abhi*... [excessively]...

"Delighting in delight" means one who delights in wholesome qualities (*kusala*); "one whose delight is in the wholesome" (*abhiratakusala*) refers to one who possesses a mind constantly intent on performing wholesome merit.
"Capable of guarding the five precepts, etc. means one who is able to protect the five precepts and so forth; and here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), for householders—
It includes the eightfold Uposatha precept, the tenfold precept for novices (sāmaṇeras), and the fourfold purification precept for monks.
"Pañcasīlādirakkho" means that which protects or is capable of protecting those things beginning with the five precepts.
For householders, there is the fivefold precept by way of constant morality; when there is the capacity for effort, [there is also] the Uposatha factor-precept.
The meaning is that he is capable of guarding the eightfold precepts and the tenfold precepts by making them unbroken, flawless, unspotted, and untarnished;
and furthermore, he is capable of guarding the ten precepts by way of the *sāmaṇera*’s virtue (*sīla*) and the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) by way of the *bhikkhu*’s virtue.
For the Blessed One said: "Monks, it is because of failure in virtue that beings, with the breakup of the body..."
“...and after death, they reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell”;
and “It is, bhikkhus, because of the perfection of virtue that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a good destination, a heavenly world”;
and “One who is perfected in virtue acquires a great mass of wealth, and a fine reputation spreads abroad.”
And because it is said: "He approaches the fourfold assembly with confidence and without timidity; he dies unconfused;
and with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a happy destination, a heavenly world. And in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary):
"There is no ornament like the ornament of virtue; there is no flower like virtue; there is no fragrance like the fragrance of virtue."
“For by relying on the perfection of virtue, one attains the threefold knowledge.
And: “One should purify virtue at the beginning. And: “Beings are purified by virtue. And: “Virtue is the beginning of the Dispensation. And:
“Among the seven purifications, purification of virtue is called the body. And: “Virtue, indeed, is a support, a foundation, an object, and a refuge.”
Because it is said, "It is a shelter, a refuge, and a resort," it is meant that one makes an aspiration for the protection of the five precepts and so forth.
"One of few wishes" (*appiccha*) means both "one who has no desire" and "one who does not desire the strands of sensual pleasure such as forms"; here, the word *appa-* has the sense of "absence.

This is like in expressions such as "free from gadflies and mosquitoes" (*appa-daṃsa-makasa-vātātapa*); or alternatively, *icchā* means "desiring," as in "one who desires the strands of sensual pleasure such as forms."

*Ichā* means craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*). The verbal root *is* signifies "to wish" and "to desire. By the rule *dhātvantassaccho*, the final *s* of the root is changed to *cch*. One who has no such wishing (*icchā*) is called *appiccho*;
the meaning is one who does not desire sense-objects such as forms and so forth. Furthermore, there are four kinds of *appiccha*:

scarcity regarding requisites (*paccaya-appiccha*), scarcity regarding learning (*pariyatti-appiccha*), scarcity regarding ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga-appiccha*), and scarcity regarding realization (*paṭivedha-appiccha*). Among these, regarding the four requisites...
One who has few desires is one who has few desires regarding requisites. Furthermore, one who takes little when much is offered, or takes less when little is offered, or does not take at all;
one who does not take everything—this is called "one who has few desires regarding requisites.

Moreover, one who, though possessing mastery of the Three Piṭakas, does not wish to make known his state of great learning—this is "one who has few desires regarding the scriptures" (pariyatti-appiccha).

...is called [contentment with requisites]. However, one who does not allow others to know that they have undertaken the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) or that they maintain those practices is called "one who is content with the ascetic practices" (*dhutaṅga-appiccha*).

Furthermore, one who, being among those such as stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), does not wish to make known their status as a stream-enterer or the like, is called "one who is content with attainment" (*adhigama-appiccha*).
And one who is endowed with these qualities of contentment (*appiccha-guṇa*)...
"I might become [this]"—this is what is meant.
"Little-anger" means being free from the defect characterized by ill-will (*dussana*). For that which "he is angry" is called anger (*kodha*); this is a designation for hatred (*dosa*).
He who has no anger is "little-anger. One who is angry does not know the goal; one who is angry does not see the Dhamma.
"Blinding darkness then prevails over the man whom anger overcomes.
Having reflected upon this teaching thus spoken, it is said that he makes the aspiration, "May I be free from anger.
"With a heart exceedingly straight" means endowed with a mind that is perfectly upright. "Arati" (dislike) proceeds—that is, it functions—by way of being non-crooked.
*Uju*: straightness, uprightness. *Ju* is the root for going; *u* is the suffix for *ari*. That which carries the object (*ārammaṇa*) is the heart (*hadaya*), that is, the mind (*citta*).

The root *har* is in the sense of carrying; *aya* is the suffix. There is the substitution of *do* for the short vowel. Alternatively, that which carries the object, goes toward it, and proceeds toward it is the heart, the mind.
The root *ay* preceded by the word *hara* is in the sense of going; *a* is the suffix. That which is both straight and the heart is "straight-hearted" (*ujuhadaya*).

"Extremely straight-hearted" (*ativujuhadayo*) means: "May his heart be exceedingly upright. Having become free from the three crookednesses—the cow’s urine-crooked, the crescent-moon-crooked, and the ploughshare-tip-crooked—he should be endowed with an exceedingly straight mind; this is the meaning.
And in that regard, he who, having committed an evil deed, says, "I did not do it," is "cow’s urine-crooked" because of his retreating as he departs.
The one who, while committing evil, says, "I am afraid of evil," is generally called *vaṅka* (crooked) because of his crookedness, like the crescent moon.
The one who, while committing evil, says, "Who would not be afraid of evil? is called *naṅgalakoṭivaṅka* (plow-tip-crooked) because he is not excessively crooked.
Or, one whose three doors of action (*kammadvāra*) are impure is *gomuttavaṅka* (cow-urine-crooked).
It is so named. That which has any two [of these] is called "crooked like a candalekhā. That which has any one [of these] is to be understood as being called "crooked like the tip of a plough.
"Possessed of psychic power" (iddhimā) means endowed with psychic power (iddhi); the etymological meaning of the word *iddhi* has already been stated above. Psychic power (*iddhi*).
"One who possesses power (iddhimā) is one for whom it exists. Here, the suffix *-mant* is used in the sense of "possessing" (*atthi-atthe*).

The meaning is that they would be fully endowed with human power during their time as a human, with divine power when arising as a deity, and with the power of a recluse (*samaṇiddhi*) when arising as a recluse.

Furthermore, "immeasurable" (*appameyyo*) means endowed with immeasurable qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth. That which can be measured is "measurable" (*pameyyo*); [this is derived from] the verbal root *mā* preceded by the prefix *pa*.

The suffix *ṇya* is used in the sense of a measure (*pamāṇe*). "Immeasurable" (*appameyyo*) means that which cannot be measured; it is called "immeasurable" because one thinks, "May I possess immeasurable qualities such as virtue.

The suffix *ṇa* is used here in the sense of existence (*assatth-atthe*). Thus, it is said that one makes an aspiration, thinking: "May I be endowed with immeasurable qualities such as virtue and with the perfection of wealth."
"Pāsaṃso" means one who is worthy of praise from virtuous persons such as the Buddhas on account of qualities like moral virtue (sīla) and so forth;

it is that which is praised or extolled. This is a noun derived from the action itself (bhāvasādhana). The verbal root *saṃs* preceded by *pa-* signifies "praise. One who is worthy of that is "pāsaṃso.

The suffix *-ṇa* is applied here according to the rule for the taddhita suffix used in the sense of "worthy of" (*arhati*). What is meant is that he should be endowed with qualities such as generosity and moral virtue, which are fit to be praised by the Buddhas and other virtuous persons.
"Pemavāco" means one who is endowed with speech that is to be cherished by the Buddhas and other noble beings because of its sweetness in both meaning and phrasing.
"Piyateti pemā" refers to speech; the verbal root *pī* signifies satisfying and desiring. "Vacitabbā" means speech;

the verbal root *vac* denotes distinct articulation, and the suffix *ṇa* is applied here. "Pema-vāco" means one whose speech is cherished; it is speech that is beloved by the Buddhas and other noble beings.
The meaning is: "One who is endowed with speech possessing four factors. Now, the speech of true persons (*sappurisa*) is endowed with four factors:
well-spoken speech, speech of the Dhamma, pleasant speech, and truthful speech. For this has been said in the *Sagāthāvagga* of the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*:
"The virtuous call well-spoken speech the highest..."
Speak the Dhamma, not what is contrary to the Dhamma—this is the second.
Speak what is pleasant, not what is unpleasant—this is the third.
Speak the truth, not falsehood—this is the fourth.
This is the application of the meaning here: The virtuous, true persons have declared that speech which is well-spoken, truly well-articulated;
one should speak what is Dhamma, one should not speak what is non-Dhamma—this they have declared to be the second kind of speech.
One should speak what is pleasant, one should not speak what is unpleasant—this they have declared to be the third kind of speech. One should speak the truth.
One should not speak what is false; one should not speak that fourth kind of speech.

A "knower of the virtues of good people" (*sujanaguṇavidū*) is one who understands the virtues, such as moral discipline, of virtuous persons beginning with the Buddhas. A "good person" (*sujana*) is a beautiful person.

It is called a "virtue" (*guṇa*) because it manifests (*guṇati*) a person as being endowed with virtues such as moral discipline; thus, it refers to the virtue of moral discipline and so forth. [The term] *guṇadhātu* [is used] in the sense of manifestation.
a. The virtue of good people—namely, Buddhas and other noble beings—is "sujanaguṇa. One who knows (*vidati*) or understands that is a "knower of the virtues of good people" (*sujanaguṇavidū*).
By adding the suffix *ū* to the verbal root *vid* (to know) with the words *sujana* and *guṇa* as prefixes, the sense is:
"one who would be capable of knowing the virtues of Buddhas and other noble beings, such as their morality, concentration, and wisdom."

*Māmako* refers to Buddhas and other virtuous persons; one who is *māmaka*. It is called *māmaka* because it "cherishes" (*mamāyati*). The verbal root *mama-* is used in the sense of honoring or love, with the suffix *ṇvu*;

its form is *māmaka*. The meaning is: "May I honor the Three Jewels, beginning with the Buddha, as well as the True Dhamma. *So* means "I, that very person. *Bhaveyyaṃ* means "may I become [or: may I am]."

This, however, is the concise explanation here: I, being one who has seen the present life—that is, having directly experienced this personal existence—and being endowed with faith, possessed of confidence;
and being fully equipped with the factors for giving, that is, endowed and fully provided with the wealth that serves as the cause for the factor of giving;
and [possessing] the object to be given, the person who receives it, and faith— *Note: The final term "saddhā" appears to be a fragment of the original text.*

Or, endowed with these three factors—fully possessed and equipped with them—he is one who bears supreme glory (*paramaśrīdharah*), that is, one who possesses the highest glory or one capable of maintaining supreme glory;
he is dispassionate (*viraktaḥ*) regarding the strands of sensual pleasure, meaning free from passion;
he is modest (*lajjī*), meaning one who shuns evil, or one endowed with modesty characterized by a loathing for evil; and he is possessed of moral shame and dread of blame (*hirottapasampannaḥ*).
He is endowed with virtuous friends and beautiful friends; he delights in skillful deeds, taking pleasure in the wholesome qualities of merit such as giving;
he is capable of guarding the five precepts and so forth; he has few desires and is free from desire, meaning he does not crave the strands of sensual pleasure such as forms;
he has little anger and is devoid of the fault characterized by malice; and his heart is exceedingly upright.
He is endowed with a straightforward mind; he is endowed with supernormal power (*iddhi*); he is immeasurable, being perfected in immeasurable qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth;
he is praiseworthy, being worthy of praise by true persons (*sappurisa*) such as the Buddhas on account of his virtues of virtue and so forth;

he possesses endearing speech, being endowed with speech that is beloved by true persons such as the Buddhas due to its sweetness in both meaning and phrasing; and he is a knower of the qualities of noble beings regarding true persons such as the Buddhas.
"May I be one who recognizes the virtues such as morality; may I be 'mine'—that is, devoted—to the Buddha and other noble beings;
and may I honor the Three Jewels beginning with the Buddha and the True Dhamma.
Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-eighth verse.
Thus, O Protector, regarding these inexhaustible qualities illuminated by their characteristics,
even a wise person who remembers but a single verse among those indicative stanzas is liberated from the four states of misery and attains the two goals of perfection.
One who has destroyed the web of calamities and is a recipient of gain and happiness,
whether as a lord of men and gods or even a sovereign of the four continents,
shall become such in his final body— or else another who possesses the white parasol.
Having mounted the vehicle of meditation, the one of noble conduct will attain equanimity;
even in this very life, he shall be healthy and long-lived.
Honored by all the worlds, his mind will delight in meditation.
"Dear to the people and pleasing—what need is there to speak of his firm retention?
(29). Having thus made his aspiration with these two verses beginning with "By this merit," he now spoke the five verses beginning with "In this world...
to show the fruits and benefits of worshipping the Buddha. However, that was not spoken by the root teachers; rather, it was [added] later.

It should be understood that this "pentad of verses" was composed by wise ones who desire our welfare. Furthermore, those verses should be understood as the *pathyāvattagāthā* (verses on the turning back of the path). Regarding them, the connection in the first verse is as follows:

"The wise person who remembers even a single verse among these verses—which indicate the qualities of the Protector and which illuminate the characteristics of this [Dhamma] in its unconditioned state (*asaṅkhaya*)—[is one who has turned away from the world].
By the word "this" (*itthaṃ*), what is meant is the manner already described by the words "the Well-Gone One" (*sugata*) and so forth.

*Asaṅkhaye*: "Incalculable" means those who are unable to count the Buddha-qualities by saying, "There are this many. *Saṅkhayā* is that which is counted (*saṅkhiyate*). Or, it is *saṅkhayā* because it is reckoned (*saṅkhiyati*) or enumerated.
It is derived from the root *sakh* with the suffix *ya*. Alternatively, they are *asaṅkhayā* because one cannot count them (*saṅkhituṃ na sakkonti*).
Even for a single Buddha, [it would take] many years to exhaustively [enumerate] these Buddha-qualities, saying, "There are this many Buddha-qualities, there are this many Buddha-qualities."
It is truly impossible even for one hundred thousand koṭis [of Buddhas] to count them, let alone anyone else—this is the meaning. And this has also been said in the Apadāna:
“Even a Buddha, speaking the praises of a Buddha, Were he to speak for an eon without uttering another word;”
“The eon might be exhausted within that very long interval, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted. And:
“It might be possible to measure the water in the ocean by means of a dry measure;”
"Indeed, it is not possible to measure your omniscient knowledge," and in the *Mahāvagga-saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*:
"The Buddhas are immeasurable; even the Buddhas themselves are unable to describe their qualities in their entirety, let alone other beings.
In the phrase "in the exposition of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇadīpite*), it should be understood by way of a secondary indication (*upalakkhaṇa-naya*).

And here, both the method of exertion (*padhānanaya*) and the method of illustration (*nidassananaya*) are found. Regarding "the qualities of the Protector" (*nāthaguṇa*), these are the qualities of the Buddha such as virtue, concentration, wisdom, and so forth;
the meaning of that term has already been explained above. As for the phrase "even a single verse among those that indicate," the word-division is *sūcakāsu ekagāthampi*.
"Among those that indicate" (*sūcakāsu*) means among those that make clear. "Verses" (*gāthāsu*) [is understood] by way of the Sugata’s verses and so forth.

Regarding the twenty-six verses of homage that have been spoken: this locative case ending is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). It is called a *gāthā* because it is sung or recited by poets (*kavīhi gāyati kathiyati*).
It is a specific type of verse. From the root *gedha*, with the suffix *tha*: the substitution of *gā* for *gedha*. Alternatively, *gaṃ* is said to mean "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*).
That which stands (*tiṭṭhati*) therein is a *gāthā*. The root *thā*, preceded by the word *gaṃ*, signifies the cessation of movement. *Gaṃ* is said to mean knowledge; [the knowledge] stands there.

It is called *gāthā* because it is bound together by poets (*kavīhi*) or because it is established and placed [in a collection]. "In those *gāthās*" means in those verses. Regarding the phrase "even a single *gāthā*":

here, the particle *pi* (even) has the sense of censure. By this, he implies: "What need is there to speak of taking refuge in the Buddha’s qualities through many verses? "Buddha" refers to one who is wise.
For he is called "Buddha" because he awakens to (*budhati*) and knows what is beneficial and what is not beneficial. "He remembers" (*sarateti*).
It is *sarati*. For the purpose of protecting one’s desire (*chandānurakkhaṇattha*), there is a substitution of the *attanopada* (middle) case-ending for the *parassapada* (active) case-ending.
30. The connection is: "He" (*so*) means "that wise one" (*budho*) would be.

"Freed from the four states of misery" (*caturāpāyamutto*) means liberated from the four miserable states known as hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts (*peta*), and the host of asuras. It is called a "miserable state" (*apāya*) because it is mostly devoid of merit (*puñña*) and because it is far removed (*apagata*) from well-being (*aya*). From well-being (*ayato*) means from happiness (*sukhato*).
"Apāya" means "gone away" (apagata). This is an *abyayībhāva* compound. Alternatively, it is called "ayo" because the three types of success (*sampatti*) go to, proceed, or occur by means of it;
thus, "ayo" refers to merit (*puñña*). The verbal root *aya* is used in the sense of "going. Or, it is "ayo" because one goes to, proceeds toward, or occurs within merit;
or because it is to be gone to or brought forth by those who perform meritorious deeds; thus, "ayo" refers to happiness (*sukha*). One who has gone away from that is an "apāya. Four...
The four states of misery (*apāya*) are the four realms of suffering; one who is released from them is "released from the four states of misery" (*caturāpāyamutta*).

Regarding the phrase *sādhakatthadvayassa ca*: the word division is *sādhako atthadvayassa ca*. "Of the two kinds of welfare" (*atthadvayassa*) refers to the two kinds of welfare consisting of those pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) and those pertaining to the future life (*samparāyika*).

Here, the word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of connection (*aṭṭhānayoga*). That [word *ca*], moreover, is connected to the words beginning with "that which accomplishes" (*sādhako*) and so forth. "That which accomplishes" (*sādhako*)...
And it is the producer. For he is called a "sādhaka" because he accomplishes (*sādheti*) and brings about (*nipphādeti*).

"With the net of calamities destroyed" means the net, which is reckoned as calamity, has been destroyed. It is "destroyed" (*hato*) because it was struck down (*hanayittha*) and removed (*apanayittha*). The verbal root *han* is used in the sense of harming.
"Calamity" (*upaddava*) is that which, having approached (*upagantvā*), plays havoc (*davati*) or harms; it refers to the sixteen calamities, such as birth-fear and so forth.
The prefix *upa* here signifies "affliction. There are sixteen kinds of such afflictions:

fear of birth, fear of aging, fear of illness, fear of death, fear of kings, fear of thieves, fear of fire, fear of water, fear of waves, fear of crocodiles, fear of whirlpools, fear of sharks, fear of self-reproach, fear of reproach by others, and fear of punishment.
"And the fear of an evil rebirth. For that by which one is caught and harmed is a *jāla* (net); thus, *macchajāla* means a net for fish. Like a net is a *jāla*, meaning a calamity.
In its primary sense (*nītāttha*), however, it is a *jāla* because by it beings are caught and harmed; it is a calamity. The verbal root *jala* is used in the sense of harming, with the suffix *ṇa*.
One by whom the *jāla*—that is, the calamity—is destroyed is "one who has destroyed the calamity-net" (*hatūpaddavajālo*). [This occurs] through the volition of saluting the Buddha.
The meaning is: "May he be one who has cast off the net known as calamity. "And a recipient of welfare and happiness" means: a recipient (*lābhī*) of both welfare (*hita*) and happiness (*sukha*).
"Gain" (*lābha*) is the act of obtaining; one who possesses that is a "recipient. That which promotes or increases is "welfare" (*hita*), meaning benefit.
That which brings pleasure is "happiness" (*sukha*); the meaning is that it makes whatever arises in one happy. Alternatively, *suṭṭhu*...

It is "sukha" because it digs up (*khanati*) suffering (*dukkha*). The root *khan* preceded by *su-* is used with the suffix *kvi* in the sense of restriction. "Hitasukha" means both welfare (*hita*) and happiness (*sukha*);
the meaning is that one would become a possessor of that. 31–32. The connection is:
"He would become the lord of men and gods, or even the sovereign of the four continents. Regarding the term "naradevānaṃ":
"Men and gods" (nara-devā) means humans and deities; this genitive case ending is used here in the sense of the object (*kamma*). "Lord" (*adhipo*) means a sovereign.
He is called "lord" because he protects (*pāti*) those dependent on him according to the Dhamma, or because he protects them having overcome them (*adhi-abhibhavitvā*).
The verbal root *pā* preceded by the prefix *adhi* signifies protection. Thus, he is the lord and sovereign of men—the human king—and the lord of the gods.
The meaning is: "He would become a sovereign, a lord, and a king of the gods. Regarding the phrase *catudīpissaropi vā*, the particle *pi* is a nipāta used in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvana*).

By it, one implies the possibility not only of being a king who rules over a single continent, but also of being a king who rules over a portion of a continent, and even of being a king who rules over all four continents.
The word *vā* is used merely for the purpose of completing the meter. As for "lord of the four continents," these are Pubbavideha, Aparagoyāna, Jambudīpa, and Uttarakuru.
The meaning is that he would even become a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti-rāja), the lord of the four continents, including Uttarakuru.
In this context, "Pubbavideha" means that which exists to the east (pubba) of Sineru; it is called "Videha" because they seek or strive (īhanti) there through knowledge (veda);
the root *īh* with the prefix *vid-* and the suffix *ṇa* denotes effort. That itself is Videha. Taking this continent as the reference point [relative] to Sineru...
Because it belongs to the eastern quarter, it is both "eastern" (*pubba*) and "Videha," thus it is *Pubbavideha*, the Eastern Island. *Apāragoyāna*:
That which exists on the other side, the western side of Sineru, is "the other" (*apara*). It is called *goyāna* because they go (*yanti*) by means of a cow (*go*) there;
the root *yā* with the prefix *go-* denotes going, and the suffix *yu* is applied. Because it belongs to the western quarter of Sineru, it is "the other" (*apara*).
*Goyāna* means Aparagoyāna, the western continent. *Jambudīpa*: it is called *jambu* because it is born (*jāyati*). It is a tree one hundred yojanas in height. *Janadhātu*:
from the root *jan* (to be born), with the suffix *u*. There is a substitution of *mo* for *na*, and the letter *ba* is inserted. *Dīpa*: it shines (*dippati*) in the midst of water;

or else, it is a *dīpa* because the True Dhamma shines (*dippanti*) and is radiant (*jotanti*) therein. *Dīpadhātu*: from the root *dīp* (to shine), with the suffix *a*. Furthermore, its word-division is *dvī-āpa*.
The term *dīpa* (island) is also appropriate as a *bahubbīhi* compound, meaning "that wherein water flows in two directions.
*Jambudīpa* is the southern continent, so called because it is marked by or known for the *jambu* tree. *Uttarakuru* refers to that which exists to the north of Sineru;
it is called *kuru* because here there is (*kaṃ*) great (*uru*) happiness (*sukha*) by the power of the five precepts established through natural law (*dhammatā*). This is a *bahubbīhi* compound.
*Ku* means "evil. Or else, it is *kuru* because they obstruct (*rundhanti*) that [evil] there. It is derived from the root *kup-pubbā-rudhi*, meaning "obstruction," with the suffix *kvi*.
There is the elision of the final part of the root. Because it is on the northern side of Mount Sineru, it is both "northern" (*uttara*) and "Kuru" (*kuru*), hence "Uttarakuru.
"Lord of the Northern Island" (*Uttaradīpa-issaro*) refers to the Cakkavatti King, who is the lord of the four islands.
Having thus shown mundane benefit, he now speaks to show supramundane benefit: "In his final body... [etc. ...well-trained. The connection is:
"In his final body, being well-trained, having mounted the vehicle of meditation (bhāvanāyāna), and bearing that white parasol, he shall go evenly.
We shall explain this according to the sequence of the meaning. "Final" (antima) means last or ultimate; it is at the end.
"At the end" means the final existence, the last body. "In that" refers to the body. It is called *deha* because it is built up (*dihati*), accumulated, and increased;
thus *deha* means the body. The root *dih* is used in the sense of accumulation, with the suffix *na*. Alternatively, it is called *deha* because merit and demerit are built up by means of it;
the meaning is "the body" existing in its final state of becoming, or as a son of noble family destined for such a state. "Well-trained" (*subbata*) means well-restrained.
Having become one who has entered the path (*paṭipannako*). One who has practiced well is "one of good conduct" (*subbato*); here, *vakāra* becomes *bb*.

"Ascending the vehicle of development" (*bhāvanāyānaṃ āruyhā*)—the word-division is "ascending the vehicle of development. The meaning is: having ascended the vehicle known as the development of insight (*vipassanā-bhāvanā*).

It is called "development" (*bhāvanā*) because it is to be cultivated and increased. Its object is the formations belonging to the three planes. Alternatively, it has that [object] as its objective support.
"Bhāvanā" means that which develops or increases; it is insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*). The verbal root *bhū* signifies "being" or "increasing," with the suffix *-ana*.
Furthermore, that development is twofold by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) cultivation.
In this context, however, by the determination of the term "another white umbrella," insight-cultivation is intended. "Yaṃ" refers to that by which one attains Nibbāna.

The vehicle (*yāna*) is the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) regarding impermanence and so forth. The root *yu* in the sense of "going" (*gati*) forms the word *yā*. A vehicle known as cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is a "cultivation-vehicle" (*bhāvanā-yāna*); or, it is a "cultivation-vehicle" because it is both cultivation and a vehicle. "Having mounted" (*āruhya*) means having ascended. The meaning is:
having ascended the vehicle of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, which is similar to an ordinary vehicle. By way of the characteristics of impermanence and so forth...
Indeed, there is no such thing as attaining the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna without [this]. Therefore, it is said: "having mounted the vehicle of cultivation.
"The other" refers to the fruit of Arahatship. For that, without overstepping the boundary first perceived by the first path, brings about the realization of the Dhamma of the Four Truths;
thus it is called "the other" (*añña*). The verbal root *ñā* preceded by *ā* signifies "realization. The prefix *ā-* has the sense of a boundary.

*Setacchattakaṃ*: a white sunshade. It is called *setaṃ* because it is served (*seviyati*), meaning white or bright; the root *si-* is used here in the sense of service. It is called *chattaṃ* because it covers the heat of the defilements (*kilesatapaṃ chādeti*);
the root *chad-* is used in the sense of covering. That very thing is *chattakaṃ*. Being both white (*seta*) and a sunshade (*chattaka*), it is a "white sunshade" (*setacchattaka*).
The sunshade of the radiance of the fruit of Arhatship is obtained. This refers to another [type of] white sunshade, namely that which is designated as the fruit of Arhatship.

"Being one who maintains" is the syntactical connection. "Peace" (*sama*) is *nibbāna*. For it is called "peace" because all the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) is calmed (*samati*), stilled (*vūpasamati*), and ceases (*nirujjhati*) therein. "He will attain" means he will reach it.
Now, showing the benefit pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika-attha*), he said: "Even in this very selfhood," and so forth. Therein, "even in this very selfhood":
The construction is as follows: "May I be free from disease, long-lived, honored by all the world, delighted in meditation, beloved by people, and pleasing.
Regarding the phrase "even in one's own person" (*attabhāve pi*), the particle *pi* here has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍanattha*). By it, the welfare pertaining to future lives is included.
"Self" (*atta*) is that by which the designation and the cognition [of "self"] arise; thus, "person" (*attabhāva*) is a designation for the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*).
"Free from disease" (*aroga*) means being devoid of all illnesses. For he is called "free from disease" because there is no disease for him.
"Long-lived" (*dīghajīvika*) means having a long lifespan. For he is called "long-lived" because his life and vitality are long.
(33) "By the whole world" (*sabbalokehi*) means by all gods and humans. "Worthy of worship" (*pūjita*) means one who is to be honored. "Delighting in mental cultivation" (*bhāvanābhiratimano*).
And one whose mind delights in the cultivation known as serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). "Beloved by the people" means he would be dear to all persons;
"pleasing" means he would be one who increases the mental joy of all beings—this is the connection.
Thus, even from a single verse among these twenty-six verses of praise, there is a fruit and benefit in the recollection of the Buddha’s qualities.
Having thus shown [the benefits], he now says, "What need is there to mention the retention of all the verses?

in order to demonstrate the manifold fruits and advantages of venerating the Buddha by memorizing all the verses. In this context, the phrase "kā kathā akhiladhāraṇā" is analyzed as "kā kathā akhiladhāraṇā.
The meaning is: "What more need be said regarding the verbal retention of all the verses for venerating the Buddhas? It is precisely that much which must be stated.

And here, the word *akhila* is an un-derived (*anipphanna*) primary noun (*pāṭipadika*) signifying "all. Alternatively, *khila* means "obstruction" (*khidhātu*); the suffix *lapaccaya* is applied in the sense of destruction.
Or, it is called *khila* because it "takes" or "seizes" destruction; thus it is "small" (*appaka*). With the word *khaya* as its prefix, the root *lā* in the sense of "seizing" takes the suffix *a*.

That which is not an obstruction is *akhila*, meaning "all verses. It is "held," which is *dhāraṇa*; [the phrase] "by all the verses, which are without obstruction" refers to *akhilāya sabbāya gāthāya*.

“Dhāraṇaṃ” means the retention of all; in that regard, by retaining even a single verse from the twenty-six verses of Buddha-vandana in one’s speech, the aforementioned fruits and benefits are obtained during the Buddha-vandana;

how much more so, then, for one who retains all the Buddha-vandana verses in their speech and performs the Buddha-vandana day after day—this is the meaning. Furthermore, by means of these five verses as stated...
This shows the exhortation: "Having understood the benefit of the fruit and possessing faith, a clansman with right view,

having memorized the verses for worshipping all Buddhas by means of speech, should worship the Buddha constantly, continuously, and uninterruptedly day and night— at dawn, at evening, during the first watch of the night, and during the last watch."
The commentary on the Five Verses is completed.
Thus, this homage, which has been venerated by the ancient teachers, is subtle, delicate, very difficult to see, and profound;

it elucidates the qualities of the Buddha that are hard to penetrate, and it is for the sake of true persons. Through the methods of word-meaning and logic, as well as the methods of prosody and poetic ornamentation... [text continues]
This commentary, titled *Buddhaguṇappadīpikā*, was composed by the Venerable Revata Thera— the foremost among the elders, a purifier of the Dispensation,

whose conduct was characterized by unshakable confidence and wisdom, and who was skilled in the Three Piṭakas together with their commentaries, thereby inspiring clarity of mind in others. Conclusion.
Furthermore, this city was founded by the Great Dhamma King Adhirāja, whose name was inscribed as Sirīpavaravijayānantayasapaṇḍita Tribhuvanādityādhipati Mahādhammarājādhirāja;
he had the Pāḷi of the Tipiṭaka engraved upon stone and, by convening the fifth council,
established it in his royal capital known as Ratanāpuñja— a place filled with various clans and abounding in the merit and grain of the virtuous.

In the great monastery (mahārāma) of the city of Mantala— described as a mine of the jewels of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, and as the dwelling place for monks endowed with virtue, concentration, and wisdom; a place that illuminates the Buddha’s dispensation like the sun and moon—
a lay follower (upāsaka) named [Name], possessed of noble qualities, together with his female attendant (upāsikā) named [Name], both desiring wholesome merit, [established this].
Having constructed two-storey Mahiṭṭhaka monasteries named Suvaṇṇavatī— which were delightful and coated with gold for the purpose of realizing Nibbāna—
he resided there, constantly and uninterruptedly reciting the Tipiṭaka together with its commentaries day by day to the monks who had come from the eight directions seeking the Dhamma,
while he himself dwelt within that Tipiṭaka along with its commentaries.

He who moves with unshakable and confident wisdom; who, in the city of Mantale, was the foremost and most eminent among the assembly of Dhamma-teachers dedicated to the welfare of the Dispensation through mastery of the scriptures;
who was graced with the titles "Revatābhipaṇḍitadhaja," "Sāsanavaṃsamahādhammarājaguru," and "Aggamahāpaṇḍita";
and who, as the eldest leader of the Great Assembly that performs the twelve fundamental duties of the Dispensation, was known as the "Teacher Wise in the Dispensation" (Sāsanāppañña Ācariya).
Having praised with words of the Buddha’s qualities— which illuminate the virtues of the Buddha as spoken by the Blessed One here and there in the Pāḷi by the renowned and eminent Mahānāyaka Thera,
the purifier of the Dispensation— and having paid homage to him who is profound in both meaning and phrasing,
like the mass of water that supports the earth, [I shall explain] by means of the mountain...
In those various commentaries and sub-commentaries, there is an exposition of the hidden meaning titled *Buddhaguṇappadīpikā* (The Lamp Illuminating the Qualities of the Buddha),
which elucidates the homage that reveals the qualities of the Buddha— qualities so difficult for worldlings to penetrate,
being as exceedingly subtle and fine as the tip of the hair of a horse split a hundredfold, or like a cloth kept hidden away.
This [work] has been composed by relying on the method of the *Saṃvaṇṇanā* for the sake of proficiency in wisdom and for the growth of the Dispensation.
And at this point:
When two thousand four hundred years of the Cakkavatti era had elapsed—
When the year eight hundred and nine of the Sakkarāj era had arrived, on the seventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phussa,
on a Buddha-day, the *Sāmaññaphala-sutta* was perfectly completed at seven hundred and seventy thousand years [after the Parinibbāna].
And by whatever merit has been accumulated by me while performing this construction,
may I, through that merit, attain supreme enlightenment and,
having delivered many beings from the cycle of existence, bring about the destruction of craving.
May I realize Nibbāna through the supreme knowledge of the Path.
May kings always protect this people by means of the Dhamma alone.
May all beings be happy; may they uphold the teaching of the Conqueror.
May the people of the Maramma kingdom always be free from calamity;
may they, with constant virtuous intentions, attain the state of the Deathless.
[This concludes] the work titled *Buddhaguṇappadīpikā*.
The Commentary on the *Namakkāra* is completed.
